### G2. How a GTA 6 clips channel can earn, and how much

**The short answer.** A channel of other creators' GTA 6 footage, reframed, captioned and credited but without permission, should be planned as earning $0 from YouTube ads: YouTube's monetisation rule refuses "promotion of other people's content (even if you have permission)", its Shorts revenue pool drops re-uploads and compilations "with no original content added", and a streamer's own consented clips channel was reported on 28 September 2026 as removed from the Partner Programme for this (money-6, money-11, money-13). Even an accepted channel would earn little from Shorts: Shorts pay about $0.07-$0.20 per 1,000 views in most niches (AIR's gaming example is $0.17, from one channel), a mainly Pakistani audience would earn less, and from 1 February 2027 Shorts ad money needs 10 million Shorts views every 90 days, so posting 24 Shorts a day pays nothing until each one averages about 4,600 views (money-3, money-8, money-m6, money-23). A new channel will almost certainly apply after 1 February 2027, when the bar for new applicants doubles to 8,000 watch hours in a year or 20 million Shorts views in 90 days (money-2). The fastest honest first dollar is paid clipping campaigns, where a game publisher or streamer supplies footage and pays per 1,000 views (about $0.70-$4.00) without the Partner Programme; the one live GTA 6 campaign we found pays $0.70 per 1,000 views on TikTok and Instagram only, and its own page says not to pull clips from other creators unless the brief allows it, while some game campaigns pay $0 for views from Pakistan, India and Bangladesh (money-15, money-16, money-m3). The route that can earn YouTube ad money over time is a long-form-led GTA 6 channel built on footage the owner records himself, with real commentary, after the game comes out on 19 November 2026 (money-9, money-22).

#### What we found

##### 1. The Partner Programme today, and what changes on 1 February 2027

- **Ad-revenue tier today.** 1,000 subscribers plus either 4,000 qualified watch hours in the last 12 months or 10 million qualified Shorts views in the last 90 days; a linked AdSense for YouTube account is required (money-1).
- **Shorts views do not help the watch-hour route.** "Any qualified watch hours from Shorts views in the Shorts Feed won't count" toward the 4,000 hours, and only Shorts set public that appear in the Shorts Feed count toward the 10 million (money-1).
- **Review.** Automated systems and human reviewers look at the whole channel, and a decision "typically" takes about 1 month, longer if several reviews are needed (money-1). After a first rejection a channel can appeal within 21 days or reapply after 30 days, then 90 days after later rejections (section A2, clips-19) (money-1).
- **Terms deadline.** Existing members must accept updated Partner Programme terms in YouTube Studio by 31 January 2027 to keep fully monetising; a dated task if a channel is ever accepted (money-m9).
- **What reviewers apply.** The channel-wide reused-content rule, the inauthentic-content rule (renamed from "repetitious" on 15 July 2025), and the spam rule against "automated tools or AI to churn out high volumes of similar content with minimal changes" (money-11, money-12b).
- **From 1 February 2027.** New applicants need 8,000 qualified watch hours in the last 365 days, or 20 million qualified Shorts views in the last 90 days (money-2). YouTube's blog does not mention the subscriber number; Tubefilter reports only the current 1,000 (money-2; the checkers did not open Tubefilter). The blog says the change "won't impact creators already in YPP" and does not say how applications pending on 1 February are judged (money-2).
- **Shorts ad money from 1 February 2027.** Only channels with 10 million qualified Shorts views over the last 90 days share in Shorts revenue; channels below stay in the programme, keep long-form earnings, and Shorts revenue sharing resumes automatically above the line (money-3, YouTube's official blog). Strictly, ads still run; the channel just gets no share (money-3).
- **The window lags.** Shorts-sharing eligibility is measured over the 90 days ending on the 15th of the month before the earnings month (money-m5).
- **What this means in time.** Today is 14 November 2026; the old thresholds last 11 more weeks, which a channel that has not launched cannot meet (money-23, own arithmetic). Plan on the 2027 thresholds.
- **The lower "fan funding" tier.** 500 subscribers, 3 public uploads in 90 days, and 3,000 watch hours in 12 months or 3 million Shorts views in 90 days unlock memberships, Super Chat, Super Thanks and Shopping, not ad revenue (money-4). Pakistan is not on that tier's country list (money-4).
- **Pakistan.** Pakistan is on the list of places where the standard Partner Programme is open (money-5).
- **What YouTube's own manager says Shorts pay small channels.** In an August 2026 interview, YouTube's Amjad Hanif said that with "only a few thousand views, you might have a few cents for that month" (money-7).

##### 2. How Shorts and long videos pay

- **Shorts revenue pool.** Ads between Shorts in the feed are pooled, split by country and by engaged views, and the creator keeps 45% of the share allocated to them (money-6, money-7). Music in a Short shrinks the pool (part goes to music partners) but "won't affect a creator's allocation ... or their revenue share rate" (money-6). Long-form videos pay creators 55% (money-7; this appears only by implication in the news article, and no official page for it was opened).
- **Views that earn nothing in the pool.** "Non-original Shorts, such as unedited clips from others' movies or TV shows", "reuploading other creators' content from YouTube or other platform, or compilations with no original content added", bot views, and views on Shorts that break the advertiser-friendly guidelines (money-6).
- **Gaming Shorts revenue per 1,000 views (RPM, the creator's share after YouTube's cut).** AIR Media-Tech, a YouTube partner network, measured 274 of its monetised channels: Shorts RPM was $0.07-$0.20 in most niches (music $0.97-$1.48) (money-8). The $0.17 gaming figure is one example channel in AIR's text ($1.79 long-form, $0.17 Shorts), not a gaming median; the gaming table is an image the text does not show (money-8, money-m7). Its median Shorts RPM by viewer country: US $0.328, Australia $0.193, UK $0.166, Canada $0.165, Germany $0.163; a US-heavy audience gives about $300 per 1 million Shorts views and a mixed global audience $150-$250 (money-8). No Shorts figure was given for Pakistan or South Asia (money-8).
- **Pakistan-type audiences earn much less.** The same AIR page says channels with large audiences in Nigeria, Pakistan or the Philippines receive only $0.20-$1.50 long-form CPM, against $8-$20 for Europe, the US or Australia, so a mainly Pakistani audience would earn far below the figures above (vendor data, money-m6). The page also gives two conflicting gaming long-form RPMs ($1.79 and $3.17) in its worked examples (money-8).
- **Gaming long-video RPM.** In AIR's 300-channel study (channels of 10,000 to 50 million subscribers, May 2025 to May 2026), the gaming median RPM was $2.05, the middle half $0.70-$3.62, median Studio CPM $4.05, about 487,000 views per $1,000 earned, with November the strongest month across niches ($2.35 median) (money-9). All sample channels were already monetised with 10,000+ subscribers, so the numbers do not describe a brand-new channel (money-9).
- **Posting more lowers pay per view.** In AIR's 282-channel within-channel comparison, small gaming channels' RPM fell from $2.33 at 3-4 videos a month to $0.63 at 5-8 (-73%); its FAQ says daily posting (30+ a month) is above the revenue-best rate in every niche except large kids channels (money-10). This is correlation, not a test, and the page admits an activity-level confounder (money-10). The top bucket measured is 16+ a month, so there is no data at 30+ and the daily-posting line is extrapolation; for medium gaming channels at 16+ a month, RPM was $1.31 and monetised playback 39.4%, against 65.6% at 1-2 a month (money-m10).
- **Caveat on all RPM numbers.** These are one network's own client channels, not a random sample, and none were brand-new clips channels (money-8, money-9).

##### 3. Can other creators' GTA 6 footage be monetised?

- **The policy definition.** Reused content is content already on YouTube or elsewhere used "without adding significant original commentary, substantive modifications, or educational or entertainment value", and the rule "applies even if you have permission from the original creator" (money-11).
- **YouTube's allowed examples (abridged).** Clips used for a critical review; reaction videos where you comment on the original; "edited footage from other creators where you add a storyline and commentary"; content that mainly features the uploading creator; edited footage with audio and visual effects that "demonstrates substantive editing" (money-11).
- **YouTube's not-allowed examples (abridged).** "Clips of moments from your favorite show edited together with little or no narrative"; "short videos you compiled from other social media websites"; "content uploaded many times by other creators"; "promotion of other people's content (even if you have permission)"; content copied "without any substantive modifications" (money-11).
- **Credit is not mentioned.** The monetisation policy page never uses the words "credit" or "credited", so it neither says credit helps nor names "credited" compilations; that reading is our inference (money-11).
- **Games are not named.** The monetisation policy page says nothing about video games, gameplay or software; the only near example is sports replays where "you explain the moves" (money-11). We found no separate YouTube page on gameplay monetisation (search budget ran out; see Risks).
- **What counts as added value (a reach rule, not a monetisation rule).** In a Creator Insider video published 1 October 2026, as reported by Search Engine Journal, YouTube Creator Liaison Rene Ritchie said remixed clips need commentary, analysis or storytelling, "not just VO descriptions of what's happening on screen, minor technical edits, or template-based bulk changes". TeamYouTube's post, quoted by Dexerto on 5 October 2026, asks for "your own original commentary, unique edits, or storytelling" rather than "minor technical edits or template-based changes simply to alter a video" (money-14). Both sources say this is about Shorts reach and recommendations; Search Engine Journal says the video does not mention monetisation (money-14, money-m2). The monetisation basis for the same point is the reused-content rule (money-11).
- **Reach falls too.** Because of this October 2026 change, reposted clips lose Shorts recommendation reach before monetisation even comes up, which lowers every view-based estimate below (money-m2).
- **So, for the owner's plan:** captions, a vertical reframe and a credit line are minor technical edits; an AI voice that narrates what is on screen is the example YouTube names as not enough for reach, and it points the same way as the reused-content rule (money-14, money-11). Credit does not change the copyright position either (section A3, policy-5).
- **Documented case.** The clips channel of Twitch streamer B0ary, run with the streamer's consent, was reported on 28 September 2026 as excluded from the Partner Programme for "recycled content" with little meaningful contribution; the operator is appealing, no outcome yet, and the source is the operator's post as reported (money-13). We found no documented case of a third-party GTA or gaming clips channel being accepted (see Risks).
- **Where the money goes instead.** If a source creator's Content ID matches the clip, the claimant can put ads on it and take the revenue, or block it (section A3, policy-2), so a claimed clip earns for the source, not for us.
- **Game-specific ad rules (advertiser-friendly guidelines).** There are two levels for game violence. Graphic game violence in the thumbnail (brutal killings or severe injuries focused on bodily fluids) gets limited ads; more severe graphic violence (such as beheadings or dismemberment) in the thumbnail or the first 7 seconds gets no ads (money-12). Also no ads: gameplay "manufactured to create a shocking experience", "aggregating non-playable characters for mass killings", and sexual games or game characters sexualised to gratify the audience (money-12). Strong profanity in titles or thumbnails gets no ads; moderate profanity gets limited ads (money-12). GTA moments that clippers favour (rampages, strip-club scenes) fall in these lines (own reading of money-12).
- **Montages lose the unedited-gameplay allowance.** Violence in unedited gameplay is generally acceptable after the first 7 seconds, but "montages where gratuitous violence is the focal point" do not get that allowance (money-m1). A GTA clips or highlight cut is edited footage, so a "best kills" or "rampage" montage is exactly that pattern (money-m1).

##### 4. Other ways clippers earn in 2026

- **Paid clipping campaigns.** A brand, studio or streamer funds a campaign and sets a brief; clippers post on their own accounts and are paid per 1,000 counted views up to a cap per clip (money-17, money-18). Content Rewards (paid out through Whop) takes a 10% creator fee on CPM campaigns (per-post and retainer campaigns: 10% under a $5,000 budget, 0% at $5,000 and above; older campaigns may show 7%); minimums are set per campaign, and at a $1 rate a $2 minimum needs a clip to reach 2,000 views; clips submitted since 25 September 2026 earn for 30 days from the day they cross the payout threshold; moving money to the Whop balance is free from $1, and a standard Whop payout to bank, PayPal or wallet can take up to 5 business days (money-17). Clips rejected for fake views are not paid, and the account can be banned; the page does not say the ban is permanent (money-17).
- **The live GTA 6 campaign.** "GTA 6 Clipping Campaign - Tokyo Girl" promotes a song, not the game; "Rockstar Games is not running it" (money-15). It pays $0.70 per 1,000 views, minimum $2.00 and maximum $35.00 per clip, on TikTok and Instagram only, with a $2,000 budget of which $88 was used by 14 November 2026 (money-15). At the $35 cap a clip needs 50,000 views, and the whole budget is shared by all clippers (money-15). It needs an ad disclosure at the start of each clip and suggests your own console footage once the game is out (money-15).
- **The campaign page rules out the owner's plan.** The page says "Don't pull clips from other creators or random uploads unless the brief says you can", and calls your own console footage "the safest kind to use"; that contradicts a "no permission, edit and credit" plan even on the campaign route (money-m3).
- **Game publisher campaigns.** World of Warcraft Forever pays $4.00 per 1,000 on TikTok and YouTube, up to $500 a clip, counting only the campaign's region (split into UK, France, DACH and Nordics campaigns, so a South Asian audience earns $0 there too); SEGA's Football Manager 27, Metaphor: ReFantazio and Stranger Than Heaven pay $2.00 (TikTok, YouTube) and $1.50 (Instagram) up to $800 a clip; Call of Duty Warzone pays $2.00 on TikTok and $1.50 on Instagram (money-16, money-m8). The full range across 62 game campaigns runs wider than $2-$4 ($0.90-$20), and Fortnite map campaigns require your own gameplay (money-16). The studio supplies the trailers and gameplay; Football Manager 27 and Metaphor pay $0 for views from Pakistan, India and Bangladesh (money-16).
- **Streamer campaigns.** TJR pays $0.75 per 1,000 up to $750 a clip and ThreadGuy $1.00 up to $500; IShowSpeed, Lacy and Clix ran as fixed pools with no per-1,000 rate given (money-18). Footage a campaign owner provides "is licensed to you only to make clips for that campaign"; some briefs allow moments from the streamer's back catalogue, and "The brief decides" (money-18, money-m4). So campaign footage cannot be reused on our own monetised channel or for other campaigns (money-m4). Dexerto (5 October 2026) reports streamer Clavicular saying Kick paid "$700,000 to promote his clips" in a month, and N3on claiming he paid clippers $1.4M over five weeks; both are unverified self-claims (money-18).
- **Rates across all campaigns.** Content Rewards' median was about $1.04 per 1,000 views over 712 live campaigns and $1.20 for YouTube on 13 November 2026 (section A2, clips-9).
- **Campaign clips and YouTube ads do not mix.** A campaign clip is paid promotion with a disclosure, which is exactly "promotion of other people's content (even if you have permission)" under the reused-content rule (money-11, money-15). Treat a campaign channel as a per-view business, not a Partner Programme channel.
- **Scams.** Content Rewards itself warns about lookalike sites; we did not read its checklist (money-17). Basic checks (own estimate): never pay to join, campaign shown on the marketplace itself, payout through the marketplace's processor.
- **Selling or transferring a channel.** The YouTube Terms we read and the spam policy page say nothing on selling or buying channels (money-19b) (unverified; the checkers did not review this item and one saw the spam page truncated). We could not confirm a rule either way; do not plan around selling the channel.

##### 5. The arithmetic for 24 posts a day (own estimate, using the sourced rates)

24 posts a day is 720 a month and 2,160 per 90 days (money-23). Only qualified public Shorts views count, and eligibility lags (money-m5), so counted views would be lower than these rows.

| Views per post | Shorts views per 90 days (all Shorts) | Meets 10M Shorts-ad line? | Meets 20M entry line? | Shorts income per month at $0.17 per 1,000, if eligible |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Low: 50 | 108,000 | No | No | $0 (below 10M); would be about $6 |
| Typical: 500 | 1.08M | No | No | $0 (below 10M); would be about $61 |
| Good: 5,000 | 10.8M | Yes, just | No (needs about 9,260 per Short) | about $612 |

| Views per long clip, 2 min average watched (assumption) | Watch hours per month (all long) | Months to 8,000 hours | Income per month at $0.70 (low) to $2.05 (median) per 1,000 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Low: 20 | 480 | about 17 | $10-$30 |
| Typical: 200 | 4,800 | about 2 | $100-$295 |
| Good: 2,000 | 48,000 | under 1 | $1,000-$2,950 |

- Every row assumes the channel is accepted; under the reused-content rule an unlicensed clips channel earns $0 in every row (money-6, money-11).
- The tables ignore AIR's finding that pay per view falls with volume, and the spam rule on mass automation, so the "typical" and "good" rows at 24 a day are optimistic (money-10, money-12b). The RPMs come from established channels with 10,000+ subscribers, a mainly Pakistani audience would sit near $0.20-$1.50 long-form CPM, and the reach cut for reposted clips lowers the views (money-9, money-m6, money-m2). 24 a day (720 a month) is far outside anything AIR measured (money-m10). The "good" long-form row (2,000 views on each of 720 long clips a month from a new channel) is far above what a new reused-clips channel should expect; section A2 estimated tens of views per upload.
- Base rate: among channels that started under 1,000 subscribers and added 52+ videos in a year, 30.77% reached 1,000 subscribers within 360 days (vidIQ, section A2, clips-20). We found no figure for the share of new channels that ever join the Partner Programme.

##### 6. Getting paid in Pakistan

- **AdSense.** Payment is released once earnings reach $100 (USD accounts); address verification starts at $10 (money-21). AdSense offers EFT, wire transfer, cheque, Western Union and PayPal Hyperwallet, varying by country; which ones work in Pakistan was not confirmed (money-21).
- **US tax.** All monetising creators must give tax info; without it Google "may be required to deduct up to 24% of your total earnings worldwide"; non-US individuals file Form W-8BEN, which expires after three full calendar years (money-19). Google files Partner Programme earnings under "Other Copyright Royalties" (money-19), but it also lists "Motion Picture & TV Royalties" and "Services" and says payments can fall into multiple categories (money-m11).
- **Treaty.** Article VIII of the 1957 US-Pakistan treaty exempts from US tax a copyright royalty (other than motion-picture film royalties) paid to a Pakistan resident with no US permanent establishment, if the consideration is fair and reasonable (money-20). A practitioner source (vidIQ, 2021) says only earnings from US viewers are subject to US withholding; no Google page we opened states this (money-19). So a correct W-8BEN claim might mean 0% US withholding, but the motion-picture exclusion and the multiple categories mean 0% on all YouTube income is not assured, we did not confirm Google applies 0% on a Pakistan W-8BEN claim, and a tax adviser must confirm; Pakistan's own tax was not researched (money-20, money-m11).

##### 7. Fastest honest route versus routes that look quick

- **Fastest honest first dollar:** a paid clipping campaign for a game whose studio supplies the footage (money-16). One clip passing 2,000 views at a $1 rate earns $2 minus the creator fee; withdrawal to the Whop balance is free from $1 (money-17). Viewer country matters: some campaigns pay nothing for Pakistani, Indian or Bangladeshi viewers, and some count only European regions (money-16, money-m8).
- **Honest route to ad money:** own GTA 6 gameplay with real commentary, long-form first (watch hours only come from long videos), a few uploads a day at most (money-1, money-10, money-22).
- **Looks quick, does not pay:** hourly reposts of other creators' clips (excluded from the Shorts pool, reused content, Content ID money goes to the claimant) (money-6, money-11); the 500-subscriber tier (not open in Pakistan, and pays no ads) (money-4); Shorts volume below 10M views per 90 days (money-3); an AI voice reading out the action, which YouTube names as not enough added value for reach (money-14).

#### What this means for our build

1. **Do not build the "no permission, edit and credit" monetisation path.** Every source we opened says it earns $0 from ads and puts money from claims in the source creator's pocket (money-6, money-11, money-13); the GTA 6 campaign page itself says not to pull other creators' clips unless the brief allows (money-m3). Build only footage sources we can record a right to: the owner's own capture, a clipping-campaign brief, or a written licence.
2. **Add a "footage right" field to every clip.** Values: own_capture, campaign:<id>, licence:<id>. The publisher refuses to upload a clip without one. Record the scope of each right, not only its source: campaign footage is licensed only for that campaign and cannot be reused on the own channel (money-m4). Campaign clips also carry the campaign's required ad disclosure as the first caption, and the campaign id goes in the upload record so payouts can be matched (money-15, money-17).
3. **Two output modes, not one.** Mode A, "campaign clips": short vertical clips, platform per brief (the GTA 6 brief is TikTok and Instagram, not YouTube), no expectation of Partner Programme money (money-15, money-16). Mode B, "own channel": long-form first, Shorts that point to the long video (money-1).
4. **Default rate: 1 long video and 2-3 Shorts a day, not 24.** Pay per view falls with volume in AIR's data, nothing measured goes near 24 a day, and mass automation is a spam-rule target (money-10, money-m10, money-12b). Make the rate a setting with a hard ceiling; raise it only if view data says so.
5. **Commentary is a required input, not a decoration.** The planner must produce a storyline or analysis per clip, and the voice track must say something the picture does not (tips, comparisons, map knowledge), since YouTube names "VO descriptions of what's happening on screen" as not enough added value; that statement is about Shorts reach, and the monetisation basis is the reused-content rule (money-14, money-11). Keep a human approval step before upload.
6. **An ad-safety check for game footage.** Reject a cut whose first 7 seconds or thumbnail frame shows graphic violence, mass NPC killing or sexualised content; keep strong profanity out of titles and thumbnails (money-12). Also check montages: a "best kills" or "rampage" compilation loses the unedited-gameplay allowance even after the first 7 seconds (money-m1). This changes the "start on the most intense moment" hook habit for GTA.
7. **Track money the honest way.** The cost meter should show revenue per source (campaign payouts, AdSense) next to cost, and the analytics pull should track Shorts views per rolling 90 days against 10M, using the window that ends on the 15th of the month before the earnings month, and watch hours per 365 days against 8,000 (money-2, money-3, money-m5).
8. **Viewer-country awareness.** Record audience country share per clip; for campaigns that pay $0 for some countries (or only count some regions), a clip with mainly local viewers earns nothing, and a mainly Pakistani audience earns far less per view anywhere (money-16, money-m6, money-m8).
9. **Separate everything from production.** New Google account, new Cloud project, new AdSense link only if and when accepted; never the company channel's token (section A3; section A2).

#### Risks and unknowns

- **Rockstar's own video policy.** Rockstar's support page on posting its material timed out three times (and twice more for the checkers); we do not know what it says about monetising GTA VI gameplay or pre-release material. Check it by hand before any own-capture plan. Leaked material is out of scope regardless.
- **No YouTube page on gameplay monetisation was found.** Our web search budget ran out before we could search for one; the monetisation policy page itself does not mention games (money-11). Check YouTube Help for "video game" guidance before the build.
- **No accepted gaming clips channel found.** We found a rejection (money-13), not an acceptance, and no rate at which channels pass review. Unknown.
- **Pending applications on 1 February 2027.** Which thresholds apply is not stated (money-2). Assume the new ones.
- **RPM for South Asian audiences.** No source gave a Shorts RPM for Pakistan or India; the only Pakistan-audience figure is AIR's long-form CPM of $0.20-$1.50 (vendor) (money-8, money-m6). GTA audiences are global and RPM varies by country. Unknown until real analytics.
- **RPM sources are one vendor's clients.** AIR's numbers are medians from a partner network's own, already-monetised channels, with some conflicting gaming examples on one page (money-8, money-9).
- **The 1 October 2026 statement is a reach rule.** It does not say how the Partner Programme reviews channels; do not read it as a monetisation definition (money-14).
- **AdSense method in Pakistan and the tax position.** Not confirmed (money-20, money-21). One checker could not read the treaty PDF, and the motion-picture exclusion and multiple tax categories make 0% on all income uncertain (money-20, money-m11). Cheap check: the AdSense payment settings page after sign-up, and one session with a Pakistani tax adviser on the W-8BEN treaty claim and local tax.
- **Clipping campaigns are thin and volatile.** The GTA 6 campaign is a $2,000 song promotion with $35 per-clip caps; publisher campaigns can end or change terms at any time (money-15, money-16). Save a dated copy of each brief.
- **Checker disagreement on fake-view penalties.** One checker read the payouts page as saying accounts are banned, the other found no "permanent" ban; we say "can be banned" and not "permanent" (money-17).
- **Not opened by any checker.** Tubefilter (money-2, money-3), AdSense payment-hold page 1714364 and any Pakistan payment-method page (money-21), an official page for the 55% long-form share (money-7), and the YouTube Community thread of 1 October 2026 (money-14). The sale-of-channel point (money-19b) was not reviewed.
- **Hardware for own capture.** GTA VI is on PS5 and Xbox Series X|S only, with no PC version listed (money-22); the owner needs a console, the game and a capture method. Cost not researched.

### G3. Rights and rules for GTA footage and for other creators' clips

**The short answer.** A GTA 6 clip has up to three owners: Take-Two (the game itself), the record labels (songs on the in-game radio and in trailers), and the creator who played, talked and edited (their commentary, face camera and edit). Rockstar's written policy only tolerates *non-commercial* fan videos, and Take-Two's terms forbid commercial use without separate written terms, so no GTA footage, even our own gameplay, has a written right to earn ads; any GTA ad income rests on Take-Two's tolerance (grules-2, grules-5, grules-6, grules-7). The owner's route, "no permission, edit and credit", cannot be relied on for ad income and puts the channel at risk of strikes: Rockstar's policy does not cover it, the source creator can have each clip removed with a strike, credit is no defence, and YouTube does not pay for clips "edited together with little or no narrative" even with permission (grules-21). Every route that YouTube's own rules allow to earn needs substantial original commentary, storyline or critical review. Our own gameplay recordings with real added commentary are the cleanest of these. Official Rockstar trailers and screenshots, or other creators' clips, used for genuine commentary or review can meet YouTube's reused-content rule but carry higher takedown and claim risk, and clips from other creators should be used only with their written permission. Every source would need its own music check (grules-11, grules-14, grules-16). No in-game GTA 6 footage may be posted before the release on 19 November 2026, five days from today, and leaked material must never be touched (grules-1, grules-3). Ask Take-Two in writing (copyright@take2games.com) before turning ads on (grules-4). A new channel should also expect close to zero Shorts ad income for months, because from 1 February 2027 Shorts revenue sharing needs 10 million qualified Shorts views in 90 days (grules-m7). This is not legal advice.

#### What we found

This builds on section 03 (section A3). That section covers general copyright strikes, Content ID, fair use, the reused-content and spam rules, the 1 October 2026 Shorts reach cut, the YouTube download ban and channel separation. Its ids are written as "03:policy-n". This section adds what is specific to GTA 6 and to game footage.

##### The game and its timing

- **Release date.** Rockstar's own GTA VI page says "Coming November 19, 2026", for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S (grules-1).
- **Delays.** Wikipedia's article lists two delays: in May 2025 to 26 May 2026, and in November 2025 to 19 November 2026. It says no PC version was scheduled as of October 2026, though some outlets reported a PC release in early 2027 (reported, not official) (grules-1).
- **What that means for us.** Until 19 November 2026 the only legitimate GTA 6 footage is Rockstar's own media. Our own gameplay needs a PS5 or Xbox Series console and a copy of the game, with the console's own capture feature or a capture device. No PC version is expected before 2027 (grules-1). The release is five days away, so the gate date must be re-read on the day.

##### Rockstar and Take-Two's rules (the game owner)

- **The core permission.** Rockstar's support page says Take-Two "does not object to our fans using materials for non-commercial uses" that do not intentionally spoil the plot. It defines "non-commercial" as "you don't make money through the game footage you post". Take-Two "reserves the right to have its copyrighted material taken down at any time" (grules-2).
- **A second limb of "non-commercial".** The definition also says you must not "use the material as part of a promotion for a product or service". This matters if the channel ever promotes the company, a tool or a sponsor (grules-m2).
- **Page date.** The page we read shows no date. Two secondary sources (For Founders Law, 31 Oct 2026; Open World Daily, 19 Oct 2026) say it was last updated on 10 January 2025 and does not name GTA 6. Tbreak (4 Nov 2026, updated 8 Nov) reports no new statement for GTA VI creators. We found no separate GTA 6 policy (grules-2, grules-7, grules-m11).
- **What gets taken down.** The page lists examples that "would result in a take-down notice" (grules-3):
  - pre-release footage from leaked copies "regardless of how the game was obtained", including "early unboxing" videos;
  - spoilers: the ending, "an edited combination of cutscenes and/or in-game plot dialogue", and any other big story reveal;
  - isolated cutscenes ("cinematics"). Cutscenes are fine "as part of a larger play-through (or in a narrated 'Let's Play' type video)";
  - in-game TV shows and comedy performances posted on their own;
  - videos that show or promote cheating, glitches, God Mode exploits or mod menus in the online games;
  - videos that promote unauthorised mods or ports;
  - anything else that breaks Rockstar's terms. The list is "not meant to be exhaustive".
- **Who the policy is for.** It covers "occasional, non-commercial in-game content use by individual members of the Rockstar fan community". It says it does not apply to using Rockstar IP for film, TV or streaming distribution, music videos, advertisements, or books and magazines. Those exclusions concern licensing Rockstar IP for those media, not ad-supported fan videos. What puts monetised videos outside the policy is the non-commercial definition above and Take-Two's terms, not the exclusion list (grules-4, grules-m3). Licensing requests go to copyright@take2games.com and must describe the content and the exact use. Spoiler questions go to the same address (grules-4). (The email address and the "occasional" wording were read by one checker only; a person should confirm them in a normal browser before anyone writes to it.)
- **Take-Two's terms of service (last updated 28 February 2025).** The game licence is for "your personal, non-commercial enjoyment". You may not "commercially exploit the Services unless subject to separate, express written terms" from Take-Two. "Custom Content" explicitly includes "gameplay clips, and livestreams", which may be used only with the services or "as authorized by us" (grules-5). Take-Two also "reserves all rights to and ownership of all Custom Content", so even our own captures are not clearly ours to license (grules-m10).
- **Rockstar's own terms.** The Rockstar legal page (rockstargames.com/legal) did not render for us, so we could not read Rockstar's own terms of service (grules-5).
- **Official media.** Rockstar's GTA VI media page offers 5 videos, 9 clips, 138 screenshots and 27 artwork items as zip downloads. Its only usage wording is "Download and share trailers, imagery, and more". It says nothing about commercial use or credit, and silence is not a commercial grant (grules-8).
- **How monetised GTA channels exist anyway.** A Canadian lawyer's article (For Founders Law, 31 Oct 2026, reviewed 12 Nov 2026) says monetised channels depend on Rockstar's tolerance, not a written permission. Open World Daily says "We do not know how Take-Two handles it, and we will not guess" (grules-7). We found no written Take-Two grant of ad monetisation for gameplay videos. Neither article addresses clip channels or reposting other creators' footage.

##### Take-Two's enforcement record

- **Leaks.** In 2022 Take-Two had YouTube videos and forum threads showing leaked GTA 6 footage taken down. In December 2023 the first trailer leaked a day early, and Rockstar released it early in response. In 2026 (August, after a leaker called "CyberLeek" posted the map and footage) Take-Two filed subpoena requests (court demands for user data) with Discord, Microsoft and X in a New York federal court, to identify a leaker. A popular GTA streamer's Discord server was among those named. In October 2025 Rockstar fired 34 staff over "distribution of confidential information"; a union disputes the reason. All of this is from Wikipedia citing IGN, Kotaku, The Verge, BBC and Bloomberg (grules-9). The enforcement is recent, not historic, so automatic launch-week scraping of "GTA 6 channels" risks ingesting leak-derived footage (grules-m12).
- **Mods and a channel.** Take-Two sent a cease-and-desist (a formal demand to stop) to the OpenIV mod tool on 14 June 2017. Nine days later Rockstar said Take-Two would not act against single-player mods. In February 2021 Take-Two sent DMCA takedowns against the re3 and reVC reverse-engineering projects, and sued the programmers in September 2021. On 23 January 2025 the YouTube channel of the "Vice City Next-Gen Edition" mod team was taken down after an appeal from Take-Two (Wikipedia citing PC Gamer, Polygon, VGC and GamesRadar) (grules-10).
- **What we did not find.** We found no documented case of Take-Two striking an ordinary monetised gameplay channel. The search tool's budget ran out before we could look further (for both checkers too), so absence of evidence here is weak, and partly survivor bias: small channels that were struck rarely make the news (grules-10).

##### YouTube's rules as they apply to game footage

- **Monetising games needs the publisher's licence.** YouTube's "What kind of content can I monetize?" page says monetising game content needs "the commercial use rights granted to you by the license from the video game publisher". Some publishers allow all their game content to be used commercially, while in other licensing agreements "publishers may not grant commercial rights for videos that simply show game play for extended periods of time". Under licensing terms, game footage should be minimal unless the commentary has "Instructional/educational value" or "Is strictly tied to the action shown" (grules-6). For GTA the practical answer is still no written grant, because Take-Two's licence is personal and non-commercial (grules-5).
- **Other people's content needs written permission.** For content made by someone else, the same page says you "must have explicit written permission granting you commercial use rights" from the rights holder. This is the clearest official text against "no permission, edit and credit" (grules-m9).
- **Violence in games (advertiser-friendly guidelines).** "Violence in unedited video gameplay is generally acceptable for advertising", for realistic and unrealistic games alike (grules-11). The page then sets three levels:
  - full ads even with graphic scenes, such as a gory attack on a person, if they come after the first 7 seconds;
  - limited ads for graphic game violence in the thumbnail, meaning "brutal killings or severe injuries focusing on bodily fluids and parts";
  - no ads for graphic game violence in the thumbnail or the first 7 seconds, for gameplay "manufactured to create a shocking experience", and for gameplay showing sexual violence, graphic torture, graphic violence against minors or against real named people.
- **Violence montages are not covered.** The same sentence says "montages where gratuitous violence is the focal point is not" acceptable, and "Aggregating non-playable characters for mass killings" is a no-ads example. A GTA highlights channel built from edited kill or rampage moments falls exactly here (grules-m1).
- **Sex, drugs and language in games.** "Sexual video games ... or sexualizing video game characters" get no ads. "Gaming and scripted content displaying drug dealings" can earn full ads, but game content that "focuses on drug usage" gets limited ads. Strong swearing (f*ck) in a title or thumbnail means no ads, moderate swearing ("shit") there means limited ads, and swearing at the start or through most of a video "may not be suitable" (grules-12).
- **Shorts.** The guidelines apply to "video, Short, or live stream, thumbnail", title, description and tags. The page has no separate Shorts rules and no dated change after 2022 (grules-12).
- **Shorts revenue sharing.** From 1 February 2027, monthly Shorts ad and Premium revenue sharing needs "at least 10 million qualified Shorts views in the last 90 days". Non-original Shorts views (re-uploads, compilations) are not counted. A brand-new GTA clip channel should plan for zero Shorts ad income, even on the own-footage route, unless it reaches that scale. Long-form own-commentary videos are the more plausible earner (grules-m7).
- **Who made it.** YouTube's reused-content page says that if "we cannot clearly tell that you made the content, monetization may be removed from your entire channel". Reuse is allowed when "the creator is either visible in the content or explains how the creator added to the content". The 15 July 2025 rename to "inauthentic content" targets "repetitive or mass-produced" content. GTA gameplay looks alike across channels, so every post needs our own voice or face. Hourly templated posting is the pattern this rule names (grules-m8).
- **Age restriction (an 18+ lock).** Age-restricted videos "can use ads", but some advertisers avoid them, so earnings may be limited or nil. Signed-out viewers and viewers under 18 can't watch them, and most other websites can't embed them. "Focusing solely on the most graphically violent part of a film or video game" is listed as a reason for age restriction. The page does not name Shorts, but it applies to "any other YouTube product or feature", so it covers Shorts by implication (grules-13). So a highlight that shows only the most violent moment risks both the age lock and fewer ads.

##### Music inside the game

- **Who can claim what.** On YouTube's Content ID page, "Video gameplay footage (by other than the game's publisher)" is not a valid reference (the file Content ID matches against). Game soundtracks are valid only when the publisher owns them and delivers them, but that rule "does not apply to licensed popular music, not originally created for the game". So record labels can claim licensed songs heard in gameplay (grules-14).
- **What happens to a claimed Short.** A Short over one minute with an active Content ID claim is "blocked globally", can't earn and isn't recommended, though the channel gets no penalty. Shorts "less than one minute" have "no changes in limitations", so the claimant's own policy (monetise, track or block) applies. The page does not say how a Short of exactly 60 seconds is treated, so claim-risk Shorts should stay under 60 seconds (grules-15, grules-m4, 03:policy-3).
- **GTA 6's radio.** Wikipedia lists radio hosts including Lana Del Rey, Morgan Wallen, Bad Bunny and Robyn. The trailers used Tom Petty's "Love Is a Long Road" (trailer 1) and the Pointer Sisters' "Hot Together" plus Wang Chung, Zenglen and Tammy Wynette (trailer 2). Justice wrote about 3 hours of original music for the game, and *Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album* (announced 17 September 2026) has 34 original songs (grules-16). Kotaku's longer song list (updated 8 Oct 2026) is compiled mostly from leaks plus official material and does not mark which songs are confirmed, so we cite only trailer songs and Rockstar-confirmed hosts here, and never use leaked material to seek songs (grules-m5). Original songs may be owned by Rockstar or by the artists' labels; we don't know which.
- **Streamer-safe radio.** One vendor article (ViceForge, 14 Oct 2026) says "Rockstar has not announced a streamer-safe radio mode for GTA VI". We found no official Rockstar statement either way, and we did not check whether GTA V or Red Dead Redemption 2 have such a mode (grules-17).
- **Honest ways to avoid music claims.** Record our own play with the car radio off and the in-game music volume at zero. Skip clips where licensed music is audible. Never use trailer audio under a Short; trailers carry licensed songs (grules-14, grules-16). Changing pitch or speed to dodge matching is circumvention and out of scope.

##### The other creator's rights

- **Who owns a let's-play or stream.** The streamer owns their commentary, face camera, overlay and edit; Take-Two owns the game footage underneath (grules-5, grules-18). Kick's terms say this directly: "The User Content you create remains yours" (grules-18).
- **Why Content ID may stay silent.** A creator generally cannot use gameplay footage as a Content ID reference (grules-14). So clips of a GTA streamer may draw no automatic claim at all. That is not permission: the creator can still send a manual takedown, which brings a copyright strike, and YouTube's Copyright Match Tool makes that a one-click request (03:policy-1, 03:policy-m6).
- **Kick's terms (dated 23 March 2026).** Other users get only "a non-exclusive license to access your User Content through the Service". Users may not copy, reproduce or distribute "User Content belonging to other Users", and may not scrape or use robots (grules-18). Kick's terms don't mention clips by name.
- **Twitch's terms.** Twitch's terms and help pages render only with JavaScript and did not open for us. We can't say what Twitch licenses for clips; this needs checking in a browser (see Risks).
- **YouTube's Clip feature.** A YouTube clip is 5 to 60 seconds, public, stays on YouTube in the Clips library, and is on by default. Creators can turn it off. The page grants the clipper no right to download, re-upload or earn money from it (grules-19). YouTube's Remix tool is no route for automatic uploads (03:policy-m5).
- **How creators treat clip channels.** Paid clipping campaigns exist for GTA-adjacent streamers. StoryCut, a vendor that sells a clipping tool, lists a GTA V roleplay campaign (NoPixel V streams, not GTA 6) paying $1.50 per 1,000 views, up to $150 per clip, through Content Rewards on Whop. The payout comes from the streamer per view, not from YouTube ads. It said that as of 4 November 2026 no GTA 6 launch campaign had been announced, and that clippers need "permission to clip" (grules-20, grules-m6). Section 02 covers clipping marketplaces in general, a consent-based streamer clip channel that still lost monetisation (02:clips-6), and a re-upload case where both the re-uploader and the original creator were terminated (02:clips-5).

##### The owner's route tested: "no permission, edit and credit" to earn ad money

- **Layer 1, the game owner.** Earning money takes the footage outside Rockstar's non-commercial policy, which defines non-commercial as not making money from the footage or promoting a product or service with it (grules-2, grules-m2). Take-Two's terms forbid commercial use without written terms (grules-5). YouTube says game monetisation depends on the publisher's licence (grules-6).
- **Layer 2, the source creator.** Credit does not make a copy fair (03:policy-5). Each clip is open to a takedown and a strike; 3 strikes end the channel and bar the people running it from other channels (03:policy-1, 03:policy-m11).
- **Layer 3, YouTube's pay rules.** "Edited together with little or no narrative" clips are not paid "even if you have permission", and non-original Shorts views earn nothing (03:policy-11, 03:policy-m3). YouTube also requires "explicit written permission granting you commercial use rights" for others' content (grules-m9). A consent-based streamer clip channel was still removed from the Partner Programme (02:clips-6). Since 1 October 2026, Shorts reach is cut for channels that mainly re-upload others' clips (03:policy-12).
- **Verdict.** This route cannot be relied on to earn ad money, and it puts the channel and its operators at risk of strikes and termination (grules-21). No GTA footage has a written right to monetise, so any GTA ad income depends on Take-Two's tolerance. Within that, the routes YouTube's own rules allow to earn all need substantial original commentary, storyline or critical review. Own captured gameplay with real commentary is the cleanest of these. Official Rockstar media or other creators' clips used for genuine commentary or review can meet YouTube's reused-content rule but carry higher takedown and claim risk, especially without the creator's permission. The binding constraint is real commentary per clip, not the footage source alone. Ideally Take-Two would confirm the use in writing (grules-6, grules-7, grules-21).

#### What this means for our build

**Risk table for GTA 6 sourcing models.** The ratings are our own judgment from the findings cited, not measured rates.

| Sourcing model | Legal exposure | Strike risk | Content ID risk | Monetisation | Evidence to keep |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Own gameplay recordings, own commentary | Low to medium: the footage is Take-Two's, and commercial use has no written grant (grules-2, grules-5) | Low, if no spoilers, isolated cutscenes, cheats or pre-release footage (grules-3) | Medium when the radio or licensed music is audible, low with music off (grules-14) | Possible, under tolerance; needs real commentary (grules-6); content must stay ad-friendly, no violence montages (grules-11); Shorts ad income unlikely before the 10M-view threshold (grules-m7) | Capture file, date and time after release, console, music-off setting, commentary script |
| Official Rockstar trailers and screenshots | Low for news or analysis use; "download and share" names no commercial terms (grules-8) | Low | High for trailer audio, which carries licensed songs (grules-16) | Only with real commentary or analysis (03:policy-11) | Rockstar media URL, download date, which asset, audio removed |
| Creators who gave written permission | Low within the licence for the creator's layer; the game and music layers stay open (grules-5, grules-14) | Low within scope | Medium (music) | Uncertain: reused-content rule applies even with permission (03:policy-11, 02:clips-6) | Signed licence naming videos, edits, platform, monetisation, term and withdrawal; music clearance |
| Creators with a public clipping programme or paid campaign | Low within the campaign terms (grules-20) | Low to medium | Medium | Campaign pays per view; YouTube ads uncertain (02:clips-6) | Dated copy of the campaign terms, campaign id, payout records |
| Other creators' videos or streams, no permission, edited and credited | High: credit is no defence (03:policy-5) | High: manual takedowns need no Content ID (grules-14, 03:policy-m6) | Medium: music claims on top | Cannot be relied on (grules-21, grules-m9) | None would make it safe: the software refuses it |
| Leaked or pre-release footage | High: Take-Two takes it down and pursues leakers in court (grules-3, grules-9) | Very high | n/a | No | None: refused outright |

**Guard rails the software must enforce.** These come on top of section 03's list: separate accounts and Cloud project, source allow-list, no YouTube downloading, circuit breakers and an audit log.

1. **Source types allowed.** Only `own_capture`, `rockstar_official_media` and `licensed_creator` (with a signed licence record). `campaign` is allowed only with a saved, dated copy of its terms. Anything else, including any clip from another creator without a licence record, is refused (grules-21).
2. **Release-date gate.** Refuse any in-game footage whose capture date is before 2026-11-19, local release time. The gate applies to a source's upload date too, not only to our own capture dates, so launch-week scraping cannot ingest leak-derived footage. Refuse any file or URL tagged leak, early copy or unboxing. Only Rockstar's media page is allowed before release (grules-1, grules-3, grules-m12).
3. **Spoiler and cutscene filter.** Refuse a clip that is mostly cutscene. Refuse cutscene compilations, mission endings and story reveals. In the first weeks after launch, keep story missions out of Shorts entirely (own default). Refuse isolated in-game TV, comedy or radio-show segments (grules-3).
4. **No cheat or mod content.** Refuse clips tagged glitch, exploit, money glitch, mod menu or modded. The titling model must never use those words (grules-3).
5. **Music check.** Music off during our own captures is the default. Run a music detector on every clip; "music detected" or "unknown" holds the clip for review. Strip trailer audio and replace it with our own voice or licensed music (grules-14, grules-15, grules-16).
6. **Ad-safety check.** No graphic violence in the first 7 seconds or in the thumbnail. No strong swearing in titles or thumbnails. Thumbnails come from a non-violent frame. Skip clips that consist only of the most violent moment, which risks age restriction. The picking model must also avoid violence montages and clips of NPC mass killings, which YouTube lists as not ad-friendly (grules-11, grules-12, grules-13, grules-m1).
7. **Real commentary required.** Every post needs our own commentary, tip or analysis tied to the action on screen (YouTube's "strictly tied to the action shown"), in our own voice or with our own face on screen. A voiceover that only describes the clip doesn't count. Hourly templated posting is the pattern YouTube's inauthentic-content rule names, so output must be limited to what a human with real commentary can supply (grules-6, grules-m8, 03:policy-m9).
8. **Shorts length.** Keep Shorts under 60 seconds unless the clip is music-free and our own capture (grules-15, grules-m4).
9. **Monetisation switch off by default.** Turn ads on only after the owner records a decision: either a written reply from Take-Two, or an explicit choice to rely on tolerance (grules-4, grules-7).
10. **Takedown response.** Any Take-Two or creator complaint pauses all uploads from that source and alerts the owner. Spoiler questions go to copyright@take2games.com before posting (grules-3, grules-4).

#### Risks and unknowns

- **Rockstar may change the policy for GTA 6.** The page reserves the right to change, and we read an undated version (grules-2). Re-read it on release day and monthly after that. Store a dated copy in the audit log.
- **Tolerance can end.** Monetised GTA channels exist on goodwill, not on a licence (grules-7). A cheap test is one email to copyright@take2games.com describing the channel. Expect slow replies or none, and don't treat silence as permission.
- **Rockstar policy text read indirectly.** One checker read the official policy page only through a third-party text reader because direct fetches timed out; the other could not open it and relied on three 2026 secondaries. The "occasional" wording and the copyright@take2games.com address are therefore confirmed by one checker only. One secondary (Open World Daily) says the page has no specific policy on pre-release footage, which conflicts with Tbreak's quote; we keep the gate because Tbreak quotes directly (grules-3, grules-4).
- **Rockstar or labels may register Content ID references.** A publisher may use its own gameplay as a reference (grules-14). We don't know whether Rockstar's trailers or GTA 6 gameplay are in Content ID. Test with 2-3 unlisted uploads first and watch for claims.
- **Original GTA 6 music ownership.** We don't know whether the 34 album songs or Justice's score are owned by Rockstar or by labels (grules-16). Treat all in-game music as claimable.
- **Streamer-safe audio.** The only source is a vendor article (grules-17). Check the game's audio settings menu on release day.
- **Twitch terms not read.** The pages need JavaScript. Open legal.twitch.com/en/legal/terms-of-service/ in a normal browser before any Twitch source is licensed.
- **Age restriction and Shorts.** The page doesn't say how age-restricted Shorts are distributed (grules-13). Avoid content that could trigger it.
- **Enforcement record gaps.** Our search budget ran out mid-research. We found no documented strike against an ordinary monetised GTA gameplay channel, but we could not search thoroughly (grules-10).
- **Whole-channel risk.** If YouTube cannot tell we made the content, monetisation may be removed from the entire channel (grules-m8).
- **Pakistan.** We didn't check local copyright law or AdSense rules for Pakistan here. Section 03 already says a local IP lawyer should confirm.
- **Cost and fit of own capture.** A console, a copy of the game, capture time and a human voice cost money and staff hours; we didn't price them. Own capture is the cleanest source but is not clean either (no written Take-Two grant), and it does not fit "automatic, one post every hour" (own estimate).

### G4. Where GTA 6 footage can come from, and which channels to clip

**The short answer.** GTA 6 launches on 19 November 2026 on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S only, five days after this was written (gsrc-1). Footage we record ourselves on a console is the only supply that we fully control: no creator can claim it, and a clipping vendor that pays for GTA 6 clips calls it "the safest kind to use" (gsrc-15). Even our own footage is not risk-free. Second-hand reports say Rockstar's video policy frames its permission around non-commercial use (nobody we opened quotes its exact wording), and it removes videos of the ending, cutscene compilations and other big story reveals, so the channel should show free-roam play and stunts, never the story (gsrc-3, gsrc-4). For the 18 creators we looked at, we found no public statement that lets anyone clip them (unverified), and Kick's terms forbid copying other users' content. Clipping them without permission therefore has no legal basis we could find, and it cannot earn ad money anyway, because YouTube refuses to monetise clips with "little or no narrative" (gsrc-12, gsrc-13, gsrc-21). Even a clip channel built on permission faces YouTube's "inauthentic content" rule if its feed is templated and mass-produced (gsrc-m2). Start with one console, one capture card (about US$160) and a person who plays, and treat creator clips as an add-on only after a creator says yes in writing (gsrc-10).

#### What we found

Our search budget ran out early in this strand (the session-wide limit on web searches was reached). After that we could only open pages whose address we already had. This is why some official pages are missing and why the permission column below is thin. See "Risks and unknowns".

##### The game and its dates

- Rockstar's GTA VI page says "Coming November 19, 2026." It lists PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, and says the game "Plays Best On" PlayStation 5. The visible page does not mention PC. Pre-load began on 10 November 2026 (gsrc-1).
- Rockstar moved the launch to 19 November 2026 on 6 November 2025, after an earlier date of 26 May 2026 (gsrc-2).
- Review copies carry watermarks that show the reviewer's name, according to one creator quoted by ARY News on 28 October 2026. The same report says journalists who share Xbox or PS5 content early could be blacklisted (gsrc-8). This is a claim we could not check, but it shows Rockstar actively polices early footage.

##### Rockstar's rules for footage (apply to our own gameplay too)

- **The policy page would not open.** Rockstar's "Policy on posting copyrighted Rockstar Games material" (support.rockstargames.com/articles/200153756) timed out six times, at four addresses and with a plain download. Everything below comes from news reports that quote it, so treat the wording as second-hand (gsrc-3).
- **Non-commercial framing.** Reports say the policy was last updated in January 2025 (Insider Gaming gives no day). It says Rockstar is "happy for fans to upload footage of their gameplay". tbreak, relying on Prepublish's reading, says the page frames that permission around non-commercial use. Bloxodes paraphrases this as "you don't make money through the game footage you post". That is a blog author's paraphrase, not Rockstar's words, and Bloxodes says the rules do not mention ad revenue by name. Nobody we opened quotes the policy's own non-commercial sentence, so the exact wording is unknown (gsrc-3, gsrc-m5). If the reading is right, a monetised GTA channel is not covered by the general permission, and Rockstar (not Take-Two, per tbreak) "reserves the right" to take material down at any time, case by case (gsrc-3, gsrc-5).
- **Take-Two's group terms (primary text).** Take-Two's Terms of Service (updated 28 Feb 2025) limit use to "personal, non-commercial enjoyment", ban attempts to "commercialize, or otherwise exploit the Services (including the Content)" without separate written terms, and list "videos ... gameplay clips, and livestreams" as content usable only as Take-Two authorises. The body does not name Rockstar or GTA VI, so whether GTA VI play falls under these terms or Rockstar's own (unreadable) terms is not confirmed. Either way, the monetised own-footage route rests on tolerance, not a licence (gsrc-m1).
- **What this means in practice.** The policy does not say Rockstar will take down monetised gameplay; it just does not promise it won't. We found no case of Take-Two removing ordinary monetised gameplay, but we could not search for one. Large GTA channels do run on monetised gameplay: DarkViperAU has 3.7 billion views over 6,715 videos (gsrc-19). That shows wide tolerance, not a right.
- **Spoilers are removed.** Videos showing "the ending of the game", "an edited combination of cutscenes and/or in-game plot dialogue" or "any other big reveal in the story" are removed. "Isolated videos of the game's cinematics will be removed." Cutscenes are acceptable "as part of a larger play-through" or "in a narrated 'Let's Play' type video". The rule has no end date (gsrc-4).
- **Other removals.** According to tbreak (relying on Prepublish's reading), the policy removes pre-release leaked footage "regardless of how the game was obtained", in-game TV shows or comedy performances "shown in isolation", and "Footage encouraging cheating in online games, or promoting mods and ports". tbreak gives copyright@take2games.com as the contact for unclear cases (gsrc-5, gsrc-m12).

##### Official Rockstar material

- Rockstar's GTA VI "Media & Artwork" page offers 5 videos (including the Launch Trailer and "An Extended Look") plus 9 clips, 138 screenshots and 27 artworks and wallpapers, each set also as a zip download. Its only usage wording is "Download and share trailers, imagery, and more." The page has no licence, no commercial-use terms and no credit rule (gsrc-6).
- Rockstar's Newswire and Legal pages did not render for our fetch tool, so we could not read the site's terms of use (gsrc-6).
- The Rockstar Games YouTube channel has 14.0 million subscribers and 435 videos; its latest upload was "Grand Theft Auto VI: Pre-Load Now" on 10 November 2026 (gsrc-7).
- So "download and share" is an invitation to share, not a licence to build a monetised channel from trailers. A channel of re-cut trailers would also fail YouTube's reused-content test, because it changes nothing of substance (gsrc-12). Trailers are fine as short reference inserts inside our own commentary or news videos, under the same fair-use test as any other clip (see section A3).

##### Recording our own gameplay

- **PS5 built-in capture.** The PS5 keeps the last 60 minutes of play in a rolling buffer at 1080p and 60 frames per second (fps) by default. 4K needs a manual recording started with the Create button. This comes from a November 2020 article that cites the PlayStation Blog FAQ. PlayStation's own support pages returned "404 Not Found" at every address we tried, so we could not confirm the current numbers (gsrc-9).
- **Moving files off the console.** Guides say to copy captures to a USB drive. PlayStation's page on auto-uploading captures to the PlayStation App also returned 404, so we could not confirm limits on that route. Xbox's support pages did not render. We know nothing confirmed about Xbox capture limits.
- **Capture card.** A capture card copies the console's HDMI picture to a computer, which records it with free software such as OBS. Elgato's Game Capture 4K S costs US$159.99. It records up to 2160p (4K) at 60 fps, but HDR capture only up to 1080p60 and only on Windows. It passes the picture through to the TV at up to 2160p60. Elgato recommends it for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series S; Series X is not on its list. It connects by USB-C and records to a computer, not on its own. Its input is described as "HDMI 2.0 (unencrypted)" (gsrc-10). "Unencrypted" means the console's copy protection (HDCP) must be off for the card to see the picture; the PS5 has a setting for this, but we did not open Sony's page that describes it.
- Elgato's older HD60 X (US$179.99) is listed as discontinued, records 4K only at 30 fps, and is recommended for PS4 and Xbox One X, not PS5 (gsrc-11).
- **File sizes (our estimate).** At a typical 12 megabits per second for 1080p60 recording, one hour is about 5.4 GB. At 40 megabits per second for 4K60, one hour is about 18 GB. The owner's laptop has about 13 GB free, so 4K recording there fills the disk in under an hour (gsrc-23).
- **Remote Play** (streaming the console to a PC) was not checked. We do not know if it is good enough for recording.

"Permission" means a statement by the creator, their programme or their platform. Silence and the existence of fan clip channels do not count. We could not open YouTube "About" pages (they returned only navigation) and could not search creator sites, so "none found" below means "none found with limited tools", not "proven absent" (gsrc-21).
