##### Platform rules for streams (Twitch and Kick)

- **Kick's terms** (modified 23 March 2026) say Kick claims no ownership of a streamer's content. Other users only get "a non-exclusive license to access your User Content through the Service". The terms class other users' content as "Company Content" and users agree not to copy, distribute or publish it. Commercial use is allowed only for a user's "on-platform activity" (gsrc-13).
- **Twitch's terms** page loaded without its text, so we could not read them.
- A clipping vendor states: "Being able to make a clip on Twitch or Kick does not give you permission to repost it for money." It says Twitch clips run up to 60 seconds and Kick clips 10-180 seconds, and that on Twitch a streamer controls who can clip their channel (gsrc-14). This is a vendor's reading, not the platforms' text.

##### Paid clipping programmes for gaming

These pay a clipper per 1,000 views on the clipper's own accounts. They do not license anyone to run an ad-earning channel of the creator's footage.

- **The only GTA 6 campaign we found** is "GTA 6 Clipping Campaign - Tokyo Girl" on Content Rewards. It promotes a song, not the game, and the page says "Rockstar Games is not running it." It pays US$0.70 per 1,000 views, at least US$2 and at most US$35 per clip, from a US$2,000 budget (US$88 spent on 14 November 2026). It accepts TikTok and Instagram only, not YouTube. Clips need an ad disclosure at the start. It calls self-captured console footage "the safest kind to use" and warns against pulling clips from other creators (gsrc-15).
- **Publisher campaigns.** SEGA and Blizzard briefs link "a content folder with trailers, gameplay and other video files"; the article does not say this for Call of Duty. Rates run US$1.50-4.00 per 1,000 views (Instagram US$1.50; TikTok and YouTube US$2-4), with caps of US$500-1,000 per clip. WoW, Football Manager 27, Metaphor and Stranger Than Heaven accept YouTube; Call of Duty Warzone Season 1 accepts TikTok and Instagram only. Football Manager 27 and Metaphor (SEGA) pay US$0 for views from Pakistan, India and Bangladesh, and WoW pays only for views from its campaign region (gsrc-16, gsrc-m7).
- **Streamer campaigns** (TJR at US$0.75 per 1,000 views capped at US$750 per clip; ThreadGuy at US$1.00 capped at US$500; pools for Lacy, Clix and others) license footage "only to make clips for that campaign", require a disclosure at the start of every clip, and are posted on the clipper's own accounts (gsrc-17). None of them is a GTA campaign.
- The same vendor says "Yes, you need permission to clip streamers" and that tagging a creator is not permission (gsrc-18).

##### What happens to clip channels without permission

- The record from the general strand applies here: a streamer's clips channel run with the streamer's consent was still removed from the Partner Programme for reused content in September 2026, and a re-upload channel was terminated, taking the original creator's channel with it (section A2, clips-5 and clips-6; gsrc-22).
- YouTube's reused-content rule names "Clips of moments from your favorite show edited together with little or no narrative" and content copied "without any substantive modifications" as not monetisable, "even if you have permission from the original creator". The page does not mention video games at all, so gameplay clips are judged by the same test (gsrc-12).
- We found no on-record statement by any GTA creator saying anyone may clip them. So the owner's "no permission" route has no public permission to turn into, for any creator on our list (gsrc-21).

##### GTA-specific monetisation trap

- YouTube's own advertiser-friendly guidelines (read 14 Nov 2026, no section date) list "unedited gameplay violence occurring after the first 7 seconds" as able to earn full ad revenue. "Graphic game violence in the thumbnail" earns limited ads. "Graphic game violence in the thumbnail or in the first seven seconds of the video" earns no ads. Also no ads: "Aggregating non-playable characters for mass killings" and gameplay "manufactured to create a shocking experience". Montages where "gratuitous violence is the focal point" are not suitable. So NPC mass-kill content earns no ads, not merely "can be" demonetised. Dexerto (4 September 2026) reports this correctly, but the official page is stricter on the thumbnail rule and on the full-ads allowance applying only to unedited gameplay, which matters for edited Shorts and for any thumbnail generator. Many typical GTA moments fall here, so the clip picker must score for this (gsrc-20, gsrc-m3).

##### Additional findings from the checkers

- **Inauthentic content rule (gsrc-m2).** YouTube's monetisation policy was renamed from "repetitious content" to "inauthentic content" on 15 July 2025. Content must "Not be mass-produced, generic, repetitive, or manipulative", and "Generic or repetitive content includes content that looks like it's made with a template". An hourly, auto-generated, templated Shorts feed made from our own GTA footage is exposed to this rule even with no copyright problem.
- **Own voice and face help (gsrc-m4).** YouTube lists "Content that primarily features the uploading creator in the video" among reused content that can be monetised. Own gameplay with our own voice-over or face-cam is the strongest position under the reused-content test.
- **Pre-launch creator videos (gsrc-m6).** MrBossFTW's latest upload on 12 Nov 2026 is "The ENTIRE GTA 6 Map Just Got Revealed...", a pre-release video whose source is unknown. Rockstar removes pre-release leaked footage, so the picker should refuse any creator footage dated before 19 Nov 2026 until its origin is checked.
- **Shorts reach cut (gsrc-m8).** On 1 Oct 2026 YouTube announced that Shorts recommendations will cut reach for channels that mainly aggregate or re-upload others' clips without meaningful changes. Minor technical edits and template-based bulk changes do not count as added value, and no start date was given. This hits the "no permission, edit and credit" route on reach, separately from monetisation.
- **Higher Partner bar (gsrc-m9).** From 1 Feb 2027 new applicants to the Partner Programme need 8,000 qualified watch hours in the last 365 days or 20M qualified Shorts views in 90 days. Shorts ad revenue share needs 10M Shorts views in 90 days. A channel started at the 19 Nov 2026 launch will almost certainly still be applying after 1 Feb 2027, so ad money from own footage will not come quickly.
- **Weak GTA 6 sources in the list (gsrc-m10, gsrc-m11).** xQc's GTA content is "GTA RP NoPixel V", which is GTA V roleplay, not GTA 6. GTA 6 launches on PS5 and Xbox Series X|S only, with no PC on Rockstar's page, so PC-based GTA RP streams of GTA 6 should not be expected at launch (our inference). gtaseriesvideos' latest upload, "GTA 6 - Pre-Load Trailer" (10 Nov 2026), appears to be Rockstar's own trailer re-posted, so clipping it would mean clipping Rockstar material through a third party, with neither's permission.

#### What this means for our build

1. **Own footage is the main supply.** Buy or use one PS5, the game, and an Elgato 4K S (US$159.99), and record on a Windows PC with OBS at 1080p60 (gsrc-10). 1080p60 is enough for Shorts and long clips and keeps files near 5.4 GB per hour (gsrc-23). Record to an external drive, not the laptop's 13 GB of free space. Built-in PS5 capture plus a USB stick is the zero-cost fallback for the first days (gsrc-9).
2. **Someone has to play.** Own footage is limited by play time. One hour of play gives perhaps a few usable moments (our estimate; nothing measured). An hourly posting rate needs many hours of play a day, so the first schedule should be set by the footage on hand, not by the clock.
3. **Turn the radio off when recording.** GTA's in-game radio plays licensed music that can draw Content ID claims (a third-party claim we saw only in a search summary, not confirmed). Removing music we have no right to use is allowed and cheap: set the radio to off or record with music volume at zero. Never use in-game TV shows or stand-up performances on their own (gsrc-5).
4. **No story, no cutscenes.** Hard rule in the picker: no cutscenes, no mission endings, no plot dialogue compilations, nothing from before 19 November 2026 (gsrc-4, gsrc-5). Default content: free roam, driving, stunts, physics, map discovery, glitches that are not cheats, and "how to" moments. Add the label `spoiler_risk` to every candidate clip and block anything flagged.
5. **Violence filter.** No graphic violence in the thumbnail or the first seven seconds of any video (thumbnail alone means limited ads; thumbnail or first seven seconds means no ads); no "kill compilation" or NPC mass-kill formats, and expect heavily edited action montages not to get the full-ads allowance, which is worded for unedited gameplay. Thumbnail and first-frame selection must use the same filter (gsrc-20, gsrc-m3).
6. **Every clip needs our own layer.** A hook, captions, a voiced or written point, a tip or a comparison, so the channel passes the reused-content test that applies even to our own footage when it is just raw play, and vary the format so the feed does not read as templated mass production (gsrc-12, gsrc-m2, gsrc-m4).
7. **Official media only as inserts.** Allow Rockstar trailer or screenshot inserts of a few seconds inside our own commentary videos, credited "Footage: Rockstar Games", never as the main content (gsrc-6, gsrc-12).
8. **Creator footage only with written permission, and nothing dated before 19 November 2026 (gsrc-m6).** Keep the `sources` allow-list from section A4: no row, no clip. Add gaming fields: platform (YouTube, Twitch, Kick), whether the permission covers downloading and monetised reuse on YouTube, music rules, and the people who appear (GTA roleplay clips show other streamers' voices and faces, and one streamer's yes does not cover them; this is our own reasoning). Do not use the Twitch or Kick clip button as a source (gsrc-13, gsrc-14).
9. **Paid clipping campaigns are a separate business.** They pay per view on the clipper's own account, need an ad disclosure, mostly exclude YouTube for GTA, and some pay nothing for views from Pakistan (gsrc-15, gsrc-16). Do not mix them into this channel.
10. **Speed matters only for own footage.** The launch week is when interest peaks, so the capture kit should be in place before 19 November 2026 if possible (gsrc-1).

##### Recommended starting set

**(a) Rights-clear sources only (recommended).**
1. Our own PS5 gameplay recorded through a capture card, radio off, no story (gsrc-4, gsrc-10).
2. Rockstar's official trailers and screenshots as short credited inserts inside our own commentary (gsrc-6).
3. Nothing else until a creator says yes in writing.

**(b) The owner asks creators for permission.** Send to the GTA-focused channels first (rows 2, 3, 4 and 5 above), then the rest. We found no data on how often creators agree; record every reply and work out the rate after 20 requests. Sample message:

> Hi [name], I run a new GTA 6 Shorts channel. I'd like to post short clips (under 60 seconds) from your GTA 6 videos, with captions and my own commentary, your name on screen and a link to your video at the top of the description. The channel earns money from YouTube ads. Can I have your written permission to download and use clips from your GTA 6 uploads for this? If yes, please tell me any limits (how many clips, which videos, anything I should not use). You can withdraw permission at any time by replying to this message, and I will take the clips down within 48 hours. Thanks, [name, channel link, email]

Store the reply, the date and the exact scope. A "yes" covers copyright only; it does not get the clips past the reused-content rule (gsrc-12).

**(c) The owner's stated preference (no permission).** We do not rank targets for this. The record shows: permission did not save a consenting streamer's clips channel from demonetisation, a re-upload channel was terminated, and three copyright strikes end the channel and any linked channels (gsrc-22; section A3 policy-1). We found no creator on our list who has said on record that anyone may clip them (gsrc-21).

##### Ten-minute vetting checklist for any GTA creator

1. **Owner (1 min).** Is the channel the creator's own official channel? If it is a fan or clip channel, stop.
2. **Written permission (3 min).** Look on the channel's About page, pinned posts, the creator's website and social bios for "clip", "clipping", "reupload", "use my content", "copyright". Copy the exact sentence, URL and date. No sentence means no permission.
3. **Programme (1 min).** Is the creator running a clipping campaign (Content Rewards, Whop and similar)? If yes, read the brief: which platforms, footage source, disclosure, and whether it allows a monetised YouTube channel. Most do not (gsrc-17).
4. **Platform (1 min).** Where does the footage live? Kick's terms forbid copying other users' content; Twitch's were not read. YouTube downloads need the creator's permission (gsrc-13; section A3).
5. **People and music (1 min).** Does the footage show other streamers (roleplay servers), webcam guests, or background music? Each is a separate rights holder.
6. **Rockstar rules (1 min).** Is the moment a cutscene, mission ending, plot reveal, in-game TV or pre-release footage? If yes, skip it (gsrc-4, gsrc-5).
7. **Enforcement (1 min).** Search "[creator] copyright strike clips", "[creator] DMCA" and "[creator] clip channel". Note dated reports.
8. **Record (1 min).** Save the result in the `sources` table with an expiry 30 days out, as section A4 describes.

#### Risks and unknowns

- **Rockstar's policy text is second-hand.** The official page timed out every time. Before launch, someone should open it in a normal browser, save a dated copy, and confirm the "non-commercial" wording. Not confirmed: the "non-commercial" wording itself and the exact update day (only "January 2025" is supported); until then the exact wording is unknown. Cost: five minutes (gsrc-3, gsrc-m5).
- **Monetised own gameplay is tolerated, not licensed.** If Take-Two ever enforces the non-commercial wording, our own footage could be claimed too. Keep the channel's add-on value high and keep a dated copy of the policy. Emailing copyright@take2games.com and keeping the reply is the cheapest way to cut this risk (gsrc-3, gsrc-5, gsrc-m1, gsrc-m12).
- **Capture numbers are old or unconfirmed.** PS5 limits come from a 2020 article citing Sony; PlayStation and Xbox support pages would not open. Test on the console itself on day one (gsrc-9).
- **Whether the PS5 allows recording of every part of GTA 6 is unknown.** Some games block capture in certain scenes. We could not check. Test it on day one.
- **The permission column is weak.** Our search budget ran out, so we did not search creator websites or social posts. A person can redo checklist step 2 for the top 5 creators in under 15 minutes (gsrc-21).
- **Twitch's terms were not read.** Open https://legal.twitch.com/en/legal/terms-of-service/ and Twitch's help page on clips in a normal browser before using any Twitch footage.
- **Which creators will stream GTA 6 is a guess.** Re-check rows 1-15 between 19 and 21 November 2026.
- **Kit and game prices for Pakistan were not checked.** Only the Elgato US price is confirmed (gsrc-10). The console and game cost should be priced locally.
- **Hourly posting from own footage may be impossible** without many hours of play a day. We have no measured ratio of usable moments per hour of GTA play. An hourly templated feed also risks the inauthentic content rule (gsrc-m2), Shorts reach is being cut for aggregated clips (gsrc-m8), and a new channel faces the higher Partner bar from 1 Feb 2027 (gsrc-m9).
- **Creator permission claim is unverified.** The statement that no creator on the list has a public clip permission is an absence claim made with limited tools (gsrc-21) (unverified).
- **Checker disagreement.** None on facts. Both checkers corrected gsrc-16; we kept the narrower wording.
- **Instruction-like text.** No page we opened tried to give us instructions.

### G5. Picking the moments in gameplay and streams

**The short answer.** In gameplay the picture carries the moment, and the one study that compared signals on game streams found video far stronger than chat (F-score about 72 for video alone against about 43 for chat alone, and about 75 with both) (gpick-12). That study used League of Legends tournament broadcasts labelled from one fan channel's highlight reels, so it is weak evidence for single-streamer GTA free-roam (gpick-m4). So the picker should find candidates with free signals first (viewer-made Twitch clips with view counts, loudness peaks from the audio, scene-change bursts, what the streamer says), then let a vision model look at small frames from those candidate windows only, and let Sonnet re-rank the best 20 (gpick-2, gpick-16, gpick-18). This costs about $0.16 of AI tokens for a 6-hour stream, about $0.03 per source hour and about $0.02 per posted clip, and half that through the Batch API (gpick-11). Those figures count AI tokens only, at list price, and assume no thinking tokens, so thinking must be switched off or kept to the minimum (gpick-m2). Even a full Haiku 5.5 scan of every 2 seconds of an 8-hour stream would cost only about $0.25, so the AI bill is not the limit; quality, the CPU work of decoding hours of video (about 18 source hours a day for hourly posting), and the right to use the footage are (gpick-7, gpick-9, gpick-11, gpick-m9). GTA 6 comes out on 19 November 2026, so the first weeks of footage will be mostly main-story play: decide now whether to avoid story spoilers. We recommend avoiding them and favouring free-roam chaos, crashes, chases and glitches (gpick-1). Clip downloads need the broadcaster or one of their editors to authorise the app, which fits the permission route and does not work for the "no permission" route (gpick-3). Live chat may be readable with a bot's own user token without the streamer's consent (our inference), but whether we may store and reuse it depends on the Twitch Developer Agreement, which we could not read (gpick-5, gpick-m3).

#### What we found

##### The game and its timing
- Rockstar's official GTA VI page says "Coming November 19, 2026", for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S (gpick-1). No PC version is listed in the page text we read (that text came back truncated in one check, so absence is likely but not fully proven) (gpick-1). No delay notice was visible, but no news search for a late delay could be run (gpick-1).
- So, as of 14 November 2026, there is no real GTA 6 gameplay to test on. The on-screen interface (death and arrest screens, mission banners, wanted level) cannot be known until release (gpick-1, gpick-20).
- The earlier game is a guide, not a promise. A fan wiki describes GTA V's death screen: the picture turns grey and slows, and the word "Wasted" appears in red in the centre, with the mission name under it (page last edited 7 June 2020) (gpick-20). If GTA 6 does something similar, such screens are easy for a model to see, and the mission name on them is itself a story spoiler (our inference from gpick-20).

##### Signals that mark a good moment, how to get each, and what it costs
- **Viewer-made Twitch clips.** Twitch's official Get Clips call returns clips for one broadcaster, one game or a list of ids, within a time window (default one week from the start date), up to 100 per page. Each clip has `view_count`, `duration`, `created_at`, `title`, `creator_name`, `video_id` and `vod_offset` (where the clip starts in the past broadcast). `vod_offset` is null when the video is not available or not yet created from the live stream, and it can stay null for minutes after a clip is made, so a null does not mean the recording is gone; `video_id` is an empty string, not null, when the video is unavailable (gpick-2, gpick-m7). An app token or a user token works (gpick-2). This is the cheapest crowd signal there is: viewers pressed "clip" at the moment and other viewers watched it. Cost: no money, only API calls (gpick-2).
- **Downloading those clips is a different matter.** Twitch's Get Clips Download call needs a token with `editor:manage:clips` or `channel:manage:clips`, and the caller must be the broadcaster or one of their editors; anyone else gets a 403 error. Its rate limit is 100 requests a minute (gpick-3). So the official way to get clip video needs the broadcaster or an editor to authorise us (gpick-3). The call takes 1-10 clip ids, returns temporary links, and gives both a landscape and a portrait download link, so a partner's clips can arrive already vertical (gpick-m8).
- **Past broadcasts (VODs).** Twitch's Get Videos call can list up to 500 videos for a game, sorted by views, with `duration` and `view_count`. It also lists `muted_segments`, the parts Twitch's audio recognition muted (usually copyrighted music), but only with a user token; with an app token that field is always null (gpick-4). Muted parts are silent, so a loudness signal sees nothing there (our inference).
- **Chat spikes.** Live chat can be read through Twitch's EventSub `channel.chat.message` event. It needs a user token with `user:read:chat`, or an app token that the chatting user granted `user:read:chat` and `user:bot` and the broadcaster granted `channel:bot` (gpick-5). The older chat connection (IRC) needs a user token with `chat:read`, and Twitch recommends EventSub over it (gpick-5). The chat guide sets a limit of 100 channels joined at once for chatbots, and joins as broadcaster or moderator, or with the broadcaster's `channel:bot` grant, do not count toward it. Our inference: a bot reading with its own user token can listen to channels that never authorised it. The docs we opened do not settle whether storing and reusing that chat is allowed (gpick-m3). Chat exists only live, so a listener must be running during each broadcast. We found no official API that returns the chat of a past broadcast: the API reference lists only Get Videos and Delete Videos under videos (gpick-5). Chat-replay downloaders exist, but they use unofficial routes, which are out of scope here (gpick-15).
- **How useful chat is.** In the League of Legends study, chat alone reached F-scores of 43.2 and 39.7 on two test sets, video alone 72.2 and 69.2, and both together 74.7 and 70.0. The best chat window was the 7 seconds after a frame, so chat reacts within seconds (gpick-12). Those models were trained with supervision on 128 and 57 labelled games, on professional esports broadcasts, so the result may not carry over to zero-shot frame picking on personality-driven streams (gpick-m4). In a later Twitch study (MINT), the authors trained on about two million user-recommended Twitch clips with their chat; per the publisher's blog it merges chat, video metadata and view count (the blog does not say it uses video frames). A user study judged its picks as enjoyable as human-recommended clips, and its picks covered failing, funny, outplay and non-game moments, while most human picks were game-winning moments (gpick-13). Chat helps, but it is a supporting signal, not the main one (gpick-12, gpick-13).
- **YouTube clips and "most replayed".** YouTube viewers can make clips of 5 to 60 seconds; clipping is on by default, and the creator sees each clip's views in YouTube Studio (gpick-6). We found no Data API call that lists clips made from someone else's video (a negative search result, which cannot prove absence, and was not repeated by the checkers) (unverified) (gpick-6). A live stream can be clipped only with DVR, a clip appears only after the stream is uploaded, and clips are removed if the original is deleted or made private, so clips are a creator-side signal, not a footage source (gpick-m10). The "most replayed" graph is not in the Data API, and scraping it breaks YouTube's developer policies (section A6: pick-12, pick-13) (gpick-21). Neither is a usable signal for other people's videos unless the source creator shares their Studio numbers with us (our inference).
- **Loud reactions and audio energy.** The app already decodes audio to 16 kHz mono and measures it in 50 ms windows, with levels that adapt to each recording (room tone at the 5th percentile, speech at the 95th), in 60-second blocks so a 3-hour file never sits in memory (gpick-18). It also measures loudness with ffmpeg's `ebur128` filter, in about 5 seconds for a 101-minute meeting (a code comment, not a measurement taken here); that call returns one integrated value per file or piece, not a loudness-over-time series, so only the 50 ms window levels are reusable for peak finding (gpick-18). Reusing the window levels, a shout or burst of laughter is a run of windows well above the source's own speech level. Those statistics are tuned for meetings: in GTA footage, game audio (gunfire, engines, sirens, radio) is almost always above the speech level, so "6 dB above typical speech" will mostly flag explosions and music rather than reactions, and a video with a music bed may flag nothing useful (our inference, not tested) (gpick-18). Cost: CPU only. The thresholds are ours to tune and must be measured on real gameplay (gpick-18).
- **Scene changes and motion.** PySceneDetect (BSD-3-Clause licence, release v0.7.3 on 8 November 2026, about 5.4k stars) finds cuts with content, adaptive and threshold detectors (gpick-16). GTA gameplay has constant camera motion, and content detectors may fire on fast driving and explosions as much as on real cuts, so "cuts per 10 s" as an action signal is untested on this footage (gpick-16). auto-editor (public domain under the Unlicense, about 5.9k stars, now written in Nim) cuts mainly on audio loudness and can also cut "motionlessness" (gpick-17). Bursts of cuts or camera motion may mark action. Long still stretches mark menus, loading, "be right back" screens and waiting rooms. Cost: CPU only (gpick-16, gpick-17).
- **What the streamer says.** The transcript still matters for gaming. It catches reactions ("no way", laughter), explanations of a glitch or trick, and sponsor reads. The existing transcript-first picker (section A6) applies here unchanged as one input (gpick-18, gpick-21).
- **On-screen game events.** Death, arrest, mission-passed banners, explosions and the wanted level are visible signals. Template matching (finding a known image inside each frame) can only be built once GTA 6 is out and we have screenshots of its interface (gpick-1, gpick-20). Until then a vision model reading big on-screen text is the only option (gpick-7).

##### A vision model looking at frames
- **How Claude counts image tokens.** Claude cuts an image into 28 by 28 pixel patches; an image costs ⌈width/28⌉ × ⌈height/28⌉ tokens (⌈ ⌉ means round up) (gpick-7). Claude 4.7 and later models use the high-resolution tier: images are shrunk to at most 2,576 px on the long edge and 4,784 tokens. A full 1920x1080 frame costs 2,691 tokens on that tier (gpick-7).
- **What small frames cost.** A 448x252 frame (16:9) costs 16 × 9 = 144 tokens. A 672x378 frame costs 24 × 14 = 336 tokens. Tiling four frames into one picture saves no tokens, because tokens follow pixels (our arithmetic from gpick-7).
- **Request limits.** One API request can carry up to 600 images, or 100 for models with a 200k-token context window. Over 20 images, every image must be at most 3,000 px on each side. JPEG, PNG, GIF and WebP are accepted; animations are not, only their first frame is used (gpick-7). Haiku 5.5 has a 1M-token context window, so the 600-image limit applies to it. The limit that matters is the Haiku price step: prompts over 100,000 tokens cost five times more, which is about 600 frames at 448x252 plus text per request (gpick-m1).
- **Prices.** Sonnet 5.5 costs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output. Haiku 5.5 costs $0.10 and $0.50 for prompts up to 100,000 tokens, and $0.50 and $2.50 above that, and each request is priced on its own. The Batch API halves these prices (gpick-9). decide/pricing.py:13-15 holds the same figures for Sonnet and the up-to-100K Haiku tier only, so a cost meter built on it would under-report any Haiku call over 100K tokens (gpick-9). Image tokens are billed as input tokens (gpick-7).
- **Thinking tokens are billed as output.** Sonnet 5.5 rejects thinking "disabled"; its lowest setting is `between_tools`, which turns off up-front thinking at high effort or below. Haiku 5.5 accepts "disabled" at high effort or below. Both default to adaptive thinking. The cost table below counts no thinking tokens, so the build must set those modes or budget extra output (Sonnet output is $10 per million), and the cost meter should read the billed usage, not the visible text (gpick-m2).
- **What the model can and can't judge.** Anthropic lists limits: Claude will not identify people by name in images, may make mistakes on low-quality or rotated images and on images under 200 pixels, and gives only approximate counts (gpick-8). A 448x252 frame is only 252 px tall, close to that warning, and in-game HUD text (speed, wanted stars, money) at that size will be unreliable; test this before titles depend on it (gpick-8). So the model can describe what happens on screen (a crash, an arrest, a ragdoll fall, a car flying), read large on-screen text, and say whether a frame looks like a cutscene or a menu. It cannot name the streamer from a facecam, and it is unreliable on tiny HUD text in small frames (our inference from gpick-7 and gpick-8). Whether a moment is funny depends on timing and sound, which still frames lose, so the transcript and loudness must go in with the frames (our inference from gpick-12).
- **A cheaper video-native option.** Google's Gemini models take video directly. By default they sample 1 frame a second, at 66 tokens a frame at the default low media resolution or 258 at higher settings, plus 32 tokens a second of audio, about 100 tokens a second in all at low resolution and about 300 at higher settings. Custom frame rate and start and end offsets work only in "static" processing mode, which the candidate-window-only test must use, so only candidate windows need to be sent (gpick-10, gpick-m5). Models with a 1M context take up to 3 hours of video per request at low resolution (gpick-m5). Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite costs $0.30 per million input tokens (the same for text, image, video and audio) and $2.50 output ($0.15 and $1.25 in batch) (gpick-10). It hears the audio and sees motion, which still frames do not, and sending windows to it could move frame decoding off our own server. But it is a second AI provider and a second place the footage is sent, and the free tier uses submitted content to improve Google's products, so only the paid tier should be used (gpick-m5).

##### Research and tools for gaming highlights
- **Research.** The League of Legends study (EMNLP 2017) used 321 games (218 NALCS and 103 LMS) from Twitch, labelled from fan-made highlight videos (gpick-12). MINT (EPJ Data Science; publisher's blog post 2 September 2021) published code at github.com/dscig/twitch-highlight-detection: 19 stars, 12 commits, no licence shown, and only clip and video ids rather than the data (full data on request) (gpick-13). Lightor (arXiv, October 2019, not peer reviewed) starts from timestamped chat and refines with how viewers interact, tested with Mechanical Turk users on two Twitch games; no code or licence is stated (gpick-14). None of these is a drop-in tool. Without a licence, MINT's code cannot be reused (gpick-13).
- **Open-source chat tools.** twitch-highlight-finder (MIT, Rust, 9 stars) counts chat message and emote frequency so that it works in any language; it gathers chat live with its own WebSocket-based collector, so it does not recover the chat of past broadcasts (gpick-15). Several other small chat-spike projects exist; the ones we saw read chat logs made by unofficial downloaders (search results, not opened) (unverified) (gpick-15). The idea (count messages and emotes per few seconds, flag bursts against the stream's own baseline) takes a few dozen lines and does not need a library (our estimate).
- **Commercial clippers.** Eklipse's own pages could not be opened (eklipse.gg returned 403), so its claimed detections (kills, clutches, eliminations, chat spikes), genre fit and supported-game counts (1,000+, 3,000+, 300+, inconsistent between pages) rest on search snippets (unverified) (gpick-19). The one review we opened (byline 22 April 2026, also marked updated 17 April 2026, says it has no affiliate links) did no testing of its own despite its title; it draws on Trustpilot, G2, Capterra and Product Hunt feedback and repeats an unsourced "community consensus" of about 80-90% accuracy on well-supported games. It says the tool works best on high-kill shooters with kill feeds and victory screens (Call of Duty, Apex, Valorant, Fortnite, League of Legends, Marvel Rivals) and worst on indie or niche titles, Just Chatting or creative streams, and "personality-driven content without in-game scoreboard events". It does not mention GTA or open-world games (gpick-19). Personality-driven content without scoreboard events describes typical GTA streams, so kill-feed detectors are a poor fit; we found no independent test of any clipper on open-world gameplay (our inference from gpick-19).

#### What this means for our build

**1. Where the footage comes from decides which signals exist.** With a partner streamer who authorises our app, we get clip downloads (possibly already vertical), clip view counts and muted-part lists through official calls, and live chat as well (gpick-2, gpick-3, gpick-4, gpick-5, gpick-m8). Live chat may also be readable without authorisation through a bot's own user token, but the Developer Agreement must be read before storing it (gpick-m3). With our own recorded gameplay we have audio, frames and our own commentary only. With unlicensed YouTube or Twitch footage we get none of the strong signals and break platform rules to get the video (section A6: pick-m6). The picker should be built for the first two cases. Better picking also cannot make a channel that mainly re-uploads others' videos "original" under YouTube's 1 October 2026 reach cut (section A6: pick-m7) (gpick-m11).

**2. Method for a 3-8 hour stream.**
- *Stage 0, crowd signal (free).* Call Get Clips for the broadcaster over the stream's time window. Every clip with a `vod_offset` becomes a candidate at [offset − 15 s, offset + duration + 10 s]. A clip with a null offset is re-polled later (offsets can take minutes) before it is dropped. Its score input is log(view_count + 1), ranked within that stream (gpick-2, gpick-m7).
- *Stage 1, cheap signals (CPU, no AI).*
  - Loudness peaks: reuse slice/silence.py's 50 ms window levels. Mark a peak where the short-term level stays at least about 6 dB above the stream's typical speech level for at least 0.5 s. These numbers are our starting guess and are likely to flag game audio; measure them on real gameplay first (gpick-18).
  - Scene and motion: run PySceneDetect on a downscaled copy and measure cuts per 10 s. Mark still stretches of 20 s or more as "dead" (menus, loading, "starting soon", "be right back").
  - Transcript: WhisperX or the source's own captions, scored with the existing sentence scorer plus a short list of reaction words.
  - Chat (live partners only): messages and emotes per 5 s against the stream's own median. Shift each spike about 5-10 s earlier, because chat follows the moment (gpick-12).
  - Muted parts and dead stretches are excluded (gpick-4).
- *Stage 2, candidates.* Merge the signals into windows of 20-90 s. Score each one as a weighted sum of ranks: clips 3, loudness 2, chat 2, transcript 1, scene burst 1. Keep the best 10 per source hour (60 for a 6-hour stream). The weights are a starting guess, to be tested on our own labelled candidates rather than taken from the 2017 study (gpick-m4), and every score is logged so it can be checked later.
- *Stage 3, Haiku 5.5 vision check (one request per candidate).* Send 16 frames at 448x252 spread over the window, the transcript lines with times, and the signal summary, with thinking disabled. The model returns event type, a one-line description of what is seen, cutscene or gameplay, spoiler risk, dead screen or not, peak frame, and sub-scores (funny, impressive, glitch, readability without sound). It must list the frame numbers that show each fact (gpick-7, gpick-8, gpick-m2).
- *Stage 4, Sonnet 5.5 re-rank.* Send the best 20, each with 6 frames at 672x378 around the peak plus Stage 3's notes and the transcript, in one request, with thinking set to `between_tools`. The output follows the existing re-rank format in decide/prompts.py:145-180, with visual fields added (gpick-18, gpick-m2).
- *Stage 5, truth check (Haiku).* For each title and hook, ask yes or no against 4 frames and the transcript: "Is X visible or said?" Drop or rewrite anything that gets a "no".
- Run Stages 3-5 through the Batch API, because none of them is urgent (gpick-9).

**3. Method for a 15-minute edited video.** It is already a highlight reel, so skip Stage 0 and the "dead" filter. Scan the whole video at 1 frame a second (448x252) with Haiku in two requests of under 100,000 tokens each (900 frames at 144 tokens is about 130k, so each half stays under the price step) (gpick-m1). Use the creator's chapters as edges (section A6: pick-17). Re-rank the best 6-8 with Sonnet and expect 1-3 Shorts. Never re-cut the creator's own edit into a near-copy of it. Prefer moments where we add something of our own; the rules section owns that call (section A3).

**4. Clean start and end (rules in code, after the model).**
- Start 3-8 s before the peak frame (set-up). Snap to a scene cut if there is one within 2 s, and never start mid-word (use transcript word times, as edl/ does today).
- Peak: the frame Stage 3 named, checked against the loudness peak.
- End after the pay-off: when loudness falls back below the stream's typical speech level for 1.5 s, or the respawn or "mission" screen ends, plus 0.5 s. Never end mid-sentence.
- Lengths: Shorts 15-45 s, hard cap 60 s, because a Short over 1 minute with an active copyright claim of any type (not only Content ID) is blocked worldwide, and Shorts may run up to three minutes (section A6: pick-24) (gpick-21, gpick-m6). Long clips: either one 3-10 minute sequence (a full chase or heist attempt) or a compilation of 6-10 moments with our own framing between them.

**5. Spoilers (if the owner wants them avoided).** Flag a candidate when any of these hold:
- The model says "cutscene or scripted story scene".
- On-screen text shows a mission name or a mission-complete banner.
- The same key frame (perceptual hash) appears in two or more different streamers' footage, which suggests a scripted scene rather than free play.
- The transcript mentions story beats ("mission", "ending", character reveals).

The default for the first 8 weeks after 19 November 2026 is to skip every flagged candidate (gpick-1). The cross-streamer hash rule is our own idea and needs testing.

**6. No near-duplicates.**
- Within one source: no more than 20% overlap with an already chosen clip.
- Across sources and posts: store a 64-bit difference hash (a small fingerprint of a picture) of 5 key frames per posted clip, plus a text fingerprint of the transcript. Reject a new clip whose key frames mostly match a clip posted in the last 90 days, or whose title shares most main words with a recent title. Thresholds are guesses, to tune on the first 200 candidates by hand (own estimate).

**7. Skipping adverts, sponsor reads and waiting screens.** Long still stretches, "starting soon" or "be right back" screens, the first and last 3 minutes of a stream, transcript sponsor reads (marked by the model) and muted parts are all removed before Stage 2 (gpick-4, gpick-16, gpick-17).

**8. Output fields per pick.** `source_id, source_kind (stream|edited), start_s, end_s, peak_s, short_start_s, kind (S|L), event_type (crash|chase|arrest|death|stunt|glitch|funny_reaction|skill|other), seen (one line), evidence_frames, evidence_lines, signals {clip_views, loud_db, chat_z, scene_rate, transcript_score}, subscores {funny, impressive, glitch, cold_readability}, rank_score, spoiler (none|possible|story), is_cutscene, dead_screen, licensed_music_suspected, dup_of (id|-), title, hook, why`.

**9. Titles and hooks true to a visual moment.** A title may claim only:
- what Stage 3 listed as seen, with frame numbers, and Stage 5 confirmed;
- words the streamer said (the existing rule: half the main words and every number said, publish/describe.py:426-441);
- names from the source's metadata or the partner agreement.

A number such as a speed or a count needs on-screen text or speech; the model's estimate is not enough, since counting is approximate (gpick-8). No name ever comes from a face (gpick-8). No "you won't believe" framing unless the clip shows a real surprise. The hook text is 6 words or fewer, drawn from what is seen or said.

**10. Learning from results, and cost.**
- Log every signal and sub-score per post. Read a weekly table by hand (by source, event type and length), and change the weights by hand. Automatic learning runs into YouTube's derived-metrics rule (section A6: pick-14, pick-m1).
- Cost per stage (own estimate from gpick-7 and gpick-9; AI tokens only, at list price; no Batch discount; no thinking tokens, so thinking must be disabled or `between_tools` (gpick-m2); transcription, decoding and rendering not included):

| Work | Tokens in / out | Model | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| Stage 3, 60 candidates × (16 frames × 144 + ~1,600 text) | ~234k / ~7k | Haiku 5.5 | ~$0.027 |
| Stage 4, 20 candidates × (6 × 336 + ~500) + 2k prompt | ~52k / ~2.4k | Sonnet 5.5 | ~$0.13 |
| Stage 5, 10 titles × (4 × 336 + 300) | ~16k / ~1k | Haiku 5.5 | ~$0.002 |
| **One 6-hour stream** | | | **~$0.16 (≈$0.08 batch)** |
| Per source hour | | | ~$0.027 |
| Per posted clip (8 posts from 6 h) | | | ~$0.02 |
| 720 posts a month (one an hour) | | | ~$14 (≈$7 batch) |
| Optional full scan, 1 frame per 2 s, 448x252 | ~289k / ~4.5k per hour | Haiku 5.5 | ~$0.03/h; ~$0.25 for 8 h |
| Same full scan | | Sonnet 5.5 | ~$0.62/h; ~$5 for 8 h |
| Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, native video at low resolution | ~360k per hour | Gemini | ~$0.11/h (price from gpick-10, token rate approximate) |

- The full Haiku scan must be split into requests under 100K tokens to keep the low price (gpick-m1). The "8 good picks per 6-hour stream" is an unvalidated assumption.
- One hourly post needs about 24 picks a day, which means about 3 streams of 6 hours a day at 8 good picks each, or about 18 source hours of video to decode every day. On a t3.large, which earns credits at a 30% per-vCPU baseline and launches in Unlimited mode by default, sustained decoding above baseline is billed extra, so decoding, not AI tokens, is the binding cost of the picker, and we have no measurement of it. The owner should not read "$14 a month" as the cost of hourly posting. That is also a lot of source footage to get legally; the hosting strand should size it (section A12) (gpick-m9).

#### Risks and unknowns
- **No GTA 6 footage until 19 November 2026.** The interface, the death and arrest screens and how much of early play is story are all unknown. Build the pipeline on GTA V or other open-world footage that we have the right to use, and add GTA 6 templates in the first week after release (gpick-1, gpick-20).
- **Rights decide the signals.** Clip downloads need the broadcaster's or an editor's authorisation (gpick-3). Without permission, there is no official way to get the video or the chat replay. Live chat may be readable with a bot's own user token, but whether storing and reusing other channels' chat is allowed sits in the Developer Agreement, which did not load (gpick-5, gpick-m3). This is a bigger problem than picking quality (section A6: pick-m6). Unofficial chat downloaders and most-replayed scrapers are out of scope.
- **Picker quality is unproven.** The best results are from research models trained on labelled data, not zero-shot models (gpick-12, gpick-13; section A6: pick-6). The "video beats chat" result is a 2017 result for one genre (League of Legends tournaments, labels from one fan channel's reels), and the only clipper review names personality-driven content without scoreboard events as the weakest case (gpick-m4, gpick-19). Vendors give no independent accuracy numbers for open-world games (gpick-19). Cheap test: for 2 weeks, have a person mark each of the top 20 candidates as "post or skip" and measure how often the model agrees.
- **Still frames miss timing.** A joke or a near-miss lives in motion and sound. If Haiku-on-frames misjudges "funny" often, try Gemini's native video on candidate windows only, in static mode, as a measured side-by-side test on 50 candidates (gpick-10, gpick-m5).
- **Thinking tokens can inflate the bill.** Stage 4 output could be several times larger than estimated unless thinking is set as described (gpick-m2).
- **Decoding cost.** Pulling frames and audio from 6-8 hours of 1080p video on a 2-vCPU t3.large may take hours, and hourly posting needs about 18 source hours a day. We have no measurement. Time one 1-hour file on the laptop before planning hourly posting (gpick-m9).
- **Loudness and scene signals are untested on game footage.** Meeting-tuned loudness thresholds will be swamped by game audio, and scene detectors may fire on fast motion (gpick-18, gpick-16).
- **Licensed music.** Game radio or a streamer's music can bring Content ID claims. Twitch's muted-part list helps only with a user token (gpick-4). Flag suspected music (section A6's YAMNet Music class) and prefer clips without it. Removing music we have no right to use is allowed; changing it to slip past detection is not.
- **The Twitch Developer Agreement page did not load its text** for any checker, so we could not check its rules on storing and reusing Twitch content, clips, VODs and chat. Read it before building on Twitch.
- **Not confirmed:** Rockstar's own policy on posting videos of its games (its support page timed out twice), any last-minute GTA VI delay beyond the official page, Eklipse's own claims (site returned 403), that other chat-spike tools read unofficial logs, that no YouTube Data API call lists clips, and the absence of a PC version (page text truncated).
- **Unconfirmed:** the MINT paper's own numbers (we read only the publisher's blog post), ffmpeg's `scdet` filter (its documentation was not opened), and the exact thresholds above, which are all our guesses.
- The web search budget for this session ran out partway through. A search for 2024-2026 research on gaming highlight detection with multimodal models was not done.

### G6. The look of a gaming Short, and rendering it with ffmpeg

**The short answer.** Render GTA 6 Shorts with ffmpeg alone, in four fixed templates: (1) streamer face camera stacked above gameplay, (2) a square 1:1 gameplay crop under a top title bar, (3) full-width gameplay for wide or HUD-heavy shots, and (4) a 9:16 centre slice only for sharp 1440p or larger sources. Do not render at 60 frames a second by default: a news outlet reports that Rockstar targets 30 fps on PS5, PS5 Pro and Xbox Series X|S (other modes are not ruled out, so check real launch footage), so 60 fps output would mostly repeat frames and double the encode time. Upload 1080x1920, because YouTube says Shorts go up to 1080p. Skip any clip where licensed music (in-game radio) is detected. Removing that music on a CPU is slow, the best-known open tool (Demucs) is no longer actively developed, and it is built to split songs into parts, not to pull a song out of game sound and voice. A good look will not make reused clips earn money or keep them safe (see the rights sections), and YouTube's monetisation rules treat template-made, commentary-free clips as not monetisable whatever the visuals. Budget about 2-3.5 minutes per 30 fps Short on a 2-vCPU box with CPU credits, or well under a minute on the laptop (unverified). These are estimates, so measure them first.

#### What we found

##### The game and its footage
- Rockstar's Newswire has a post titled "Grand Theft Auto VI is Now Set to Launch November 19, 2026". The page body would not render, so we read only the title (glook-1).
- Notebookcheck (10 Nov 2026) reports that Rockstar confirmed a 30 fps target on PS5, PS5 Pro and Xbox Series X|S. A 60 fps mode is unconfirmed. PS5 Pro adds PSSR upscaling and ray-traced shadows. Launch is on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, and no PC version is mentioned. This is a news outlet's summary of Rockstar's post, which we could not open (glook-2).
- What this means for footage: at launch, GTA 6 gameplay clips are expected to come from a console running at 30 fps. This is a target, not a guarantee: Notebookcheck says Rockstar has not ruled out more graphics modes and mentions datamined 120 Hz references and talk of a 40 fps mode, so check real footage (glook-m7). A stream or video published at 60 fps would still carry 30 new game frames a second, and the in-between frames repeat (our inference from glook-2). A streamer's face camera can be a true 60 fps (our inference).
- Rockstar's Newswire also has a post titled "Announcing Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album, Coming November 19". Only the title rendered. Search summaries said the album is made with Atlantic Records, but we did not open a page that says so. So the game very likely has commercial licensed music in it. Which in-game radio songs are licensed, and whether they are in Content ID, is unknown (glook-21).
- Rockstar's video policy page timed out twice. Search summaries said it allows only non-commercial use, removes spoilers and cutscene compilations, and was last updated on 10 January 2025. We did not read it, so treat all of that as unverified. It matters for the rights sections, not for the look (glook-19) (unverified).
- We have not seen GTA 6's HUD, the on-screen game information such as the minimap, health and money. Where it sits on screen is unknown until launch, so templates must not hard-code HUD positions (no source; the game launches in 5 days).

##### YouTube's limits that shape the render
- YouTube's Shorts help page says Shorts can be uploaded "with a maximum resolution of 1080p" and can be up to 3 minutes long (glook-3).
- YouTube's upload page (read by section A7) recommends H.264 at the recorded frame rate: about 8 Mbps for 1080p at 24-30 fps and 12 Mbps at 48-60 fps, with AAC or Opus audio at 48 kHz (384 kbps stereo) (glook-22). These are recommended bitrates, not caps (glook-m6).
- Any Short over 1 minute with an active copyright claim of any type, including manual claims, is blocked worldwide (section A7, look-17). It cannot be played, recommended or monetised, and the block lifts once the claim is resolved. Shorts under 1 minute are not affected. Content ID is YouTube's automatic copyright matching. For gameplay, a claim is our judgement of a near certainty to plan around, not an edge case (glook-16, glook-m3).
- HDR uploads must be PQ or HLG with Rec. 2020 colour, at 10 or 12 bits. YouTube makes "an automatic SDR downconversion" for devices without HDR. HDR (high dynamic range) is the brighter, wider-colour format some consoles and capture cards record. The help page does not mention Shorts (glook-4).
- Safe zones. The Shorts player draws buttons on the right and the title and channel name at the bottom. A third party reads Google's ad safe-zone image as top 288 px, bottom 672 px, left 48 px and right 192 px on a 1080x1920 frame. This is not official (glook-8).
- Since 31 March 2025 a public Shorts view counts every start and every replay. Engaged views leave out loops, and YouTube has not said that loops help ranking (section 01, growth-2) (glook-15). YPP eligibility and Shorts ad revenue still use engaged views, so public view counts will overstate earning progress (glook-m2).
- YouTube's monetisation policy (updated July 2025) treats "inauthentic" content, meaning content that looks template-made or mass-produced and repetitive, as not monetisable. Its reused-content rules exclude edited clips with little or no narrative and short videos compiled from other sites. So rotating visual templates at hourly volume do nothing for eligibility: only real commentary or a new storyline does (glook-m1).

##### Turning 16:9 gameplay into 9:16: what each layout costs
All numbers are our own arithmetic for a 1920x1080 source shown 1080 px wide. "Upscale" above 1.0 means YouTube viewers see made-up pixels and soft HUD text (glook-7).

| Layout | Source window kept | Share of source width | Scale to 1080 wide | Height on screen |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Full width over blurred or branded bars | 1920x1080 | 100% | 0.56 (shrinks HUD text to 56%) | 608 px (32%) |
| 1:1 square crop with bars | 1080x1080 | 56% | 1.00 (pixel for pixel) | 1080 px (56%) |
| 4:5 crop with bars | 864x1080 | 45% | 1.25 | 1350 px (70%) |
| Gameplay part of a face-cam stack (1080x1280) | 911x1080 | 47% | 1.19 | 1280 px (67%) |
| 9:16 centre slice | 608x1080 | 32% | 1.78 | 1920 px (100%) |

- From a 2560x1440 source, the same windows scale by 0.75 of those factors. The 9:16 slice needs only 1.33x and the 1:1 and 4:5 crops are downscaled, so they stay sharp (glook-7).
- What a centre slice loses: anything in the outer 34% of each side. In most third-person games that is the minimap, the money and the mission text. Whether that holds for GTA 6's HUD is unknown (glook-7, layout point above).
- Face camera size: a streamer's face camera is often a small box. Our example, not a measurement: a 480x270 box shown 1080 wide is a 2.25x upscale, which looks soft. Source quality caps how good the stack can look (glook-7).
- Evidence on which layout holds viewers: we found none that is independent. The one vertical-clip vendor page we opened (StreamLadder) gives no retention data, only usage totals and one creator's word (glook-20). We ran out of web searches before checking more vendor and Twitch pages, so this is "not found", not "does not exist" (see Risks).

##### What the app's slice package already does
- `slice/layout.py` picks one layout per clip (screen, speaker, gallery or fit) from 2 fps gray frames 480 px wide, and falls back to fit when unsure. It has no face detection, no face-camera detection and no per-shot handling. Its speaker focus is the centroid of moving pixels, which for gameplay means the whole moving screen, not a subject (slice/layout.py:19-21, 280-282, 413-424) (glook-6).
- `build_short_graph_new` in `slice/ffmpeg_wrapper.py` already builds a blurred, darkened background (quarter size, box blur, `eq=brightness=-0.3:saturation=0.7`), a 4:5 panel 1350 px tall at y=285, a full-frame fit, a 9:16 full crop with a fixed x, burned-in ASS captions, gain plus a peak limiter, and short audio fades (slice/ffmpeg_wrapper.py:535-544, 577-581, 604-688) (glook-6).
- There is no stacked (vstack) layout. The crop x is a constant, not a function of time (slice/ffmpeg_wrapper.py:577-581, 635-662) (glook-6).
- The encode keeps the source frame rate (`-r` from the probe). The HD Shorts profile is libx264 medium, CRF 20, with a fixed `-maxrate 8M`, so it is not raised for 60 fps. Audio is AAC 128 kbps. The non-HD Shorts path uses the standard profile (veryfast, CRF 24, 2500k cap) (slice/profile.py:23-43, 64-68) (glook-6).
- `probe_media` records the colour tags but nothing converts HDR. A PQ or HLG source would be squeezed into 8-bit `yuv420p` and come out washed out (our inference from slice/profile.py:96-98, 178-181 and glook-4) (glook-6).
- The server image takes ffmpeg 9.0.1 from `mwader/static-ffmpeg` (Dockerfile:13, 48). The current README for that build lists libzimg (the `zscale` filter used for HDR-to-SDR conversion), libass, libx264, libx265, libsvtav1, libvmaf, freetype, harfbuzz, fribidi and rubberband. libplacebo is not listed. The README describes the current build, not 9.0.1 specifically, and does not name zscale itself (glook-5).

##### Sound
- The app already measures loudness once and applies one gain toward -14 LUFS, with a -1.5 dBFS peak limiter (section A7, look-5). LUFS is the standard loudness unit. This suits game audio: it does not pump, and the limiter catches gunshots and explosions (our judgement).
- A clip from another creator arrives as one mixed stereo track. The streamer's voice and the game sound cannot be rebalanced without source separation (our inference).
- Demucs is the best-known open separation tool. It is MIT-licensed, but the original facebookresearch repository was "archived by the owner on Jan 1, 2025". The author now keeps an "officially maintained" fork at github.com/adefossez/demucs (v4.1.0, dated 11/07/2026, read as 11 July 2026) but says he is "not actively working on Demucs anymore", so expect slow replies and no new features (glook-9, glook-m5).
- Its README says CPU processing takes "roughly equal to 1.5 times the duration of the track". The fine-tuned model takes 4 times longer, and two-stem mode is no faster (glook-9).
- Its outputs are music parts (drums, bass, vocals, other). A radio song's singer would land in the "vocals" part together with the streamer, and the instrumental would land in "other" with the car and gun sounds. It is not made to delete a song from a game mix (our inference from glook-9).
- inaSpeechSegmenter (MIT) labels audio as speech, music or noise, but it counts "speech over music" as speech. It would miss a radio song under a talking streamer, which is the common case (glook-10).
- PANNs (MIT) tags 527 AudioSet sound classes, including "Music", and some variants give a frame-by-frame timeline. The README gives no CPU speed (glook-11).
- YouTube Audio Library music and sound effects can be used in monetised videos and "won't be claimed". Creative Commons tracks need an artist credit in the description, and the standard licence needs none (glook-12).
- ffmpeg's `sidechaincompress` turns one sound down whenever a second one plays (ducking). Defaults: threshold 0.125, ratio 2, attack 20 ms, release 250 ms (glook-13).
- /brag ships CC0 sound effects. CC0 means free to use with no credit (section A8, hf-3).

##### Text and fonts
- Anton, a tall condensed display face suited to a top title bar, is under the SIL Open Font License 1.1. The licence allows it to be bundled and used in commercial work, and documents made with it are not bound by it. Each copy shipped with the software must keep the copyright notice and licence, so OFL.txt goes in the font folder (glook-14). Section A7 found that OFL text burned into a video needs no extra licence or credit, and that Montserrat is also OFL (look-20).

#### What this means for our build

**1. Four templates, chosen per clip by rules.** One fixed style at hourly volume reads as templated (section A8). Pick by content, not at random. Varying the templates is a look decision only: YouTube's policy on inauthentic and reused content treats clips with little or no narrative as not monetisable however they are framed, so it does nothing for eligibility (glook-m1):

- **T1 Stack** (the source has a face camera): face camera at y=0-640 (1080x640), gameplay at y=640-1920 (1080x1280). Captions sit on the seam, roughly y=560-720, one line, 2-4 words. The gameplay crop must leave out the face-camera box so the face does not show twice.
- **T2 Square** (default for gameplay with no face camera):
  - A top title bar at y=300-500: a solid brand-colour box with black Anton text, 64-72 px, at most 2 lines. A small 34-36 px credit line sits under it ("Gameplay: <creator> on YouTube").
  - A 1:1 gameplay crop, 1080x1080, at y=520-1600, so 1080p sources need no scaling. About a third of it (y=1248-1600) falls under the bottom overlay on the third-party margins (glook-m8).
  - Captions inside the panel, with the bottom edge at or above y=1240.
  - Below y=1600, the blurred background. That area sits under YouTube's title and channel text anyway.
- **T3 Full** (wide driving, scenery or HUD-dependent moments): the same top bar, full-width gameplay at y=540-1148, and one caption line at y=1160-1240. This is the only template that keeps the whole HUD, but the HUD shrinks to 56%.
- **T4 Slice** (only when the source is 1440p or larger and the action is centred): full-bleed 9:16 with a top text box. On 1080p sources the 1.78x upscale is too soft (glook-7).
- Bars: offer two background styles: the app's existing blurred copy, and a flat or gradient brand colour (cheaper, more "branded"). A/B them. Keep everything else fixed while testing.
- Panning that follows the action: not in version 1. GTA's third-person camera mostly keeps the player near the centre (our observation of the genre, not checked for GTA 6). The app's moving-pixel centroid is useless here because the whole picture moves when the camera turns. Use a fixed crop per shot, cut on shot changes, as section A7 plans. A later version can try a smoothed time-based crop `x(t)` (A7, look-9).
- Stay inside the safe band: no text above y=288, below y=1248 or right of x=888 (glook-8). Check it once on a phone (see Risks).

**2. Finding the face-camera box automatically.** Run this once per source channel, then reuse the box while checking it on each clip:

1. Sample gray frames with the existing `sample_frames` (2 fps, 480 px).
2. Run YuNet face detection on them (section A7, look-12). A face camera shows as a face in the same small region in more than about 60% of samples. In-game faces move and come and go. The 60% figure is our guess, to be tuned.
3. Find the box edges around that face with the long-edge finder already in `layout.py` (`_vertical_edges` and `_horizontal_edges` on the mean frame, limited to the area around the face). If the edges are unclear, grow the face box by fixed factors and clamp it to the frame.
4. Store the box per source channel with a thumbnail. The owner approves each new channel's box once in the web panel. If a later clip's face is outside the stored box, fall back to T2.
5. Treat other stream overlays the same way (chat boxes, follower alerts, donation pop-ups). They should stay outside the gameplay crop where possible, because they show other people's usernames.

**3. Frame rate, resolution, bitrate.**
- Default output is 30 fps for GTA 6 console footage (glook-2), confirmed against real launch footage first, since other modes are not ruled out (glook-m7). A 60 fps option applies only when the source has 60 real fps (later PC footage, or a stack where a smooth face camera matters).
- Detecting real 30 fps inside a 60 fps file (how many neighbouring frames are the same) is a cheap check on the sample. We did not verify a specific ffmpeg filter for it this session.
- 1080x1920 H.264 High, `yuv420p`, CRF 18-19 (gameplay has more motion than talk), `-maxrate 8M -bufsize 16M` at 30 fps and `12M/24M` at 60 fps (glook-22). YouTube's 8 and 12 Mbps are recommended bitrates, not caps, so this ceiling is our own choice and may starve fast driving scenes. Benchmark it (glook-m6). Write BT.709 tags. No 1440x2560 uploads (glook-3).
- AAC-LC, 48 kHz stereo, 256-384 kbps (glook-22). Today's 128 kbps profile is too thin for explosions and music-free game mixes.
- HDR: at download, prefer YouTube's SDR version of a source, since YouTube makes one for every HDR upload (glook-4). If a file still probes as PQ or HLG, convert it with `zscale` plus `tonemap`. zscale should be in our ffmpeg build (glook-5; the README describes the current build and names libzimg, not the filter, so run `ffmpeg -filters | grep zscale` in the pinned 9.0.1 image first), but we could not open ffmpeg's tonemap documentation this session, so test the exact chain on a sample. Otherwise skip the clip.

**4. Sound.**
- Keep the measure-once gain to -14 LUFS with a limiter (A7, look-5). No noise reduction on game audio.
- Music gate (required): run PANNs on each candidate clip's audio. Reject the clip if "Music" scores above a tuned threshold for more than a few seconds (glook-11). inaSpeechSegmenter is not good enough on its own, because it misses music under speech (glook-10).
- Do not use Demucs to remove radio music in version 1 (glook-9). Muting the music segment also mutes the streamer, so skipping the clip is cheaper and cleaner. Removing music we have no right to use is allowed in principle; the issue is cost and quality, not principle. The maintained fork does not change this.
- No music beds or whooshes on gameplay with voice. If a voiceless montage needs a bed, use only YouTube Audio Library tracks marked "Attribution not required", ducked under the game sound with `sidechaincompress` (glook-12, glook-13). Log every track used per video.

**5. Text.**
- The top title bar is one ASS style with an opaque box. The repo's captions are ASS already. We did not re-check the ASS box style syntax this session; `drawbox` is the fallback.
- Word-by-word captions only when someone is speaking. Get word times from WhisperX alignment, as A7 plans. Gameplay with no speech gets no captions, only the title bar.
- Ship two fonts in the new system's own folder: Anton for the bar and Montserrat ExtraBold for captions, each with its OFL.txt. Both are OFL (glook-14). Never take fonts from `public/fonts/`.

**6. Credit and ending.**
- Burn in a credit for the whole clip (T2/T3 under the title bar, T1 at the seam corner). Put the full source link in the description. Credit is courtesy, not a licence (A7, look-18).
- No end card. End on an action beat, and cap the total at 59 s (glook-16). We will not engineer seamless loops, because replays inflate public views but not engaged views, which are what YPP and Shorts earnings use (glook-15, glook-m2).

**7. Render design and timings.** Use one analysis step and one ffmpeg command per Short, extending the A7 design:

1. **Analysis.** `sample_frames` → shot cuts, face camera (YuNet), HUD-heavy check (later) → template plus crop boxes per shot. In parallel, PANNs on 32 kHz mono audio for the music gate. Save the result as JSON so a re-render never re-analyses it.
2. **One ffmpeg command:**
   - `-ss/-t` input → `split`.
   - T1: `crop` face box → `scale=1080:640`, and `crop` gameplay → `scale=1080:1280:flags=lanczos` → `vstack`.
   - T2-T4: background (quarter-size blur, or a `color` source for brand bars) plus foreground crop/scale → `overlay`.
   - Then `subtitles=clip.ass:fontsdir=…`, then `format=yuv420p` → libx264. Audio: trim, gain, limiter, fades.
   - Static brand art, such as a bar texture or logo, goes in as one PNG with `overlay`, which costs almost nothing.
3. **Checks.** The app's existing frame-count, duration and loudness probes.

Expected time per 45-second Short (estimates, not measured):

| Machine | 30 fps (1,350 frames) | 60 fps (2,700 frames) |
|---|---|---|
| t3.large-class box (2 vCPU = 1 core, 2 threads), CPU credits available (unverified) | 1.7-3.4 min | 3.4-6.8 min |
| Same box in Standard credit mode with credits used up (about 3.3x slower; in Unlimited mode, the T3 default, it keeps full speed and bills extra per vCPU-hour instead) (unverified) | 6-11 min | 11-22 min |
| Owner's laptop (6-core Ryzen AI 5 340) | about 20-60 s (guess) | about 40-120 s (guess) |

- Analysis and alignment add about 10-50 s, and the PANNs pass is unmeasured (glook-17, glook-18). The model behind these times counts two threads as two cores and leaves out 1440p/2160p decode and 50-60 fps sources, so real times are likely longer than the low end (glook-17).
- At 24 Shorts a day, 30 fps output uses about 40-80 minutes of a 2-vCPU box a day, and 60 fps about 1.4-2.7 hours. Either fits inside one small separate machine, never the production server. A t3.large earns 864 credits a day, and 24 Shorts at 30 fps use roughly 82-163, so rendering alone would not exhaust them, but WhisperX and PANNs add to that. If the box runs in Unlimited mode (the T3 default), price the extra CPU surcharge rather than a slowdown. We do not know which mode production uses (glook-18, glook-m4).
- If the 2-vCPU box is too slow, try x264 `-preset faster` before buying hardware. It is quicker, but it needs more bits for the same quality, and the 8M cap may then bite on fast driving scenes. This is untested.

**8. Where browser-rendered overlays help.** Use Hyperframes only to pre-render a few animated pieces once: a 1-second title-bar slide-in, a channel sting, a lower-third credit. Export them with transparency (WebM VP9 alpha or ProRes 4444) and overlay them with ffmpeg. Per-Short browser renders cost 1.5-3 minutes each on the laptop and add no proven value (section A8, hf-9 and its cost table). ASS already covers word-by-word captions.

**9. Build boundary.** Everything above goes in new modules on the clp branch, for example `clip/look.py` and `clip/render.py`, copying the small helpers from `slice/ffmpeg_wrapper.py` (`_even_box`, `SHORT_BG_BLUR`, `subtitles_filter`). Production's `slice/` stays untouched. New dependencies (opencv-python-headless for YuNet, a PANNs runtime with torch) live only in the clip system's own environment.

#### Risks and unknowns
- **Not confirmed:** Rockstar's video policy text and the in-game music licensing (glook-19, glook-21). Neither page body could be read.
- **Looks do not fix rights.** A well-framed clip of another creator's GTA footage is still reused content, can be claimed by the creator, Take-Two or a music label, and may break Rockstar's non-commercial terms (glook-19, unverified). This section only says how to make clips look right if the rights question is settled.
- **Monetisation is a separate wall.** Templated or commentary-free clips are not monetisable under YouTube's policy, however good they look (glook-m1).
- **The GTA 6 HUD and frame rate are unconfirmed for us.** The 30 fps target comes from a news outlet's summary (glook-2), and other modes are not ruled out (glook-m7). The HUD layout is unseen. Cheap check: on launch day, read Rockstar's post in a normal browser and look at 5 real gameplay videos (frame rate in the player's "Stats for nerds", HUD positions) before freezing the templates.
- **No evidence on which layout holds viewers** (glook-20). The web search limit for this run was reached before Twitch's own clip-editor pages and more vendor studies could be checked. Plan an A/B of T1/T2/T3 with "Stayed to watch" as the measure, as earlier sections propose.
- **Render times are estimates** (glook-17, unverified). Cheapest check: on the laptop, with a static ffmpeg the owner chooses to install, render one 45-second Short per template at 30 and 60 fps with preset medium and faster. That is 8 renders, about 10 minutes of work.
- **Music detection thresholds are unknown.** PANNs' CPU speed and false-alarm rate on game audio are unmeasured (glook-11). Car engines and game score may read as music. Test on 30 hand-labelled clips first.
- **Copyright claims may still hit game audio itself**, or music we failed to detect. The 59 s cap avoids the worldwide block but not the claim itself, and a manual claim by a source creator would also block a 61-180 s clip (glook-16, glook-m3).
- **Face-camera detection** will fail on cartoon avatars (VTubers), cameras with green-screen cutouts and no box, and layouts that change mid-stream. The fallback is T2, and the owner approves boxes per channel.
- **Safe-zone clash in T2.** On the third-party margins, the 1080x1080 gameplay square (y=520-1600) runs below the y=1248 line, so about 352 px (33%) of the picture sits under YouTube's title and channel overlay, and the right 192 px button column covers gameplay in every template (glook-m8).
- **Safe-zone margins are third-party** (glook-8). Check with one private test upload with coloured guide bands, viewed on Android and iPhone.
- **Checker wording difference on Demucs:** one checker called "archived and unmaintained" true only of the old repo, the other called it slightly overstated because of the fork. We used the more cautious wording (glook-9).
- **Not verified this session:** ffmpeg's `tonemap` and `scdet` documentation (the page text was cut off before those sections), whether the pinned 9.0.1 image exposes `zscale`, the ASS opaque-box style, Rockstar's video policy text, Twitch and Kick clip-editor layouts, any frame-repeat detection filter, whether production's t3 box runs in Standard or Unlimited mode, and the laptop CPU model.
