### G7. Titles, hashtags and channel identity for a GTA 6 channel

**The short answer.** The game comes out on 19 November 2026, five days from today, on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, so any gameplay footage dated before then is pre-release footage that Rockstar's reported policy removes, and we must never use it (gpack-1, gpack-4). Titles can and should use the game's own official words: "GTA 6" or "GTA VI", Jason, Lucia, Leonida, Vice City, and named vehicles. Every title must describe what the clip really shows, and must not name story events, because Rockstar removes ending clips, cutscene compilations and other big story reveals (gpack-2, gpack-4). Violence is the main money risk in packaging, not words: graphic game violence in the thumbnail or the first 7 seconds earns no ads, and a clip that is only the most violent moment can be age-restricted (gpack-6, gpack-7). The channel must look like a fan channel and must not look like Rockstar: no Rockstar logo, no "Official", no copied Rockstar art or colours, and "fan" in the name or handle (gpack-10). Set every upload to "not made for kids" and Gaming category, keep titles in English at first, and do not expect the money to come from Shorts: from 1 Feb 2027 YouTube's page says a channel needs 10 million qualified Shorts views in 90 days (re-checked every month) to share in Shorts ad revenue and the YouTube Premium share, and reuploads of other creators' videos never count (gpack-15, gpack-16, gpack-m3). Packaging cannot make the owner's route (other creators' clips, edited and credited) eligible for money, and Take-Two's terms say it owns recorded gameplay clips, so crediting the source creator gives us no rights (gpack-12, gpack-m1).

#### What we found

This builds on section A10 (`section A10`), which covers the general rules for titles, descriptions, hashtags, tags, channel images, handles, verification and quota. Its finding ids (pack-N) are cited where we rely on them and are not repeated here. Everything below is what changes for a GTA 6 gaming channel.

##### The game's own words (the vocabulary a program can use)

- Rockstar's game page says Grand Theft Auto VI is "Coming November 19, 2026" on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S. It names the two lead characters, Jason and Lucia, the state of Leonida and Vice City. Its newest posts are dated 3, 5 and 10 November 2026; pre-load started on 10 November (gpack-1).
- Rockstar's downloads page gives the full names Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, the vehicles "'95 Grotti Cheetah" and "'55 Vapid Stanier", and "Hawk & Little Morgan Revolvers". It shows the ESRB rating (the US age rating board) as Mature, with the descriptors blood and gore, intense violence, mature humor, nudity, strong language, strong sexual content, and use of drugs and alcohol, plus in-game purchases. "Mature" appears only as the rating badge image, not as text (gpack-2).
- A news site lists six regions of Leonida credited to Rockstar: Vice City, Leonida Keys, Grass Rivers, Port Gellhorn, Ambrosia and Mount Kalaga. We did not see these six on a Rockstar page in this session, so they are second-hand (gpack-3).
- We found no official list of missions. After launch, mission names will exist in the game, but naming a story mission can itself spoil the plot (our inference, see spoilers below).
- **Search words without scraping.** A10 already covers the allowed tools: the Studio Trends and Research tabs (only useful once we have viewers), Google Ads Keyword Planner, the Analytics API's top search terms per video, and Search Console. The Google Trends API is an alpha for few testers (pack-16, pack-17, pack-18). YouTube's Terms forbid automated access, so scraping autocomplete or other channels is out (A10, channel_features-15). We did not open Google Trends pages for GTA 6, so we have no search-volume numbers. Whether people type "GTA 6" more than "GTA VI" is unknown to us; using both is our inference.

##### Rockstar's rules on footage, spoilers and money

- Rockstar's official page "Policy on posting copyrighted Rockstar Games material" timed out three times in this session. We could not read it. What follows comes from news reports of it (gpack-4, gpack-5).
- A news article dated 4 Nov 2026 (updated 8 Nov 2026) reports that the policy removes endings, edited cutscene compilations and isolated cinematics. Cutscenes inside a longer playthrough are fine. It bans "pre-release leaked footage of any kind", "regardless of how the game was obtained". It frames the permission to upload around non-commercial use. It says the policy was last updated in January 2025 and covers all Rockstar games (gpack-4).
- A 2013 Game Informer report of the GTA V version of the policy says the permission covered "non-commercial" use, spoilers would be removed, and the policy "can be changed at any time" (gpack-5).
- Take-Two's own terms of service (last updated 28 Feb 2025) govern "our games, apps, products, websites, and other services", so they cover the games themselves, not only websites. They list its "trademarks, logos, trade names, trade dress" as reserved, limit use to "personal, non-commercial" use, and bar commercially exploiting the services without separate written permission. Section 5.3 defines "Custom Content" to expressly include "recordings of in-game audio, gameplay clips, and livestreams", usable "only with the Services and/or only as authorized by us", and section 5.4 says Take-Two "reserves all rights to and ownership of all Custom Content". The terms do not name YouTube or Rockstar's video policy; section 6.3(11) points to separate per-game Community Standards. Whether this makes a monetised clip channel a breach is a legal question (gpack-12, gpack-m1).
- The same news report also lists as removed: in-game TV shows or comedy performances shown in isolation, and footage that encourages cheating or promotes mods and ports. It says narrated Let's Play videos are allowed, and it tells creators planning monetised launch-week content in the UAE, Saudi Arabia or Egypt to read Rockstar's original policy first, which points to region-specific caveats we have not read (gpack-m4, gpack-m9).
- Whether a monetised fan channel of *our own* gameplay is "non-commercial" under Rockstar's policy is a question for the rules strand. For packaging, the point is narrower: spoiler titles and isolated cutscene clips are exactly what the policy names for removal (gpack-4).

##### Violence, age limits and ads (titles, thumbnails, first seconds)

- YouTube's advertiser-friendly guidelines say "Violence in unedited video gameplay is generally acceptable for advertising", including violence after the first 7 seconds (gpack-6).
- Graphic game violence in the thumbnail limits ads. Graphic game violence "in the thumbnail or in the first seven seconds of the video" earns no ads. "Graphic game violence" includes "brutal killings or severe injuries focusing on bodily fluids and parts" (gpack-6).
- Profanity: "hell" or "damn", or bleeped or abbreviated swearing, in a title or thumbnail keeps full ads. Moderate profanity (like "shit") in the title or thumbnail limits ads. Stronger profanity (like "f*ck") in thumbnails or titles earns no ads. The rules cover thumbnail, title, description and tags (gpack-6).
- YouTube's age-restriction page lists "A video focused on violent or gory imagery, such as focusing solely on the most graphically violent part of a film or video game", and "heavy profanity in the title, thumbnail or associated metadata". Age-restricted videos cannot be watched by viewers under 18 or signed out, and "may have limited or no ads monetization" (gpack-7).
- YouTube's thumbnail policy bans "Violent imagery that intends to shock or disgust", "Graphic or disturbing imagery with blood or gore", sexual imagery, and a thumbnail "that misleads viewers to think they're about to view something that's not in the video". A thumbnail that is not suitable for all ages but breaks no rule may get the video age-restricted or the thumbnail removed with no strike; a violating one is removed and may bring a strike (gpack-8).
- The same guidelines say violence in unedited gameplay is acceptable but "montages where gratuitous violence is the focal point" are not, and list "a video compilation of such graphic scenes" as limited ads. Under no ads they list gameplay "manufactured to create a shocking experience", for example aggregating non-playable characters for mass killings, and gameplay showing graphic violence directed at minors or at real named persons (gpack-m8).
- Strikes: "If you get three strikes in 90 days or your channel is dedicated to violative content, your channel may be terminated." The first violation is usually a warning that can expire after 90 days with policy training (gpack-m5).
- GTA 6 is rated Mature for blood and gore, intense violence, nudity and strong sexual content (gpack-2). So the risk is built in: a program that picks "the most exciting moment" will often pick the most violent one, which is the exact pattern YouTube names for age restriction (gpack-7, our inference).

##### Made for kids

- YouTube's made-for-kids page lists the factors: subject, intended and actual audience, child actors, characters or toys that appeal to children, language meant for children, and so on. Content with "sexual themes, violence, obscene, or other mature themes not suitable for young audiences" is likely not made for kids, and it lists "A gaming video that features adult humor" as general audience (gpack-9).
- The page does not list the features lost by a made-for-kids video in the text we read. It says such videos are "more likely to be recommended alongside other kids' videos" (gpack-9).
- The app already sends `selfDeclaredMadeForKids: False` on every upload (`publish/youtube.py` line 433) (gpack-17).

##### Game title, category, hashtags and tags

- The YouTube Data API `videos` resource has no field for a game title. `topicDetails.relevantTopicIds` is marked deprecated as of 10 November 2016 and `topicDetails.topicIds` is deprecated and no longer returned; the gaming topic list on the page is labelled as of February 2017. `topicDetails.topicCategories` (Wikipedia URLs) exists, and the page does not say it is writable. None of these is a way to tag the game. `categoryId` is settable and is required when updating the snippet (gpack-13).
- YouTube's "Edit video settings" help page says nothing about game titles or linking a video to a game. It says only that the category helps "viewers find your video more easily" (gpack-14). We could not find, in this session, the help page on how YouTube links a video to a game; how and whether the game gets attached to our uploads is unknown.
- Hashtags: A10's rules hold. Up to 3 show by the title; they must relate directly to the video; misleading or unrelated hashtags can get a video removed; #Shorts is not needed (pack-10, pack-m5, shorts_views-12). For this channel, relevant ones are the game's name and the place or character the clip shows (our inference from those rules).
- Tags: minimal role, mainly for misspellings, 500-character cap (pack-11, pack-12). For GTA 6 the spelling variants ("GTA 6", "GTA VI", "Grand Theft Auto 6", "Grand Theft Auto VI") are exactly the misspelling-type case tags are for (our inference).
- The app hard-codes the hashtag `#FloLabs` (`publish/describe.py` line 332) and adds it first to every hashtag line (line 576). The clip build must not reuse that function unchanged (gpack-17). More FloLabs branding is hard-coded: `ORG_LINE` (describe.py:316), "FloLabs <Series>" title suffixes (describe.py:378, :385), playlists.py:30, the caption track name "English (FloLabs)" (caption_track.py:22) and the playlist templates (settings.py:133-135). The clip build must replace all of them (gpack-m7).

##### Channel name, handle, icon and banner

- YouTube's impersonation policy covers "individuals, channels or entities". It bans "Real" or "Official" in the name, names "phonetically identical or visually similar to an established entity", and copying an entity's "profile pictures, banners, or specific color schemes". A fan channel must "state so explicitly in your channel name or handle", and "It should be obvious to your viewers that your channel doesn't represent the original creator, artist, or entity". The page adds that "YouTube also enforces trademark holder rights" (gpack-10).
- YouTube's trademark policy bans use of a trademark "likely to cause confusion". Videos can be blocked and the channel "may also be suspended". YouTube forwards each complaint to the uploader and does not mediate (gpack-11).
- Rockstar's downloads page offers artwork, logos and wallpapers but shows no licence terms for them; its only usage line is "Download and share trailers, imagery, and more", which is an invitation to share, not permission to use the art as channel branding (gpack-2, gpack-m6). We found no permission to use them on a channel icon or banner, and YouTube's impersonation policy separately bars copying an entity's profile pictures, banners or colour schemes (gpack-10).
- A10 covers image sizes, handle rules, and the ban on `<Creator> Shorts` style names (pack-5, pack-6, pack-7, pack-m1).

##### Credit for the source creator

- A10 covers the credit block and its limits: credit gives no rights, Shorts description links are not clickable, and pinned comments cannot be set by API (pack-2, pack-9, channel_features-9). Nothing GTA-specific changes that.
- For gaming, the clip often has no speech, so a spoken credit or a transcript match is not available (our inference). On-screen credit has to come from the source's metadata.

##### Languages, markets and money per view

- Shorts ad revenue is pooled and split per country, "based on their share of total engaged views from monetizing creators' Shorts in each country". Creators keep 45% of their share. So money per view depends on where viewers are (gpack-15).
- "Non-original Shorts, such as unedited clips from others' movies or TV shows, reuploading other creators' content from YouTube or other platform, or compilations with no original content added" do not earn from the pool (gpack-15).
- The same page says that from 1 Feb 2027 a channel needs "at least 10 million qualified Shorts views in the last 90 days" to earn a share of Shorts ad revenue from the Creator Pool and YouTube Premium revenue for each month. Views are measured over the 90 days ending on the 15th of the month before the month being paid, so it is re-checked monthly. That is about 111,000 qualified views a day; at 24 Shorts a day, about 4,600 per Short on average, every day for 90 days (gpack-16).
- Shorts revenue needs Partner Program membership and acceptance of the Shorts Monetization Module; "Shorts views accrued prior to accepting the Shorts Monetization Module are not eligible", so the first weeks or months of a new channel earn nothing (gpack-m3).
- "Shorts over one minute in length that contain claimed content are blocked and not eligible for monetization." A clip channel whose Shorts may carry Content ID claims (other creators' streams, in-game radio music) should keep Shorts at 60 seconds or less, or accept that claimed long Shorts are blocked (gpack-m2).
- We found no source, in this session, for ad rates by country for gaming, and none on Urdu or Hindi gaming channels. We don't know how much less a view from Pakistan or India earns than one from the US.
- Earlier local research chose Hindi as one of six translation languages by YouTube audience size; Urdu was not on that list (gpack-18). A10 says auto-dubbing skips videos with copyrighted content and recommends turning it off (pack-4).

##### Posting times

- Nothing GTA-specific was found. A10's finding stands: posting hour is a minor lever, and one vendor study (Buffer, 24 Jul 2026, engagement not views) found Shorts did best on Friday 4 p.m. and evenings 6-11 p.m. in the viewer's local time (pack-19, algorithm-8, shorts_views-1).

##### Real title examples

- We did not collect real titles from top GTA channels. Our web-search budget ran out early in this strand, and reading YouTube pages by program is against YouTube's Terms (channel_features-15). Any title pattern below is our design, not an observed pattern.

#### What this means for our build

**1. A date gate before anything else.** Reject any source published before 18 Nov 2026 10:00 UTC (midnight on 19 Nov in the earliest time zone, UTC+14). We do not know Rockstar's exact unlock time, so a person can move this floor once launch-day reports are in. Rockstar removes leaked footage "regardless of how the game was obtained" (gpack-1, gpack-4). Official trailers are Rockstar's own copyrighted videos; do not clip them either (pack-2).

**2. A spoiler rule set.** Rockstar removes endings, cutscene compilations and isolated cinematics (gpack-4). So:
- Also reject isolated in-game TV and comedy segments and any mod or cheat footage (gpack-m4). Reject source clips that are another creator's recording only if we add original content; the source creator may not own the footage (gpack-m1).
- Do not cut a clip that is mostly a cutscene. If the picker can tell gameplay from cinematics (for example by on-screen HUD presence), mark cutscene-heavy clips as rejected.
- Titles, thumbnails and descriptions must not name a death, betrayal, ending, final mission or "the twist". Keep a banned-word list (ending, final mission, dies, death of, betrays, twist, secret ending, post-credits) and send any title that hits it to review, not to upload.
- Keep a 30-day "story-quiet" window after launch: no title may name a story mission. This number is our choice, not a rule; Rockstar names no window.

**3. A vocabulary file, not live scraping.** Keep `gta6_vocab.json` with fields: `game_names` ("GTA 6", "GTA VI", "Grand Theft Auto VI"), `characters` (Jason, Lucia, Jason Duval, Lucia Caminos), `places` (Leonida, Vice City; the six regions marked "second-hand" until seen on a Rockstar page), `vehicles` ("Grotti Cheetah", "Vapid Stanier"), `weapons`, `activities` (filled by a person after launch). Every word has a source URL and date (gpack-1, gpack-2, gpack-3). A person reviews it weekly with the Studio Trends tab once we have viewers (pack-16).

**4. Title rules (`gta_title()`):**
1. Start with the game name: "GTA 6" for Shorts (short), "GTA 6" or "GTA VI" for long clips. Then one concrete subject from the vocabulary file or the clip (place, vehicle, activity). Then the hook.
2. Lengths: Shorts 25-50 characters, never over 60; long clips 40-70, with the game name and subject in the first 45 (A10 rules, pack-20, pack-21). These bands are vendor-based style choices.
3. Grounding: the current `_grounded()` returns True when the clip has no text (`publish/describe.py` lines 431-432), and gameplay clips often have little speech (gpack-17). The clip build needs its own check: every named place, vehicle or character in the title must appear in the source title, source description, the source's captions, or an on-screen-text read of the clip. If none can confirm it, drop the name.
4. No caps-lock words beyond the game name, at most one emoji, no "you won't believe", no "insane"/"broken" unless the clip shows it. Misleading titles and thumbnails break the spam and thumbnail policies (pack-1, gpack-8).
5. Profanity: a filter that blocks strong swearing in titles, thumbnails, descriptions and tags, and bleeps or masks moderate swearing. Strong swearing there means no ads (gpack-6, gpack-7).
6. Never "Official", never "Rockstar" as if we speak for it, never "leak", never "early access" (gpack-4, gpack-10).
7. Variety: at least four title shapes, rotated, and refuse a title too close to any of the last 50 (A10, pack-m11). Example shapes (ours): `GTA 6: <subject> <what happens>`; `<What happens> in GTA 6's <place>`; `GTA 6 <vehicle> <test or result>`; `How <activity> works in GTA 6` (long clips only).

**5. Hashtags and tags (`gta_tags()`):**
- Hashtags: at most 3, on the description's last line: `#GTA6` always, then one of the place or character in the clip if the grounding check in title rule 3 confirmed it (pack-10). No `#FloLabs`, no `#Shorts`, no trending tags that do not match the clip (pack-m5).
- Tags: 6-10, within 500 characters: the four game-name spellings, the subject, the source creator's channel name only if credited (pack-11, pack-12).
- `categoryId`: Gaming, looked up once with `videoCategories.list` and stored in config (pack-11). Do not hard-code a number we have not looked up.
- Game title: not settable by API; do not rely on deprecated topic fields (gpack-13). After the first 5 uploads, a person checks in Studio whether YouTube attached "Grand Theft Auto VI"; if Studio offers a game-title field, the owner sets it by hand for a sample and we compare.

**6. Thumbnails and the first 7 seconds (`gta_thumb_ok()`, long clips only):**
- Pick frames from the moment the title is about, sharp and centred (packaging-7). Reject frames with blood, gore, nudity, or a body as the subject. Prefer vehicles, places, characters' faces or the HUD action (gpack-6, gpack-8, our design).
- Add 2-4 words of text, no swearing, matching the title (packaging-6, gpack-6).
- No Rockstar logo, no official key art, no "GTA VI" logo lettering copied from Rockstar, no Rockstar colour scheme (gpack-10).
- For Shorts, do not set custom thumbnails at first (A10).
- Run the same violence check on the first 7 seconds of each clip; if the clip opens on a graphic kill, move the start point or reject it (gpack-6).
- Score each clip for "focus on violence" and reject clips where most of the run time is killing or injury (gpack-7). Also score against the montage and shocking-gameplay rules: avoid compilations of violent scenes and mass-killing rampages (gpack-m8).
- Stop-on-first-warning: if YouTube issues any Community Guidelines warning or strike, the autopilot pauses uploads until a person reviews, because at one upload an hour a systematic error could reach three strikes in 90 days quickly (gpack-m5, gpack-8).

**7. Upload settings for every clip:** `selfDeclaredMadeForKids=false` (keep the current behaviour, gpack-9, gpack-17); `containsSyntheticMedia=false`; `defaultLanguage=en`; `defaultAudioLanguage` = the source's spoken language, or leave unset when there is no speech; auto-dubbing off (pack-4). Read back the age-restriction status after processing and log it; if a clip is age-restricted, stop and send that clip shape to review (gpack-7).

**8. Channel identity (owner sets in Studio):**
- Name pattern: `<Our word> + GTA 6 + Fan` style, for example "Leonida Fan Clips" or "Vice Fan Desk". Avoid "Rockstar", "Official", "Real", "GTA 6 News" (sounds like an outlet), or any creator's name plus a format word (gpack-10, pack-m1). Put "fan" in the name or the handle, as YouTube's policy asks of fan channels (gpack-10).
- Handle: 3-30 characters, include "fan" if the name does not (pack-6, gpack-10).
- Icon and banner: original art made by us (a simple wordmark and a palm or sunset motif in our own colours). No Rockstar logo, key art, screenshots of official art, or the "VI" logotype (gpack-2, gpack-10, gpack-11).
- Channel description line: "Unofficial fan channel. Not affiliated with or endorsed by Rockstar Games or Take-Two." plus a removal-request contact (gpack-10, gpack-11). This line lowers confusion; it gives no rights (pack-2).

**9. Credit:** Keep A10's credit block. For gaming, also burn an on-screen credit for the first 3 seconds: "Gameplay: <channel name> on YouTube", taken from the source metadata, never from guessing (pack-2, our design). The pinned comment stays a manual Studio step (channel_features-9).

**10. Language:** English titles and descriptions only for the first 8 weeks. Do not add Urdu or Hindi titles until Analytics shows where viewers are. A Hindi or Urdu *commentary* channel is a separate product (our own voice over gameplay), and would be original content, which matters more for money than the language does (gpack-15). We have no data on ad rates by country.

**11. Posting times:** Store times in UTC. Until Analytics has 28 days of data, follow A10: Shorts weighted to US and UK evenings, and keep the queue spread across the day (pack-19). The hourly plan is a volume decision for other strands.

#### Risks and unknowns

- **We could not read Rockstar's policy page.** It timed out three times. The spoiler, cutscene, leak and non-commercial points come from news reports (gpack-4, gpack-5). Cheap check: the owner opens it in a browser and saves a PDF before launch day.
- **The 10 million Shorts views rule.** Both checkers read the full passage: from 1 Feb 2027 it gates the Creator Pool and the YouTube Premium share, re-checked monthly (gpack-16). A new clip channel will not earn from Shorts in 2027 unless it is very large.
- **Clips of other creators' Shorts do not earn from the pool** under the non-original rule (gpack-15). Packaging cannot fix this.
- **Game title attachment is unknown.** No API field exists (gpack-13); we did not find the help page. Check by hand on the first uploads.
- **The six region names are second-hand** (gpack-3). Check them against Rockstar's site before putting them in the vocabulary as confirmed.
- **No real title examples.** The title shapes are our design. Cheap check: a person reads 50 titles from 5 large GTA channels in a browser after launch and records length, first words, emoji and caps.
- **Search volumes unknown.** We have no figures for "GTA 6" against "GTA VI" or place names. Cheap check: the owner looks at Google Trends in a browser once after launch.
- **Violence detection is hard.** A vision model check per clip adds cost; a cheaper first pass is to sample 3 frames and ask the existing LLM. False negatives mean limited ads or age restriction (gpack-6, gpack-7).
- **Trademark complaints.** Rockstar or Take-Two can complain about the name or the art; YouTube may block videos or suspend the channel (gpack-11).
- **Take-Two's terms** reach gameplay clips and livestreams as "Custom Content" that Take-Two says it owns, and bar commercial exploitation without written permission. Whether that makes a monetised clip channel a breach is a legal question for the rules strand; it weakens the "edit and credit" route (gpack-12, gpack-m1).
- **Region caveats** in Rockstar's original policy (UAE, Saudi Arabia, Egypt) are unread (gpack-m9).
- **Not checked:** how age restriction affects Shorts feed distribution; whether the YouTube help text on game titles exists; the A10 (pack-N) findings.
- **No page we opened contained instructions aimed at AI readers.**

### G8. Getting footage from streams and from our own recordings

**The short answer.** Twitch gives us good free signals about other creators' GTA 6 moments: its API lists clips by game, ranked by views, with the time of each clip inside the stream (gingest-1, gingest-2). But Twitch's official clip-download tool works only for channels where you are the broadcaster or an editor, and Twitch has no official way to download past broadcasts by program (gingest-3, gingest-6). Kick's public API, as far as its docs show, has no clips or past-broadcast endpoints, and Kick's terms bar scraping, copying and editing other users' content (gingest-9, gingest-10, gingest-m3). So for "no permission, edit and credit" there is no official route to the files on either platform. Our own recordings (console capture to USB or cloud, then a watched folder) are the only source we fully control, and they should be built first (gingest-14, gingest-15). Use the stream sites as a signal layer (what is hot, when), not as a file supply, unless a creator gives us a file. The one official, permissioned file route on Twitch is a creator who makes our account a channel editor, so we can cut and download 5 to 60 second clips from their own broadcasts (gingest-m1). Whichever route we take, write one provenance record per source and per clip from day one (gingest-20, unverified).

#### What we found

##### 1. Twitch: what the official API gives us

- **Get Clips** works with any valid token, including an app access token (a token for our own app, no user login needed). You can filter by `game_id` (look it up with the Search Categories API) and by `started_at` and `ended_at` in UTC. If `ended_at` is left out the window is one week. Results come back ordered by views, highest first (gingest-1).
- Each clip carries `id`, `url`, `broadcaster_id`, `broadcaster_name`, `creator_id`, `video_id`, `game_id`, `language`, `title`, `view_count`, `created_at`, `duration`, `vod_offset` and `is_featured` (gingest-1, gingest-2).
- `vod_offset` is the clip's start, in seconds from the start of the stream video. If the stream video has been deleted, `video_id` is empty and `vod_offset` is null. For new clips these fields can be empty for several minutes (gingest-1).
- One query can return only about 1,000 clips in total across pages. The docs say to use several smaller time windows to get more (gingest-2). Lookup by clip id takes up to 100 ids; paging and date filters are ignored in that mode (gingest-1).
- Clips are 5 to 60 seconds long when created through the API (gingest-1). Clips that viewers make on the site are not covered by that statement. So a Twitch clip is a short, already-chosen moment, which makes it a useful hint about what viewers liked.
- **Get Videos** (`GET /helix/videos`) takes one of `id`, `user_id` or `game_id`. `type` can be `archive` (past broadcast), `highlight` or `upload`; `sort` can be `time`, `trending` or `views`; pages hold up to 100. A `game_id` query returns at most 500 videos. Fields include `duration`, `view_count`, `created_at`, `url`, `viewable` and `muted_segments`. `muted_segments` is always null with an app access token (gingest-4).
- A changelog entry dated 2026-11-10 says Get Videos now lists `past_premiere` and `premiere_upload` types (these appear only in responses for lookups by id, not as request filters) and corrects the `duration` format. The `duration` string looks like `3m21s` (gingest-4).
- **Rate limit:** each app has a bucket of points per minute; most calls cost 1 point; running out gives HTTP 429. Response headers `Ratelimit-Limit`, `Ratelimit-Remaining` and `Ratelimit-Reset` show the state. The page does not state the bucket size as a rule (an example header shows 800). App-token and user-token requests use separate buckets, and some endpoints can return 429 for reasons unrelated to the bucket (gingest-5). The download endpoint has its own limit of 100 requests per minute (gingest-3).
- **Authentication for our needs:** an app access token comes from a POST to `id.twitch.tv/oauth2/token` with a client id and secret (`client_credentials`). That needs a Twitch developer account and a registered app, which we do not have yet. The app token cannot see `muted_segments` (gingest-4, gingest-5).

##### 2. Twitch: downloading, and what the terms allow

- **Get Clips Download** (open beta 2025-09-19, generally available since 2025-10-30) returns temporary links to the video files. It needs a user token with `editor:manage:clips` or `channel:manage:clips`, or an app token that an editor has already authorised with those scopes. It applies to editors of the channel; the broadcaster uses their own token. A user who is not an editor gets 403. Up to 10 clips per call. Each item has `landscape_download_url` and `portrait_download_url`, either may be null. The docs say the links are temporary and give no expiry time (gingest-3).
- So the official download tool is built for a channel's own team. It does not cover other creators' clips: the docs state outright that clips that belong to a different broadcaster are left out of the list. This is documented behaviour, not only our reading (gingest-3, gingest-m2).
- **Past broadcasts:** a forum user (BarryCarlyon; the page shows no staff or moderator badge) answered on 2026-03-20 that there is no official way to download a VOD (past broadcast) by program, and that downloads are manual from the dashboard. A January 2026 thread asking Twitch to add a VOD download endpoint like the clips one had no staff answer on the page. No official Twitch page saying this was opened; the official API offers only clip-level download and Create Clip From VOD (editor-only) (gingest-6).
- **Storing data:** the forum quotes the Developer Services Agreement as saying "Do not store copies of Twitch Content or Program Materials" and as allowing caching only for 24 hours without sharing with third parties. A Twitch voice (user `jbulava`, no staff title shown) wrote on 2025-07-14 that an OAuth flow that gets a user's permission generally complies when storing that user's data beyond 24 hours. Nobody answered whether public data, such as clip lists fetched with an app token, must be deleted after 24 hours. This is the forum's quotation; the agreement text itself could not be checked (gingest-7).
- We could not open the Developer Services Agreement or the Twitch Terms of Service text: the pages loaded only their navigation, for both checkers. We therefore cannot quote the rules on copying, reposting or commercial use. A search summary of a 2022 Spanish copy of the Terms said the licence is for personal or internal business use and excludes resale, commercial use and public performance of the materials. We did not open that text, so treat it as a lead, not a finding (gingest-8, unverified).
- Twitch-side muting: a vendor claims Twitch mutes VOD segments where music matching fires. This is a vendor claim (gingest-12). For GTA 6, in-game radio music is a likely cause (our inference).
- **Create Clip From VOD** (open beta 2025-12-19, generally available 2026-02-05) creates a 5 to 60 second clip from a broadcaster's VOD on behalf of the broadcaster or a channel editor, with the same `editor:manage:clips` or `channel:manage:clips` scopes. It fails if the VOD does not belong to that broadcaster. Combined with Get Clips Download, a creator who adds our account as a channel editor lets us cut and download clips from their past broadcasts through the official API. Nothing added in 2025-2026 gives a third party official file access to other creators' footage (gingest-m1).

##### 3. Twitch: how long past broadcasts stay

- Twitch's API page says normal broadcasters' VODs are deleted after 14 days and "all others like partners" after 60. Highlights and uploads do not expire. Past broadcasts exist only if the streamer turned storage on (gingest-11).
- A search summary of Twitch's help centre (we could not open the page, for either checker) says Partners, Prime and Turbo users keep 60 days, Affiliates 14, everyone else 7, and that a higher-quality (2K or vertical) copy expires after 7 days. The API page and the help centre disagree for non-partners. Which is current is unconfirmed (gingest-11).
- For us: plan for a 7 to 60 day window and treat the stream video as short-lived. A clip's `video_id` becomes empty when its stream is deleted (gingest-1, gingest-11).

##### 4. Twitch chat replay

- There is no official endpoint for chat of a past broadcast. A forum answer on 2023-06-27 says there "never has been a supported/documented API for VodChat". The Twitch changelog to 2026-11-10 shows no such endpoint added. A search summary says people use an undocumented endpoint and that Twitch called it unsupported and not meant for third parties. We did not open that part (gingest-13).
- Live chat can be received in real time. We have no source on whether recording live chat of other channels is allowed (gingest-13).
- Chat is therefore not a dependable signal for us. For our own recordings there is no chat at all.

##### 5. Kick

- Kick's public developer docs (GitHub `KickDevDocs`, and `docs.kick.com`) have a changelog (day-first dates) from 2025-04-01 to 2026-08-11 (11 August 2026, Get Channels subscriber counts). Later entries include Livestreams V2 with pagination (2026-06-23), livestreams by user IDs (2026-07-03), Categories V2 (2026-01-15) and Channel Rewards (2025-12-03). The table of contents lists Categories, Users, Channels, Channel Rewards, Chat, Moderation, Livestreams, Public Key, KICKs, Ads, FAQs, Events, Organizations and Drops. There is still no clips, videos or VOD endpoint, no rate-limit page and no developer terms. So we cannot confirm any official clip or past-broadcast endpoint. Re-check docs.kick.com before the build (gingest-9, gingest-m3).
- Search results show third-party wrappers that scrape Kick's internal, undocumented endpoints. Those are not Kick's API (gingest-9, search summary only).
- **Kick's Terms of Service** (page shows "Date Modified: 23 March 2026"): copying, distributing or disclosing any part of the Service is barred, "including by scraping" (1.4(a)); bots, spiders and offline readers are barred (1.4(b)); accessing content by means not provided or authorised, and bypassing copy-prevention, are barred (1.4(k), 1.4(l)); other users' content may not be copied, reproduced or redistributed, and section 3 also bars publishing, adapting, editing or creating derivative works from it. Users keep ownership of their content and give other users a licence to use it "as permitted through the functionality of the Service and under these Terms" (2.1). Commercial use of your own content is allowed only if submitting it for commercialisation purposes, and commercial solicitation is barred (1.2, 1.4(h)) (gingest-10).
- **Replays:** Kick's help centre says verified streamers keep replays up to 30 days and non-verified 7 days. A verified channel can hold 30 replays at once and a non-verified one 16. The page shows only "Updated over 2 weeks ago" and says nothing on downloading (gingest-10).
- A vendor post (2026-04-27, updated 2026-10-31) says Kick's archive is less policed on music. A vendor claim; it gives no retention numbers (gingest-12).

##### 6. YouTube Live

- YouTube's help page says streams under 12 hours can be archived automatically; a stream over 12 hours "may not be captured at all". It says nothing on how long an archive stays, and recommends a local backup. The page shows no date (gingest-16).
- Archives are ordinary videos once processed. Everything in section A5 of this report (RSS, `videos.list`, captions, yt-dlp, the 720p format string in our `ingest/youtube.py`) applies. The Data API's `liveBroadcastContent` value tells live from finished (A5 gingest/ingest-4).
- yt-dlp's `--live-from-start` is "experimental and only supported for YouTube, Twitch, TVer, and mellow-fan"; the default downloads from the current time (gingest-17).
- Terms on downloading YouTube content are covered in A5 (ingest-23) and not repeated here.

##### 7. Long recordings of 3 to 10 hours

- yt-dlp's `--download-sections` fetches only a time range. Cuts without re-encoding land on keyframes; exact cuts need `--force-keyframes-at-cuts`, which the project FAQ calls slow (gingest-17, A5 ingest-13). Whether range download works on Twitch past broadcasts was not stated in anything we opened. Test it on one (gingest-17). These flags are a capability, not a permission: for other creators' Twitch or Kick streams the terms read so far point the other way, so they belong only to sources we own or have written permission for.
- `--concurrent-fragments N` fetches several pieces at once for DASH and HLS streams (default 1); `--limit-rate` caps speed; `--download-archive FILE` skips ids already fetched (gingest-17).
- Sizes (our estimate, assuming a stream rate of about 6 Mbit/s, which we did not confirm from a Twitch page): 6 Mbit/s is 0.75 MB/s, about 2.7 GB per hour. A 6-hour stream would be about 16 GB, more than the laptop's 13 GB of free space and most of a 20-30 GB server disk. Fetching all of it is never right (gingest-19).
- A 60-second clip with 10 seconds of padding each side is an 80-second window, about 60 MB at that rate (a 70-second window is about 53 MB). Twenty such windows are about 1.2 GB (own arithmetic, gingest-19).
- The 6 Mbit/s rate is unsourced. YouTube's own live-encoder guidance recommends 10-17 Mbit/s H.264 for 1080p (minimum 5-6) and 35-50 Mbit/s for 4K, and the bitrate of a downloaded rendition differs from the ingest bitrate. Real sizes depend on the source, so measure on real files before setting disk caps. Console 4K captures could be far larger than the figures above (gingest-19, gingest-m5).
- The server's existing rule refuses a job below 3 GiB free disk and cleans up below 4 GiB (core/config.py:304-317) (gingest-18).

##### 8. Our own recordings

- **PS5.** A 2020 article says PS5 videos can be saved as WebM ("most efficient") or MP4 ("most compatible"), up to 3840 x 2160, changed under Settings > Captures and Broadcasts > Captures. Copying to USB goes through the Media Gallery menu (gingest-14).
- Search results (not opened) say the USB drive needs FAT32 or exFAT, and one says files over 4 GB fail on FAT32. We found no official Sony page (two official URLs returned 404). HDR, codec and clip-length limits are **not confirmed** (gingest-14).
- **Xbox Series.** One vendor blog (2026-09-04, promotes its own capture tool and a competing product) says the Share button saves the last 30 seconds; manual recordings run up to 10 minutes on internal storage and about an hour on external USB; 4K HDR shortens the maximum; uploads to the Xbox network are deleted after 90 days unless downloaded; a USB copy has "full quality". It names no container or codec and states these as fact with no sources. Search results (not opened) disagree on length caps, and say early reports found 4K and HDR clips not auto-uploaded to OneDrive. Treat all numbers as unconfirmed (gingest-15).
- Neither official support page would open for us (a 404 or an empty page). Our plan must not depend on these numbers; the intake code should accept whatever the console writes and report what it got (gingest-14, gingest-15).
- **Our upload endpoint.** `api/main.py:363` already has an upload route taking a `file` (and an optional transcript). Its docstring calls it a hidden path for tests and regression, so it is not a polished drop-in. `ingest/validate.py:90` comments that real-world files, notably Matroska, need care (read lines, not run). `ingest/` holds `store.py`, `validate.py`, `youtube.py` and `zoom.py`. There is no watched-folder code in the repo (a case-insensitive search for "watch" and "inbox" found nothing relevant) (gingest-18).

##### 9. Words (speech-to-text)

- faster-whisper's own benchmark: `small` model, int8, 13 minutes of audio, 1 min 42 s and 1,477 MB RAM on 8 threads of an Intel i7-12700K; with `batch_size=8` it was 51 s and 3,608 MB. That is a fast desktop chip, not a t3.large with 2 burstable vCPUs. The repo runs WhisperX (faster-whisper plus alignment and a diarization model), so this benchmark is a lower bound for the repo's time (gingest-21, gingest-m6, A5 ingest-18).
- It can drop non-speech stretches with the Silero VAD (voice activity detection): `vad_filter=True`, by default removing silences longer than 2 seconds, tunable with `min_silence_duration_ms` (gingest-21). WhisperX's README says VAD reduces hallucination (made-up words) with no loss in accuracy, says overlapping speech is "not handled particularly well", says words such as "2014." or "£13.60" get no timing, and says int8 "may reduce accuracy" (gingest-22).
- Whisper was trained on 680,000 hours of data and "approaches" human robustness per its authors (paper submitted 2022-12-06). The abstract says nothing about music or game noise (gingest-22).
- We found **no source** measuring accuracy on game audio (gunfire, radio music, engines) or on commentary over it. That is unknown (gingest-22).
- Paid API prices (Deepgram, AssemblyAI, OpenAI) are in A5 (ingest-19): about $0.15-0.36 per audio hour.

##### 10. Provenance

- Nothing we opened says what a platform or a rights holder will accept as proof of source. The record below is our own design (gingest-20, unverified).
- Twitch's 24-hour cache clause and "do not store copies of Twitch Content" language (as quoted on the forum) mean we should store only ids and our own facts about the clip, not Twitch's titles or chat, unless the broadcaster has given permission (gingest-7).
- Twitch clip ids and ranges must be stored as our own copy, because the platform ids go empty or null when a VOD is deleted (gingest-1).

##### 11. Added by the checkers

- **gingest-m1.** Create Clip From VOD plus Get Clips Download is the official permissioned route to Twitch files: a creator who adds our account as a channel editor lets us cut and download 5 to 60 second clips from their past broadcasts. Both calls are broadcaster or editor only (see section 2).
- **gingest-m2.** Get Clips Download explicitly drops clips that belong to a different broadcaster: "Clips that weren't found, that the editor may not access, or that belong to a different broadcaster are left out of the list."
- **gingest-m3.** Kick's Terms section 3 bars publishing, adapting, editing or creating derivative works from other users' content, and 2.1 limits other users' licence to use content to what the Service's functionality permits. The "no permission, edit and credit" route is expressly barred for Kick sources, separate from any copyright question. Kick's docs are also newer than first read (changelog to 2026-08-11), still with no clips or videos API.
- **gingest-m4.** For creators who agree to supply footage, the routes Twitch supports for their own VODs are local recording (which also avoids Twitch music muting), multistreaming to YouTube, and the manual Video Producer export to YouTube. A YouTube upload or export from them is a more reliable file route than anything on Twitch.
- **gingest-m5.** Disk sizing should use measured bitrates: YouTube recommends 10-17 Mbit/s H.264 for 1080p and 35-50 Mbit/s for 4K, well above the assumed 6 Mbit/s. This matters on a laptop with 13 GB free.
- **gingest-m6.** Server realism. The repo transcribes with WhisperX (core/config.py:129-132), so the faster-whisper CPU benchmark understates its time. AWS lists the t3.large at 30% baseline per vCPU (36 CPU credits per hour), with sustained use above baseline in unlimited mode billed at $0.05 per vCPU-hour. `max_queue_depth` is 1 (core/config.py:298), so one job runs at a time and any clp work on the production server would delay company jobs. clp should run elsewhere.
- **gingest-m7.** The signal layer is worth less than it looks. Get Clips by `game_id` tells us which moments and creators are popular, but we cannot officially get those files. The signal can feed only outreach to those creators for written permission, or ideas for our own recordings. It cannot supply 24 clips a day by itself.
- **gingest-m8.** Registering a Twitch developer app (client id and secret) is needed even for read-only Get Clips polling. That is an owner action under the Developer Services Agreement, whose text nobody has read yet. Read it before registering.

#### What this means for our build

**Source order (what I would do).**
1. **Own recordings first.** It is the only route with files we hold, no platform terms to break, full quality and no yt-dlp. It still has a rights question with the game's publisher; that belongs to another strand and I did not research it.
2. **Stream sites as a signal only.** Twitch Get Clips by `game_id`, in 6-hour windows, sorted by views, tells us what moments and which creators are hot. We store the clip id, view count, `broadcaster_id` and `created_at`, and keep the data short-lived. We do not download the file. The signal feeds creator outreach or our own recording plans; it cannot supply daily clips by itself (gingest-m7).
3. **Creator-supplied files** (a creator sends us a clip or a stream segment with a written yes, or makes our account a Twitch channel editor so Create Clip From VOD and Get Clips Download work). This is the only way a Twitch or Kick video file enters the pipeline in a way the terms we could read allow. Record the permission (gingest-3, gingest-6, gingest-10, gingest-m1, gingest-m3).
4. **YouTube videos from other creators** stay in A5's territory. Treat the same way: metadata first, files only with permission.

**Own-recording intake (simple for a non-technical person).**
- One shared folder per recorder (Google Drive or OneDrive or Dropbox) named `inbox`. The person drops files; a worker on the laptop watches the folder and moves each finished file to `incoming`, then `done` or `failed`. A file counts as finished when its size has not changed for 60 seconds (my default).
- Naming: `YYYY-MM-DD_HHMM_console_title.ext` made by the worker from the file's creation time, not from what the person typed. Keep the original name in the provenance record.
- Accept `.mp4`, `.webm`, `.mkv`, `.mov`. Run `ffprobe` on each file first and record codec, size, frame rate, length and whether it is HDR. Convert only what the editor cannot read (usually HDR 4K to 1080p SDR with tone mapping) into an `edit-source` file, and keep the original until the clips are posted. Do not run this on the production server (see the A5 and G-series cost advice; the server's job slot and disk are the production system's, and the queue holds one job at a time, gingest-m6).
- Console to PC: USB stick (exFAT) in, copy by hand or by phone app to the cloud folder. Write one-page instructions with pictures once we know which console is used (gingest-14, gingest-15).
- Do not extend the production upload route. Copy the idea into the `clp` branch (`api/main.py:363` is a test path).

**Signals before downloads.**
- Per game, poll Get Clips every 15 minutes with a 6-hour window, up to 100 per page, and keep the top 20 per window. At about one request per page that is far under any limit (gingest-1, gingest-2, gingest-5).
- Use `vod_offset` plus `duration` to say where, inside a stream, viewers found something worth clipping. That is the cheap way to avoid reading hours of video.
- For our own recordings the equivalent signals are cheap audio measures: loudness peaks, speech starts, and the player's own markers if we have them. Another strand covers scoring.

**Long recordings.** If a source ever arrives as a long file:
- Never load a whole 3-10 hour file into one job. Cut candidate windows first with `ffmpeg -ss ... -t ...` stream copy, and render from those windows.
- Cap working disk at 5 GB for the worker and refuse above it; delete the window file after the clip is made. Keep the original only for our own recordings, where we have the space plan on the laptop's 13 GB. Set the real caps after measuring file sizes with `ffprobe` (gingest-m5).
- For YouTube live archives use ranges, not whole files, and prefer a creator's own file (gingest-16, gingest-17, gingest-19).

**Words.**
- Transcribe only candidate windows, padded by 10 seconds, with `vad_filter=True`. Whole-stream transcription of 3-10 hours on the server is not needed.
- Use the existing `small` int8 setting (`core/config.py:131`) until a test shows poor results on GTA audio. My estimate that a 60-second window takes well under a minute is unmeasured: it ignores model load time, WhisperX's extra alignment steps and the t3.large's CPU-credit limit. Measure on the actual machine before relying on it, and run this off the production server (gingest-21, gingest-m6).
- Run one test first: 20 candidate windows of our own GTA 6 footage with commentary over game audio, compared against a person's transcript. If the error is high, lower the game volume in the recording or use a paid API on those windows only (gingest-22).
- Where there is no commentary, skip speech-to-text and title from the game event instead. That saves cost and removes a failure mode.

**Provenance record (build this as a table from the first day).**
One row per source file or source moment, with these fields (my design, unverified):
- `source_id` (our id), `platform` (twitch, kick, youtube, own, creator_file), `source_url`, `platform_video_id`, `creator_name`, `creator_channel_url`.
- `rights_status`: `own`, `permission_written`, `no_permission`, `unknown`; plus `rights_evidence` (a link or file to the email or message).
- `fetched_at`, `fetch_method`, `file_sha256`, `original_filename`.
- `range_start_s`, `range_end_s` (the part of the source used).
- `clip_id`, `youtube_video_id` of what we posted, `posted_at`.
- `takedown_state` and `takedown_note`.
- A unique key plus an overlap check, so the same moment cannot be used twice. A key on (`platform`, `platform_video_id`, `range_start_s`, `range_end_s`) does not stop overlapping ranges, and for a Twitch clip whose VOD is deleted `platform_video_id` is empty, so key on the clip id (or our `source_id`) and run an overlap check on ranges. A second query "all clips from creator X" gives a takedown list in one step (gingest-20).
- Storing `creator_name` and `creator_channel_url` conflicts with keeping Twitch data short-lived (gingest-7) unless the creator gave permission. Decide which applies per row.
- The pipeline must refuse to render a clip whose source row has `rights_status` of `no_permission` or `unknown`. If an owner override exists at all, it must be a named, manual, per-clip action and must not exist on the automated hourly loop. This is a guard rail, not a legal opinion. For Kick sources a `no_permission` row is barred outright by Kick's section 3 (gingest-m3).

#### Risks and unknowns

- **No official file route for others' streams.** Everything we found says Twitch downloads need channel editor status, and past-broadcast downloads are unsupported (gingest-3, gingest-6, gingest-m2). Kick has no documented clip or video API and bars scraping, copying and editing (gingest-9, gingest-10, gingest-m3). Third-party download tools exist, but we did not research them and they sit outside what the pages we read allow. This conflicts with the owner's "clip other GTA 6 channels" idea. Cheap check: email 5 creators and ask for files with a written yes (or for channel-editor access on Twitch); see how many answer in a week.
- **We could not read Twitch's Terms and Developer Agreement** (neither checker could). The pages gave only navigation. Open them in a normal browser before the plan is final and before registering an app, and quote the actual text on copying, reposting and commercial use (gingest-7, gingest-8, gingest-m8).
- **Twitch retention is disputed:** 14/60 days on the API page against 7/14/60 in a help-centre summary we could not open (gingest-11).
- **Console capture specs are unconfirmed.** We had no official Sony or Microsoft page. Clip lengths, codec, HDR behaviour and exFAT rules come from blogs (gingest-14, gingest-15). Cheap check: someone records 5 minutes at the highest setting on the actual console and sends us the file; `ffprobe` gives the real answer in a minute.
- **Not confirmed: the 6 Mbit/s stream rate** behind the size figures; YouTube's table suggests 10-17 Mbit/s for 1080p. Measure real files (gingest-19, gingest-m5).
- **Game audio and speech-to-text:** no source measures it (gingest-22). Run the 20-window test above.
- **Whether GTA 6 can be recorded and posted at all** (publisher rules, console capture blocks in cutscenes, if any) is for other strands. I did not research it.
- **Twitch app registration:** a developer account and client secret are needed for Get Clips. That is an owner action; I did not sign in or register (gingest-m8).
- **Rate-limit sizes** for Twitch's general bucket are not stated as a rule on the page we read (gingest-5).
- **Source of the `muted_segments` data** needs a user token, which we will not have for other channels (gingest-4).
- **Server capacity:** t3.large CPU credits and one-job-at-a-time queueing mean clp work should not run on the production server (gingest-m6).
- **Costs.** Metadata polling is free. A cloud folder for own recordings is free at small sizes (we did not research plan limits). Paid transcription is cents per hour and only on windows.

## 4. Research on YouTube, clips channels and the code we have

- A1. How Shorts get views now, and whether posting every hour helps
- A2. How clips channels really grow, and why many die
- A3. The rules: copyright, YouTube policy, and what makes clipping allowed
- A4. Which channels to clip: candidates and how to vet them
- A5. Getting the source videos and their words
- A6. Picking the moments worth posting
- A7. Making the Short look good with ffmpeg
- A8. Hyperframes and /brag: what they can do for clips
