### A1. How Shorts get views now, and whether posting every hour helps

**The short answer.** Posting every hour (24 a day) is the wrong default for this system. No official source rewards upload volume. The one large data set on gaps between Shorts links back-to-back posting (under 1 hour apart) with fewer views per Short. A new channel also runs into an unpublished daily upload limit. The bigger danger is what gets posted, not how often: on 1 October 2026 YouTube announced that channels mostly re-posting other creators' clips without adding their own work will likely see less distribution in the Shorts feed (no start date was given). Permission from the source channels does not fix this or the monetisation rules. Its spam and termination rules can end a channel, and they bar the terminated owner from having any other channel, which could put the company channel at risk. Start at 1 Short a day, avoid posting less than 1 hour apart and prefer at least 3 hours (a precaution, not a finding), raise the rate only when Stayed-to-watch holds, cap it at about 4-6 a day by week 8, and judge each Short on Studio's Stayed-to-watch and engaged views at 48 hours and 7 days, never on raw views.

#### What we found

##### How the Shorts feed tests a new Short

- YouTube first shows a new Short to a small "seed" audience. Reach then grows or shrinks with how those viewers respond, mainly whether they keep watching or swipe away. YouTube publishes no threshold (growth-1).
- The signals YouTube names are viewing behaviour, likes and dislikes, satisfaction surveys and channel quality. YouTube's Shorts lead said in 2023 that there is no upload-count threshold, that posting time matters only for news, and that deleting and re-uploading a Short can be read as spam (the spam reading is the reporter's paraphrase; the source is three years old and second-hand) (growth-1).
- "Stayed to watch" (Studio's name for what used to be "viewed vs swiped away" (unverified)) is the share of times viewers kept watching past the first seconds of a Short. YouTube does not say how many seconds (growth-2).
- Since 31 March 2025 a public Shorts view counts every start and every replay, with no minimum watch time (the date comes from the Analytics API revision history and Help 10059070, not Help 12220281). "Engaged views" is the old, stricter count: viewers who stayed past the first seconds, not counting loops. Average view duration is worked out only over viewers who stayed (growth-2).
- In one vendor case, engaged views were about 56% of public views. Earlier research estimates raw views at about 1.5-2 times engaged views (unverified) (growth-2).
- Loops raise public views but are left out of engaged views. We found no official statement that loops help ranking (growth-2).
- Since August 2026 public views in all formats count from the first frame, including autoplay and hover (API revision history, 2026-08-27). Vendor studies that span this change (growth-16, growth-19) mix two view definitions (growth-m6).

##### The October 2026 originality change, which matters most for a clips channel

- On 1 October 2026 YouTube announced, in a TeamYouTube Help Community post and a Creator Insider video, that it will "further prioritize original content and reduce the reach of content re-uploaded from other creators." Channels "identified as primarily aggregating or re-uploading other creators' videos" without significant changes will likely get less Shorts-feed reach. 1 October is the announcement date, not a stated start date. The quotes rest on news reports (SEJ, PPC Land), not the primary post (growth-4).
- YouTube's Creator Liaison said that, to count as your own work, a clip of someone else's video needs commentary, analysis or storytelling: "not just VO descriptions of what's happening on screen, minor technical edits, or template-based bulk changes." VO means voice-over (growth-4).
- No effective date, threshold, notice or appeal process was given. Nothing was said about clips posted with the owner's permission, clipping programmes or podcasts, or a creator's own long-video cuts. A channel that moves to original work will have its reach "re-evaluated," with no timeline given. Creators who want to feature someone else's video were pointed to the Posts tab (growth-4).
- This is a reach rule. It is separate from the monetisation rule. The reused-content policy applies "to your channel as a whole." It names as not allowed: "Clips of moments from your favorite show edited together with little or no narrative", "Short videos you compiled from other social media websites" and "Content uploaded many times by other creators." It allows clips used for critical review and reaction videos with commentary (growth-5).
- The inauthentic-content rule (renamed on 15 July 2025) bars "similar or repetitive content with low educational value, commentary, narratives, or minimal variation across videos" and says a channel "shouldn't have content that appears to be produced using a template" (growth-5).
- The reused-content policy "applies even if you have permission from the original creator" and is not based on copyright, permission or fair use. Licensing clips from top channels does not make them monetisable (growth-m1).
- Shorts ad revenue: the Creator Pool excludes views of reuploaded other creators' content, compilations with no original content added, and unedited clips from others' movies or TV shows. A light-edit clips channel would earn nothing from those views even before reach cuts. The same page notes a 10 million qualified Shorts views (90-day) threshold starting 1 February 2027 (growth-m3).

##### What high-volume automation risks under YouTube's rules

- The spam policy bans "Using automated tools or AI to churn out high volumes of similar content with minimal changes." It also bans "Re-posting material from other websites or platforms, or other videos without adding anything of your own." It says "posting a few variations of a video is ok" (growth-6).
- Under the spam policy YouTube can remove content and issue a warning or strike, suspend monetisation, or terminate the channel. Three strikes in 90 days may end the channel (growth-6).
- The terminations page lists "A single case of severe abuse (such as predatory behavior, spam, or pornography)" as grounds to end a channel. It adds: "If your YouTube channel is terminated, you are prohibited from using, possessing, or creating any other YouTube channels" (growth-7).
- That circumvention rule applies to all existing channels, any new channels you create or acquire, and "any channels in which you are repeatedly or prominently featured." This widens the risk to the company channel if the same people appear on both. The monetisation policy separately says violations can disable monetisation "on all or any of your accounts" and, for some behaviour, "could lead to termination of all channels" (growth-m2).
- Since about November 2026, YouTube has been testing a 30-day "locked" state for some channels flagged for spam. Locked channels are hidden and cannot upload, and the owner can fix the videos, delete them all, or appeal. YouTube calls it an experiment for "certain channels" only. This rests on news; the official Help thread's text did not load for the checker (growth-8).
- A news article (Fstoppers, 2026-07-19) describes a Google research paper on a "Scalable Cluster Termination System" that flags templated narratives and "non-human publishing frequency", groups accounts likely to share an origin script or API, and terminates the whole cluster. The article says it is unconfirmed whether this runs on live YouTube. Hourly automated posting from the same app, API project or server as the company channel is the pattern it describes (unverified) (growth-m8).

##### Posting frequency: what the sources say about 1, 3, 5, 10 and 24 a day

- **Official.** Volume on its own is neither rewarded nor penalised. No "post X a day" rule exists (growth-1).
- **Daily upload limit.** YouTube limits "how many videos a channel can upload in a 24-hour period across desktop, mobile and YouTube API." It publishes no number. The limit varies by country or region and channel history, and strikes reduce it. The error says to try again in 24 hours (growth-9).
- **Raising the limit.** "Higher daily upload limits" are an advanced feature. That needs phone verification first, then enough channel history or an ID or video check, which usually takes 24 hours and is not open to everyone (growth-9).
- **Who can verify.** Only the primary channel owner can do the identity check; Brand Accounts and supervised accounts get an error. One phone number can verify only 2 channels. A separate clips channel may therefore not easily get higher upload limits or the Related video link. ID-verifying the new channel with the same owner's identity is also one concrete way the two channels become linked (growth-m4).
- **API.** The Data API counts uploads in a separate bucket: each `videos.insert` costs 1 unit, with a default of 100 calls a day. Quota is therefore not what stops 24 a day; the channel's own limit is (growth-10). Hourly extras do draw on the 10,000-unit pool: thumbnails.set 50, captions.insert 400, playlistItems.insert 50. At 24 posts a day, captions.insert alone would use 9,600 units (growth-m7).
- **Notifications.** A channel can send each viewer at most 3 new-video notifications a day. More than 3 publishes in a short window may pause notifications for 24 hours (the page says "may"; that hourly posting would keep them paused is our inference). A brand-new channel with no subscribers sends almost none, so this is a weak reason to cap volume (growth-14).
- **Gaps between Shorts (vendor data, 18,148 Shorts, 1,221 channels, Aug-Oct 2026).** Shorts posted less than 1 hour after the channel's previous Short had a median of 7,978 public views. Gaps of 1-3 h had 25,190, 24-48 h had 24,022, and 48-72 h had 33,189 (growth-12).
- Within the same channel, Shorts posted under 3 hours apart got about 0.82 times the views of those spaced 12-48 hours apart. 129 of 197 channels did better with longer gaps. This is an association, not proof. The data argues against sub-hour bursts: 1-3 h vs 12-48 h was only 0.92x, against 0.80x for under 1 h. A 3-hour minimum is a precaution, not a finding. The vendor's sample may over-represent successful channels, and its medians are not benchmarks for a new channel (growth-12).
- **Cadence (vendor data, 799,718 videos from 71,177 accounts).** Each Short did best per post when its channel posted 2-4 Shorts a week. Metricool asserts "no real ceiling" on the monthly total but gives no figures for it. Channels posting about 5 Shorts a month averaged 8,789 views per long-form video, against a 5,985 global average and 4,364 for channels with no Shorts. Channels posting 35 or more a month fell back to roughly the level of channels posting none. No data is shown between 5 and 35 a month, so "5 a month is the peak" is not established, and Metricool calls the link possibly correlational (growth-13).
- **Practitioner advice.** An agency guide advises about 5 Shorts a week for 8 weeks, then tracking retention and changing frequency "only if quality stays stable." It warns that a repeated premise and falling quality reduce reach. It gives no data for its "10+ a day doubles views" remark, so we disregard that remark (growth-13).
- **Counter-evidence on volume.** vidIQ's upload-frequency study (2026-07-08; 10.2M channels with at least 1,000 subscribers; Shorts and long-form combined) finds median monthly view growth rising at every tier up to 12 or more uploads a month (2.18% vs 0.89% at 1-3). It is correlational, has no tier above 12 a month and no per-video data, and excludes channels under 1,000 subscribers. Some volume may help channel totals, but there is no evidence for 24 a day (growth-m9).
- **The only high-volume new-channel test we found** (practitioner, summarised by a third-party page that gives no date of its own; the year is not stated): 300 fact- and quote-style Shorts (text written by ChatGPT, made in Canva) in 30 days, about 10 a day. The creator could upload 16 a day before hitting the limit, so that limit cannot be dated or assumed to apply in 2026. The test brought about 131,000 views and 318 subscribers. 228 of 300 Shorts got under 100 views, and 111 got under 10 (growth-11).
- We found no test of 24 Shorts a day, and no official or data-backed numbers for 3, 5 or 10 a day on a new channel. We don't know what hourly posting would do beyond the points above.

##### Cold start: the first 10-50 uploads, and the myths

- vidIQ studied channels created January-June 2025 that posted at least 10 Shorts in their first 90 days (367,243 channels). The median 30-day public views were about 1,362 for the first Short, 1,275 for the fifth and 1,344 for the tenth: flat, with no warm-up curve. The median best Short of the first 10 had 8,832, and 48% of channels had one Short above 10,000 within 30 days, but only 20.9% of individual Shorts reached 10,000. The sample leaves out channels that quit early, so these medians are optimistic, and the cohort predates the October 2026 originality change (growth-15).
- **No "warming up."** Neither YouTube nor the vidIQ data shows early uploads unlocking reach (growth-1, growth-15).
- **"View jail" and hard caps.** In vendor data on 32,069 Shorts from July-September 2026, view counts show no cliff at 500, 1,000 or 10,000. Two-thirds of channels with a Short under 10,000 also had one above it. This weakens the "view jail" idea but does not rule out staged testing (growth-16).
- **Shadow bans.** We found no official YouTube statement. The real, documented reach cuts are the originality change and spam enforcement (growth-4, growth-8).
- **Deleting weak Shorts.** YouTube documents no benefit from it, and deleting and re-uploading can be read as spam (growth-16).
- **Best posting time.** YouTube says it doesn't matter except for news (TechCrunch 2023, not a current Help page). A vendor's engagement data favours local evenings, but gives no effect size for Shorts (unverified) (growth-17).
- **The #shorts tag.** It isn't needed: any vertical or square video of 3 minutes or less is a Short. Up to 3 hashtags show above the title, and more than 60 means all are ignored (growth-17).

##### Format

- **Length limits.** Shorts can run up to 3 minutes. But a Short over 1 minute with any active copyright claim, manual or Content ID, is blocked worldwide: it cannot play, be recommended or earn. YouTube names no ideal length (growth-18). For clips of other people's channels, where claims are likely, this is a hard reason to stay at 60 seconds or less. Staying at 60 s or less avoids only that automatic rule: a Content ID owner can still choose to block a video at any length, and actions can vary by region (growth-m10).
- **Length data (vendor, 16,537 Shorts, Oct 2026).** 16-30 s Shorts had the highest pooled median (36,970 public views), against 18,849-20,938 for 46-90 s. Within channels, 16-30 s beat 61-180 s on 58.8% of 85 channels, at a median 1.29 times. 121-180 s also did well in some cuts (it had the highest channel-balanced median, 29,492, and split 13-13 against 16-30 s on 26 channels). Public views favour short clips because replays count. Shorts were classified by duration only, not confirmed as Shorts-feed eligible, and the data spans the August 2026 view-count change (growth-19).
- **Talk and interview clips.** On 37 comparable company channels, meeting, talk and talking-head Shorts were the weakest format, with a median of about 600 views. Hardware demos had about 2,300 and presenter-led explainers about 3,550 (growth-20). Talk channels without a famous host stay at a few hundred views per Short even with large audiences (growth-20). This rests on raw public views from tech-company channels and transfers only loosely to a clips channel.
- **Opening, captions and pacing.** The earlier study found indirect support for opening on the strongest line with readable text in the first frame, and for a bigger vertical picture. Burned-in captions and cutting pauses are plausible but untested on organic Shorts, and there is no evidence for glossy motion-graphic extras (research/youtube-growth/02-shorts-editing-and-cost.md lines 68-78). We found no 2025-2026 official YouTube page that gives a hook length in seconds; the "first 3 seconds" figures in third-party guides cite no data.

##### Beyond the view: subscribes, the long-video link, shares

- A Short can link to a longer video only through Studio's Related video field: one link per Short, on the same channel, added after upload, and only with advanced feature access. The Data API cannot set it. YouTube's July 2026 advice is to ask for the click in the last 5 seconds and to deliver the Short's promise in the long video's first 5-10 seconds. It publishes no conversion numbers (growth-21).
- An agency study of 18,000 channels (March 2025-March 2026) put the best Shorts share at 25-40% of uploads, with long-form doing worse above 55%. It quotes a Short-to-long conversion rate rising "from 0.04% to 0.5%" with the Related video link and a spoken call to action, but does not say how it measured this (growth-21).
- In science and tech, channels posting only long videos had about 16% more subscribers than mixed channels at 1M-10M subscribers (284,000 vs 244,500). That is correlation only (growth-21).
- On one audited channel, Shorts brought about 91% of views but about 6% of watch hours. This comes from a different AIR page (updated 2026-10-23), not the 18,000-channel study (growth-21).

##### Measuring

- Studio gives, per Short: Shown in feed, Stayed to watch, engaged views, views, average view duration and subscribers (02-shorts-editing-and-cost.md lines 31-35; growth-2).
- The YouTube Analytics API gives engagedViews, views, averageViewDuration, averageViewPercentage, likes, shares, comments, subscribersGained, retention curves and traffic sources. It has no Shorts-specific metric: no Stayed-to-watch and no Shown-in-feed (growth-3).
- API data usually runs 48-72 hours behind (stated on the Data Model page, not the Metrics page) (growth-3).
- The API's engagedViews definition was updated on 2026-08-27 and now reads "viewed past the first frame, or the user clicks/taps to play". That differs from Studio's "past the initial seconds, not including any loops", so API and Studio engaged views may not match one to one. Do not mix data from before and after August 2026 (growth-m5).
- In a report filtered to one video, subscribersGained "will only include statistics from the specified video's watch page." It may therefore undercount subscribes made in the Shorts player; we could not confirm this (growth-3).
- **Our own baseline.** The company channel's app-made Shorts had a median of 16 public views from 30 Oct to 14 Nov 2026, at 35-50 a week, posted in bursts. One Short held about 27% of all views (growth-22). Views per Short are heavily skewed, so judge on medians and on the share of Shorts above a mark, never on averages.

#### What this means for our build

1. **Cadence and ramp-up (our estimate, built on growth-1, 9, 11, 12, 13 and 14).** Default to 1 Short a day in week 1, 2 a day in week 2, and 3 a day by week 4 if the gate below holds. Allow up to 4-6 a day by week 8, never more than 6. Never post less than 1 hour apart, and keep at least 3 hours between public go-lives as a precaution (growth-12; the data supports avoiding sub-hour bursts, not a specific 3-hour rule). Longer clips count toward the same daily cap. Make the cap a setting, not a constant. The notification pause (growth-14) is a weak reason on a new channel; the cap rests on policy risk and the unknown upload limit.
2. **Ramp gate.** Raise the rate only when all of these hold over the last 20 Shorts that are at least 7 days old:
   - The median Stayed-to-watch is no lower than in the previous step.
   - Median engaged views are not falling.
   - There are no policy emails, strikes, Content ID claims on Shorts or limit errors.
   If any fails, step back one level for a week.
3. **Upload limit handling.** Upload privately with a scheduled publish time well ahead of the slot, so a "Daily upload limit reached" error never leaves a slot empty. On that error, stop uploading for 24 hours and log it; never retry in a loop (growth-9). Do the channel's phone verification on day 1, and ID verification if offered, to raise the limit (growth-9); only the primary channel owner can do the ID check and Brand Accounts get an error, so confirm early that the new channel can get it (growth-m4). API quota is not the constraint for uploads (growth-10), but budget thumbnail, caption and playlist calls against the 10,000-unit pool (growth-m7).
4. **Originality gate before upload. This is the main way to protect views (growth-4, 5, 6).** Each Short must carry something of ours beyond crop, captions and a template:
   - a spoken or on-screen framing line written for that clip (a claim, a question, a "why this matters");
   - a sourced context card;
   - or a combination of two sources.
   The pipeline should reject a Short whose only change from the source is a re-frame, captions and a branded wrapper. Vary the layout and the opening style from clip to clip so the channel does not look templated (growth-5). Never post the same moment twice (growth-6). Permission from the source channel does not replace this gate (growth-m1).
5. **Keep every clip of someone else's footage at 60 seconds or less** (growth-18). Default to 20-45 s (growth-19). Allow 46-60 s only when the idea needs it.
6. **Open on the claim.** The first second shows readable text that states the point, and the clip starts on the strongest line, not the setup (02-shorts-editing-and-cost.md lines 68-78). Make captions readable and keep them light. No glossy motion-graphic extras until they win an A/B test. This is the first place /brag-style editing would have to prove itself, measured on Stayed-to-watch, not looks.
7. **Packaging.** Use a plain search phrase in the title and 1-3 topic hashtags, and drop #shorts (growth-17). Don't build posting-time optimisation (growth-17). Don't auto-delete weak Shorts (growth-16).
8. **Long-video link.** Each longer clip goes live before the Shorts that point to it. Add a spoken and on-screen pointer in the last 5 seconds. Make a weekly Studio task list of the top Shorts by engaged views that need their Related video set, since the API can't do it (growth-21).
9. **Measurement module.**
   - At 48 hours, read Studio's Shown in feed and Stayed to watch by hand or from a Studio export, plus public viewCount from `videos.list`.
   - At 7 and 28 days, pull engagedViews, averageViewPercentage, shares, comments and channel-level subscribersGained from the Analytics API (growth-3). Check API engagedViews against a Studio export before treating them as equal, and do not mix data from before and after August 2026 (growth-m5, growth-m6).
   - Store everything per Short together with its source channel, length, opening style and layout, so formats can be compared.
   - Judge a change only after about 20-30 Shorts per arm are 7 days old, compared on medians (our estimate, given how skewed the views are, growth-22).
10. **Separate channel, separate blast radius.** Run this system on its own channel, never the company channel, and keep its uploads at the cautious end of every policy (growth-7). Avoid sharing an app, API project, server, ID verification or featured people with the company channel where possible, since YouTube's rules reach channels linked to a terminated owner (growth-m2, growth-m8). Settle this as an owner decision before building. See owner decisions.

**Early signs that a Short worked (our estimate, to be recalibrated after the first 60 Shorts):**
- At 48 h: Shown in feed is more than about 10 times the channel median. Alternatively, Stayed to watch is above the channel's running median.
- At 7 days: engaged views are above the channel's 75th percentile, with at least 1 subscriber.

Realistic starting range for a new clips channel: medians in the tens to low hundreds of public views per Short for the first 4-8 weeks. This rests on our own median of 16 (growth-22), the 300-Short test where 76% of Shorts got under 100 views (growth-11), and talk clips at about 600 on established channels (growth-20). The vidIQ cohort's roughly 1,300 is an optimistic upper reference (growth-15); vendor medians from OverseerOS cover established channels and predate the October 2026 originality change.

#### Risks and unknowns

- **Reach cut for being "mainly re-uploads" (high impact, likely if clips are lightly edited).** YouTube defines neither "primarily" nor "significant", and gave no start date (growth-4). To check cheaply, watch Shorts-feed views by traffic source each week. A steady fall while other sources hold is the sign. Compare Shorts with a framing line against plain clips.
- **Termination spreading to the company channel.** The rule bars a terminated owner from "using, possessing, or creating any other YouTube channels", and covers channels where the same people are prominently featured (growth-7, growth-m2). We could not confirm how YouTube links channels to an owner (same Google account, Brand Account managers, payment profile, ID verification). Treat it as a real risk until someone asks YouTube support.
- **Unknown daily upload limit.** The only data point is an undated anecdote of 16 a day (growth-11). A cautious ramp will find our channel's limit without breaking the schedule.
- **Permission does not make a clip original.** Even with the source channels' consent, the reused-content policy still applies and the views earn nothing from the Shorts Creator Pool (growth-m1, growth-m3). Copyright and Content ID are another strand's subject; for views, a claim on a clip over 60 s blocks it (growth-18).
- **Most numbers here are vendor data on public views, which count replays.** They favour short, loopable clips and may overstate effects (growth-12, 13, 19). None is causal.
- **No official hook length, no official benchmark for Stayed-to-watch, and no per-Short subscriber count from the API that we can trust** (growth-3). Use Studio and our own running medians.
- **The 30-day lock is an experiment** with unknown eligibility (growth-8). Don't plan on getting a grace period.
- **"Shorts that convert to long views" is poorly measured.** The only figure we found has no stated method (growth-21).
- **View definitions changed.** Two changes (March 2025 and August 2026) mean older and newer view numbers are not comparable (growth-m6).
- **Source limits.** The growth-4 quotes rest on news reports, not the primary TeamYouTube post. Growth-1's official statement is from 2023.

- Earlier project research (local): research/youtube-growth/02-shorts-editing-and-cost.md section 3 (lines 29-99); data/shorts-verified-findings.json (shorts_views-1, -2, -3, -6, -8, -11, -12; crosspost-2, -10, -15); data/traffic-verified-findings.json (algorithm-7, algorithm-10, api-10, api-12). Written 2026-11-14.

Checked on 2026-11-14 by 2 independent fact-checker(s) (primary; realism): 27 confirmed, 4 corrected, 0 removed, 1 unverified.

### A2. How clips channels really grow, and why many die

**The short answer.** The clips channels that grow in our kind of niche (tech, AI, business, podcasts) are almost all run by the show itself, sit on top of a main channel with millions of subscribers, and post about one item a day, mostly horizontal cut-downs of 10-30 minutes, not dozens of Shorts (clips-12, clips-13, clips-14, clips-15). A channel that automatically re-posts other people's clips is the exact pattern YouTube is acting against right now: on 1 October 2026 YouTube announced that channels "primarily aggregating or re-uploading other creators' videos without significant changes" will likely see less distribution within the Shorts feed (announced that day, no start date given) (clips-3), and the monetisation rule rejects promoting other people's content "even if you have permission" (clips-1). Posting every hour does not fix this and probably makes it worse: Diary of a CEO tested doubling its clips output and total views stayed flat (one practitioner anecdote, with an unclear measurement window) (clips-13), and a termination on one channel can bar the same person from every other channel they run; copyright strikes are the more likely route for clips and reach "any associated channels", which reaches the company channel (clips-4, clips-m1). If the owner still wants a clips channel, the version with a real chance is: a new separate channel on a separate Google account, a short allow-list of sources that gave written permission, one long topic clip a day plus one or two Shorts on that same channel, each with real added context, and a person approving every upload. Expect most new channels to stay small: even among new channels that added 52 or more videos in a year, about 69% did not reach 1,000 subscribers (clips-20).

#### What we found

##### 1. The operating models in use, 2025-2026

- **Creator-owned clips channels.** The show runs a second channel for cut-downs. Diary of a CEO runs a clips channel of horizontal 10-30 minute cut-downs, a main channel that now carries Shorts too, and phased out a separate Shorts channel (clips-13). These are the channels in our niche that grow steadily (clips-12, clips-15). Caveat: the Diary of a CEO Clips monthly views jumped from about 16-20M to 47-48M in Sep-Oct 2026, so its 28-day figure is a recent spike, not a steady rate (clips-m9).
- **Authorised clippers and paid clipping campaigns.** A creator or brand posts a "bounty"; clippers post clips on their own accounts and are paid per verified view (clips-8). Whop opened a public clipping marketplace in March 2025; typical pay was $1-5 per 1,000 views with a cap per campaign, and Whop took 10% (clips-8). On the Content Rewards listing the median rate on 13 November 2026 was about $1.04 per 1,000 views across 712 live campaigns, $1.20 for YouTube (411 campaigns), with half of campaigns between $1 and $2 (clips-9). Other named marketplaces: Vyro (backed by MrBeast, about $3 per 1,000 views reported), Clipping.io, and agencies such as Clipping Culture (clips-10). Some streamers spend heavily: one reportedly paid clippers $1.4M over five weeks (his own claim, reported by Dexerto, not verified) (clips-11). At realistic early views these campaigns pay very little (clips-m12).
- **Fan clippers without permission.** Anonymous accounts race to cut the same moments; one clipping-tool vendor says a big moment from a well-watched streamer is routinely 30-90 minutes from first clip, with leading channels inside 30 (vendor claim, no data or method) (clips-21). They carry copyright risk (Content ID claims and strikes, policy-8 in 01-traffic-research.md:1213) and reused-content risk (clips-1).
- **Automated AI clip and content farms.** High-volume, templated channels. This is the group being removed: from late 2025, speeding up in January 2026, YouTube terminated 11 and wiped 5 large templated AI channels with about 35M subscribers and 4.7B lifetime views between them, under its spam and inauthentic-content rules (clips-7). These were AI-generated original-style channels, not clip re-uploaders, so they are an analogy for templated automation, not a clips precedent (clips-7).
- **Who grows, who is removed.** Growing: creator-owned clips channels with a big parent (clips-12, clips-15). Stalling: older clips channels with heavy volume or Shorts-heavy output (clips-14, clips-16, clips-17). Removed or demonetised: templated mass producers (clips-7), re-uploaders (clips-5) and, as of September 2026, even a streamer's clips channel run with the streamer's consent (clips-6).

##### 2. The rules that decide whether a clips channel lives

- **Reused content (monetisation rule).** Not allowed: "Clips of moments ... edited together with little or no narrative", "Short videos you compiled from other social media websites", "Content uploaded many times by other creators", "Promotion of other people's content (even if you have permission)", and content copied "without any substantive modifications" (clips-1). Allowed: clips used for critical review, reaction with commentary, "Edited footage from other creators where you add a storyline and commentary" (clips-1). The rule "applies even if you have permission from the original creator", is judged on "your channel as a whole", and a breach can remove monetisation from the entire channel (clips-1). This is a monetisation rule, separate from copyright: a channel can be fine on copyright and still fail here (clips-1).
- **Inauthentic content (renamed 15 July 2025).** Not allowed: templated storylines with little narrative, and "AI-generated content made with generic or unoriginal templates giving the impression of mass production"; the same intro and outro is fine if the bulk of each video differs (clips-2). Channels "where content feels interchangeable from video to video are not allowed to monetize", which templated automatic clips would hit (clips-m3). Earlier research already covers the spam rule on automated mass-production, which applies whether or not a channel is monetised and can end a channel (02-shorts-editing-and-cost.md:97).
- **Shorts reach, announced 1 October 2026.** YouTube announced (a TeamYouTube community post and a Creator Insider video) that Shorts recommendations will "reduce the reach of content re-uploaded from other creators without adding anything of your own", and that channels "primarily aggregating or re-uploading other creators' videos without significant changes" will "likely see less distribution within the Shorts feed" (clips-3). YouTube's Creator Liaison said added value is "not just VO descriptions of what's happening on screen, minor technical edits, or template-based bulk changes" (clips-3). This is a recommendations change, not a monetisation rule. There is no start date, no timescale for re-evaluating a channel that changes (Ritchie said reach is re-evaluated, no timeframe), no detection method, no notice or status indicator, and nothing on clips posted with permission or under licence; 9to5Google (via Dexerto) notes there is no clear threshold for how much original input is enough (clips-3, clips-m4). Long-form clips are not named, so the Shorts-feed effect may not reach horizontal long clips (clips-m4). We could not read the official post's body (see Risks).
- **What reviewers look at.** YouTube's own monetisation page says reviewers may check, for the channel overall, its main theme, most-viewed videos, newest videos, biggest share of watch time, the About section and video metadata (titles, thumbnails, descriptions); for reused content, the videos, channel description, titles and descriptions; and apply the rule if they "cannot clearly tell that you made the content" (clips-1, clips-22). The added claim that a licence or fair use also does not make reused content eligible comes from an agency guide (AIR Media-Tech), not from YouTube's text (clips-22).
- **Termination spreads to other channels.** If a channel is terminated (any termination, not only a Community Guidelines one), "You are prohibited from using, possessing, or creating any other YouTube channels", covering new or acquired channels, existing channels, and channels where you are "repeatedly or prominently featured", which YouTube does not define (clips-4, clips-m2). For a clips channel, copyright strikes are the most likely route to termination: after 3 strikes "Your account, along with any associated channels, is subject to termination" and "You can't create new YouTube channels" (clips-m1). Content ID claims usually do not give strikes, but removal requests do, and a clips channel on the same Google account as the company channel would put the company channel at direct risk (clips-m1). Monetisation penalties can spread too: creator-responsibility violations may turn off monetisation or terminate accounts, possibly across all channels, and earnings can be held up to 90 days during an investigation (clips-m10). A gaming creator lost his own channel after a re-upload channel that had copied his clip was terminated; support's reply, as the article words it, was that he had posted "a terminated user's content", and he was not reinstated as of 10 December 2025 (clips-5).
- **Money thresholds.** Today: 1,000 subscribers plus 4,000 watch hours in 12 months or 10M Shorts views in 90 days; decisions typically in about a month; after a first rejection, appeal within 21 days or reapply after 30 days, and after later rejections 90 days (clips-19). From 1 February 2027, per YouTube's blog of 10 August 2026, new applicants need 8,000 watch hours in 365 days or 20M Shorts views in 90 days, and Shorts ad and subscription revenue needs 10M Shorts views in 90 days; this does not affect creators already in the Partner Programme for entry, but existing members below 10M Shorts views in 90 days keep long-form earnings and lose Shorts revenue share (clips-19, clips-m6).

##### 3. Case studies (data from vidIQ's public stats pages, read 14 November 2026; YouTube's public counts are shortened to three significant digits, so vidIQ sees 10K steps at 1M+ and a "0" month means under about 10K net, not zero (clips-m5); vidIQ estimates the Shorts split)

| Channel | Relationship to source | Created | Subs | Videos | Uploads (our arithmetic) | Lifetime views per video (our arithmetic) | 2026 trend | Id |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| The Diary Of A CEO Clips | Owned by the show (team interview) | 2022-02-17 | 2.95M | 1,420 | about 0.8 a day; team says 1 a day | about 324K | +80K to +140K subs a month; 41.7M views in last 28 days (a recent spike from 16-20M a month to 47-48M in Sep-Oct 2026) | clips-12, clips-13, clips-m9 |
| Huberman Lab Clips | Named as the show's clips; ownership not checked | 2021-07-28 | 1.51M | 582 | about 9 a month | about 242K | +10K to +20K subs a month; 6.8M views in 28 days | clips-15 |
| Lex Clips | Named as the show's clips; ownership not checked | 2019-08-06 | 1.65M | 9,376 | about 3.5 a day | about 68K | 0 to +10K subs a month except January (+30K); 2.65-9.78M views a month | clips-14 |
| JRE Clips | Named as the show's clips; ownership not checked | 2017-01-18 | 8.32M | 6,101 | about 1.7 a day | about 1.0M | Flat or falling subs (-10K in Oct 2026); 13-21M views a month | clips-16 |
| Theo Von Clips | Not checked | 2018-05-14 | 1.47M | 2,294 | about 0.7 a day | about 246K | +20K to +50K subs a month in early-to-mid 2025, about +10K a month in 2026 (0 in June, +20K in July) | clips-17 |
| FLAGRANT CLIPS | Not checked; format of latest upload not checked (tagged #podcast #superbowl #jayz, not #shorts) | 2020-03-20 | 1.04M | 3,187 | about 1.3 a day | about 280K | No change in rounded public sub count in every 2026 month except February (+10K); 2.1-14.8M views a month | clips-17, clips-m13 |

What the table shows (our reading, not a study):
- The fastest-growing clips channel posts about one long clip a day (clips-12, clips-13). The highest-volume one (Lex Clips, about 3.5 a day) earns the fewest views per video and almost no new subscribers in 2026 (clips-14). FLAGRANT CLIPS also posts about 1.3 a day and its subscriber count barely moves, which fits the "high volume stalls" reading (clips-17). That fits YouTube's own statement, cited in earlier research, that volume by itself is neither rewarded nor penalised, and a 37-channel sample where Shorts count had no link to views per Short (02-shorts-editing-and-cost.md:97). Lex Clips posts about 6 times as often as Huberman Lab Clips but gets similar monthly views, which also supports falling per-video returns with volume (clips-14).
- Diary of a CEO tested 2 clips a day against 1 a day: total channel views stayed flat while views per clip fell, and they went back to 1 a day (clips-13). The measurement window is unclear (the guest says a 30 day period, the host's recap says three days), the team's explanation (a per-channel feed cap) is speculation, and this is one anecdote from a mature channel with a famous parent, not a controlled study (clips-13).
- Subscriber counts are a poor success measure for clips channels: FLAGRANT CLIPS gained almost no subscribers in 2026 yet drew 2-15M views a month, and JRE Clips' subscribers were flat while it drew 13-21M views a month (clips-m13).
- Every channel here has a parent show with a large audience and its guests, and all are 4-10 years old. None is a third-party automated channel. This is survivor bias: we found no third-party automated clips channel in these niches with public, checkable growth numbers.
- Title patterns differ by brand. Diary of a CEO Clips leads with an authority label and a warning ("Godfather of AI WARNS", "War Expert WARNS") and capital letters; Lex Clips uses plain "topic | Guest and Lex Fridman" titles (clips-18).

##### 4. Failures and what triggered them

| Case | Date | What happened | Trigger | Id |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Large templated AI channels (11 terminated, 5 wiped; about 35M subs, 4.7B views) | Late 2025 to early 2026 | Terminated or emptied | Spam, deceptive practices and inauthentic content; high-volume templated output (AI-generated channels, not clip re-uploaders) | clips-7 |
| A streamer's clips channel run with the streamer's consent | Sept 2026 (date inferred from the article's publication date) | Removed from the Partner Programme; operator contests it as an error | Reused content: no noticeable contribution to existing content | clips-6 |
| Evolution Army, a re-upload channel | Late 2025 | Terminated | Re-uploading other creators' videos (probably unlicensed) | clips-5 |
| SplashPlate, the original creator of a clip | Late 2025 | Terminated by association, not reinstated as of 10 Dec 2025 | YouTube linked his upload to the terminated channel's copy | clips-5 |

Two lessons for us: permission from the source did not save the streamer's channel (clips-6; the channel was demonetised, not terminated), and enforcement can spill over to linked people and channels (clips-4, clips-5).

##### 5. Shorts versus long clips

- Long horizontal clips of 10-30 minutes drive the strongest creator-owned clips channel; Shorts sit on the main channel, where the team found they did not reduce long-form views and converted better than on a separate Shorts channel (clips-13). A separate Shorts channel cannot link to the long video on the main channel, while Shorts on the same channel can link to it and "it converts" (clips-m7).
- Money from Shorts needs scale a new channel will not have: 10M Shorts views per 90 days for Shorts ads from 1 February 2027, and ads pause below it, so a new clips channel earns no Shorts ad money even after joining the Partner Programme (clips-19, clips-m6). Watch hours from Shorts in the Shorts feed do not count toward the watch-hour route (clips-19).
- Shorts over 1 minute with any copyright claim are blocked (policy-8, 01-traffic-research.md:1213), and clips of other people's footage are the most likely to be claimed.
- Earlier research already found the per-channel sweet spot is low: Shorts did best at 2-4 a week per channel, and long-form views peaked near 5 Shorts a month (Metricool, 02-shorts-editing-and-cost.md:95).
- So: long clips should be fewer and better, and Shorts should point at them. We found no evidence that 24 posts a day beats 1-3.

##### 6. Speed

- We found no measured data on how soon after a source video winning clips go up. The only figure (routinely 30-90 minutes for a big moment from a well-watched streamer, leading channels inside 30) comes from a clipping-tool vendor with no method or dataset, published 27 April 2026 and updated 12 November 2026; it gives no figure for podcasts (clips-21).
- An off-the-shelf vendor (AutoClip, paid Starter, Pro and Scale plans) already sells a monitor-sources, cut and auto-publish pipeline, the same automatic flow the owner proposes, so being fast and automatic is commodity, not an edge (clips-m8).
- For podcast sources that run their own clips channel, the source posts its own cut-downs, so a third party competes with the owner for the same moment, and copies uploaded many times are named in the reused-content rule (clips-1, clips-12).

##### 7. Honest expectations (our estimates, not measurements)

The base rate: in vidIQ's September 2026 study of 32.9M channels, among channels starting under 1,000 subscribers, 30.77% of those that added 52 or more videos in 360 days reached 1,000, versus 8.65% for 12-51 videos (clips-20). The study is observational and has no bucket above 52 videos, does not separate formats, and has no clips or reused-content cut (clips-20).

| Cadence | 30 days | 90 days | 180 days |
|---|---|---|---|
| 24 a day, automatic, no added commentary | Likely early views from a few Shorts, then falling reach as the October 2026 change applies; real risk of a spam or reused-content action | Likely demoted; a Partner application would most likely be refused for reused content; possible termination that reaches the owner's other channels | Most likely dead or demonetised |
| 3-6 a day, automatic, light templates | Tens to low hundreds of views per upload, a rare outlier | Under 1,000 subscribers is the most likely outcome | Partner review is a coin-flip at best; template edits are named as not enough |
| 1 long clip + 1-2 Shorts a day, with permission, real context, human approval | Tens of views per upload | A few hundred subscribers if a source fits the niche | 1,000 subscribers plausible but under 50% (base rate clips-20); 4,000 watch hours unlikely within 6 months |

These are judgments from the cases, the base rate and the rules. Correcting for survivor bias: the successful channels above all had a famous parent, and we found no checkable success story for a third-party automated clips channel in these niches. Most such channels likely get nowhere; the 69% figure from clips-20 is an estimate for the most active new channels in general, not a bound for clips channels.

#### What this means for our build

1. **Never post to the company channel.** Build the clips system to upload only to a new, separate channel, with its own OAuth credentials and its own config. Hard-code a refusal to use the production channel's token. Reason: the reused-content rule judges the whole channel (clips-1), and the October 2026 change cuts Shorts-feed reach for aggregating channels (clips-3).
2. **A separate channel is not full isolation.** A termination can bar the same person from using other channels (clips-4), copyright strikes put "any associated channels" at risk (clips-m1), and enforcement has spread to linked creators (clips-5). So the new channel must not be a brand account or channel under the same Google account as the company channel, and the plan must treat termination as a risk to the company channel, not only to the clips channel. Get the owner's explicit sign-off on this risk.
3. **Source allow-list with permission records.** Only clip channels on an allow-list, each with a stored written permission (or a paid clipping campaign brief) and the date. No permission, no clip. Permission does not satisfy the monetisation rule (clips-1, clips-6), but it removes most copyright-strike risk (policy-8) and opens paid-per-view campaigns, which at early-stage views would pay only a few dollars a month, so do not count on them as meaningful income (clips-8, clips-9, clips-m12).
4. **Every upload must add something.** Required, not optional: a topic angle across several sources (for example "what three AI founders said about agents this week"), on-screen context cards written for the clip, and a description that explains the context. AI voice-over that describes the screen and template edits are named as not enough (clips-3). Best option: a short recorded human intro or commentary per long clip.
5. **Default cadence: 1 long clip and 1-2 Shorts a day, at least 3 hours apart.** Hard ceiling configurable, default 4 uploads a day. Hourly posting stays off. Reasons: clips-13 (one anecdote: doubling output gave flat views), 02-shorts-editing-and-cost.md:92 (notifications pause after more than 3 publishes in a short period), and the spam rule on mass-production (02-shorts-editing-and-cost.md:97).
6. **Formats.** Long clips: horizontal 8-20 minutes, one idea each (clips-13). Shorts: 60 seconds or less (policy-8), each linking to its long clip. Post the Shorts and the long clips on the same new channel so the Shorts can link to the long clips (clips-m7).
7. **Skip what the source already posted.** Before rendering, check the source's own clips channel and Shorts for the same moment and drop duplicates ("content uploaded many times by other creators", clips-1).
8. **Speed is not the strategy.** Poll sources every 30-60 minutes, but aim to publish within 24 hours after human approval. Our edge is context and topic grouping, not being first or being automatic (clips-21 has no data behind the speed race; clips-m8).
9. **Human approval on every upload for at least the first 90 days.** Fully automatic posting of third-party clips is the pattern under enforcement (clips-3, clips-7).
10. **Kill switches.** Pause all uploads on: any Content ID claim or copyright strike, any Community Guidelines warning, a Partner rejection, YouTube's automatic pause after unusual activity (gap3-14, 01-traffic-research.md:208), or a source revoking permission.
11. **Measure and gate.** Track views at 7 and 28 days and percentage viewed per upload; do not gate on subscribers, which move little even on channels with millions of views (clips-m13). YouTube gives no status indicator or notice for Shorts-feed demotion, so the build needs its own view-trend detection (clips-m11). Gate at day 30 and day 90: if median views per upload stay under about 100 at day 90, stop rather than raise volume.
12. **Set the privacy status on every upload explicitly.** Earlier local research records that the rule forcing uploads from unaudited API projects to private was lifted on 2 November 2026, so an upload with no privacy setting now goes public. Upload as private or scheduled until a human approves (clips-m14).

#### Risks and unknowns

- **We could not read the official 1 October 2026 post** (support.google.com/youtube/thread/470890423 returned only navigation, also with ?hl=en). Its wording comes from news reports (Search Engine Journal, PPC Land, Dexerto) quoting it and YouTube's Creator Liaison (clips-3). The Creator Insider video was not opened. Cheap check: open the post in a browser while signed out.
- **How YouTube treats licensed clips under the new Shorts rule is unknown** (clips-3). The monetisation rule says permission does not help (clips-1). Cheap check: ask TeamYouTube or the channel's partner manager before launch.
- **Linked-channel termination.** We don't know how YouTube decides two channels are linked (shared Google account, shared payment, shared person on camera; "repeatedly or prominently featured" is not defined). This is the main risk to the production channel (clips-4, clips-5, clips-m1). Ask counsel or YouTube support before building.
- **vidIQ figures are third-party estimates,** rounded to 10K subscribers (YouTube's public counts have three significant digits), with no published Shorts/long split (clips-12 to clips-17, clips-m5). Ownership of Lex Clips, Huberman Lab Clips, JRE Clips, Theo Von Clips and FLAGRANT CLIPS was not checked.
- **No third-party success case.** We found no checkable numbers for a third-party automated clips channel in our niches, so the expectations table is a judgment.
- **Speed data is vendor marketing** (clips-21).
- **Marketplace rates move** (clips-9; a 10 Nov article on the same site gave different figures) and earlier figures came from guides with a stake in the market (clips-8, clips-10).
- **The owner's "top 6 channels" are not named.** If they have their own clips channels or Content ID, our clips will compete with or be claimed by them. Check each source for an official clips channel and a clipping campaign before building.
- **The B0ary case may be reversed on appeal** (clips-6). Watch for the outcome. It is a single case sourced from the operator's own post, and the article says it is unclear whether it was a mistake or stricter enforcement.
- **Whether the 1,000-subscriber minimum stays for new Partner applicants after 1 February 2027** was not confirmed in the official blog fetch; secondary coverage says it stays.
- **Not fully checked:** the Lex Clips title pattern (second half of clips-18) and the last part of the Nathan Barry transcript.
