### A3. The rules: copyright, YouTube policy, and what makes clipping allowed

**The short answer.** Posting clips of other people's channels without written permission is the fastest way to lose a channel. Three copyright strikes end the channel, every channel linked to it, and the right to start new ones (policy-1, policy-14). A credit line or a "no copyright intended" note doesn't protect us (policy-5). Even with permission, YouTube's reused-content rule can keep a pure clip channel out of monetisation (policy-11), and views on non-original Shorts earn nothing, so plan for zero Shorts revenue (policy-m3). Since 1 October 2026 the Shorts feed also cuts reach for re-uploads that add nothing of their own, judged at the channel level (policy-12, policy-m10). So the clip system should only post (1) our own footage, (2) clips we hold a written licence for, or (3) properly checked CC BY or public-domain videos. It should add real commentary or framing to every clip, and it must run on a Google account and Cloud project with no link to the company channel. Because a termination bars the person and not only the account, the people who run it should have no role on the company channel (policy-m11). Ask a lawyer before launch, and get written answers from the rights holders. This section is not legal advice.

#### What we found

Earlier research already covers our own-footage risks: Content ID on Shorts, the spam rule's mass-production clause, strikes that block uploads, the consent rules for automatic uploads, privacy complaints and synthetic-media labels. See 01-traffic-research.md lines 1208-1218 (its ids policy-4, policy-6, policy-8, policy-12 and policy-14) and 02-shorts-editing-and-cost.md section 7, lines 272-318. The ids below are new to this section. Where an old file's id appears, it is written as "01:policy-8".

##### Copyright strikes, claims and counter-notices

- **Copyright strike.** A strike means YouTube removed a video after a legal takedown request (a formal complaint from the rights holder, also called a DMCA notice) that looked valid. It is separate from a Community Guidelines strike (policy-1).
- **How long a strike lasts.** A strike expires after 90 days, but only once the channel has finished "Copyright School", a short YouTube course (policy-1).
- **Three strikes.** At 3 active strikes, "your account and any associated channels" can be terminated, and "You cannot create new channels" (policy-1). YouTube's 2025 "second chance" pilot, which lets some terminated creators ask for a new channel after a year, excludes creators terminated for copyright infringement (policy-1).
- **Linked channels.** If a linked channel reaches 3 strikes, your channel can be terminated too, and the other way round. Deleting the video doesn't remove the strike, except for a "scheduled" takedown, where you get 7 days to delete it first (policy-1).
- **Content ID claim.** This is an automatic match against a rights holder's reference file. It is not a strike. The owner can block the video, put ads on it and take the money, or just track it, and the choice can differ by country (policy-2).
- **Disputing a claim.** After a dispute the claimant has 30 days to answer, and 7 days to answer an appeal. At any point the claimant can switch to a legal takedown, which gives us a strike. Abusing disputes is penalised (policy-2).
- **Claimed Shorts.** A Short longer than 1 minute with an active claim is blocked "regardless of the policy". Vertical videos of 1-3 minutes have counted as Shorts since 15 October 2024 (8 December 2025 for Official Artist Channels and channels linked to a music Content Owner). A video over 3 minutes, or a Short of 1 minute or less, is not blocked automatically, but the claimant's chosen policy (monetise, track or block, possibly by country) still applies, so it can still be blocked (policy-3). For clips of other creators' videos, any Short over 60 seconds that matches is gone, and one at 60 seconds or less can still be claimed or blocked.
- **Counter-notice.** This is the formal answer to a takedown. It may only be filed if the removal was a mistake or a misidentification, fair use included. It needs a person's full legal name, address and phone number, and YouTube must pass all three to the claimant. It also needs a statement made under penalty of perjury. An uploader outside the US consents to the courts of the judicial district where YouTube is located (policy-4).
- **After a counter-notice.** The claimant has 10 US business days to show it has started a court case. If it doesn't, the video comes back (policy-4). In practice, a counter-notice invites a US lawsuit.

##### Fair use and similar exceptions

- **Who decides.** YouTube doesn't decide fair use, and Content ID can't. Only courts can (policy-5).
- **What doesn't help.** Credit lines, "I do not own this", "no infringement intended" and "for entertainment only" don't make a copy fair. Nor do your own additions if they bring no new meaning or message (policy-5).
- **Outside the US.** The EU allows only listed uses: quotation, criticism, review, caricature, parody and pastiche. Other countries use "fair dealing", which works differently (policy-5).
- **The US test.** The US Copyright Office says courts judge each case on its own facts. No length of clip is safe. Courts weigh the harm to the original's market, including what would happen if the practice became widespread (policy-6).
- **Case: reaction video, fair use.** A 14-minute reaction video used about 3 minutes 15 seconds of a 5 minute 24 second skit. It was found fair use because criticism ran all the way through it and it couldn't replace the original. The court said not every reaction video is fair use (policy-7).
- **Case: clip service, not fair use.** TVEyes sold clips of TV broadcasts. The appeals court accepted that the service served a transformative purpose, but still found it not fair use, because it made available "virtually all" of Fox's content that clients wanted and deprived Fox of revenue that properly belongs to the copyright holder (policy-8).
- **What that means for us.** A clip channel posting a creator's best moments with light edits looks like TVEyes, not like the reaction video (own reading of policy-7 and policy-8).
- **UK example.** UK law allows fair dealing for criticism, review and quotation. For criticism or review the work must already be public and the acknowledgement must be sufficient (unless that is impossible). A quotation needs the same, and in addition the extent can be no more than the specific purpose requires (policy-9). So outside the US, credit is a precondition but never enough on its own.
- **If the company is outside the US.** It still faces YouTube's US-law process, because counter-notices bind it to US courts (policy-4). Its home country's law applies on top. We don't know the company's country, so a local lawyer must confirm which exceptions apply.

##### YouTube's own rules that hit clip channels

- **Spam policy.** It bans "using automated tools or AI to churn out high volumes of similar content with minimal changes". It also bans re-posting "other videos without adding anything of your own" and malicious clickbait. Penalties are removal, a warning, strikes (3 in 90 days can end the channel), loss of monetisation or termination (policy-10).
- **Hourly posting.** At one post an hour, 24 automatic posts a day, an unlicensed clip channel fits the first two bans word for word (own reading of policy-10).
- **Reused-content rule (who can earn money).** These are not allowed: clips "edited together with little or no narrative", and "Short videos you compiled from other social media websites". The rule "applies even if you have permission from the original creator" (policy-11).
- **What reused content is allowed.** Reaction videos with commentary, "edited footage from other creators where you add a storyline and commentary", and clips used for a critical review (policy-11).
- **Inauthentic-content rule.** It was renamed on 15 July 2025, and the page lists no change since. It excludes templated, mass-produced content, including AI content made "with generic or unoriginal templates" (policy-11).
- **The 1 October 2026 Shorts update.** YouTube said it will "reduce the reach of content re-uploaded from other creators without adding anything of your own". Channels "primarily aggregating or re-uploading" get less distribution, and "minor technical edits or template-based changes" are not enough (policy-12).
- **Where the update came from.** The source is a YouTube Help Community post, which we read only through news coverage. No rollout date was given, and it doesn't say whether licensed clips are treated differently (policy-12).
- **Impersonation.** Copying a creator's name, avatar, banner or colour scheme is banned. So is adding "Backup", "Shorts" or "Live" to their name. A fan channel must state so explicitly in its channel name or handle; the page doesn't require the literal word "fan". Using someone's AI-generated likeness or voice to falsely imply they own or authorise the content is also banned, and disclosing the AI use doesn't excuse it (policy-13).
- **Termination and new channels.** Terminated users may not use, own or create other channels to get round it. That covers existing channels, new ones and channels where the person is "repeatedly or prominently featured". Appeals must come within 1 year, and at most 2 are allowed (policy-14).
- **YouTube Terms of Service, effective 15 December 2023.** They ban downloading any content "unless expressly authorized" or with written permission. They ban access "using any automated means (such as robots, botnets or scrapers)" except for public search engines or with YouTube's prior written permission. They ban harvesting information that identifies people, faces included (policy-15).
- **Our existing downloader.** The repo already has a yt-dlp downloader (ingest/youtube.py line 99, `download_youtube`) (policy-24). Pointed at other people's channels, it would break the download ban (own reading of policy-15).
- **A creator's licence is not YouTube's permission.** The download exception needs YouTube's prior written permission "and, if applicable, the respective rights holders". A creator can license their copyright to us, but that covers only the rights-holder half; YouTube's own permission is still needed (policy-15, policy-m2). A lawyer should still confirm.

##### YouTube API rules for an automatic uploader

- **Developer policies.** An API client (our uploader app) must not "download, import, backup, cache, or store copies of YouTube audiovisual content" without YouTube's prior written approval. It must not facilitate copyright infringement or scrape (policy-16).
- **Automatic uploads are allowed with consent.** The app needs the user's "prior specific and express consent", and the user must keep "final control" over what is published. Nothing we read bans scheduled automatic uploads as such (policy-16).
- **Audits.** YouTube may survey, monitor or audit how an app uses the API, and a quota increase needs a compliance audit for the approved use only. Changing the use case means resubmitting the audit (policy-16).
- **API Terms of Service.** YouTube may monitor and inspect the app, and suspend or end its API access. The terms grant no right to reproduce or distribute audiovisual content (policy-17).
- **What that means for us.** An audit would look at the app's whole use case. A clip uploader sharing a Cloud project with the production app puts that app's API access at risk (own reading of policy-16 and policy-17). The developer policies also make a separate project a rule (policy-m1).

##### What makes clipping allowed

- **Written licence.** Content Rewards, a clipping marketplace and an interested vendor, says a campaign's permission covers that campaign's footage only, on the stated platform (policy-23).
- **What a licence doesn't clear.** The clipper still promises to clear music and other third-party material, and to get releases from identifiable people (policy-23). So a licence must name what it covers: the source videos, editing, platform, monetisation, length, duration of the deal and how to withdraw. It must also cover what the creator doesn't own (own estimate).
- **Shorts Remix.** This is YouTube's built-in tool for using another video's clip in a Short. Remixing is on by default, and creators can opt out. Remixes link back to the original. If the original is deleted, video remixes are deleted (policy-19).
- **Remix doesn't cover our uploads.** Copyrighted material used in Shorts made outside YouTube's tools may still get a Content ID claim or a takedown (policy-19). So Remix is not a licence for files we upload through the API.
- **Creative Commons CC BY.** This is a licence that lets anyone reuse a work if they credit it. A creator sets it in Studio, and viewers find CC videos with the search filter or in the description. Users must credit the title, author, source address and licence. A video with a Content ID claim can't carry CC BY. YouTube can't grant rights to someone else's content (policy-18).
- **The risk of a wrong label.** If the uploader didn't own what they marked CC BY, the label gives us nothing (own reading of policy-18). Keep CC BY sources to channels that clearly own their footage.
- **Public-domain and government material.** We didn't check this in this session. US federal works are generally public domain, but that is background knowledge, not checked here. Record the legal basis for each source and have a lawyer confirm the category.
- **People shown in clips.** Anyone uniquely identifiable can file a privacy complaint. Making the video private is not an accepted fix. YouTube suspends accounts that violate privacy, and re-posting the same people invites more complaints (policy-20).

##### Disclosures and extras

- **AI label.** Realistic AI or altered content needs the "altered or synthetic" label. That includes making a real person seem to say or do something they didn't, AI music as the main focus, or altered real events (policy-21).
- **What needs no label.** Captions, colour fixes, AI-written titles and scripts, and cloning your own voice (policy-21).
- **What the label does.** It doesn't limit reach. Repeatedly skipping it can bring a forced label, removal or suspension from monetisation (policy-21).
- **An AI voice over a real creator's clip.** If it could pass for that creator, it is also impersonation (policy-13, policy-21).
- **Made for kids.** Every video must be marked "made for kids" or not, wherever the creator lives. Getting it wrong can bring YouTube penalties and legal consequences under COPPA, the US children's privacy law (policy-22).
- **Music.** Music inside a source clip is usually owned by a third party, and Content ID matches music most often (policy-2). The creator's licence doesn't clear it (policy-23).

##### Added by the fact-checkers

- **One API project per client (policy-m1).** The developer policies say each API client must have exactly one API project, and one project must not serve several clients. So the clip uploader needs its own Cloud project, as a rule. They also bar creating new accounts, credentials or projects to get round a suspension, and the API terms bar circumventing quota. Extra quota may be used only for the approved use case, and a changed use case means a new compliance audit.
- **The download exception needs both parties (policy-m2).** The ToS wording is "prior written permission from YouTube and, if applicable, the respective rights holders". A creator's licence alone does not meet it. Having creators send files directly is the only clean path.
- **Shorts monetisation for clip channels (policy-m3).** Views on non-original Shorts (unedited clips from others' movies or TV, re-uploads of other creators' content, compilations with no original content) are ineligible and not counted for revenue. From 1 February 2027 a channel needs at least 10 million qualified Shorts views in the last 90 days to share Shorts ad revenue. The page is ambiguous about whether this already applies. A new clip channel should plan for zero Shorts revenue.
- **The 60-second cap is narrow (policy-m4).** Keeping Shorts at 60 seconds or less only avoids the automatic block on claimed Shorts over 1 minute. The claim, and a claimant's block policy (possibly by country), still apply (policy-3).
- **Remix is no route for real clips (policy-m5).** The Cut option takes only a 1-5 second segment. Audio remixes of a deleted original are muted, set to Unlisted and deleted after 30 days. The page describes Remix only in the app and Studio, with no Data API path, so the automatic uploader can't use it.
- **Copyright Match Tool (policy-m6).** It shows rights holders matching videos on YouTube and offers a one-click removal request or "Contact channel". That makes takedowns of re-uploads easy for the source channels. The page doesn't say how partial clips are detected, and says partial song use isn't surfaced.
- **Bot-check workarounds in our downloader (policy-m7).** ingest/youtube.py lines 60-68 add a cookies file and a proxy to get past YouTube's bot check. Reusing that path for high-volume pulls from other channels would compound the ToS automated-access ban (policy-15), so the clip system should not carry these options over.
- **Retraction ends a strike (policy-m8).** Besides Copyright School and counter-notices, a retraction by the claimant resolves a copyright strike. That supports getting written licences from rights holders who can retract (policy-1).
- **A voiceover that only describes the clip is not enough (policy-m9).** In a Creator Insider video, as reported by Search Engine Journal (2026-10-01), YouTube's Rene Ritchie said remixing another creator's clip needs real added value, "not just VO descriptions of what's happening on screen, minor technical edits, or template-based bulk changes". An automatic voiceover that only recaps the clip is the case named as not enough.
- **The reach cut is judged by channel (policy-m10).** Per the same report and Social Media Today (2026-10-01), YouTube gives less Shorts distribution to channels "primarily aggregating or re-uploading" and will re-evaluate reach when a channel shifts to original content. A new channel made mostly of other people's clips would be classed that way from day one, and one good clip would not lift it. YouTube suggests sharing other creators' videos in the Posts tab instead (PPC Land summary).
- **Termination binds the person (policy-m11).** A terminated user is "prohibited from using, possessing, or creating any other YouTube channels", existing ones included. If the owner or a company manager runs the clip channel and it is terminated, that person may lose the right to use the company channel, however separate the Google accounts are. Separate accounts do not shield the people.
- **Reused-content violations are judged channel-wide (policy-m12).** The page says the policy "applies to your channel as a whole" and that "monetization may be removed from your entire channel" (policy-11).
- **Quota at 24 posts a day (policy-m13).** On the official quota page, videos.insert has its own bucket of 100 calls a day, so 24 uploads fit. On the shared 10,000-unit bucket, captions.insert costs 400, thumbnails.set 50, playlistItems.insert 50 and videos.update 50. By the checker's arithmetic, 24 x (400 + 50 + 50) = 12,000 units, over 10,000. Uploading caption tracks for every hourly post would need a quota extension, and so an audit of a clip-uploader use case.
- **Unverified API projects (policy-m14).** The videos.insert page says uploads from unverified API projects are not restricted to private viewing mode, and no longer mentions the July 2020 audit lock. A new project's uploads would not be stuck private before an audit.
- **New accounts and long videos (policy-m15).** New accounts can upload videos only up to 15 minutes until phone verification. This matters for any longer clip format.

#### What this means for our build

**Risk by sourcing model.** "Strike risk" means a legal takedown. "Content ID risk" means an automatic claim. The ratings are our own judgment from the findings cited, not measured rates.

| Sourcing model | Legal exposure | Strike risk | Content ID risk | Monetisation | Evidence to keep |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Own content | None for our own footage. Third-party media inside it is still a risk (01:policy-8) | Low | Low, except music or screen shares | Yes, if not templated mass output (policy-11) | Source meeting id and consent register (02 section 7) |
| Written permission or licence | Low within its scope. Music and people in the clip aren't covered (policy-23) | Low within scope. High if outside scope or after withdrawal | Medium: the licensor's own Content ID may still match. Ask the licensor whether they can exempt our channel (not checked this session) | Uncertain: reused-content rule applies "even if you have permission" (policy-11). Non-original Shorts earn no Shorts revenue (policy-m3) | Signed licence naming videos, platform, edits, monetisation, term, withdrawal process, any Content ID exemption; licensor contact; dated copy |
| Public clip policy or clipping programme | Low within the published terms, which can change (policy-23) | Low to medium | Medium | Uncertain (policy-11). Paid programmes may need a sponsorship disclosure (vendor claim, policy-23) | Dated capture of terms each time we use it; campaign id; payout records |
| CC BY on YouTube | Low if the uploader really owned the work. High if the label is wrong (policy-18) | Low to medium | Low (a claimed video can't carry CC BY when labelled), but a claim can arrive later | Uncertain (policy-11) | Dated capture of the licence and channel page; attribution text used (policy-18) |
| Public domain or government | Low, but depends on country and work (not checked this session) | Low | Medium: others sometimes register PD material in Content ID (unverified) | Uncertain (policy-11) | Legal basis per work; original source link; lawyer note |
| No permission, heavy commentary or transformation | Medium: fair use is decided case by case, by courts only (policy-5, policy-6, policy-7) | Medium: the owner can still file a takedown, and we'd have to counter-notify under US jurisdiction (policy-4) | High: Content ID matches regardless of commentary (policy-5) | Possible only with real commentary (policy-11) | Script showing the commentary; ratio of our runtime to theirs; lawyer opinion |
| No permission, light edits | High (policy-8) | High: 3 strikes end the channel and linked channels (policy-1) | High | No (policy-11). Also downranked in Shorts (policy-12) and a spam-policy match at volume (policy-10) | None would help: don't do it |

1. **Separate everything from production.** Use a new Google account and a new Brand Account, and never add company channel managers to it. Give it its own Google Cloud project and OAuth client (the developer policies require one project per API client, policy-m1), its own server process or machine, and a different branch (clp). The clip system must never receive a production token. Never create new accounts or projects to get round a suspension or quota (policy-m1). YouTube terminates "associated" and "linked" channels, and we don't know how it decides they are linked, and a termination bars the person from other channels too, so the people who run the clip channel should have no role on the company channel (policy-1, policy-14, policy-17, policy-m11). So separation lowers the risk but doesn't remove it. That is why the content rules below still matter.
2. **Source allow-list with a rights record.** The system ingests only from sources on a list kept in the repo. Each entry has:
   - the channel or URL and the rights holder;
   - the basis: own, licence, programme, CC BY or public domain;
   - the evidence file (the signed licence, a screenshot of the programme terms with its date, or a CC BY page capture with its date);
   - what is allowed: platforms, monetisation, maximum clip length and edits;
   - an expiry date and a revoked flag.
   With no rights record, or an expired one, nothing is ingested (policy-11, policy-18, policy-23).
3. **No downloading from YouTube by default.** Licensed sources send files directly (a shared drive or a download link). `download_youtube` is disabled in the clip system unless a source's rights record holds YouTube's written permission (as well as the rights holder's) or a lawyer's sign-off (policy-15, policy-16, policy-24, policy-m2). Its cookies-file and proxy options are not carried over (policy-m7).
4. **CC BY check.** At ingest, store a dated capture of the licence shown on the page and the uploader's channel. Reject the source if the channel looks like a re-uploader (re-uploads, mixed watermarks). Re-check the licence before each upload (policy-18).
5. **Attribution text.** Every description must start with the template the rights record requires, for example "Clip from <title> by <creator>, <url>, <licence>", plus a music credit where needed. Credit is required for CC BY and UK fair dealing, but it is never a defence on its own (policy-5, policy-9, policy-18).
6. **Real transformation, or don't post.** Every post needs at least one of these: commentary, analysis, or context that makes up a large part of the runtime. A voiceover that only describes what is on screen doesn't count (policy-m9). One template stamped on every clip doesn't count (policy-10, policy-11, policy-12). A step before upload rejects outputs with no added track. If an AI voice is used, it must not sound like the clipped creator, and synthetic media is flagged where it applies (policy-13, policy-21).
7. **Length and music.** Shorts from third-party sources stay at 60 seconds or less. This only avoids the automatic block on claimed Shorts; the claim and any block policy still apply (policy-3, policy-m4). Strip or replace source music unless the licence names it. Run music detection, and treat "unknown" as a hold (policy-2, 01:policy-8).
8. **Rate limit.** The volume is set in settings, not fixed at hourly. Start at a few posts a day (own estimate) and raise it only while claims and warnings stay at zero (policy-10, policy-12). Never post two near-identical clips from the same source window. Keep per-post extras cheap: caption-track uploads at 24 posts a day would exceed the default quota and force an audit (policy-m13).
9. **Circuit breakers.** Any copyright strike, Community Guidelines warning or strike, takedown notice or automatic security pause stops all uploads and alerts the owner (policy-1, 01:gap3-14). A Content ID claim pauses that source. Two claims on one source in 30 days, or three channel-wide, pause the channel (own default). A human must restart it.
10. **Takedown handling.** On a takedown notice or a rights holder's complaint, remove every clip from that source within 24 hours (own default), set the source to revoked, and log it. Don't counter-notify without a lawyer, because it shares a person's legal name and contact details and invites a US court case (policy-4). Don't automate disputes (policy-2).
11. **Privacy queue.** A privacy complaint deletes the video; making it private is not enough (policy-20). Block re-uploads that show the same person.
12. **Upload settings set explicitly.** Set made-for-kids (normally false) and synthetic media on every upload (policy-21, policy-22). Keep the user's final control and consent records as the API rules ask (policy-16).
13. **Audit log.** One append-only record per post: the source and rights record id, licence evidence hash, clip times, edits made, attribution text, upload time, video id, and every later claim, warning, takedown or removal. That is the evidence for a licence dispute, an API audit or an appeal (policy-14, policy-16).
14. **Channel identity.** Use our own name and art. Never use a source creator's name, logo or look, and never add "Clips" or "Shorts" to their name (policy-13).

#### Risks and unknowns

- **Linked-channel risk.** We don't know how YouTube decides two channels are "associated" (policy-1, policy-14). The cheap check is to ask a YouTube partner manager, if the company has one, or a lawyer. The safest default is full separation, including the people (policy-m11).
- **The 1 October 2026 update.** We read the post only through news coverage, the original Help Community post did not open for us, and licensed clips may or may not be exempt (policy-12). Find out by reading the original post, then compare Shorts-feed views on 10-20 licensed test clips with and without commentary.
- **Monetisation.** A licensed clip channel can still fail the reused-content review (policy-11), and non-original Shorts views earn nothing (policy-m3). Plan for no ad revenue until real commentary is proven.
- **The company's country.** We don't know it, so the local copyright exceptions, image rights and privacy law are unconfirmed (policy-5, policy-9). A short call with a local IP lawyer settles it.
- **The ToS download ban with a licence in hand.** A creator's licence alone doesn't meet the ToS exception, which also needs YouTube's written permission (policy-m2). Whether YouTube would grant it for licensed creators' own videos is unconfirmed. Avoid the question by having creators send files directly.
- **Public domain and government works.** These weren't checked this session. Check each source's legal basis before use.
- **Clipping-programme terms.** These differ per programme and can change mid-campaign. The only terms we read came from one vendor (policy-23). Save a dated copy of each programme's terms in the rights record.
- **Hourly volume.** No official page gives a safe number of posts per day. Any number we pick is a guess, so watch warnings and reach and ramp up slowly (policy-10). The quota maths also argues against hourly posts with caption uploads (policy-m13).
- **Page dates.** Most YouTube Help pages show only "©2026 Google", and we read them on 14 November 2026. Rules can change without notice, so re-read the key pages before launch.
- **Not checked by the fact-checkers.** The second citation for policy-14 (answer/2802032), the full Hosseinzadeh and TVEyes opinions, the original Help Community post for policy-12, the automatic-pause page (answer/17366810), whether the synthetic-media and made-for-kids flags can be set through the Data API, any daily channel upload cap, Content ID allowlisting, and public-domain material.
- **Account-level monetisation reading.** The Shorts revenue threshold of 10 million qualified views from 1 February 2027 is ambiguous on whether it already applies (policy-m3).

Checked on 2026-11-14 by 2 independent fact-checker(s) (primary; realism): 35 confirmed, 4 corrected, 0 removed, 0 unverified.

### A4. Which channels to clip: candidates and how to vet them

**The short answer.** None of the big AI, robotics or podcast channels we checked publishes a permission to clip their videos, and two of them (TED and Huberman Lab) publish rules that forbid what an automated clip channel would do (sources-5, sources-6, sources-12, sources-13, sources-15). So "the top 6 channels" cannot be clipped legally on day one; each one needs a written yes first. The material we can use today without asking is public-domain NASA video and talks from the Chaos Computer Club (CCC) archive that state CC BY 4.0 (the licence is set per talk and must be read each time), taken from their own download sites, not from YouTube (sources-4, sources-8, sources-9). YouTube's reused-content rule still applies even when we have permission, so every clip needs real added value, not just a re-cut (sources-3). Even then, YouTube said on 1 Oct 2026 that it is cutting Shorts reach for channels that mainly re-upload other creators' videos, so a channel made only of licensed clips may be down-ranked and a high-volume feed risks strikes (sources-m6, sources-m5). Start with NASA and CCC plus a vetted pool of CC BY videos, at a volume where each clip gets real editorial input, send written permission requests to six field channels the same week, and add each channel only after it says yes in writing.

#### What we found

##### How YouTube marks a video's licence and how to check it

- YouTube offers uploaders only two licences: the standard YouTube licence and Creative Commons Attribution (CC BY). CC BY means anyone may reuse the video, including commercially, as long as they credit the author (sources-1, sources-2).
- YouTube's Help page says to find CC content with the "Creative Commons" search filter and to "look in video descriptions" for licence information. It also says that you must credit the author when you reuse CC BY work (title, author, source URL, licence) and that a video with a Content ID claim cannot be given a CC BY licence (sources-1).
- The Data API shows the licence of any public video in `status.license`, which is either `creativeCommon` or `youtube`. `search.list` can filter with `videoLicense=creativeCommon` (it needs `type=video`) and costs 1 unit from the separate Search Queries quota bucket, which is capped at 100 calls a day (sources-2, sources-m1).
- An uploader can mark someone else's video CC BY by mistake or on purpose. The flag shows what the uploader claimed, not who owns the rights. That is why the checklist below also asks who made the footage.

##### YouTube's own rules that limit any clip channel

- **Downloading.** YouTube's Terms of Service (effective 15 Dec 2023, English US version) forbid users to "access, reproduce, download, distribute..." any content except where the service expressly allows it or YouTube and the rights holders give prior written permission. They also forbid access "using any automated means (such as robots, botnets or scrapers)" (sources-4). Fetching other people's videos with yt-dlp (`ingest/youtube.py`) conflicts with this, even for CC BY videos. A CC licence comes from the rights holder. It is not YouTube's permission to download. (That reading is our interpretation of the Terms, not a quote and not legal advice.)
- **Reused content.** The rule says: "This policy applies even if you have permission from the original creator." It also says it "applies to your channel as a whole". Its examples of content that cannot earn money include "clips of moments from your favorite show edited together with little or no narrative" and content copied "without any substantive modifications". Clips used for a critical review, or footage with added storyline and commentary, are allowed (sources-3). The rule controls monetisation (YouTube Partner Program, YPP). Removal risk comes from the separate spam policy below, and reach risk from the October 2026 change (sources-3, sources-m5, sources-m6).
- **Volume.** The earlier study already found that the spam policy (Help 2801973) applies to all channels, monetised or not. It covers large volumes of similar automated content and can lead to strikes and channel termination. See `research/youtube-growth/02-shorts-editing-and-cost.md` line 97 (sources-20). An hourly feed of clips from other people falls squarely under that rule, so who we clip and how much we add matter as much as what we post.

##### Added by the fact-check

- **sources-m1. Search quota cap.** `search.list` has its own quota bucket capped at 100 calls a day (`videos.insert` has the same 100 a day). `videos.list` and `channels.list` cost 1 unit each from the normal 10,000-unit budget. Discovery of a CC BY pool through the API is limited to about 100 searches a day, so cache results and re-check licences with `videos.list` (sources-m1).
- **sources-m2. Share-alike cannot be carried on YouTube.** ESA (CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO), MIT OCW and SEE (CC BY-NC-SA) require derivatives to carry the same licence. YouTube's upload licence choices are only Standard or CC BY, so a share-alike clip cannot carry its matching licence there. This is our inference from the pages, not a quote, and it weighs further against MIT and ESA in set (b) (sources-m2).
- **sources-m3. CC BY 4.0 duties.** CC BY 4.0 requires attribution, a link to the licence and a note if changes were made. It also warns that publicity, privacy or moral rights may limit use. Our credit template needs a licence link and a "clip edited from the original" note, and people in CC footage still need care (sources-m3).
- **sources-m4. Promoting others' content.** The reused-content policy lists "Promotion of other people's content (even if you have permission)" as not monetisable. This weakens reading (b) further, where we run paid clipping campaigns on our channel (sources-m4).
- **sources-m5. Spam policy covers scraped content and networks.** The spam policy (a Community Guidelines rule, so removal and strikes, with termination after 3 strikes in 90 days) names "Scraped content": "Re-posting material from other websites or platforms, or other videos without adding anything of your own". It also covers "coordinated networks of channels", which matters if the owner splits the clip feed over several new channels to protect the company channel (sources-m5).
- **sources-m6. October 2026 Shorts originality change.** On 1 Oct 2026 YouTube said it is "updating our recommendation systems to further prioritize original content" and will "reduce the reach of content re-uploaded from other creators without adding anything of your own". Channels identified as mainly aggregating or re-uploading other creators' videos will likely see less Shorts distribution. The classification works at channel level and the reports do not say permission or licence exempts anyone. So a clip-only channel, even of NASA or CC BY footage, should expect suppressed Shorts reach, not just lost monetisation. These quotes come from news reports; the official thread did not render when opened (sources-m6).
- **sources-m7. A templated commentary line is likely not enough.** YouTube's Creator Liaison said originality means "not just VO descriptions of what's happening on screen, minor technical edits, or template-based bulk changes" (as quoted in news reports). An LLM-templated lead-in on every hourly clip is close to "template-based bulk changes", so the gate needs real, varied editorial input at much lower volume (sources-m7).
- **sources-m8. Supply is smaller than the headline counts.** The 6,202 NASA and 5,920 CCC figures are YouTube upload counts, not rights-cleared, downloadable, on-topic items. CCC licences are per talk, the archive includes conferences run by other organisations, and most recent titles are German. NASA uploads include livestreams, press conferences and segments with outside personalities that carry privacy and third-party caveats (sources-m8).
- **sources-m9. Realistic view expectations.** An established 221K-subscriber AI channel (Machine Learning Street Talk) has a median of about 1.6K views on its own Shorts (range 318 to 11,747), and CCC's recent long uploads average about 10.9K views on a 274K channel (arithmetic from one read of the feeds, not a forecast). A brand-new aggregator channel that may be down-ranked would likely do worse (sources-m9).
- **sources-m10. Content ID false claims happen on public-domain footage.** NASA's own Curiosity landing video was blocked in Aug 2012 after a TV company's Content ID claim (an old case, written up in 2021). A NASA-based clip channel should plan for claims and disputes (sources-m10).

##### What "clipping programmes" really are

- Paid clipping campaigns are run by brands and shows that pay clippers per view. Neither page says where the clips are posted; that they go on the clippers' own accounts is our inference. A vendor reports rates of about $0.80-3.00 per 1,000 verified views ("observed market ranges, not guaranteed rates", figures checked August 2026) and says permission is needed unless a show's campaign authorises clipping; it says the show owner, a network or a guest's company usually funds it (sources-11).
- The Content Rewards marketplace's FTC terms (last updated 13 Nov 2026) require a clear disclosure such as "#Ad" or "Sponsored by [Brand Name]" at the start of the video (within the first 10 seconds if spoken) and at the top of the caption. They say "#Collab" or a brand tag alone is not enough (sources-11).
- So reading (b) of "top 6" (channels that invite clipping) mostly means paid adverts for other brands. Running them on our channel would turn it into an advert feed for other companies and would need a paid-promotion disclosure on every post. We found no tech or AI show that grants a standing, unpaid licence to clip.

##### Permission can change overnight

- Netflix's exclusive podcast deals with Barstool Sports and The Ringer cap how many clips their shows may post on YouTube (Tubefilter, 6 Mar 2026, relaying Bloomberg). The cap is of undisclosed size and applies to the shows' own clips; the article does not say how it affects third-party clippers. Our reading is that a business deal can change what a source allows at any time (sources-22).

##### Crowding

- Several of the strongest field channels already cut their own Shorts. In their last 15 uploads, Dwarkesh posted 11 Shorts, Machine Learning Street Talk 15 and Y Combinator 8 (sources-13, sources-14, sources-15). Our clips of them would compete with the owner's own cuts of the same moments, and the owner's channel would win on authority. NASA, Stanford Online, Two Minute Papers, Lex Fridman and CCC post almost no Shorts of their own, so there is more room there (sources-9, sources-12, sources-17, sources-18, sources-8).

#### What this means for our build

1. **A source allow-list, not open crawling.** The system clips only channels in a `sources` table, where each row holds: channel ID, permission type (`public_domain`, `cc_by`, `written_permission`, `policy_conditional`), the evidence URL or email, the date it was checked, any conditions (maximum clip length, credit wording, commentary required, non-commercial), and an `expires_on` date for re-checking (default 30 days). With no row, nothing is clipped (sources-3, sources-22).
2. **Ingest from the owner's own download site, not from YouTube.** Use NASA's own media sites and media.ccc.de's direct downloads, which invites downloads. Store the licence for each CCC talk, not once per channel (sources-8). Keep yt-dlp only for channels that grant written permission that explicitly covers downloading (sources-4, sources-9). This also takes YouTube bot checks out of the critical path.
3. **Check the licence of each video, every time.** For YouTube-hosted CC BY sources, call `videos.list` with `part=status` before cutting and refuse anything that is not `creativeCommon`. The check costs 1 quota unit. Store the result with the clip (sources-2). Plan CC-pool discovery around the 100 searches a day cap (cache results) (sources-m1).
4. **Credit is automatic and fixed.** Every post's description starts with: original title, creator, source URL, licence name and link, and "clip edited from the original by [us]". Add an on-screen credit line for 3Blue1Brown-style rules (sources-1, sources-7, sources-m3). Never use NASA or ESA logos as our branding, and never word a title so it implies their endorsement (sources-9).
5. **A commentary gate with real editorial input.** Since permission does not exempt us from the reused-content rule, each clip must carry something of ours: a spoken or written lead-in, a "why this matters for robotics" line, or a comparison with the lab's own work. An automatically templated line on every clip is likely not enough under YouTube's October 2026 originality stance, so the gate needs varied human or editorial input and a volume low enough to supply it. The system refuses to publish a clip whose added material is empty (sources-3, sources-7, sources-m6, sources-m7).
6. **Blocklist from day one:** TED (all channels), Huberman Lab, and any channel whose policy says "non-commercial" or "no edits", until a person approves a licence (sources-5, sources-6, sources-10).
7. **Supply is deep but smaller than the headline counts.** NASA has about 6,200 videos and CCC about 5,900 on YouTube (sources-18), but those are upload counts, not rights-cleared, on-topic items (sources-m8). The build needs a deep, rights-clear back catalogue plus a few permitted live sources, and should measure how many items pass the licence and fit checks before promising one post an hour.
8. **Track crowding.** For each source, record how many Shorts the owner posts in its last 15 uploads. Do this through the Data API (`playlistItems.list` or `channels.list`, 1 unit each), not by polling the RSS feed, because robots.txt disallows it and the Terms forbid automated access (sources-19). Lower the priority of sources whose owners already post Shorts most days.

##### Recommended sets for each reading of "top 6"

**(a) Top channels in our field.** We recommend these only after written permission arrives.
- Six: Boston Dynamics (robot demos, closest to a robotics lab), Stanford Online (robotics and AI lectures, few Shorts of its own), Y Combinator (AI founders), Lex Fridman (long AI interviews, almost no own Shorts), IEEE Spectrum (robotics news), Machine Learning Street Talk (AI research, but crowded by its own Shorts).
- Reserves: Two Minute Papers, No Priors, Dwarkesh Patel (heavily self-clipped), All-In.

**(b) Channels that invite or allow clipping, plus rights-clear sources.** We recommend starting here.
- Six: NASA (public domain), media.ccc.de (CC BY 4.0, checked per talk), a vetted CC BY pool found with `videoLicense=creativeCommon` searches on robotics and AI terms (each video checked), 3Blue1Brown (only inside our commentary, under 60 s), MIT OpenCourseWare (only if the owner accepts the non-commercial and share-alike terms, which YouTube cannot carry), ESA (only items expressly marked CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO, with the share-alike problem, and only after commercial terms are confirmed).
- Reserves: ROSCon talks from Open Robotics (a forum post says they carry a CC licence, but no licence text was found, so ask first), Stanford Engineering Everywhere (CC BY-NC-SA, same caveat as MIT), university robotics labs that mark videos CC BY (found through the filter), IEEE Spectrum (ask).

**(c) Top podcasts and interview shows overall.** We do not recommend this set.
- Six: The Diary of a CEO, The Joe Rogan Experience, TED, Huberman Lab, Lex Fridman, All-In.
- Reserves: Dwarkesh Patel, Y Combinator, No Priors, Machine Learning Street Talk.
- None has a public permission, two forbid it, and their clip markets are the most crowded. Their audience overlap with a robotics lab is also weak.

**Which set to start with.** Set (b), narrowed to NASA, CCC and the CC BY pool for the first 2-4 weeks. It is the only set we can post from without anyone's permission, and NASA's rover and robotics footage fits a robotics lab. Because of the October 2026 originality change, start at a volume where each clip gets real editorial input, well below one an hour, and watch reach before raising it. In the same week, send permission requests to the six channels in set (a). Add each one to the allow-list only when a written yes covers clipping, Shorts, downloading and use on a company channel.

#### Risks and unknowns

- **Weak fit.** Space footage and CCC security talks are rights-clear, but they are not what the lab's viewers come for. Views may come from people who never care about the lab. We don't know the size of the effect; measure engaged views and subscribers per source after 4 weeks.
- **Reach suppression.** YouTube's October 2026 change targets channels that mainly re-upload other creators' videos, at channel level, and no report says a licence exempts anyone. An hourly clip feed is the pattern it describes (sources-m6, sources-m7). Expect low views even with every licence in order (sources-m9).
- **Company channel at risk.** One strike, a "scraped content" finding or a reused-content finding applies to the whole channel (sources-3, sources-20, sources-m5). If the clips go on the company channel, its existing search traction is exposed. A separate channel removes that exposure at the cost of starting from zero, but splitting the feed over several channels runs into the "coordinated networks" rule (sources-m5) (owner decision below).
- **CC flags can be wrong.** A re-uploader can mark someone else's footage CC BY. Check that the uploader is the original creator before trusting the flag.
- **CCC caveat.** The licence is set per recording, and the CC BY sentence on the streaming page may not cover the slides or the performance. CCC asks people not to share raw stream dumps (sources-8). Use the finished cuts only, and skip talks that show third-party video or music.
- **NASA caveats.** Third-party material inside NASA videos, identifiable people in commercial use, and the insignia (sources-9). Content ID false claims on public-domain footage have happened (an old 2012 case) (sources-m10).
- **Not confirmed:** that commercial use of ESA images and videos needs ESA's written authorisation (the terms pages returned 404), the MIT OCW support page (403), the official Boston Dynamics terms page (404), Stanford Online's and SEE's licence, and any Lex Fridman or Dwarkesh Patel clip policy. Cheap check: open each page by hand, or email the press contact.
- **Share-alike mismatch.** A share-alike clip (ESA, MIT, SEE) cannot carry its matching licence on YouTube (sources-m2). This is our inference.
- **Stats are third-party estimates.** vidIQ counts and RSS views were read once on 14 Nov 2026. Re-read them through `channels.list` (1 unit) when the build starts.
- **Legal reading.** Whether a company growth channel counts as "commercial" under the NC terms (MIT, Stanford SEE, Huberman) is a legal question we cannot settle. Our default is to treat it as commercial.

##### Ten-minute vetting checklist (run on any channel)

1. **Who owns it?** Is the uploader the original creator (the official channel of the person, company or event)? If not, stop.
2. **Licence flag.** Open 3 recent videos and look at the licence line under "Show more", or call `videos.list part=status`. Write down `creativeCommon` or `youtube` (sources-1, sources-2).
3. **Written policy.** Search the creator's site for "clips", "copyright", "usage policy", "licensing" and "terms". Copy the exact sentence, the URL and the date. With no sentence, the status is "no public permission found", which means no.
4. **Red words.** "Non-commercial", "no derivatives", "may not edit", "no clips", "no re-upload" or "educational only" means no for us without a signed licence (sources-5, sources-6, sources-10).
5. **Conditions.** Note the maximum length, credit wording, link rules and any "must add context" rule (sources-7).
6. **Download route.** Does the creator offer its own download (an archive site, press kit, media library)? If YouTube is the only route, we need written permission that covers downloading (sources-4).
7. **Inside the video.** Check for third-party footage, music, logos and bystanders who could be identified (sources-8, sources-9).
8. **Pace and crowding.** Open the RSS feed by hand (do not automate it): count long videos in the last 30 days and the share of the owner's own Shorts (sources-19). Search YouTube for "<channel name> clips" and count how many clip channels already exist.
9. **Enforcement.** Search "<channel> copyright strike clips" and "<channel> takedown". Note any reports with their dates.
10. **Fit.** Would a viewer of this content also care about a robotics and AI lab? Answer yes or no in one line.
11. **Record and re-check.** Save the result in the `sources` table with an expiry date 30 days out (sources-22).

Checked on 2026-11-14 by 2 independent fact-checker(s) (primary; realism): 27 confirmed, 4 corrected, 0 removed, 1 unverified.

### A5. Getting the source videos and their words

**The short answer.** Noticing new uploads on six channels is cheap: the free RSS feed or push notifications (WebSub, a standard way for a site to call our server when a feed changes) can do it, but the feed has had multi-hour outages since December 2025, so keep a `playlistItems.list` fallback. The YouTube Data API can check each new video for about 2 quota units. Getting the video itself is the hard and risky part. YouTube's Terms forbid downloading without "prior written permission from YouTube and, if applicable, the respective rights holders". The download tool (yt-dlp) now needs a JavaScript runtime and changes every few weeks. YouTube's API Developer Policies also bar separating or modifying the audio or video of YouTube content, which bears on cutting and re-uploading clips. YouTube also blocks most cloud server addresses, including AWS. So the clean route is for each source creator to give us the files (a shared folder or their podcast host's export), and the yt-dlp route should never run on the production server. Get the words from YouTube's own captions first: they are free, and the app already parses them. Use local WhisperX only when captions are missing. A paid API costs about $0.15-0.26 per hour of audio if it returns word times (Deepgram, AssemblyAI); OpenAI's cheaper models return no word times, and the one that does (whisper-1) shuts down on 26 Feb 2027. Production EC2 never runs WhisperX; a video without captions fails with transcript_not_ready there. Fetch captions and pick the moments before downloading any video, then download only the chosen minutes. That cuts download size, time and exposure by roughly 90% for an hour-long source, about 73% for a 30-minute one (my estimate, unverified).

#### What we found

##### 1. Noticing new uploads

- Every channel has a public feed at `https://www.youtube.com/feeds/videos.xml?channel_id=UC...`. Practitioner write-ups (a 2023 blog, the gPodder docs) say it lists only about the 15 newest uploads. No official page states this limit. YouTube's push guide gives the topic URL as `https://www.youtube.com/xml/feeds/videos.xml?channel_id=...` (with `/xml/`) (ingest-1).
- The feed is not reliably up. YouTube's feed server intermittently answers all feeds with 404 for hours at a time; reports run from 27 Dec 2025 to at least 2 May 2026 with no official response, and Feeder's help page (updated 10 Nov 2026) confirms it. Polling must survive multi-hour outages and fall back to `playlistItems.list` on the `UU` uploads playlist, 1 unit a call (6 channels x 96 polls a day = 576 units a day) (ingest-m1).
- Push notifications go through Google's hub, `https://pubsubhubbub.appspot.com/subscribe`, with that same feed URL as the "topic". YouTube's guide says the hub notifies on three events: an upload, a title change and a description change. It promises only "near real-time" delivery. It says nothing about deletions, retries or how long a subscription lasts (ingest-2).
- Under the WebSub standard (W3C), every subscription expires after a lease and must be renewed before then. The hub first checks the callback with a GET request that carries a `hub.challenge`, and it can sign each message with an HMAC secret. YouTube's hub page asks subscribers to renew "just before hub.lease_seconds elapse" (ingest-2).
- Data API costs from the official quota page: `playlistItems.list` 1 unit, `videos.list` 1 unit, `channels.list` 1 unit. `search.list` is 1 unit but limited to 100 calls a day. `captions.list` is 50 units. The default allowance is 10,000 units a day, reset at midnight Pacific (ingest-3). The earlier research checked the upload cost as well: 1 unit, in its own bucket of 100 a day (01-traffic-research.md:1247, api-1). The official revision history (4 Dec 2025 entry) describes an upload as about 100 units, which conflicts with the quota page, so check the new project's quota in the Cloud console (ingest-m9).
- The `videos` resource tells us about live streams. `snippet.liveBroadcastContent` is `live`, `upcoming` or `none`, and `liveStreamingDetails` appears for upcoming, live and completed live broadcasts, premieres included. `contentDetails.duration` is an ISO 8601 length such as `PT15M33S`. The resource has no field that marks a Short or a members-only video, and aspect ratio is readable only by the owner. `contentDetails.contentRating.ytRating` flags age restriction, and `status.madeForKids` also exists (ingest-4).
- Undocumented playlist IDs split a channel's uploads by type: `UULF` + channel ID holds long videos, `UUSH` Shorts, `UULV` live streams and `UUMO` members-only videos. Each comes from swapping the channel ID's leading `UC`. Two practitioner sources describe them: the ArchiveTeam wiki (edited 2 July 2025) marks UU, UULV, UUMO and UUSH "Fully functional", and a June 2025 blog lists UULF, UUSH, UULV and UUMF. YouTube does not document them (ingest-5).
- yt-dlp reports `live_status` as `not_live`, `is_live`, `is_upcoming`, `was_live` or `post_live`. It reports `availability` as `private`, `premium_only`, `subscriber_only`, `needs_auth`, `unlisted` or `public`. It also reports `duration` in seconds and `was_live`. `live_status` can also be `None` (unknown), which a skip rule should treat as skip or recheck, not as `not_live` (ingest-6, ingest-m7).

##### 2. Getting the video

- yt-dlp now needs an outside JavaScript runtime to solve YouTube's challenges. Deno (2.3.0 or newer) is the one turned on by default. Node (22 or newer) has to be switched on with `--js-runtimes node`. The solver scripts come in the `yt-dlp-ejs` package, which `yt-dlp[default]` installs, and the project says it "SHOULD be updated alongside yt-dlp". The `[default]` extra pins `yt-dlp-ejs==0.8.0` exactly, so a pinned yt-dlp release pins the solver too (ingest-7, ingest-m3).
- yt-dlp's default YouTube clients are now `tv_samsung,visionos,web`. With no JavaScript runtime, "`web` and `tv_samsung` are omitted". The production image installs no Node and no Deno (Dockerfile:29-31; the server has no Node, per 00-context.md). Its YouTube downloads therefore run without two of the three default clients, leaving only `visionos`, whose caption and format behaviour is undocumented (ingest-8, ingest-m5).
- From April 2025 the `web` client got only SABR streams, YouTube's own streaming protocol, which yt-dlp could not download directly. The suggested workarounds were other clients or a PO token. The issue's last visible activity is August 2025, and we found no 2026 source on the current state (ingest-24).
- YouTube "is gradually enforcing" a PO Token ("proof of origin" token), which yt-dlp cannot generate itself. The `web` client needs one for video streams and for subtitles. The `tv`, `web_embedded` and `android_vr` clients need none. Tokens are bound to each video and may last as little as 12 hours (some reports say months). The guide's table does not list `tv_samsung` or `visionos`, so their token needs are undocumented (ingest-m5). Third-party plugins such as bgutil-ytdlp-pot-provider make them (ingest-9).
- The bgutil plugin's own README warns that on data-centre addresses "Sign in to confirm you're not a bot" can persist even with a token, and cookies may also be needed (ingest-11).
- yt-dlp's wiki gives rate limits of about 300 videos an hour for a signed-out session and about 2,000 for a signed-in one. It recommends a 5-10 second pause between downloads. It warns that using an account risks a temporary or permanent ban, suggests a throwaway account, and says to export cookies from a private window that is never reopened, because YouTube rotates cookies in open tabs (ingest-10).
- Cloud addresses are widely blocked. The youtube-transcript-api README says "YouTube has started blocking most IPs that are known to belong to cloud providers". This repo already notes that YouTube answers EC2 with "Sign in to confirm you're not a bot" (core/config.py:146-148), and DEPLOY.md says "YouTube URLs may fail from AWS" (DEPLOY.md:397-398). yt-dlp's FAQ says 429 errors mean the service is blocking your IP address because of overuse (ingest-11).
- yt-dlp changes often. There were five releases between 9 June and 26 October 2026, (2026.06.09, 07.04, 08.19, 10.21, 10.26). Two changed YouTube default clients: 2026.10.21 made `tv_samsung` a default, and 2026.08.19 added `visionos` and removed `android_vr` from the defaults. 2026.06.09 raised the minimum Deno and Node versions, and 2026.07.04 fixed YouTube extraction, so four of the five touched YouTube. Production installs yt-dlp from the GitHub head with no pin (requirements.txt:15) (ingest-12).
- yt-dlp can fetch part of a video; `--download-sections` needs ffmpeg, which the laptop lacks (ingest-m10). `--download-sections "*START-END"` downloads only a time range. `--force-keyframes-at-cuts` makes the cuts exact but "requires a re-encode". The `-t sleep` preset adds `--sleep-requests 0.75 --sleep-interval 10 --max-sleep-interval 20 --sleep-subtitles 5`. `--download-archive` records finished video IDs so nothing is fetched twice, and `--match-filters` can skip by any field, for example `live_status` or `availability` (ingest-13).
- Today's code asks for H.264 at 720p or lower (ingest/youtube.py:92-95), because meeting recordings gained nothing visible above that. A clip channel probably wants a 1080p source. We could not confirm on any page we opened which 1080p formats YouTube serves in late 2026 or how large they are; one forum page that might have shown this blocked us with a bot check (ingest-14).

##### 3. Getting the words with timings

- The app already reads YouTube captions through yt-dlp. It prefers creator-written captions over automatic ones and json3 over VTT, rejects machine translations, and falls back to WhisperX when no original English track exists (transcribe/native.py:573-599, 616-680) (ingest-14). That is code behaviour: production EC2 runs `REQUIRE_NATIVE_TRANSCRIPT=true`, which never runs WhisperX, so a video without a platform transcript fails with `transcript_not_ready` (README.md:50-51), and a copied `native.py` brings that switch along (ingest-m4).
- Its json3 parser keeps one timed line per caption event, not per word (native.py:498-534), so the captions it stores today are phrase-level. A 2021 practitioner post reports that YouTube's automatic captions carry word-level times in the `srv2` format, fetched with `yt-dlp --write-auto-sub --skip-download --sub-format srv2`. That post is over four years old, and caption fetches via the `web` client now need a PO token, so whether srv2 still carries word times is untested (ingest-15).
- The official API is no use for other people's captions. `captions.download` costs 200 units and "requires the user to have permission to edit the video"; anyone else gets a 403 error (ingest-16).
- youtube-transcript-api returns segment-level text, start and duration. Its cookie login is "currently not available", and it recommends rotating residential proxies because "YouTube will ban static proxies after extended use" (ingest-17).
- Local speech-to-text: the faster-whisper project measured its `small` model (int8) transcribing 13 minutes of audio in 1 min 42 s on 8 threads of an Intel i7-12700K, using 1.5 GB of RAM. WhisperX's "70x realtime" claim is for a GPU. For CPU, its README gives only the flags (`--device cpu --compute_type int8`). The app runs `small`, int8, batch 16 (core/config.py:129-131; whisperx_backend.py:21-26) (ingest-18).
- The t3.large earns 36 CPU credits an hour, which is a 30% baseline per vCPU. Running above that costs $0.05 per vCPU-hour in Unlimited mode. Earlier research estimated that once credits run out, everything runs about 3.3 times slower (data/shorts-owner-questions-and-skeptic.json:222) (ingest-18).
- Paid transcription prices, read 14 Nov 2026 (ingest-19):
  - Deepgram Nova-3: $0.0043 a minute ($0.26 an hour), with $200 of free credit.
  - AssemblyAI: Universal-2 $0.15 an hour, Universal-3.5 Pro $0.21 an hour, $50 free (page updated 10 Nov 2026).
  - OpenAI: gpt-4o-mini-transcribe $0.003 a minute ($0.18 an hour), gpt-transcribe $0.0045, Whisper $0.006 ($0.36 an hour).
  - None of these pages says whether word timestamps are included in the base price. OpenAI's `timestamp_granularities[]` works only with whisper-1, and whisper-1, gpt-4o-transcribe and gpt-4o-mini-transcribe shut down on 26 Feb 2027; uploads are capped at 25 MB. So the cheap OpenAI options give no word times for karaoke captions. AssemblyAI returns per-word times (accurate to about 400 ms) and Deepgram includes per-word start and end, so the realistic word-timed range is about $0.15-0.26 an hour (ingest-m2).

##### 4. Public signals that help pick moments

- yt-dlp exposes a `heatmap` field, a list of points with `start_time`, `end_time` and a value from 0 to 1. This is the "most replayed" graph (ingest-20).
- YouTube Help says the graph may not appear when the channel has active strikes, when the content is potentially inappropriate, or "if the video is too new or has too few views" (ingest-20).
- Chapters: yt-dlp gives `chapters` (start, end, title); automatic chapters are on by default for new uploads, so they may be machine-made, not creator-chosen (ingest-m8). YouTube's rules are that the first timestamp is 00:00, there are at least three in ascending order, and each chapter is at least 10 seconds long. Creators can turn automatic chapters on or off (ingest-21).
- Comments: `commentThreads.list` costs 1 unit for up to 100 comments, sorted by `time` or `relevance`. The page does not say whether timestamp links come through in the text (ingest-21).
- SponsorBlock, a crowd-sourced database of ad reads, offers `GET /api/skipSegments` with categories such as sponsor, selfpromo, interaction, intro and outro. A privacy mode sends only the first 4 characters of a hash of the video ID. yt-dlp can mark or cut those segments. The API and database are licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, which means attribution, **non-commercial use only** and share-alike, "unless you have explicit permission" (ingest-22).

##### 5. What the terms say (facts only; another strand judges the risk)

- The YouTube Terms of Service (effective 15 Dec 2023, English page) say you may not "access, reproduce, download, distribute" any part of the Service or Content except "as expressly authorized by the Service" or "with prior written permission from YouTube and, if applicable, the respective rights holders". They also forbid access "using any automated means (such as robots, botnets or scrapers)" other than public search engines (ingest-23).
- The YouTube API Services Developer Policies say API clients must not "download, import, backup, cache, or store copies of YouTube audiovisual content without YouTube's prior written approval" (III.E.1.a). They forbid scraping (III.E.6). Most stored API data must be deleted or refreshed within 30 calendar days (III.E.4) (ingest-23). They also bar separating, isolating or modifying the audio or video components of YouTube content (III.I.7), promoting those components separately (III.I.8), facilitating copyright infringement (III.E.1.c, III.I.18), and selling ads placed in YouTube audiovisual content without written approval (III.G.1.c). The clip system would be an API client that uploads through `videos.insert`, so these apply to uploads as well as downloads (ingest-m6).

##### 6. Volume, disk and time

- We don't know the six channels, so we don't know their weekly hours. My working range for talk, podcast or interview channels is 1-6 long videos a week each, 0.5-2 hours each, which gives 3-72 source hours a week in total. This is an estimate, not a measurement (ingest-25).
- Posting every hour means 168 posts a week. To fill that, the source hours needed depend on how many usable clips each hour gives, a number another strand has to supply (ingest-25).

#### What this means for our build

**Detect (cheap, safe, no video touched).**
- Poll each channel's RSS feed every 15-30 minutes. It is free and needs no key, but it goes down for hours at a time, so fall back to `playlistItems.list` on the `UU` uploads playlist (1 unit a call) when it returns 404 (ingest-m1).
- WebSub can be added later for speed. It needs a public HTTPS callback, a lease-renewal job and HMAC checks, which is more moving parts than six channels justify.
- For each new ID, call `videos.list` once (1 unit for up to 50 IDs) to read `duration`, `liveBroadcastContent`, `liveStreamingDetails` and `status`. Six channels cost under 50 units a day.
- Use a **separate Google Cloud project and API key** for the clip system, so a bug in it can never use up the production project's 10,000-unit day (ingest-3). Since 2 Nov 2026, uploads from unverified projects are no longer forced private, so such a project is practical; check its upload quota in the console (ingest-m9).
- Skip a video if any of these holds:
  - `liveBroadcastContent` is not `none`, or `liveStreamingDetails` is present (live, upcoming and premieres; check premieres on a real one).
  - `live_status` is `None` (unknown): skip or recheck (ingest-m7).
  - It is a Short: the ID is in the `UUSH` feed, or yt-dlp shows a duration of 180 s or less with height greater than width.
  - It is in the `UUMO` feed, or yt-dlp shows `availability` other than `public`.
  - It is age-restricted (`contentRating.ytRating`).
  - It is shorter than a minimum length, say 8 minutes.
- Because the playlist prefixes are undocumented, treat them as hints and keep the yt-dlp fields as the final check (ingest-4, ingest-5, ingest-6).
- Wait at least 24-48 hours after upload before clipping. The heatmap does not exist for new videos, captions often appear late, and SponsorBlock data builds up over time. This waiting period is a default the owner can change.

**Get the words first, the video last.**
- For each kept video, fetch only metadata (`skip_download`): captions, chapters and heatmap. Reuse `transcribe/native.py` by copying it into the new branch, not by importing it from production code. Remember the copy brings the `REQUIRE_NATIVE_TRANSCRIPT` switch (ingest-m4).
- Extend the parser to read word times from `srv2`/`srv3` or json3 segment offsets. Check first on one real track that the times are present (ingest-15).
- Let the LLM pick moments from that transcript. Then download only the chosen ranges with `--download-sections "*START-END"`, padded by about 5 s on each side, and cut exactly in our own ffmpeg render. That avoids `--force-keyframes-at-cuts` and a second encode (ingest-13).
- Ask for 1080p, preferring H.264 and taking VP9 or AV1 when H.264 is missing. We re-encode every clip anyway, so the source codec only affects decode CPU.
- If a video has no captions, use a paid API that returns word times: Deepgram (about $0.26 an hour) or AssemblyAI ($0.15-0.21 an hour), not OpenAI's cheaper models, which give no word times (ingest-19, ingest-m2). The saving over local CPU is not large: both vCPUs flat out cost about $0.10 an hour in surplus credits (own arithmetic from the AWS rate), the same order as the API. The real reason to avoid production CPU is that it blocks the single job slot and the credits (ingest-18, ingest-m11). On the laptop or a separate worker, local WhisperX is free.

**Where downloading runs.**
- **Never on the production EC2.** It would share the disk (which has already filled up once, 01-traffic-research.md:77), the single job slot and the CPU credits. If its IP address gets flagged, production's own YouTube URL jobs would fail too.
- The best route is files the creators give us: a shared Drive or Dropbox folder, or the video or audio files a podcast host already publishes. It needs no yt-dlp, gives no ToS question about downloading from YouTube, and gives master-quality files.
- If the owner chooses yt-dlp anyway, run it on a separate small machine or on the laptop. A home connection is not a cloud address. The laptop has Node 24, which meets the Node 22 minimum, but it has no ffmpeg, which yt-dlp needs to merge streams and cut sections, so installing ffmpeg (and about 13 GB of free disk) is a setup step (ingest-m10).
- Pin one yt-dlp release together with yt-dlp-ejs. Upgrade on purpose, with a smoke test of one known video, not from the git head. Install Deno, or pass `--js-runtimes node`, and smoke-test captions as well as video, since without a runtime only `visionos` remains (ingest-7, ingest-12, ingest-m3, ingest-m5).
- Use no cookies by default. If cookies become necessary, use a throwaway account, **never the company channel's Google account** (ingest-10).
- Use `-t sleep`, `--download-archive`, and at most one download at a time (ingest-10, ingest-13).

**Signals.**
- Use the heatmap peaks and chapter boundaries as ranking hints when they exist (ingest-20, ingest-21).
- Don't call SponsorBlock until the owner settles its non-commercial licence (ingest-22). Instead, have the LLM flag ad reads ("this episode is brought to you by", promo codes) in the transcript and drop those segments. A rule-based phrase list is the cheap first layer.
- Store comment text only briefly and refresh or delete it within 30 days (ingest-23).

**Storage policy (my estimates).**
- A section download of 6 clips × about 70 s at 1080p is roughly 50-150 MB per source video, against roughly 1-2 GB for a full hour.
- Keep each section file only until its clip is rendered and uploaded, then delete it.
- Keep the caption JSON and our moment picks for 30 days, then delete.
- Keep a hard cap of 5 GB of working disk on the laptop or a small worker, and refuse new downloads above it.

**Time per source video (my estimate).**
- Metadata and captions take seconds.
- Sections at home broadband speed take under a minute.
- Paid transcription, when needed, takes minutes.
- None of this is the bottleneck. Rendering and review are.

#### Risks and unknowns

- **Terms and permission.** Downloading from YouTube with yt-dlp falls outside what the Terms expressly allow, even when a creator agrees, because the Terms ask for permission from YouTube as well (ingest-23). Only creator-supplied files avoid that question entirely. The Developer Policies' limits on modifying audio and video (III.I.7) also apply to uploads (ingest-m6). Another strand judges this. The cheapest way to find out is to ask the six creators whether they will share files.
- **yt-dlp breakage.** Two YouTube client changes and four YouTube-touching releases of five in four months (ingest-12) means it can stop working without warning. Plan for a 1-3 day gap a few times a year (my estimate). The system should keep posting from a backlog of at least 3 days of rendered clips when downloads fail.
- **IP flagging.** We could not find any official statement on how YouTube treats AWS addresses. The evidence is project READMEs, our own code comments and community reports (ingest-11). It is unknown whether a home connection stays clean at about 10-30 videos a week. Test with a week of metadata-only fetches before any video download.
- **Not confirmed: current state of the web client SABR limit.** The issue's last visible activity is August 2025 (ingest-24).
- **1080p formats and sizes.** These are not confirmed for late 2026, and the PO Token Guide does not cover the new default clients (ingest-m5). Run `yt-dlp -F` on one video from each source channel before writing the format string.
- **Word-level caption times.** These are confirmed only by a 2021 blog for `srv2`. Check one real auto-caption track before building karaoke-style captions on them. If they are missing, or a PO token blocks the fetch, align with WhisperX on just the 60-second clip; earlier research measured this as cheap (02-shorts-editing-and-cost.md:143).
- **RSS delay, outages and the 15-entry limit.** These come from practitioners only; see ingest-m1 for the outages. Log the time from upload to first sight for two weeks. A channel posting more than 15 videos between polls would hide some, which is very unlikely at a 30-minute poll.
- **Premieres.** We assume they show `liveBroadcastContent: upcoming` and then `was_live`/`post_live` in yt-dlp. Check this on one real premiere.
- **Heatmap timing.** We don't know how many days or views a video needs before the heatmap appears (ingest-20).
- **Storage and volume estimates (unverified).** The 50-150 MB range has no source and may be low: about 480 s at an assumed 1-4 Mbps is roughly 60-240 MB. The 90% saving holds only for sources near an hour long (ingest-25).
- **Source hours.** These are unknown until the owner names the six channels. Check each channel's last 30 days of uploads (titles and durations through RSS plus `videos.list`, a few units) before sizing anything.
