### A6. Picking the moments worth posting

**The short answer.** No clipping tool has shown, with independent evidence, that its "virality score" picks clips that get more views, and the best public study found that off-the-shelf language models only modestly beat a simple baseline at finding the parts of podcasts people replay (on its F1 measure; on its hit-rate measure the zero-shot models did clearly better than the baseline, though they saw only summaries). So treat the AI's picks as a shortlist that will often be wrong, and plan to learn from our own results. Reuse what the app already has (score sentences, re-rank the best moments, snap to sentence edges, start on the claim, check that title words were said) and add three things for other people's interviews and podcasts: an "it makes sense on its own" check with a hard ban on back-references like "as I said earlier", filters for adverts and off-topic chat, and a near-duplicate check across everything already posted. Picking costs very little: about $0.18 of Sonnet tokens for a 1-hour source and $0.42 for a 3-hour source, or about $0.01-0.02 on Haiku 5.5. A Haiku-then-Sonnet split costs about $0.08-0.14, and the Batch API would halve each figure. Automatic learning from YouTube numbers runs into YouTube's ban on derived metrics, so start with a weekly human read of the raw numbers, and apply for the amendment before turning on any automatic learner (a bandit, explained below). The amendment needs an audit and an "analytics use case", so plan for the manual loop to be permanent.

#### What we found

##### What clipping tools say they do, and what is proven
- OpusClip's help page says its score runs from 0 to 99 and covers four things: Hook (does the opening grab attention and fit the topic), Flow (does it move logically to a satisfying end), Value (does it resonate emotionally) and Trend (does it match current interests). The page makes no claim that the score has been validated, and only paid plans show it (pick-1).
- Vizard's "Model v2" post (13 Jul 2026) names three sub-scores: hook strength, clear takeaway and story flow. It says the model keeps about 13 "high-confidence" clips per hour of video and that each clip includes setup, insight and payoff. It gives no performance data (pick-2).
- OpusClip's own data post (17 Apr 2026) covers clips processed by its product from Jan-Mar 2026. In a public TikTok cross-check, top-10% clips had a median length of 41 s against 50 s for all clips. The post never defines "viral" for its main sample, its sample is self-selected, and the author works for OpusClip. It has no YouTube Shorts figures, so it says nothing direct about YouTube (pick-3).
- Earlier repo research found no independent test showing that any clipping tool's features raise views. The only number linking a score to results is one unverified review, in which clips scored 80+ got about 2.3x the TikTok views of clips scored under 50. That review also found an ACL 2025 paper in which an LLM predicted video popularity with up to 85.5% accuracy, helped by asking it to reason first (pick-4).
- Our own reading: every tool scores the same few things (hook, stands alone, payoff, emotion). None of them can see what viewers will do. Their scores rank clips; they do not predict views (pick-1, pick-2, pick-4).

##### Research on finding highlights in long talk
- RHAPSODY (COLM 2025, arXiv v2 dated 7 Sep 2025) is the closest public study to our task. It covers 13,364 episodes from 90 popular YouTube podcast channels, averaging about 27 minutes and 4.7K words. It splits each episode into 100 equal segments and labels a segment a highlight when YouTube's "most replayed" graph is above 0.5 (at most 20 per episode). It also corrects a replay spike on the first segment, which appeared in 75% of episodes before correction (pick-5). Most-replayed graphs exist only for videos with enough views (typically at least 50K), so a new channel's own uploads will not have that signal (pick-m10).
- In that study's test set, zero-shot GPT-4o (F1 0.057, hit rate 0.265) and Gemini 2.0 Flash (F1 0.065, hit rate 0.327) beat the random (F1 0.039, hit rate 0.220) and frequency (F1 0.051, hit rate 0.224) baselines only modestly. F1 is a 0-1 accuracy score. A fine-tuned 1-billion-parameter Llama reached F1 0.163 on text alone and 0.197 with HuBERT audio features (hit rate 0.452 and 0.490), and the authors call the task "very challenging". The paper never defines "hit rate". The zero-shot models saw only the episode title and 100 per-segment summaries, not the full transcript, and they are 2024-2025 models, so the result does not show how Sonnet 5.5 would do on full transcripts. The labels are replay peaks over roughly 16 s segments, not "a good stand-alone clip". It is fair evidence that zero-shot picking is weak, not proof that it cannot beat chance (pick-6).
- An ACL 2025 industry paper describes LLM-made podcast previews (short snippets of an episode's key moments) that replaced a feature-engineered expert-model system and were deployed at scale. In an online A/B test they raised engagement with previews by 4.6% and processed 5x more efficiently. Offline raters found them easier to understand, clearer in context and more interesting. The metric is engagement with in-app podcast previews, not views of stand-alone clips in a YouTube feed (pick-7).
- Together: an LLM can pick clean, understandable moments better than hand-built rules (pick-7), but it can't reliably guess which moments viewers will replay (pick-6). Real gains come from training on real viewer data, which we will only have for our own uploads (pick-6, pick-14).

##### Open-source projects we could reuse
- ClipsAI: an MIT-licensed Python library for podcasts, interviews and talks. It splits a WhisperX transcript into coherent clips with TextTiling (a method that finds topic shifts from changes in word use; clipsai/clip/texttiler.py) over sentence-transformers embeddings from all-roberta-large-v1 (RoBERTa), and reframes to 9:16 using pyannote speaker diarisation (speaker-diarization-3.0, which needs a Hugging Face token). It has about 571 stars, 68 commits, no releases, and its newest commits are from 16-17 Jan 2024, so it is dormant (not archived): reuse the idea, not the library (pick-8).
- Lighthouse (LINE): an Apache-2.0 library for moment retrieval and highlight detection, the task of finding the part of a video that matches a text query. Version 1.2 came out on 20 Nov 2025 and it has 274 stars. It works from video features and its README says the maximum video duration is 150 s because of the benchmark datasets it was trained on, so it does not fit hour-long talk. It also has an audio-only moment-retrieval API, still query-based (pick-9).
- laughter-detection: MIT-licensed, 298 stars. Its model was last updated in Aug 2021. It outputs (start, end) laughter segments with a 0.5 threshold and a 0.2 s minimum length. It is useful for comedy podcasts and of little use for technical interviews. Its README says it was tested on Python 3.6.1, librosa 0.8.1 and PyTorch 1.3.1, so it may need porting to run on the server's Python 3.12 (our inference, not tested) (pick-10).
- YAMNet (TensorFlow models): labels 0.96 s frames (50% overlap) of 16 kHz mono audio with 521 AudioSet classes, including Laughter (13), Applause (62), Cheering (61), Music (132) and Silence (494). Its subfolder page states no licence, but it lives in the tensorflow/models repository, which is Apache License 2.0; the licence of separately hosted model weights (for example TF Hub or Kaggle) was not checked. Its README warns that it relies on Keras 2 and is incompatible with Keras 3, which adds a pinned TensorFlow/Keras 2 dependency to the image (pick-11).
- SponsorBlock: a crowd-sourced database of advert and other segments in YouTube videos. Its categories include sponsor, selfpromo, interaction, intro, outro, preview, filler and poi_highlight, a single "point of interest" timestamp. Its API can be queried by a hash prefix of the video ID, so the exact ID isn't revealed. The data is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (non-commercial) unless the maintainer grants other terms (pick-18). The wiki also lists "hook", "chapter" and "exclusive_access" categories, and forbids automated submissions; its "hook" and "preview" segments are spans a clipper should skip (pick-m5).

##### Signals we can and can't use
- The Data API's video resource has no "most replayed", heatmap or per-second engagement field. It has no chapters field either: chapters exist only as timestamps inside snippet.description, so using them means parsing the description (pick-12).
- YouTube's developer policies ban scraping YouTube and ban getting API data by any means other than the API. So we cannot take the most-replayed graph of other channels' videos, even though RHAPSODY used it for research (pick-12, pick-13). The YouTube Terms of Service separately ban accessing the Service by automated means ("robots, botnets or scrapers") without written permission, and third-party "most replayed" scrapers exist, which is a temptation the plan should rule out explicitly (pick-13).
- Comment timestamps: we found no paper that uses YouTube comment timestamps to find highlights (a negative search result, which cannot prove absence). The nearest work uses crowd-sourced on-screen "time-sync" comments (Bilibili/niconico (unverified)) and has to correct for the lag between a moment and the comments about it. Reading comments costs 1 quota unit per call, but stored comments count as other channels' data (30-day limit), and counting them may count as a derived metric (pick-17, pick-15, pick-19).
- For our own uploads, the Analytics API gives engagedViews, estimatedMinutesWatched, averageViewDuration, averageViewPercentage, likes, shares and subscribersGained. Engaged views are views past the first frame, or a click or tap to play. Its retention report returns audienceWatchRatio (which can go above 1 with rewatches), relativeRetentionPerformance (0-1 against similar-length videos), startedWatching and stoppedWatching, and the video filter must name a single video ID (audienceType, subscribedStatus and youtubeProduct are optional). The metrics page lists no Shorts-only metric, but the creatorContentType dimension has a SHORTS value (pick-16, pick-m2).
- Earlier research: Studio's Shorts "Stayed to watch" share has no API (01-traffic-research.md:593). Per-video tests at a few hundred impressions are mostly noise (analytics-7). A randomised packaging test needs about 170-280 videos (analytics-9) (pick-23).
- The Analytics API dimension creatorContentType has a SHORTS value (also LIVE_STREAM, STORY, VIDEO_ON_DEMAND), so per-format reports for Shorts vs long clips can be pulled by API even though no Shorts-only metric exists. The retention report does not accept creatorContentType. The traffic-source dimension insightTrafficSourceType=SHORTS (swiped in from the previous Short) and insightPlaybackLocationType=SHORTS_FEED (documented 2026-11-06) also split Shorts by feed versus other traffic (pick-m2).
- On 2026-08-27 YouTube aligned public view counting ("YouTube will count public views the moment a video begins to play"), and since 2025-03-31 Shorts "views" count every start and replay. So use engagedViews, not views, as the learning reward (pick-m8).
- Since 2026-01-15 the Reporting (bulk) API offers channel reach reports (channel_reach_basic_a1 and channel_reach_combined_a1) with video_thumbnail_impressions and video_thumbnail_impressions_ctr, which gives a CTR signal for long clips' titles. The docs do not say whether Shorts are included (pick-m9).
- Getting the source transcript is itself a gap. The section assumes a WhisperX transcript of other channels' videos, but there is no sanctioned way to get one: captions.download requires permission to edit the video and costs 200 units, and the YouTube Terms of Service forbid downloading content and automated access without YouTube's written permission. Picking therefore depends on a download step that breaks the Terms unless the source owners grant permission (pick-m6).

##### What the app already does that carries over
- Sentences are scored 0-10 in chunks of 60 with 3 context lines each side. The best 60 moments go to one re-rank call, which returns score, category, clip lines a-b, short-worthy y/n, title, why, hook, stands_alone 0-10 and short_start. Scores are then replaced by rank, because the model's absolute scores swing from run to run (decide/prompts.py:145-180, edl/highlights.py:89-112) (pick-20).
- Clips snap to sentence edges, drop filler at both ends, may not start on "which/and/so", and Shorts start at short_start: the claim itself, with at most one sentence of setup (decide/prompts.py:160-179, edl/highlights.py:322-345) (pick-20).
- Title grounding: a title counts only if at least half its main words, and every number in it, were said in the clip (publish/describe.py:426-441). Hooks must be at most 6 words, made only of words said in the clip, with no names (decide/prompts.py:172-174). Today's prompt bans people's names in titles (decide/prompts.py:170) (pick-20).
- Measured cost: on a real 98-minute meeting (1,061 sentences) the whole decide stage used about 100k input and 15k output tokens (README.md:422). Prices in decide/pricing.py:13-15, in $ per 1M tokens (input / output): Sonnet 5.5 2.00 / 10.00, Haiku 5.5 0.10 / 0.50 for prompts up to 100K tokens, and 0.50 / 2.50 above that. README.md:90-92 still says the default model is claude-haiku-4-5 at about $0.18 for this run, while core/config.py:27 defaults to claude-sonnet-5-5, so that README text is stale and the 100k/15k figure may come from an older model run (pick-21).
- Earlier research relevant to picking: a Short over 1 minute with any active copyright claim is blocked worldwide (shorts_views-6). On 1 Oct 2026 YouTube said it would cut Shorts-feed reach for channels that mainly re-upload others' videos without significant changes (shorts_views-4). Opening on the strongest line has indirect support (shorts_editing-3) (pick-24). That update works at channel level, and minor technical or template-based edits (auto-captions and crops are exactly that) do not count, so picking better moments does not make the channel "original" and picker quality cannot fix a reach cut (pick-m7).

##### Storage and quota rules that shape the learning loop
- The 30-day rule depends on the type of data. Analytics API and Reporting API data, and statistics such as view counts, that the channel owner authorised (Authorized Data) may be stored as long as needed, if the client re-checks every 30 days that authorisation still holds (III.E.4.b). Other Authorized Data (III.E.4.c) must be deleted or refreshed within 30 calendar days. Non-Authorized Data, meaning anything fetched without user credentials (other channels' titles, descriptions, chapters, comments and view counts), may be kept only in limited amounts for at most 30 days (III.E.4.d), and Non-Authorized statistics never beyond 30 days. API data may be aggregated only across channels under the same content owner, viewable only by that owner (III.E.2.a). So our own channel's learning table can keep its history, but source-video metadata stored per posted clip (title, description, chapters, guest names taken from them) must be refreshed or deleted within 30 days (pick-15).
- The derived-metrics policy lets accepted clients store statistical and derived metrics for up to 36 calendar months, while titles, descriptions and comment text stay under the 30-day rule. You apply through the quota extension form (support.google.com/youtube/contact/yt_api_form, "Section 5", then "Analytics & Reporting"). The service "must reflect an analytics use case on YouTube", and an auto-posting bot may not qualify, so the Phase 2 bandit may never be allowed (pick-m1).
- videos.insert now has its own 100-calls-a-day bucket at 1 unit per call, so 24 uploads a day fits. Any plan that assumes the old high per-upload cost should be rechecked by the publishing strand (pick-m4).
- Picking is not latency-sensitive, so the Message Batches API halves the token cost: Sonnet 5.5 $1 / $5 and Haiku 5.5 $0.05 / $0.25 per MTok. Haiku 5.5 prompts over 100,000 tokens cost 5x more ($0.50 / $2.50), so every Haiku call must stay under 100K tokens, which 10-minute chunks do (pick-m3).

#### What this means for our build

**1. Candidate generation (no AI first, then one cheap pass).**
- Inputs: a WhisperX transcript with word times and speaker labels (the source of the audio and transcript is an open compliance question, see Risks), plus the source video's title, description and chapters from videos.list (1 unit). Creator-written chapters give free topic edges for long clips (pick-17).
- Cut out before any AI call: the first and last 60-90 s (intros, outros, "like and subscribe"), long music stretches (YAMNet Music, optional) and advert spans. For adverts, the default is that the LLM marks lines as `ad`. SponsorBlock only with the maintainer's permission, because the channel is commercial (pick-11, pick-18).
- Pass 1 (Haiku 5.5): chunks of about 10 minutes with 5 lines of overlap. The model proposes up to 6 candidates per chunk as line ranges, each tagged S (Short, 20-60 s) or L (long clip, 3-12 min). This replaces per-sentence keep/remove, which the clip system does not need, and cuts output tokens. Keep every Haiku call under 100K prompt tokens (pick-21, pick-22, pick-m3).
- Optional audio bonus, phase 2: laughter, applause and loudness peaks from YAMNet or laughter-detection add a small bonus to a candidate. Audio helped only fine-tuned models in RHAPSODY (pick-6, pick-10, pick-11).
- Long clips: use creator chapters or TextTiling-style topic edges, ClipsAI's idea reimplemented in a few lines rather than adopting a dormant library (pick-8).

**2. Scoring (Sonnet 5.5 re-rank over the shortlist).**
- Send the best 30 (1-hour source) to 50 (3-hour source) candidates with about 15 s of context on each side to one re-rank call. Ask for separate sub-scores, never one "virality" number: hook (does the first sentence work cold), stands_alone, payoff (does it end on a conclusion), novelty/emotion, and searchability (does it name a tool, person or question people search). Keep ranking by rank position, as calibrate_by_rank does (pick-20).
- Combine sub-scores with fixed starting weights (stands_alone and hook count double). Log every sub-score so the weights can later be checked against results (pick-4, pick-6).
- Quality floor: a slot with no clip above the floor stays empty. Posting a weak clip to fill an hourly slot adds volume, and volume has no proven value and carries policy risk (shorts_views-4) (pick-24).
- Run pass 1 and the re-rank through the Batch API, since picking is not latency-sensitive; it halves the token cost (pick-m3).

**3. Clean start and end points (rules in code, after the LLM).**
- Start: the start of a sentence, never inside a speaker overlap, and the first word is not a connective ("and", "so", "but", "which", "because", "that's why").
- Reject when the first two sentences match a back-reference list ("as I said", "like I mentioned", "earlier", "going back to", "we talked about", "that point", "this guy") or contain an unresolved "he/she/they/it/that" with no noun before it. The LLM also returns `needs_context y/n`.
- End: on sentence-final punctuation after the payoff, with the cut placed in the next word gap of at least 250 ms plus about 0.3 s of pad. Never end on a question the clip doesn't answer.
- Shorts: open at short_start (the claim or question) with at most one sentence of setup, as today. Don't reorder sentences ("punchline first, then setup"): that changes what the speaker said and in what order, which conflicts with the truth rule (pick-20, pick-24).
- Lengths: Shorts 20-60 s, target 30-45 s. Keep them at 60 s or less, because a clip of someone else's show is likely to draw a copyright claim, and a claimed Short over 1 minute is blocked worldwide. Long clips 3-12 min on one topic (pick-3, pick-24).

**4. Near-duplicates.**
- Within one source: reject any clip overlapping a chosen one by more than 20% of its length (the app already blocks any overlap for Shorts).
- Across sources: guests repeat the same story on many shows. Store a text fingerprint of every posted clip (TF-IDF or small-embedding cosine over its transcript) and reject a new clip above about 0.85 similarity to anything posted in the last 90 days, or with a title sharing most main words with a recent title. Thresholds are our estimate; tune them on the first 200 candidates by hand (own estimate).

**5. Titles and hooks that stay true.**
- Keep `_grounded` unchanged: half of the main words and every number must be said in the clip (pick-20).
- New: allow the speaker's name and the show's name, which today's meeting rule bans. A name may appear only if it is in the source video's title or description, or said in the transcript. It must never come from the model's guess about who is speaking, because diarisation only gives SPEAKER_00-style labels (pick-20).
- Pattern: "<what is said or claimed, in the speaker's words> - <Guest> on <Show>". Quote marks only for verbatim words. No claim, number or outcome that isn't in the clip.
- The description names the source channel, links the original video at the clip's start time, and states that this is an excerpt. The copyright strand decides whether that is enough.
- Hook text on screen: at most 6 words, all said in the clip (current rule) (pick-20).

**6. Learning from results.**
- Store per posted clip: source channel, source video ID and times, guest, topic words, kind (S/L), length, all sub-scores, hook and title style, posting hour. Then pull raw Analytics numbers at 48 h, 7 days and 28 days: engagedViews, views, estimatedMinutesWatched, averageViewDuration, averageViewPercentage, likes, shares, subscribersGained. For long clips, also pull the retention curve (one call per video). Use engagedViews, not views, as the reward (pick-16, pick-m8).
- Shorts "Stayed to watch" is Studio-only. Export it weekly by hand (pick-23).
- Phase 1 (legal now): keep our own channel's Analytics numbers as raw numbers (re-checking the channel's authorisation every 30 days), refresh or delete any data about the source channels (titles, descriptions, chapters, guest names taken from them, comments) within 30 days, and have a person read a weekly table by source, length band and title style, then change the weights by hand (pick-14, pick-15).
- Phase 2, only after the derived-metrics amendment is approved (which may never happen, since the service must reflect an analytics use case): a Thompson-sampling bandit. A bandit is a method that shifts more posts toward options doing well while still trying the others. Its arms would be a few coarse choices (source channel, length band, title style), its reward the log of 48-hour engaged views, stratified by source, with at least 20% exploration (pick-14, pick-m1).
- When a signal is real (our estimate, assuming the spread of log views has a standard deviation of 1.0-1.5): telling a 2x difference between two options needs about 33-74 posts per option, and a 1.5x difference needs about 96-215 per option. At 24 posts a day that is about 3-6 days for 2x and 1-3 weeks for 1.5x. Measure the real spread in the first two weeks before trusting any comparison, since a new channel's Shorts views are heavy-tailed and the spread may be larger, and interleave arms in time because views trend upward as the channel ages. The source channel will likely swamp everything else, so compare options within a source (pick-23).

**7. Cost per source and per posted clip (estimate, prices from decide/pricing.py).**
Assumptions: 174 words a minute (RHAPSODY's 4.7K words per 27 minutes); about 1.3 tokens per word plus 15% for line numbers and speakers; about 15.5k transcript tokens per hour of source; a 2,000-token prompt per chunk; 6 candidates of 70 output tokens per 10-minute chunk; a re-rank over 30 or 50 candidates at 450 tokens each in and 110 out; plus 20% for retries (pick-5, pick-22). The yield of 6 posted clips from 1 hour and 12 from 3 hours is an assumption that a quality floor and de-duplication may cut. Figures assume chunked Haiku calls under 100K tokens and no Batch API discount, which would halve them.

| Source | Tokens in / out | Sonnet 5.5 | Haiku 5.5 | Haiku pass 1 + Sonnet re-rank |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 hour | ~54k / ~7k | $0.18 | $0.009 | $0.083 |
| 3 hours | ~134k / ~16k | $0.42 | $0.021 | $0.141 |
| Per posted clip (6 from 1 h, 12 from 3 h) | | $0.030-0.035 | $0.0015-0.0018 | $0.012-0.014 |
| 720 posts a month (one an hour) | | about $22-25 | about $1-1.3 | about $8.5-10 |

Check against a real run: the 98-minute meeting's full decide stage (~100k in / 15k out) would cost about $0.35 on Sonnet 5.5. That stage also labels every sentence keep or remove, which clip picking skips (pick-21). Transcription and rendering are not in these figures, and they will likely dominate.

Recommended default: Haiku 5.5 for pass 1 and Sonnet 5.5 for the re-rank, titles and hooks, where wording and truth checks matter most.

**Draft prompt structure (re-rank call).**
System: role ("you pick stand-alone clips from someone else's interview for a YouTube channel that credits the source"); the owner's criteria string (as highlights_criteria today); the rules (clean start, no back-references, end on the payoff, no adverts or sponsor reads, no off-topic chat, titles from said words only, names only from the METADATA block); the output format. User: a METADATA block (show, channel, video title, guest names from title/description, chapters), then candidate blocks `#<id> <kind> core <a>-<b>` with numbered lines `[n mm:ss] SPK: text` and `~` context lines.
Output, one line per candidate, pipe-separated, as today:
`id|rank_score|kind|a|b|short_start|hook_s|alone_s|payoff_s|novel_s|search_s|needs_context(y/n)|backref_line(-|n)|ad_or_offtopic(y/n)|speaker_name(-|name from METADATA)|title|hook_text|search_phrase|why`

#### Risks and unknowns
- The big unknown is whether any picker beats chance on views. RHAPSODY suggests zero-shot models do only modestly better than baselines, on summaries and older models (pick-6). Cheap test: for the first 2 weeks, post the top pick and a random clip that passes the floor from the same source, then compare within each source.
- The derived-metrics rule may cover even simple medians or rankings worked out from API data. The text makes no exception for internal tools (pick-14, analytics-11). Apply for the amendment early; until then, keep the loop manual. Approval needs an audit and an analytics use case, so the manual loop may be permanent (pick-m1).
- Source transcripts and media: there is no ToS-compliant way to get other channels' transcripts or video. captions.download is owner-only and the Terms ban downloading and scrapers without written permission. This breaks the picking pipeline unless the source owners grant permission, and is bigger than any picking-quality question (pick-m6).
- Copyright claims and the Oct 2026 originality update may matter more for views than picking does (shorts_views-4). Other strands own this, but the picker must leave room for "significant changes" such as commentary. We don't know what YouTube counts as significant, and template-based edits do not count (pick-m7).
- Speaker names: wrong name-to-voice matching would make titles false. Use only names from metadata or the transcript, and never put a name on screen next to a face unless a person has checked it.
- Token and sentence counts for podcasts are estimates. Real speaking rate and sentence length vary by show. Read job.llm_usage on the first 10 sources to replace the table.
- YAMNet is Apache-2.0 via the tensorflow/models repository; only the licence of separately hosted weights is unchecked, and it needs Keras 2. laughter-detection's upkeep is unconfirmed and it may need porting off Python 3.6-era dependencies. Both are optional (pick-10, pick-11).
- SponsorBlock data is non-commercial by default. Don't use it without written permission (pick-18).
- The near-duplicate thresholds (20% overlap, 0.85 similarity) are guesses. Tune them by hand on real candidates.
- Hourly posting gives fast samples, but that is a reason to measure, not proof that hourly posting helps. The quality floor should be allowed to leave slots empty.
- The RHAPSODY venue (COLM 2025) is shown on the arXiv abstract page per one checker and was not stated on the HTML page the other checker read. The 2.3x score test and the 85.5% ACL figure (pick-4) are second-hand in youtube_research.md and their original sources were not opened.

### A7. Making the Short look good with ffmpeg

**The short answer.** ffmpeg alone can make a clean, phone-first Short from someone else's landscape video, and most of the pieces already exist in this repo's Shorts renderer (layout guess, blurred-background fit, libass captions with a hook card, loudness levelling, an HD encode). For a clip channel the main things to add are: a crop that follows faces shot by shot (not one fixed crop per clip), a stacked layout for two-person shots, real word timings so captions can highlight the spoken word, an on-screen source credit, and a hard 60-second cap, because YouTube blocks any Short over one minute that has an active Content ID claim. Keep the look plain: there is no independent evidence that zoom punches, progress bars, emoji, sound effects or music raise retention, and the only related study we found (on keyword highlights for language learners, not word-by-word highlights) called them too distracting for everyday viewing. Encode 1080x1920 H.264 at the source frame rate, about 8 Mbps (12 Mbps for 50-60 fps), with AAC at 48 kHz, which is what YouTube itself recommends. Render time is unmeasured; our estimate of about 2-3.5 minutes per 45-second Short on a t3.large with CPU credits is a floor, not a range (the model leans optimistic and leaves out decoding 1440p/2160p sources), so 24 a day plausibly fits on small hardware, but it must not run on the production server.

#### What we found

##### What the app already does (local code, read 14 Nov 2026)

- The Shorts renderer guesses one layout per clip (screen share, speaker, gallery or "fit") from gray frames sampled at 2 fps and 480 px wide, and falls back to "fit" (the whole frame) whenever it is unsure or the picture switches inside the clip (look-1). Only some of today's Shorts use this new look, because the default `shorts_style` is 'alternate', so the rest use the classic one (look-1).
- The "speaker" crop is a single fixed 9:16 window for the whole clip, centred on where pixels move most. There is no face detection, no tracking and no handling of camera cuts (look-1).
- "Fit" and the screen/gallery panels sit over a blurred, darkened copy of the same video (quarter-size box blur plus `eq=brightness=-0.3:saturation=0.7`); a slide panel is shown 1080 px wide between y=480 and y=1130 (look-2).
- Captions are an ASS file burned in with libass (the subtitle renderer inside ffmpeg). Zoom gives sentence-level text, so word times are spread by word length; cues are at most 5 words or 28 characters and 2 rows, 80 px, white with a black outline, bottom edge at y=1330. A yellow hook card shows from frame 0 for 2.5 seconds, a small title after it, and an end line over the last 2.5 seconds (look-3).
- The font is whatever the system has: DejaVu Sans on Linux, Arial on Windows, unless FONT_FILE is set (look-3).
- Estimated word times are off by a median of 0.3-0.4 seconds and up to 2.3 seconds, which is fine for phrase captions but not for a word highlight; WhisperX forced alignment (matching known text to the audio to get exact word times) took about 7 seconds of model time and under 1 GB on 2 threads for a 50-second Short on the dev PC; the earlier research estimates 20-40 seconds on a t3.large, never run there. It aligns known text only, so third-party YouTube clips, which have no Zoom transcript, also need a transcript from ASR or the source's captions, and that cost is not in this figure (look-4).
- Sound: a gain toward -14 LUFS (a standard loudness measure) with a peak limiter at -1.5 dBFS; noise reduction (`afftdn`) exists but is off by default. Video: the HD Shorts profile is libx264 preset medium, CRF 20, capped at 8 Mbps; audio is AAC 128 kbps, 48 kHz stereo (look-5).
- Tests already cover this: tests/test_layout.py, tests/test_shorts_render.py, tests/test_shorts_style.py, tests/test_shorts_pauses.py, tests/test_shorts_selection.py, tests/test_render_loudness.py (file names only; not run, per the read-only rule).

##### Turning 16:9 into 9:16

- Centre crop: a 9:16 window cut from a 1920x1080 frame is about 608x1080 px, so it is upscaled about 1.78 times to fill 1080x1920 (my arithmetic). From a 3840x2160 source the same window is about 1215x2160 and needs no upscale (my arithmetic). Sharp speaker crops therefore depend on getting the highest source resolution.
- Smart crop needs a face detector. OpenCV's YuNet is MIT-licensed, scores 0.834 / 0.824 / 0.708 AP on WIDER Face easy/medium/hard, and runs in 0.69 ms per frame at 160x120 input on an Intel i7-12700K and 6.23 ms on a Raspberry Pi 4B (look-12). That latency is for the 2023mar model at 160x120 and does not carry over to the 640 px input planned below; the model page also gives a second eval table with different AP figures, and a newer default model (2026may, dynamic input) exists (look-12, look-m2). YuNet detects faces of about 10x10 to 300x300 pixels, so frames must be downscaled for close-ups and tiny faces in wide shots will be missed (look-m2).
- Google's MediaPipe face detector (BlazeFace) runs at 2.94 ms per frame on a Pixel 6 CPU (short-range model, 128x128 input); that model is tuned for front-facing phone-camera faces, and it installs with `pip install mediapipe` (Python 3.9-3.14; Linux x86_64 needs glibc 2.28 or later); the repository is Apache-2.0 (look-13). The same guide also lists full-range and sparse full-range models for wider images, but only short-range has a published latency (look-m3).
- Active-speaker detection (working out which visible face is talking) exists in open source: Light-ASD (CVPR 2023) is MIT-licensed, has 1.0M parameters and 0.6 GFLOPs, and scores 94.06% mAP on the AVA-ActiveSpeaker validation set. Neither its README nor its abstract gives a CPU speed (look-14).
- No vendor or study we opened measures which 9:16 layout performs best for clipped talk content, or how often auto-reframe fails. We don't know. The repo's own data says what fails on slides: even a 2x crop of a shared screen leaves body text at about 19-25 px, under a 28 px phone-readability line (look-21). Face trackers have nothing to follow on slides, screen shares and wide shots, so those shots need the fit layout.
- ffmpeg's crop filter evaluates its x and y expressions on every frame, can use the frame time `t` and frame number `n`, and accepts runtime commands for w, h, x and y. A precomputed x/y crop path can therefore be written straight into the crop expression, in one pass, with no extra tool (look-9). The w and h options are not per-frame: they are evaluated at configuration, on a command, or when the input size changes, so a time-varying crop size (a zoom punch) needs sendcmd/zmq commands or a fixed crop followed by a time-varying scale or zoompan; none of those was verified (look-m1).

##### Captions

- The ASS subtitle format, which libass renders, has karaoke tags: `\k` switches a syllable from the secondary to the primary colour when it starts, `\kf` sweeps it left to right, both in centiseconds. `\t` animates style changes, `\fad` fades, `\pos` places text (look-11). That is everything needed for a word-by-word highlight from word timestamps. The page is Aegisub's documentation, not libass's; that libass renders each tag the same way was not verified (unverified) (look-11).
- Evidence on highlighted words is thin. A 2023 online study (49 language learners) found time-synchronised keyword highlights (selected keywords, not every spoken word) were the preferred design for learning but "too distracting to replace standard captions" in everyday viewing; it did not test word-by-word karaoke highlighting, so it is indirect evidence at best (look-15). Vendor blogs claim 20-35% more watch time from animated captions without published methods; those claims come from search results that were not opened, and we did not count them as evidence (unverified) (look-15).
- The earlier research already found no independent evidence that word-by-word animated captions, progress bars, emoji, whooshes, stock B-roll or zoom punches raise retention; background music hurt learning in lab studies; and the evidence leans toward lightly produced clips. Opening on the strongest line with something readable in the first frame has indirect support (look-16).
- Safe areas: YouTube publishes no safe zone for organic Shorts that we could find. Google's help page on vertical video ads shows a 1080x1920 safe-zone image but its text gives no margins (look-8). A third-party tool that says it read that image lists top 288 px, bottom 672 px, left 48 px and right 192 px (like, comment and share buttons on the right; channel name, title and subscribe at the bottom), leaving about 840x960 px clear (look-8). Other tools give smaller margins (bottom about 300 px, right 96-192 px) (look-8). Our current caption bottom at y=1330 is inside the stricter tool's bottom margin, which starts at y=1248 (my arithmetic).
- Fonts: text rendered into a video with a SIL Open Font License font needs no extra licence or credit; the licence applies only if the font file itself is redistributed (OFL FAQ, updated 9 Nov 2026). Montserrat is OFL 1.1 (look-20); an ExtraBold static weight was not confirmed. If font files are bundled in the new system's repository, the copyright statement, licence notice and OFL text must ship with them (look-m8).

##### Opening, sound and encode

- YouTube's upload page recommends MP4, H.264, the same frame rate the video was recorded at, 8 Mbps for 1080p at 24-30 fps and 12 Mbps at 48-60 fps (16 and 24 Mbps for 1440p), and AAC-LC or Opus audio at 48 kHz, 384 kbps for stereo (look-6). The same page asks for High Profile, 4:2:0, the moov atom at the front (Fast Start) and no edit lists; whether ffmpeg's MP4 muxer writes an edit list when trimming with -ss/-t was not verified, so check the output (ffprobe or the elst atom) (look-m4).
- The claim that uploading at 1440x2560 makes YouTube serve a cleaner stream comes from vendor blogs with no test data; YouTube's page does not say it (look-7).
- ffmpeg's loudnorm filter implements EBU R128, defaults to -24 LUFS integrated, 7 LU range and -2 dBTP true peak, has one-pass and two-pass modes, and upsamples to 192 kHz in dynamic mode (look-10). The app instead measures once and applies one fixed gain plus a limiter, which avoids pumping (look-5). YouTube publishes no loudness target (earlier research, 01 retention-8).

##### Credit, length and endings

- Any Short over one minute with an active Content ID claim of any type, including manual claims, is blocked worldwide: it cannot be played, recommended or monetised until the claim is resolved; there is no channel penalty, and Shorts can be up to three minutes (YouTube Help, read 14 Nov 2026) (look-17). A 59-second cap avoids that block but not the claim itself, which can still route revenue to the claimant or block the Short in some regions under the rights holder's policy (look-m7).
- Giving credit to the owner does not by itself turn a non-transformative copy into fair use, and there are no "magic words" (look-18).
- YouTube's reused-content rule is a YouTube Partner Program monetisation rule: it names "clips of moments ... edited together with little or no narrative" as not allowed to monetise, and allows commentary or an added storyline; removals and strikes come from other policies (copyright, spam) (look-19). It also lists "Short videos you compiled from other social media websites" and content "downloaded or copied from another online source without any substantive modifications", and applies even with the original creator's permission; templated content is not monetisable either (renamed "inauthentic content" on 15 July 2025). Reframing to 9:16 plus captions is not stated anywhere to be a substantive modification (look-m5). On-screen polish does not change this.
- End screens need a video of at least 25 seconds; the page does not mention Shorts (look-23). Setting a Short's Related video is described only in desktop Studio, needs advanced feature access (which a brand-new channel may lack) and a public or unlisted target from the same channel; the Data API shows no field for it (look-23, look-m6).

##### Render cost

- The earlier cost model, an estimate never measured on the server, prices plain ffmpeg at 0.1 vCPU-seconds per 1080x1920 frame and crop + lanczos scaling + HD encode at 1.5-3 times that; the app's own comments say HD medium costs up to 65% more on gallery content, and that full-frame HD takes about 2.15 times the standard encode; without CPU credits a t3.large runs about 3.3 times slower (look-22). The model's own authors say it leans optimistic, because a t3.large's 2 vCPUs are hyperthreads of one core; it also leaves out decoding 1440p/2160p sources (informally VP9 or AV1 rather than H.264, unverified) and 50-60 fps sources, which double the frame count (look-22).

#### What this means for our build

**1. Layout, chosen per shot, not per clip.** Our sources (other people's podcasts, interviews and talks) cut between cameras, so one crop per clip will often frame an empty chair.

- Find shot cuts first (a frame-difference pass over the same 2-5 fps gray sample the app already takes in slice/layout.py), then decide the layout for each shot.
- One face, medium or close shot: full-bleed 9:16 crop around the face, with the eyes about a third of the way down. Default to a fixed crop per shot (the look of a camera operator who doesn't move). Add slow tracking only when the face moves more than about 10% of frame width within the shot: a dead zone, then a low-pass filter, written as a piecewise-linear `x='...'` expression in the crop filter (look-9).
- Two faces side by side (a two-shot): stacked layout, top half and bottom half each a 1080x960 crop around one face, captions on the seam. This needs no speaker detection.
- Slides, screen shares, wide shots, B-roll or no face found: the app's existing "fit" layout (whole frame over blurred background), with the hook above and captions below (look-1, look-2, look-21).
- Face detector: YuNet through OpenCV (MIT, tiny, fast on CPU) (look-12). MediaPipe is the alternative, but its short-range model targets phone selfies (look-13). Run it at about 5 fps and 640 px wide, downscaling so close-up faces stay under 300 px (look-m2); the app's sampler outputs gray frames while YuNet's demo uses colour frames, so plan a separate colour sample (unverified) (look-m9); my estimate is 5-15 seconds per 45-second clip on 2 vCPU. opencv-python-headless is not in requirements.txt today, so it is a new dependency for the separate system only.
- Active-speaker detection: leave it out of version 1. Light-ASD is light as models go (look-14), but it needs face tracks plus audio and has no published CPU speed. If switching between two speakers is wanted later, use the transcript's diarisation (speaker turns) plus face position first, and test ASD on the laptop before it goes anywhere near a server.

**2. Captions.** Keep the app's ASS approach and change the defaults for a clip channel:

- 2-4 words per cue (today up to 5 words or 28 characters), one row where possible, never more than two.
- Bold OFL sans font shipped with the new system (Montserrat ExtraBold or similar), about 80-90 px at 1080 wide, white with a 6-8 px black outline and a small shadow. Don't depend on system DejaVu (look-3, look-20).
- Position: centre the text block left of the button column (MarginL about 60, MarginR about 192), and keep the caption bottom at or above about y=1240 until a phone check shows the 672 px bottom margin is too cautious (look-8).
- Active-word colour change (yellow on the spoken word), built as one ASS event per word slice with an inline colour tag, or with `\k` tags (look-11). It costs nothing to render, but the evidence is weak and the only related study (keyword highlights, not word-by-word) calls them distracting (look-15), so ship it as an A/B style, not as the default truth.
- Word times: get them by forced alignment of a transcript to the clip audio (WhisperX, already used by the app; about 7 seconds per Short on the dev PC, estimated 20-40 seconds on a t3.large). Third-party clips have no Zoom transcript, so the text must first come from ASR or the source's captions, which adds cost (look-4). Run it in a subprocess so its memory is freed.
- Accuracy: a per-source glossary of names and product words, applied before alignment. Drop captions in cues where the alignment score is low rather than show wrong words.

**3. The opening.** Start the cut on the strongest line, not the setup, and show a hook of 6 words or fewer, readable from frame 0, for about 2-3 seconds (the app's hook card already does this) (look-3, look-16). Do not add zoom punches, progress bars, emoji, whooshes, B-roll or a music bed in version 1:

- Zoom punch: cheap to render, but not as a time expression on the crop filter, because crop's w and h are not per-frame (look-m1); it needs sendcmd/zmq or a crop followed by a time-varying scale, none verified. No evidence it helps. Keep it as a later A/B option only.
- Progress bar: about free (one `drawbox` with a time-based width), no evidence, and it reads as an ad. Skip.
- Emoji: needs a colour emoji font in libass, which we did not verify. Skip.
- Sound effects and music: licensing work, and music hurt learning in lab studies. Skip (look-16).
- B-roll: stock licences plus selection work, and no evidence. Skip.

**4. Sound and encode defaults.**

- Audio: keep the measure-once gain toward -14 LUFS with the -1.5 dBFS limiter (look-5). YouTube-hosted sources are usually already mixed, so leave `afftdn` off. Encode AAC-LC 48 kHz stereo at 256-384 kbps, following YouTube's 384 kbps recommendation; at 45 seconds that adds about 1.5 MB at most (look-6).
- Video: 1080x1920, H.264 High, yuv420p, the source's own frame rate (no 60 fps conversion), CRF 18-20, preset medium, `-maxrate 8M` for 24-30 fps and `12M` for 50-60 fps, `+faststart`, BT.709 colour tags written explicitly (look-6). This is the app's HD Shorts profile plus a frame-rate-aware cap (look-5).
- Do not upload at 1440x2560 by default. Most sources are at or below 1080p, so the extra pixels would be made up. Test it once (same Short at both sizes, compare the served stream) before paying the extra encode time (look-7).

**5. Credit and ending.**

- Burn a small credit line for the whole clip ("Clip: <source channel> on YouTube"), about 34-40 px, semi-transparent box, top-left under the hook and inside the 288 px top margin plus 48 px left margin. Put the full source link and title in the description too. This is courtesy and good practice; it is not a licence and does not make the use fair (look-18, look-19).
- No branded end card: it adds non-content at the loop point (the 05 plan made the same call). Use a 2-2.5 second end line instead ("Full episode: <source>" or "Follow for more").
- Related video: Studio-only, so the system cannot set it; leave it as an optional manual step for the best Short of the week (look-23).

**6. Length.** Cap every clip at 59 seconds, including the hook, credit and end line, because a Short over one minute with any Content ID claim is blocked worldwide (look-17); the cap does not prevent the claim itself (look-m7). The "longer clips" the owner wants are regular 16:9 videos and need no 9:16 render at all.

**7. One-pass ffmpeg design.** Per Short, one analysis step and one encode:

1. Analysis (Python + numpy + OpenCV): sample gray frames at 5 fps and 640 px, find shot cuts, run YuNet per sampled frame, and pick a layout and crop window per shot. Smooth the windows and write them out as keyframes. Store the result as JSON next to the clip, so a re-render never re-analyses.
2. Captions (Python): aligned words → 2-4-word cues → ASS with the hook, credit, captions and end line, all in one file. One `subtitles=` filter draws all of the text, so drawtext is not needed (look-3, look-11).
3. Encode (one ffmpeg command): input trimmed with `-ss`/`-t` → `split` → [background: scale to quarter size, box blur, darken, scale up] and [foreground: per-shot `crop` with an x/y expression of t, `scale=1080:-2:flags=lanczos`] → `overlay` → `subtitles=clip.ass:fontsdir=fonts/` → `format=yuv420p` → libx264. Audio in the same command: trim, gain, limiter, short fades. The stacked layout is two crops plus `vstack` in place of the single foreground. This is a small extension of `build_short_graph_new` (look-2, look-9).
4. Checks: frame count, duration and loudness probes, as the app already does for Shorts (look-5).

Expected time (my estimates, not measured; treat as a floor): 45 seconds at 30 fps is 1,350 frames; at 0.15-0.3 vCPU-seconds per frame that is about 200-400 vCPU-seconds, or about 1.7-3.4 minutes on a t3.large with credits only if both vCPUs give full throughput, plus 10-50 seconds of analysis and alignment (alignment alone is estimated at 20-40 seconds there, before any transcription), and about 3.3 times longer with no credits; decoding 1440p/2160p or 50-60 fps sources adds unmeasured time (look-22, look-4). At 24 Shorts a day the model's 202-405 vCPU-seconds each is 81-162 CPU credits a day against 864 earned, so volume plausibly fits (look-22). A modern 6-8-core laptop should be roughly 3-5 times faster than a t3.large (an unmeasured guess). Memory: one x264 encode at 1080x1920 with medium lookahead plus the frame sample should stay well under 1 GB (estimate); WhisperX alignment adds under 1 GB in its own process (look-4). Hourly posting is 24 Shorts a day, about 1.5-3 CPU-hours of rendering a day.

Where quality is lost, in order: (a) the source is already compressed by YouTube, then by us, then by YouTube again; (b) the 1.78x upscale when cropping 9:16 from a 1080p source; (c) chroma subsampling, which softens coloured caption edges a little; (d) camera-cut frames if a crop change lands one frame late (avoid it by cutting crop changes exactly on detected shot boundaries).

**What is new versus the app.** Reuse: the blur background, fit layout, ASS/libass caption pipeline with hook card and end line, gain and limiter, HD profile and frame/duration checks. Add: shot-cut detection, YuNet face crops per shot, the stacked two-face layout, a time-based crop expression, 2-4-word cues with an optional active-word colour, a bundled OFL font, the stricter safe band, a credit line, a frame-rate-aware bitrate cap, 384 kbps audio and a hard 59-second cap. Build it as new modules in the new system on the clp branch, copying the small graph-building helpers rather than editing slice/ in place, so the production renderer is untouched.

#### Risks and unknowns

- **Rights are the real risk, not the look.** A beautiful clip of someone else's video can still be claimed or blocked (look-17, look-18), and a channel that auto-clips other creators' videos risks being refused or losing monetisation under the reused/inauthentic content rules, even with the creator's permission (look-19, look-m5). The look cannot fix that; see the rights strand.
- **Render time is unmeasured.** Every time figure here is an estimate from an unmeasured model that leans optimistic (look-22). Include 1440p/2160p decode and 50-60 fps sources in the benchmark. Cheapest check: render 5 sample Shorts on the laptop with a static ffmpeg build (installing it is the owner's call) and time each step; then one run on the target machine.
- **Safe-zone margins are not official.** The 288/672/48/192 px figures come from a third party that says it read Google's ad image (look-8). Check: upload one private test Short with coloured guide bands and screenshot it on an Android and an iPhone.
- **Face crops fail** on profile views, small faces in wide shots, masks, screen shares and fast camera moves. Mitigation: a minimum face size (about 6% of frame height, a guess to tune), fall back to fit, and log the layout per shot so bad crops can be found.
- **Word highlight may hurt.** The only related study (keyword highlights for language learners) says it distracts, and it did not test word-by-word highlighting (look-15). Treat it as an A/B style with Stayed to watch as the measure (see the earlier test design in 02 section 5).
- **A uniform style at hourly volume** matches the "templated, mass-produced" pattern the earlier research flagged (02 section 3). Vary the layout per source, and don't stamp heavy branding on every clip.
- **Not verified this session:** libass support for each Aegisub tag, the vendor caption claims, Montserrat's ExtraBold weight, whether YuNet accepts gray input, current per-resolution codec availability, ffmpeg's `scdet`, `zoompan` and `sendcmd` documentation (the page cut off before those sections), libass colour-emoji support, MediaPipe AutoFlip's support status, and whether 1440p uploads look better (look-7).
- **Source resolution** depends on what the download step gets; sharp speaker crops need 1440p or 2160p sources.
