Checked on 2026-11-14 by 2 independent fact-checker(s) (primary; realism): 27 confirmed, 4 corrected, 0 removed, 1 unverified.

### A8. Hyperframes and /brag: what they can do for clips

**The short answer.** /brag itself cannot make our Shorts: it turns a code project into a 15-25 second launch promo, it has no way to take a video clip, and it needs a person (or an expensive AI run) for every video. Hyperframes, the HTML-to-video renderer under it, can help, but only as a fixed template that our Python fills with data (words and timings, hook text, colours) and renders with no AI call per Short. The cheapest safe use is to have Hyperframes pre-render a few short branded pieces once (hook card, end card, sting) and let ffmpeg join or lay them on each clip; the next step up is a transparent caption overlay per Short, rendered on a separate machine, never on the production server. Nothing we found links this extra motion to more views, and template polish does not make other people's clips "original" in YouTube's eyes (the October 2026 change cuts reach per channel for channels that mainly re-upload others' videos, and rotating template variants is itself a "template-based change"), so treat it as packaging, not as the growth lever. Spend one hour on the experiment at the end of this section before building any of it.

#### What we found

##### /brag and /brag-slim: what they make
- /brag reads a software project's code and turns it into a short launch video with a plan, a brief, a rendered `brag.mp4`, a poster frame and share copy (hf-1).
- Its own rules default the length to 15-25 seconds and fix the shape at hook, reveal, 2-3 highlights, punchline (hf-1). The 15-25 s cap is /brag's; /brag-slim accepts `--duration` (default about 20 s) and a vertical 1080x1920 format, but still takes only a project or a URL (hf-1).
- It has no input for existing footage. Its inputs are a project folder, or a website URL in /brag-slim (hf-1).
- On Claude Opus 5.5, /brag hands the job to /brag-slim unless you pass `--full` or `--voice`, and /brag-slim says it uses "No Hyperframes" at all. It builds the video with whatever tools the machine has (hf-1).
- The latest release is brag 0.5.0 (23 October). The copy on this laptop is 0.4.0. The repository is MIT-licensed with about 21.4k stars (hf-2).
- It ships five music beds (CC BY 4.0, by Sascha Ende of ende.app) and about 260 sound effects (CC0, mostly from Kenney) (hf-3). The SFX licence is confirmed in the skill's audio notes; the music licence is not confirmed from a primary source (the bundled music README names ende.app but states no licence, and ende.app returned HTTP 403) (unverified).
- On the earlier research's reading, CC BY music needs a credit line in every video's description and Content ID claims on these tracks are possible (hf-3) (unverified).
- The owner's own test (23 October) produced a 23-second landscape video in 6 scenes, built on hyperframes 0.8.186 (hf-4).
- On this laptop each full render of that video took 48 s and 63 s. The laptop is a Ryzen AI 5 340 with 6 cores, 15 GB RAM and an RTX 5050 GPU (hf-4).
- From the written plan to the first finished render took about 13-14 minutes of agent time; counting from the project scaffold (13:28) the run to first render was about 19 minutes, and about 23 minutes to the second render (hf-4).
- That composition is graphics and music only, with no `<video>` layer, so its 2.1-2.7 s of rendering per output second does not stand for footage renders (hf-4).

What could serve a clips pipeline:
- the craft rules: a hook in the first 2 seconds, about 0.3 s on screen per word, a chosen poster frame as frame 0 (hf-1);
- the CC0 sound effects, for one soft hit on the hook (hf-3);
- the idea of one composition per video with scenes as sub-compositions (hf-6).

What could not serve it: the planning steps, the storyline choice, the tone system, the music (licence duty, claim risk) and the 15-25 s default length (hf-1, hf-3).

##### Hyperframes today
- **Version and licence.** npm `hyperframes` 0.9.45 is current on 14 November 2026. It is Apache-2.0, needs Node 22 or newer, and unpacks to 25.1 MB (hf-5).
- **Release pace.** Ten releases (0.9.36 to 0.9.45) came out between 11 and 14 November, so any build must pin one exact version (hf-5).
- **How a video is built.** A video is an `index.html` page with timed elements (`class="clip"`, `data-start`, `data-duration`) and one paused GSAP timeline per composition. GSAP is a JavaScript animation library (hf-6).
- **How it renders.** Hyperframes steps headless Chrome through the timeline frame by frame, captures each frame and encodes the frames with FFmpeg (hf-6).
- **Rules for the page.** No clocks, no unseeded random numbers and no network fetches during the render. Every frame must depend only on time (hf-6).
- **A clip inside a composition.** A `<video>` element keeps its own sound with `data-has-audio="true"`. `data-media-start` trims the start of the source (hf-7).
- **Frame timing.** The docs say Hyperframes "owns media playback and seeking" and injects video frames at render time. Source frames are extracted before capture (hf-7).
- **Audio trimming trap.** The audio mixer reads only `data-media-start`. If a clip uses another attribute name, the picture is trimmed but the sound is not (hf-7).
- **Keyframes.** Footage whose keyframes are more than about 1 s apart freezes on seek, so re-encode it with a keyframe every second first (hf-7).
- **Templates.** A composition can declare variables and bind a video to one with `data-var-src` (hf-8).
- **Clip length.** The docs say the output "takes the length and the sound of the clip you pass": a 3-second placeholder swapped for a 5-second clip renders 5 seconds (hf-8).
- **Correction to earlier research.** This changes what the earlier research said (02, section 2): one composition can take clips of any length (hf-8). The variables page says the root's length follows the clips it plays, but the skill contract says the video's length is the root's `data-duration` (overrun is cut, an early end holds the last frame). The docs do not say what happens with an unset root duration, so our generator should write `data-duration` per Short from the clip length, and the experiment must check it (hf-8, hf-m5).
- **What variables cannot change.** Variables cannot change the canvas size, frame rate, output format or an explicit root duration (hf-8).
- **Variable types.** There are seven: string, number, colour, boolean, enum, font and image. None of them is a list, so a word list has to travel as a JSON string read by the page's script, or be written into the HTML (hf-8).
- **Batch mode.** `render --batch rows.json` renders one output per row (hf-8). `--batch-concurrency` defaults to 1 (hf-m4).
- **Transparent (alpha) output.** "Alpha" means see-through pixels. Three formats keep them: `--format webm` (VP9 with alpha), `--format mov` (ProRes 4444) and `png-sequence` (RGBA frames in a folder) (hf-9).
- **Cost of transparency.** The docs say transparent WebM is CPU-heavy (performance guide) and that a transparent MOV/WebM request falls back to SDR (rendering guide; producer docs say HDR and alpha are not one supported path) (hf-9).
- **A docs conflict.** The rendering guide says `--prores-profile` can pick hq/422/lt/proxy, which have no alpha and render transparent areas black, while the CLI page says MOV always uses ProRes 4444 (hf-9).
- **Caption parts.** The catalog index lists 17 caption styles under "Captions" and 12 items under "Lower Thirds" (11 lower thirds plus a News Ticker). It has no "title cards", "progress" or "outro" category. Only 2 items are title cards proper (Titlecard Calm, Titlecard Lockup), about 8 item names contain "title", there is one progress ring (Conic Progress Ring) and 2 logo closers (Logo Outro, Logo Brand Close) (hf-10).
- **How a caption style takes data.** The one we opened (Pill Karaoke) takes an inline word list of `{text, start, end}`. It is fixed at 1920x1080 and 8 seconds, and it loads gsap@3.14.2 from cdn.jsdelivr.net and Poppins 700 from Google Fonts. Its item page states no licence (hf-10).
- **What that means.** Each caption style needs adapting to 1080x1920 and to local files before an offline renderer can use it (hf-10).
- **Built-in caption rules.** Groups of 2-3 words for high energy. On a vertical frame, captions sit about 600-700 px from the bottom, inside a 168-1330 px band clear of the app's buttons (hf-11).
- **Safe-area check.** Since 0.9.44, `check` warns when text leaves the 9:16 safe areas (hf-11).
- **Memory.** Each render worker is a separate Chrome of about 256 MB (hf-12).
- **Low-memory mode.** On a host with 8 GB of RAM or less, a slow "low-memory" mode turns on by itself: one worker and screenshot capture. It reads the host's RAM, not container limits (hf-12).
- **Fast capture.** The fast capture path, BeginFrame, is described for Linux with the bundled chrome-headless-shell (hf-12). The docs do not say it is Linux-only, and low-memory mode forces screenshot capture anyway, so on an 8 GB box it gives no speed-up unless low-memory mode is overridden (hf-12).
- **Windows.** Multi-worker capture on Windows is screenshot-based and writes frames to disk unless `HF_CAPTURE_PARALLEL_STREAM=true` is set (hf-12).
- **Speed, graphics only.** A 10-second 1080p motion-graphics clip took about 26 s on a 2-core VM with no GPU in default (low-memory) mode, and about 14 s with `--no-low-memory-mode --workers 2`, which does not apply on a host of 8 GB or less unless forced (hf-13).
- **Speed with a clip.** A 10-second 1080x1920 clip with one video took 35 s in a 4-CPU Docker VM (hf-13).
- **Speed with treated footage.** Blurred or colour-graded footage fell to about 2 frames a second without a GPU (hf-13).
- **Known bug: stalls in Docker.** Bug #5473 is still open and labelled stale. A single 44-second clip stalled under `--docker` (reporter's update), and no fix has been confirmed; a maintainer suggested 0.8.150 might help, unconfirmed, with no linked PR (hf-14).
- **Known bug: missing fonts.** Bug #7406 is still open. On Linux, when fontconfig lists zero fonts, the render exits 0 with no text, and check, validate, snapshot and doctor all pass. PR #7413 is open and unmerged, and it is not clear it fixes this (hf-15).
- **Install footprint.** About 135 MB for the CLI, 261 MB for the cached headless Chrome, 3.33 GB for the Docker render image, and at least 2 GB free for the frame cache (hf-16).
- **Windows render fixes.** Two Windows render bugs were fixed in the last week: failed exports (0.9.41) and coloured fringes on text (0.9.43) (hf-17).
- **Sandbox.** In Docker, Chrome runs without its sandbox. `HYPERFRAMES_CHROME_SANDBOX=1` makes it required instead (hf-18).
- **Telemetry.** It can be turned off with `HYPERFRAMES_NO_TELEMETRY` and `DO_NOT_TRACK` (hf-18).
- **Skill behaviour.** The skills tell an agent to read stored login credentials (`usage`) and to post feedback to a public channel after each render (hf-18).
- **Node API.** There is a Node render API (`createRenderJob`, `executeRenderJob` with a cancel signal) and a distributed plan / render-chunk / assemble mode (hf-21).

##### Added by the fact-checkers
- **hf-m1. WebM alpha decode trap.** The rendering guide says of transparent WebM: only browsers decode the alpha, and every video editor renders the transparent areas black. FFmpeg's default VP9 decoder can also produce an opaque image from a file that contains alpha, so `-c:v libvpx-vp9` must be set before the input (`ffmpeg -c:v libvpx-vp9 -i overlay.webm ...`). The guide recommends MOV (ProRes 4444) as the editor-grade transparent intermediate. Our static ffmpeg 9.0.1 must be tested for libvpx (rendering guide).
- **hf-m2. An embedded font is no defence.** In bug #7406 the page embedded a web font, yet all text was still missing when fontconfig listed zero system fonts, and check, validate, snapshot and doctor all passed. Vendoring a font into `assets/` is not enough: the render box needs at least one system font installed, and the post-render pixel check is the only guard (issue #7406).
- **hf-m3. Bug #5473 may close without a fix.** A stale bot said on 8 November it closes the issue in 7 days without a comment, so it may show as closed around 15 November. A close is not a fix. The same thread has a maintainer confirming a separate bug: `--no-low-memory-mode` does not reach Docker renders (issue #5473).
- **hf-m4. Batch renders run one at a time by default.** `--batch-concurrency` defaults to 1; the docs say to raise it only after one real render is stable and memory allows (cli.md, variables.md).
- **hf-m5. Root duration.** The skill contract says the video's length is the root's `data-duration`; the variables page says the root length follows the clips it plays and does not cover an explicit root duration. Write `data-duration` per Short rather than rely on leaving it unset (SKILL.md:21; variables.md).
- **hf-m6. The 1 October 2026 change is about reach, per channel.** It changes Shorts recommendations for re-uploaded content: minor technical edits and template-based changes do not count as added value, and the target is channels "primarily aggregating or re-uploading other creators' videos without significant changes". It gives no definition of "significant", no start date and no recovery window. For a channel that reposts other channels' clips, this bears on reach beyond the monetisation reused-content rule. The primary YouTube thread did not render for the checkers; this rests on quoted secondary coverage (Dexerto 5 Oct 2026; PPC Land 2 Oct 2026).
- **hf-m7. The API spend cap is organisation-wide.** At the cap, requests return HTTP 429 (`enforced_spend_limit_reached`) with no retry-after until 00:00 UTC on the 1st, and SDK retries keep failing, so production's decide step would stop too. A separate organisation or a workspace spend limit would protect production (a spend limit cannot be set on the default workspace), but the organisation cap still applies to everything (rate-limits page).
- **hf-m8. Closer analogue for a small box.** On a 2-core, 3.8 GB VM on defaults (low-memory mode), the 10-second 1080p graphics clip took 34.1 s, slower than the 26 s above (ComputingForGeeks, updated 25 Oct 2026).
- **hf-m9. Footage time on one worker.** The only single-worker footage figure is a 44-second composition that took 9 minutes at 1 worker and 2 minutes at 4 workers, outside Docker (about 12 s per output second) (issue #5473). Earlier research put option (b) at 9 min or more, probably 15-30+ min on a t3.large, and about 3.3x that once CPU credits run out (02, lines 108 and 149).
- **hf-m10. A render box is a second machine.** The "$0 extra" cost needs a box we already pay for, but rule 1 keeps all of this off the production server. A t3.large is $0.096 an hour, $70.08 a month in Frankfurt (02, line 117); a laptop left on 24/7 is the only $0 option.
- **hf-m11. Low-memory mode can be overridden.** On a 7.8 GB, 2-core VM, `--no-low-memory-mode --workers 2` cut a 10-second render from about 26 s to about 14 s, and a 4-worker render peaked at 1,823 MB for the whole box. On an 8 GB render box this is the lever to benchmark (ComputingForGeeks).
- **hf-m12. PR #7413 is narrower than it looks.** It covers Linux render and doctor only, counts fonts with `fc-list`, and its author says check and snapshot do not run that preflight. So even after it merges, a passing check proves nothing and the per-Short pixel check stays (PR #7413).
- **hf-m13. The GPU will not help alpha.** `--gpu` is rejected for 444 output and some other formats, and Docker turns browser GPU off by default. The laptop's RTX 5050 therefore will not speed up ProRes 4444 or alpha encodes (rendering guide; preview-render.md:135-136).
- **hf-m14. GSAP licence.** GSAP, which every composition needs and which the plan copies into `assets/`, is under Webflow's "Standard No Charge" licence (effective 30 Apr 2025), not Apache-2.0. Commercial use is free, but it bans use in tools that compete with Webflow and requires keeping its notices (gsap.com/licensing).

##### Templates versus an agent per Short
- A fixed template needs no AI call per Short. The data goes in as variables or as HTML written by our own code (hf-8, hf-10).
- An agent designing each Short costs about $1.13-7.26 per Short on Sonnet 5.5, typically $2.10-2.30, and takes 17-43 minutes (earlier estimate, hf-19).
- At 24 Shorts a day (about 720 a month), that is about $1,510-1,660 a month in a typical month and $810-5,230 at the extremes (my arithmetic on hf-19).
- That is above the $500 monthly cap of the API's Start tier (the Build tier cap is $1,000). The cap is organisation-wide, so it would also stop the production app's decide step (hf-19, hf-m7). The "typical" figure is optimistic: the earlier research says clips would probably land toward the heavy end (02, line 335).
- The owner's own /brag run took about 13-14 minutes of agent time from plan to first render (about 19 minutes from scaffold) for one 23-second video (hf-4).

##### Does the polish earn views?
- The earlier research found no source that links motion polish to more Shorts views (hf-20).
- YouTube's 1 October 2026 originality update says template-based edits do not make a video original. That bears directly on a channel that reposts other people's clips (hf-20). It is applied per channel and affects reach; the wording is known only from secondary coverage, because the YouTube thread did not render for the checkers (hf-20, hf-m6).
- No Hyperframes overlay or variant rotation addresses that: no amount of packaging makes this channel's model original (hf-m6).

#### What this means for our build

**The three ways, worked through.** These times are estimates for a 45-second 1080x1920 Short at 30 fps (1,350 frames). They scale the measured figures in hf-4 and hf-13. Nothing has been run on the t3.large.

| | (a) ffmpeg clip + Hyperframes transparent overlay | (b) whole Short as a Hyperframes composition | (c) Hyperframes only for pre-rendered stings |
|---|---|---|---|
| Look | Animated word captions, hook card, lower third, progress bar, end card. Close to (b) | Best: punch-ins and moves on the clip itself, text behind the speaker | Branded open and close; captions stay ffmpeg/ASS |
| Laptop time, render only | about 1.5-3 min. The graphics render is 2.1-2.7 s per second of output (hf-4, graphics only, no video layer); the VP9 alpha encode adds an unmeasured amount, and the GPU does not help alpha (hf-m13) | about 3-10 min. Footage capture is 3.5-15 s per second of output on CPUs (hf-13), less with the RTX GPU | 0 per Short. A few seconds once per sting |
| Server-class time (2 vCPU, ≤8 GB, low-memory mode) | about 2.5-5 min, plus about 1 min for ffmpeg. About 3.3x slower once CPU credits run out | about 9-30+ min (the only single-worker footage figure is 9 min for 44 s on a laptop, hf-m9; low-memory mode forces one worker). Can stall in Docker (hf-14) | about the same as today's ffmpeg render (about 1 min, 02 section 4) |
| Memory | 1 Chrome, about 256 MB per worker, plus Node | Same, plus extracted frames and the decoded video. Earlier research found memory growth with injected video | ffmpeg only |
| What breaks | Missing system fonts give an empty overlay with exit 0, even with an embedded font (hf-15, hf-m2). Alpha is lost on decode with ffmpeg's default VP9 decoder (hf-m1). CDN or Google Fonts unreachable offline (hf-10) | All of (a), plus the Docker stall (hf-14), audio trim attribute (hf-7), keyframe freezes (hf-7), slow blur (hf-13) | Almost nothing at run time: files are pinned and checked once |
| Install on the render box | Node 22+, hyperframes 0.9.45 pinned, chrome-headless-shell, fonts: about 0.5 GB without Docker (hf-16) | Same, plus at least 2 GB free for the frame cache (hf-16) | Nothing. Render once on a throwaway box and copy the MP4 or MOV files |
| Cost per Short (no AI) | $0 extra only on a box we already pay for, but rule 1 needs a second machine: about $70 a month for a t3.large, or a laptop left on (hf-m10). A burst above baseline costs $0.05 per vCPU-hour (02 section 4), at most about $0.01 | at most about $0.03 at the surplus rate | $0 |
| 24 Shorts a day | Laptop: about 1-2 h of rendering a day, if it stays on. Second 2-vCPU box: about 1.5-2.5 h a day of 2-vCPU work, inside a t3's credit earn if little else runs (my estimate) | Laptop: possible, about 1.5-4 h a day. Second 2-vCPU box: 2-8 h a day, likely over its credits once download and transcription are added | Any machine |

**What I would do.**
1. **Keep it off the production server.** Hyperframes, Node, Chrome and /brag never run on the production server. The clip system runs on its own small machine, or on the laptop for the first weeks. The earlier research reached the same rule for the meetings app (02 section 6).
2. **Default to (c) plus ffmpeg captions.** ffmpeg cuts and reframes. ASS subtitles (the ffmpeg subtitle format that can animate text, and is already in our static ffmpeg) draw per-word captions in the safe band. Hyperframes renders 2-3 variants each of a hook card, a sting and an end card once, as ProRes 4444 MOV files (the documented editor-grade alpha format), or as VP9-alpha WebM only if ffmpeg is told `-c:v libvpx-vp9` before the input (hf-m1). They are pinned by sha256 and laid on by ffmpeg. Per-Short cost and risk are close to zero.
3. **Build (a) only if a measured test says the captions matter.** Then use one fixed Jinja-generated composition. "Jinja" is the Python template library. Python writes `index.html` per Short with the word list inline, the hook text, the speaker label, the colours and the clip length, then calls `npx hyperframes@0.9.45 render --format mov` (or `webm`, with the decoder caveat above). It writes `data-duration` per Short from the clip length (hf-m5). There is no AI call, and no `--docker` path, which is what bug #5473 affects.
4. **Settings on the render box.**
   - `PRODUCER_LOW_MEMORY_MODE` set explicitly; benchmark `--no-low-memory-mode --workers 2` on the 8 GB box (hf-m11).
   - At least one system font installed (fontconfig not empty), because an embedded font does not prevent silent text loss (hf-m2).
   - `HYPERFRAMES_NO_TELEMETRY=1` and `DO_NOT_TRACK=1`.
   - `HYPERFRAMES_CHROME_SANDBOX=1` outside containers.
   - One installed font family with its licence file.
   - GSAP and fonts vendored into `assets/` (copied in locally), with no CDN links.
   - A post-render check that the overlay is not empty: sample 3 frames and count non-transparent pixels. A clean exit code proves nothing (hf-15).
5. **Hook frame.** Frame 0 shows the hook text. Captions sit at y 168-1330 px. Run `check` once when the template changes, not per Short (hf-11).
6. **Skip (b) for automated posting.** Its gain over (a) is moves on the footage, which ffmpeg can also do (crop and zoom), at 3-5 times the render time and with the open stall bug.
7. **No agent per Short, and no /brag in the pipeline.** Use an agent (or /brag --full) once, in a throwaway VM with no credentials, to design the 2-3 template variants. Then freeze them.
8. **No music by default.** Other people's clips already carry audio. CC BY music needs a credit line in every description, and Content ID claims are possible (hf-3). If a sound is wanted, use one CC0 hit at the hook.
9. **Rotate the variants, but do not expect it to help with originality.** Rotate 2-3 template variants and keep the overlays short, so the channel does not look like one stamp on many clips. Rotation is itself a "template-based change" in YouTube's wording, so it does not lower the reach risk for a channel that mainly re-uploads others' clips (hf-20, hf-m6).

**The one-hour experiment (on the laptop, later, with approval; nothing is run now).**
1. Install ffmpeg (static build) and set `HYPERFRAMES_FFMPEG_PATH`. Run `npx hyperframes@0.9.45 doctor --json` (10 min).
2. Write one 1080x1920 composition with an adapted caption style, a hook card, a progress bar, an end card, 45 seconds of real word timings from a test transcript, local GSAP and a local font (25 min).
3. Render it three ways: `--format webm`, `--format mov`, and once as (b) with a 45-second test clip as the video layer. Time each one and record peak RAM (15 min).
4. Overlay the WebM and the MOV on the clip with our pinned ffmpeg 9.0.1. Check that the alpha survives, the captions line up within 1 frame, the audio is untouched and the file sizes (10 min).

**Pass:** (a) renders in 3 minutes or less with correct alpha and text present.
**Kill:** the overlay takes more than 6 minutes, alpha is lost, or text goes missing. If that happens, stay with ffmpeg/ASS plus pre-rendered stings.

#### Risks and unknowns
- **Render time on a 2-vCPU box is unmeasured.** Every server figure above is my estimate scaled from other machines. Find out with the one-hour test, then one render on the second box.
- **Fast-moving tool.** About ten releases came out in four days. Pin 0.9.45 (or the version tested), install from a lockfile with install scripts off, and upgrade only on purpose (hf-5).
- **Silent text loss (#7406).** Without system fonts the render "succeeds" with no text, even if a font is embedded. A pixel check per Short catches it, and stays necessary even after PR #7413 merges (hf-15, hf-m2, hf-m12).
- **Docker stall (#5473).** It matters for (b) and for any `--docker` use. We don't know whether it hits plain local renders on Linux. The stale bot may close it around 15 November; a close is not a fix (hf-14, hf-m3).
- **Alpha decode in our ffmpeg.** The rendering guide documents that ffmpeg's default VP9 decoder can drop the alpha, so `-c:v libvpx-vp9` must come before the input, or use MOV. Not yet tested on our static ffmpeg 9.0.1 (check libvpx is included); ProRes 4444 files are large. Settle both in the experiment (hf-m1).
- **Originality and reach.** The October 2026 change is per channel and has no stated definition or recovery window; it is known only from secondary coverage (hf-m6).
- **Shared API cap.** Any AI use in the clip system should run under a separate organisation or workspace spend limit, since the $500 cap is organisation-wide (hf-m7).
- **GSAP licence.** GSAP is under Webflow's "Standard No Charge" licence, not Apache-2.0; keep its notices with the vendored copy (hf-m14).
- **Root duration.** Docs differ on whether an unset root `data-duration` follows the clip; the generator writes it explicitly and the experiment checks it (hf-m5).
- **Not confirmed: music licence.** The CC BY 4.0 reading, the credit-line duty and Content ID claims rest only on earlier research; the bundled music README states no licence and ende.app returned HTTP 403 (hf-3) (unverified).
- **Docs conflict on ProRes profiles (hf-9).** Use the default MOV and check the alpha with ffprobe.
- **Caption catalog items are landscape and online by default (hf-10).** Adapting one takes a few hours (my estimate). Its licence is not stated on the item page, so check the repository licence (Apache-2.0) covers the catalog before using it.
- **Laptop as a renderer.** It must stay on 24 hours a day for hourly posting. It has 17 GB free on C: and 11 GB on D:, and Windows had two render bugs fixed only this week (hf-17). Fine for a trial, weak for production.
- **Polish may not move views (hf-20).** Measure it with an A/B split of overlay versus plain captions before building more than (c).
- **Supply chain and agent behaviour.** npm install-time malware, telemetry, and skills that read credentials or post feedback (hf-18). Keep the render box free of API keys and YouTube tokens. Hand it only the clip and a JSON file.
- **brag's music licence page.** Not confirmed from a primary source (hf-3) (unverified); low impact because the section recommends no music.

### A9. The YouTube API: can we post every hour?

**The short answer.** Yes on quota, but quota is not the main risk. A new Google Cloud project gets 100 upload calls a day plus 10,000 units for everything else, so 24 uploads a day with a thumbnail, a playlist add and a readback each (about 2,500 units) fits without asking Google for anything (api-1, api-2). Give the clip system its own Cloud project and its own sign-in. Google's developer policy says one project per app, and sharing production's project would let a clip bug or a failed audit hurt the company channel (api-5, api-13). The real unknown is the channel itself. YouTube publishes no number for a channel's daily upload limit, and a brand-new channel starts on the lowest, "limited" tier (api-7, api-8). A channel of other people's clips may also be held back from the higher tier, and automated high-volume reposting is named in YouTube's spam policy, so channel standing and API-project suspension are larger risks than quota (api-m1, api-m7, api-m10, api-m12). So start at a few posts a day, upload each video private with a scheduled release time, and climb toward hourly only while YouTube keeps accepting uploads.

Note on ids: this section's own findings are api-1 to api-22. Findings from the earlier research file are written as 01:api-N or 01:gap5-N (research/youtube-growth/01-traffic-research.md and data/traffic-verified-findings.json).

#### What we found

##### Quota today (read on the official page on 14 Nov 2026)

- **What quota is.** Quota is the daily allowance of API calls that Google gives each Cloud project. It is counted in "units" (api-1).
- **Three buckets, one project.** Each project gets 100 `videos.insert` (upload) calls a day, 100 `search.list` calls a day, and 10,000 units a day shared by every other method (api-1).
- **Upload cost.** An upload costs 1 unit from its own "Video Uploads" bucket, not from the 10,000 (api-1).
- **Other costs (units per call):** `videos.update` 50, `videos.list` 1, `thumbnails.set` 50, `playlistItems.insert` 50, `playlists.insert` 50, `captions.insert` 400, `captions.list` 50, `channels.list` 1, `commentThreads.insert` 50. Each extra page of a list costs the price again (api-1).
- **Reset.** Every quota resets at midnight Pacific Time (api-1).
- **How we got here.** The upload price fell from about 1,600 units to about 100 on 4 Dec 2025. The separate buckets started on 1 Jun 2026. `videos.batchGetStats` got its own 10,000-unit bucket on 3 Jun 2026 (api-3).
- **The repo agrees with the official page.** `publish/youtube_extra.py` lines 18-20 use 50, 400 and 50 units. `publish/quota.py` lines 4-12 count uploads in their own bucket and reset at Los Angeles midnight. `DEPLOY.md` line 187 says "roughly 100 uploads per day per project" (api-1). Old blog figures of 1,600 units per upload are out of date (api-3).

##### More quota, audits and the private lock

- **More quota needs an audit.** To go above the default, you fill in the "YouTube API Services - Audit and Quota Extension Form". The audit checks that the project follows YouTube's API Terms of Service. The page gives no timeline beyond "as soon as possible" and lists no questions (api-4).
- **Extra quota is tied to one use case.** Approved quota may be used only for the use case that was approved. A changed use case needs a new audit (api-5).
- **The private lock is gone.** Since 2 Nov 2026, uploads from unverified (unaudited) API projects are no longer forced to private. This reverses the 28 Jul 2020 rule (api-3). The upload page says it outright: such uploads "are not restricted to private viewing mode" (api-2).
- **No privacy setting means public.** An upload that leaves out `privacyStatus` goes public. Some accounts default to private because of their own settings (api-2). The earlier research said the same (01:api-2).
- **One project per app.** The developer policies say you "must create exactly one (1) API Project" for an API Client (an app) and must not use that project for several apps (api-13). "API Client" means any website or application you build that uses the API (api-13).
- **Quota is per project.** The audit page says the allowance is given per project (api-4).

##### Channel-side limits

- **A separate limit from quota.** The API's error list says `uploadLimitExceeded` means "The channel's daily video upload limit has been reached". It adds that this "is entirely separate from your Google Cloud project's API quota" (api-6).
- **No number is published.** YouTube Help says standard channels (no verification) can upload videos and Shorts with a "limited daily limit". Advanced access "usually has higher limits". No page we opened gives a number, a reset time, or says whether private or scheduled uploads count (api-7, api-8). The earlier research found the same and thought private and scheduled uploads very likely count (01:gap5-6, 01:gap5-7).
- **What each tier unlocks** (api-7):
  - Standard: on at channel creation, as long as there are no active Community Guidelines strikes.
  - Intermediate (phone verification): videos over 15 minutes, custom thumbnails (with a daily limit), live streaming from a computer.
  - Advanced (enough channel history, or ID or video check): higher daily upload limits, related videos on Shorts, pinned comments, clickable links, chapters, "additional channels", multi-language features, A/B testing. ID and video checks are not offered to every creator.
- **Hitting a limit.** On advanced access you wait 24 hours before using that feature again (api-7).
- **Thumbnails have their own limit.** `thumbnails.set` can return 429 `uploadRateLimitExceeded`: "The channel has uploaded too many thumbnails recently" (api-9).
- **Strikes freeze schedules.** During a strike's penalty period, scheduled videos do not publish. They are set to private and must be rescheduled afterwards (api-15).
- **Unusual activity.** Since 21 Oct 2026 YouTube may pause uploads for about 24 hours on channels that show unusual activity, and may make recent videos private (01:gap3-14, unverified: not re-checked today). Trade press describes it as aimed at suspected hacked accounts, with no named trigger (api-m13).
- **More channel-side limits.** Standard-tier channels also have a "limited daily limit" on playlists, and custom thumbnails on the intermediate tier have one too (api-m3).

##### Errors and backing off

- `quotaExceeded` is HTTP 403, the project's daily quota (api-6).
- `uploadLimitExceeded` is HTTP 400 on `videos.insert`, the channel's own limit (api-6).
- `rateLimitExceeded` appears in the error list only for `videos.reportAbuse`, not for uploads (api-6).
- For uploads, retry only HTTP 500, 502, 503 and 504, with exponential backoff (wait longer after each failure). Treat every other 4xx and 5xx as permanent. Resume a cut-off upload from the last byte received. An upload link eventually expires, and then returns 404 (api-10).
- Every request costs at least 1 unit, even an invalid one, so blind retries use up the 100 upload calls (01:gap5-8).

##### Signing in to a second channel

- **Scopes (permissions).** Uploads accept `youtube.upload`, `youtube`, `youtubepartner` or `youtube.force-ssl` (api-2). `thumbnails.set` accepts `youtube.upload` (api-9). `youtube.force-ssl` covers editing videos, comments and captions (api-11). Google says to ask for the narrowest scope that works (api-11). Production asks for `youtube.upload` and `youtube.readonly`, plus `youtube.force-ssl` and `yt-analytics.readonly` (`publish/youtube.py` lines 32-37).
- **The 7-day trap.** If the consent screen is "External" and still in "Testing", refresh tokens expire in 7 days (api-12). A refresh token is the long-lived key the server uses to keep posting without a person signing in again.
- **Testing limits.** A project in Testing allows at most 100 test users. In production, Google shows an "unverified app" warning for sensitive scopes until the app is verified (api-12). `DEPLOY.md` lines 162-163 record that production lives with this warning.
- **Token count limit.** There can be at most 100 refresh tokens per Google Account per OAuth client. A new one past that silently kills the oldest (api-12).
- **Other ways a token dies.** The user revokes access, or the token goes unused for six months (api-12).
- **Brand accounts.** A brand account is a Google identity that owns a channel and can be managed by several people. No official YouTube page we found explains how to pick a brand-account channel at consent (api-14).
  - Practitioner reports say a "Choose your account or a brand account" screen appears when the Google account manages several channels (api-14).
  - One report (a single Make community post, 16 May 2024, no resolution) says an "Internal" (Workspace-only) app fails with `org_internal` when you pick a brand channel. Google's Cloud help supports the mechanism: Internal apps show `org_internal` to users outside the organization (api-14).
- **New-user cap.** An unverified-app screen caps new users at 100 over the project's whole life, and the cap cannot be reset. Harmless for owner-only use, but each re-consent by a new Google identity uses one (api-m2).
- **Name the channel.** Policy requires the app to "clearly identify the YouTube channel" behind each request that needs a user's sign-in (api-13).

##### Scheduling

- **How publishAt works.** `status.publishAt` is the planned public time. It can be set only on a private video that has never been published. A time in the past publishes at once (api-16).
- **Changing a time.** When `videos.update` changes the time, it must also send `privacyStatus: private` (api-16). In Studio, a scheduled time can be changed only while the video is private (api-15).
- **What YouTube does not say.** No page we opened limits how far ahead you can schedule or how many videos can wait (api-15).
- **Shorts can't premiere.** "Shorts aren't supported for Premieres" (support.google.com/youtube/answer/9080341) (api-15).
- **Scheduled Shorts.** No official page confirms or rules out scheduling a Short through the API. The documented rules suggest it works (01:gap5-4).
- **notifySubscribers.** This is a yes/no setting on the upload call, and it is on unless you turn it off (api-2).
- **If our side fails.** We found no page that says what happens to scheduled videos when the token dies or quota runs out. Since `publishAt` is stored on the video at YouTube, already-scheduled videos should still go live without further calls. This is our inference, not a documented fact (api-16).

##### Shorts by API

- **What makes a Short.** There is no "Short" field. A video counts as a Short if it is square or vertical and up to three minutes long (since 15 Oct 2024 for standard channels) (api-17, api-18).
- **The #Shorts hashtag.** Neither Shorts help page we opened mentions it, so we have no official evidence that it matters (api-17, api-18).
- **Copyright blocks long Shorts.** A Short longer than one minute with any active copyright claim, including a manual claim, "will be blocked globally". It can't be played, recommended or monetized. This matters most for a channel built from other people's clips (api-17).
- **Fields the API can set** (api-19):
  - title (up to 100 characters, no < or >), description (up to 5,000 bytes), tags (500 characters in total, commas included), category;
  - text language (`defaultLanguage`) and spoken language (`defaultAudioLanguage`), recording date;
  - privacy, `publishAt`, licence (`youtube` or `creativeCommon`), embeddable, public stats;
  - made-for-kids (`selfDeclaredMadeForKids`) and the altered or synthetic content flag (`containsSyntheticMedia`);
  - paid product placement, and `brandPartner` (added 7 Jul 2026, api-3).
- **Custom Shorts thumbnails.** Since 3 Nov 2026, `thumbnails.set` can set a custom thumbnail on a Short, but only after processing finishes (api-3, api-9). The file can be up to 50 MB (raised from 2 MB on 14 Sep 2026, so older 2 MB caps are out of date) (api-9, api-m5). On a channel that is not phone-verified, `thumbnails.set` returns 403 `forbidden`, a permanent per-channel state, not something to retry (api-m6). Custom thumbnails need phone verification (intermediate tier) (api-7).
- **What the API cannot do.** We found no field for collaborations or co-creators on the video resource (api-19). The earlier research found no API for the Shorts related-video link, pinned comments, end screens or cards (01:api-16). Related videos on Shorts and pinned comments also need advanced access (api-7).

##### Results by API

- **Analytics API.** It needs `yt-analytics.readonly`, which production already requests (`publish/youtube.py` line 36).
- **Shorts metrics.** Per-video numbers include `views`, `engagedViews`, `estimatedMinutesWatched`, `averageViewDuration`, `averageViewPercentage`, `subscribersGained`, `likes` and `shares` (api-20).
  - `creatorContentType = SHORTS` separates Shorts from other videos (api-20).
  - Traffic source `SHORTS` means views from swiping in the Shorts feed (api-20).
  - Playback location `SHORTS_FEED` was added on 6 Nov 2026 (api-21).
- **Delay.** Analytics data typically lags 48-72 hours (api-20, api-21).
- **Analytics quota.** Each request counts as one unit. The actual limits are shown only in the Cloud console (api-20).
- **Reporting API.** You create a "job" once. It then makes one report per Pacific day, ready within about 48 hours, with "historical data" reports covering the 30 days before job creation. Standard reports stay downloadable for 60 days, historical-data reports for 30 (api-22).
- **What views mean now.** Since 24-27 Aug 2026, public views count from the first frame. Engaged views keep the old method (api-21, 01:api-12).
- **Storage rules** (api-13):
  - Statistics fetched without the user's sign-in may be kept at most 30 days.
  - Data fetched with the user's sign-in must be refreshed or deleted after 30 days, and the app must re-check every 30 days that it still has permission.
  - Making new "derived" metrics needs an approved amendment (01:api-13).

##### Items the fact-checkers added (api-m1 to api-m14)

- **api-m1. Developer policy bans copyright infringement and replacement projects.** III.I.18 forbids API clients that "infringe copyrights or exploit copyright-infringing materials". III.D.6 forbids creating new projects or credentials to regain access after a suspension. For a channel that reposts other people's clips, the risk is losing the API project itself, and a suspended clip project cannot be replaced.
- **api-m2. Unverified-app cap.** Apps showing the unverified-app screen are capped at 100 new users over the project's life, with no reset.
- **api-m3. More daily limits.** Standard-tier channels have a "limited daily limit" on playlists as well as uploads, Shorts and Posts. Custom thumbnails on the intermediate tier have one too. The 24-a-day plan with a playlist and thumbnail on each post may hit channel-side limits the quota arithmetic does not show.
- **api-m4. videos.list batch size.** The official `videos.list` page states no maximum for `id`, and says `maxResults` (1-50) is not supported together with `id`. The earlier "up to 50 IDs per call" figure is unverified.
- **api-m5. Thumbnail size.** The upload limit rose from 2 MB to 50 MB on 14 Sep 2026.
- **api-m6. Thumbnail 403.** `thumbnails.set` returns 403 `forbidden` when the user may not set custom thumbnails. Expect it before phone verification and treat it as permanent for that channel.
- **api-m7. Advanced tier may be withheld.** YouTube Help lists repeatedly uploading content you don't own, and posting the same content repeatedly across channels, among actions that can delay or restrict advanced feature access. The higher upload limits sit in that tier, so a clip channel may stay on the limited tier and the ramp may stall.
- **api-m8. Related channels share standing.** "Maintaining channels that are related to another policy-violating channel" is a listed reason to restrict features. Separate Cloud projects isolate quota only, not channel standing, if the clip channel is linked to the company channel (same account, owner or phone).
- **api-m9. Phone verification cap.** A phone number that has verified 2 channels cannot verify more. The clip channel may need a different number from the company channel.
- **api-m10. Ingest conflicts with the rules.** Developer Policies III.E.1 bar API clients from downloading, caching or storing copies of YouTube audiovisual content without written approval, or using the API to facilitate copyright infringement. The YouTube Terms of Service bar downloading except as authorized and bar automated access without written permission. Pulling other channels' videos and uploading them through the API is exposed on both counts, whichever Cloud project it uses.
- **api-m11. Audits happen anyway.** YouTube "conduct[s] periodic audits" and can monitor and audit API access without notice and suspend it. Staying on the default quota does not avoid audits.
- **api-m12. Spam policy.** It names "using automated tools or AI to churn out high volumes of similar content with minimal changes" and "re-posting material from other websites or platforms, or other videos without adding anything of your own". Consequences: suspended monetization, strikes, and channel or account termination (3 strikes in 90 days). Hourly automated reposting is the main channel-level risk, ahead of quota.
- **api-m13. The unusual-activity pause is about suspected hacking.** During it no one can upload, edit, add to playlists, set thumbnails or switch Private to Public. The report names no trigger and says nothing about upload rate or API use, so the idea that hourly regularity could trip it, and the random-offset fix, are speculation. Whether scheduled releases fire during such a pause is undocumented.
- **api-m14. 30-day spam lock test (unverified).** One practitioner article reports a test announced 29 Oct 2026 that locks channels for 30 days over certain spam violations before deciding on termination, with mass-produced automated content as a likely trigger. The source thread did not load.

#### What this means for our build

1. **A separate Cloud project, OAuth client and consent screen for clips.** Never reuse production's project, client ID or token file. The one-project-per-app rule points this way (api-13). So does quota: production plans 1,100-1,700 units per meeting and up to 4,000 units a day of back-fill (01 lines 1051-1053), and that would compete with the clip system's units. If the clip project draws an audit problem or abuse flag, production stays clean.
2. **Consent screen: External, In production, owner-only.** Never leave it in Testing, or the token dies every 7 days (api-12). Accept the "unverified app" warning, as production does. Don't use Internal, which reportedly blocks brand-account channels (api-14, practitioner).
3. **Scopes: `youtube.upload` + `youtube.readonly` to start.** Add `youtube.force-ssl` only when playlists or edits are built (01 line 1039), and `yt-analytics.readonly` for results. Do not request `youtube` or `youtubepartner` (api-11).
4. **Guard against posting to the wrong channel.**
   - Use a separate token file under a separate storage folder, and a separate settings key.
   - After sign-in, call `channels.list?mine=true` (1 unit) and save the channel ID.
   - Before every upload, check the token's channel ID against `CLIP_CHANNEL_ID`. Refuse if it differs, and refuse hard if it equals production's channel ID.
   - Show the channel name and ID on every panel screen (api-13).
5. **Upload private with `publishAt`, as a rolling buffer, never all at once.**
   - Upload roughly one video an hour, each scheduled 12-24 hours ahead. YouTube then releases them hourly on its own.
   - If the uploader, token or quota fails, the next 12-24 hours of posts still go out (api-16, inference).
   - Uploading 24 at once is more likely to trip the unknown channel limit (api-7). It may also look odd to the unusual-activity pause, but that link is speculation (api-m13).
   - Always send `privacyStatus` explicitly, and read each upload back with `videos.list` (1 unit per call; the batch size per call is unverified) (api-2, api-16, api-m4).
6. **`notifySubscribers=false` on most clips.** At hourly volume, a notification on every post would spam subscribers. Allow at most one notifying post a day (api-2; earlier research I5 used 1 a day or fewer).
7. **Shorts: vertical 9:16, 60 seconds or less.** The three-minute limit is technically allowed, but a claimed Short over one minute is blocked worldwide (api-17). Don't rely on #Shorts (api-18). Set `containsSyntheticMedia` honestly and `selfDeclaredMadeForKids=false` on every upload. Send category and languages explicitly too, because Studio defaults don't apply to API uploads (01:gap5-13).
8. **Error handling that keeps the two limits apart.**
   - `quotaExceeded` (403): stop the calls that use units until the next Pacific midnight. Uploads may still be possible, since they draw on their own bucket. Production's `publish/quota.py` `mark_exhausted()` is the model.
   - `uploadLimitExceeded` (400): stop all uploads for 24 hours, log the count of uploads in the last 24 hours, and lower the daily cap by one step. Never retry within the hour; each retry burns an upload call (api-6, 01:gap5-8).
   - 5xx: resume with exponential backoff (api-10). `uploadRateLimitExceeded` (429) on thumbnails: skip the thumbnail and retry it hours later (api-9).
   - Production's `is_account_wide_error` lumps quota and upload-limit errors together (`publish/youtube.py` lines 562-571, line 571 is the lumping). The clip system should not.
9. **A daily cap the scheduler respects:** `min(upload_calls_left, channel_cap, units_left / units_per_post)`, where `channel_cap` starts low and climbs only after 7 days with no `uploadLimitExceeded`. The climb rule is our estimate, not a YouTube rule. The ramp to hourly may never be reachable for a clip channel (api-m7), and the 30 units of checks in the arithmetic below is low if the build polls for processing status before each thumbnail (about 240 units a day at ten polls per video, still well inside 10,000; our estimate).
10. **Phone-verify the new channel before launch.** That unlocks custom thumbnails, including Shorts thumbnails since 3 Nov 2026 (api-3, api-7). Treat a 403 `forbidden` from `thumbnails.set` as a permanent per-channel state, not a retry (api-m6). Use a phone number not already used for two verified channels (api-m9). Expect related videos and pinned comments to be unavailable until advanced access (api-7).
11. **Analytics.** Pull per-video `engagedViews`, `views`, `averageViewPercentage` and `subscribersGained`, split by `creatorContentType`, once a day for the day three days back, to allow for the 48-72 hour lag (api-20).
    - Store raw numbers only, and refresh or delete them every 30 days (api-13).
    - A person works out ratios from Studio exports until the derived-metrics amendment is granted (01:api-13).
    - Create a Reporting API job on day one, because its historical-data reports reach only the 30 days before job creation (api-22).

##### The arithmetic: 24 posts a day

Units per post (api-1):

| Item | Units | Bucket |
|---|---|---|
| Upload (`videos.insert`) | 1 | upload bucket (100/day) |
| Readback (`videos.list`, batched) | about 1 | 10,000 |
| Custom thumbnail (`thumbnails.set`) | 50 | 10,000 |
| Playlist add (`playlistItems.insert`) | 50 | 10,000 |
| One later edit (`videos.update`) | 50 | 10,000 |
| Caption track (`captions.insert`) | 400 | 10,000 |

Daily totals for 24 posts, plus about 30 units of checks (`channels.list`, processing polls):

| Kit per post | Upload calls | Units from the 10,000 | Fits a new project? | Fits if shared with production? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Upload + readback | 24 | about 55 | yes | yes on quota, but against policy (api-13) |
| + thumbnail | 24 | about 1,255 | yes | tight: production plans 2,200-3,400 a day plus back-fill |
| + thumbnail + playlist | 24 | about 2,455 | yes | likely to clash on back-fill days |
| + thumbnail + playlist + one edit | 24 | about 3,655 | yes | no |
| + all of the above + caption track | 24 | about 13,255 | **no** (over by about 3,250) | no |

- **Uploads.** 24 posts a day leaves 76 of the 100 upload calls for retries. If the channel limit allows it, 100 posts a day is the quota ceiling.
- **Captions.** Burned-in captions cost 0 units, so caption tracks are the one item to drop. With everything else attached, about 15 caption tracks a day fit (about 6,345 units left / 400).
- **What fits today with no approval:** on quota, hourly posting (24 a day) with thumbnail, playlist and one edit each, in its own project. On the channel side we don't know. Start a new channel at about 4-6 posts a day and step up (estimate), because the "limited" standard tier has no published number (api-7, api-8).

#### Risks and unknowns

- **The channel upload limit is unpublished.** It is the most likely blocker for hourly posting on a new channel (api-7, api-8). We could not confirm whether private and scheduled uploads count toward it.
  - Cheap test: run a ramp (4, 8, 12, 16, 24 a day over 2-3 weeks) and log every `uploadLimitExceeded` with the count of uploads in the previous 24 hours.
- **Scheduled Shorts.** No official page confirms that a Short scheduled through the API goes live on time as a Short (01:gap5-4).
  - Cheap test: one private scheduled Short, checked when its time comes.
- **Unusual-activity pause.** The pause is documented for suspected hacked accounts, not for upload rate (api-m13; 01:gap3-14 unverified, not re-checked). Whether regular hourly uploads could trigger it is speculation. Small random offsets of a few minutes on release times are cheap, and alert on the first pause.
- **Copyright and spam policy.** For a channel of other people's clips, claims block Shorts over 60 seconds worldwide (api-17), strikes stop scheduled videos from publishing (api-15), and the developer policies and spam policy name infringement, downloading and automated reposting as grounds for losing the API project or the channel (api-m1, api-m10, api-m12). A suspended clip project cannot be replaced with a new one (api-m1). Separate projects do not protect the company channel if the channels are linked (api-m8). Not confirmed: a reported 30-day spam lock test (api-m14).
- **Audits.** An audit for more quota checks Terms of Service compliance (api-4), so a reupload channel may fail one. Plan never to need more than the default quota, but note that periodic audits can happen on the default quota too (api-m11).
- **Copyright blocks and the ramp.** The Shorts copyright rule does not make clips of 60 seconds or less safe: under one minute the claimant's own policy still applies (our inference from the "regardless of the policy" wording on the page) (api-17).
- **Disagreement note.** The checkers disagreed on nothing material. One detail: api-14 is a single dated 2024 report, so keep it low confidence.
- **Policy reading.** "One project per API Client" is our reading of section III.D.1.c (api-13). Google gives no example for two systems run by one owner. Separate projects satisfy it either way.
- **Brand-account sign-in.** The brand-account consent flow is documented only by practitioners (api-14).
  - Cheap test: sign in once and confirm with `channels.list?mine=true` before any upload.
- **"Additional channels" is an advanced feature** (api-7). Creating a second channel under the same Google account may need advanced access on that account; we don't know. A separate Google account or brand account avoids the question.
- **Token loss.** A new token past 100 for the same account and client silently kills the oldest (api-12). Don't reconnect in a loop. Store the token encrypted, as production plans to.
- **Analytics limits.** The Analytics API quota numbers are not published (api-20). Check the Cloud console after the first week.
- **notifySubscribers on scheduled release.** We don't know whether the setting made at upload still applies when a private scheduled video goes public later (01 line 155). Check the first few releases.
- **Undated pages.** The official pages we opened carry no "last updated" date. The revision history entries (latest 3 Nov 2026 for the Data API, 6 Nov 2026 for Analytics) are the dated record.
