- YouTube Terms of Service. https://www.youtube.com/t/terms?hl=en&gl=US. Official, effective 15 Dec 2023. Read 14 Nov 2026.
- YouTube halts uploads on suspected hacked channels. https://ppc.land/youtube-halts-uploads-on-suspected-hacked-channels-typically-for-24-hours/. Trade press, 21 Oct 2026.
- YouTube channel lock for spam. https://outlierkit.com/resources/youtube-channel-lock-spam-grace-period/. Practitioner, 3 Nov 2026. Unconfirmed.
- Local: publish/quota.py (lines 1-15, 41-52), publish/youtube.py (lines 32-37, 409-419, 535-571), publish/youtube_extra.py (lines 18-20), publish/settings.py (lines 44-69, 159-160), DEPLOY.md (lines 160-205), research/youtube-growth/01-traffic-research.md (lines 200-228, 1012-1062), research/youtube-growth/data/traffic-verified-findings.json (01:api-6, 01:api-8, 01:api-16, 01:gap3-14, 01:gap5-4, 01:gap5-6, 01:gap5-7, 01:gap5-8).

Checked on 2026-11-14 by 2 independent fact-checker(s) (primary; realism): 18 confirmed, 4 corrected, 0 removed, 2 unverified.

### A10. Titles, descriptions, hashtags and setting up the channel

**The short answer.** Words on the video cannot make clipping other people's videos safe. YouTube's spam policy names "re-uploads popular clips in full" without anything added as a violation, and a credit line or a "no infringement intended" note does not give us rights (pack-1, pack-2, pack-3). Within that limit, the packaging rules are simple and a program can follow them. Put the topic, and the guest's name when people search for it, in the first 40 characters. Every claim in the title must be said in the clip. Write a unique opening line, then a credit block that names and links the source, then 1-3 relevant hashtags and about 10 tags. Send every field on every upload, because YouTube's upload defaults only apply to uploads made in a web browser (pack-13). Put this on a new, separate channel that is not linked to the company's account, because three copyright strikes can end linked channels too (pack-m9). Keep clipped Shorts to 60 seconds or less, because a claimed Short over a minute is blocked worldwide (pack-m8). The owner can try ID or video verification before the first upload, but it is not available to every creator, so the first uploads must not depend on description links, chapters or the Related video link (pack-8, pack-m2). Leave auto-dubbing and translations off at the start: dubbing skips videos with copyrighted content anyway (pack-4).

#### What we found

Earlier research already settled most of the general packaging rules. We cite those findings by their ids from `research/youtube-growth/01-traffic-research.md` and `research/youtube-growth/data/traffic-verified-findings.json` (ids like packaging-1). Shorts ids come from `data/shorts-verified-findings.json` (ids like shorts_views-1). Everything marked pack-N is new in this strand, and pack-mN items were added by the fact-checkers.

##### What YouTube's rules forbid for a channel that posts clips

- The spam policy bans "Scraped content". It describes this as re-posting other videos "without adding anything of your own". Its example of a violation is a channel that re-uploads popular clips in full, without transformative editing, reaction or an educational breakdown (pack-1).
- The same page bans "Automated or synthetic mass-production": "Using automated tools or AI to churn out high volumes of similar content with minimal changes" (pack-1). An earlier finding showed that this applies to every channel, including private and unlisted videos (policy-4).
- The page's own mass-production example is "Channels that use the exact same background music and repetitive AI generated imagery across many videos". The reused-content page also bars content that "looks like it's made with a template". One fixed template with the same music, used many times a day, matches this pattern. The template, the music and the on-screen look need real variation, not only the titles. Testing tools or posting "a few variations" is fine, so the line is volume plus sameness (pack-m11).
- Titles, thumbnails or descriptions that are "maliciously misleading" are banned as malicious clickbait (pack-1, packaging-2). Unrelated hashtags, tag lists in the description and repeated sentences in the description can each get a video removed and bring a warning or strike (policy-9).
- Giving credit "doesn't automatically give you the rights" to someone else's content. Disclaimers such as "no infringement intended" don't either. Only a court decides fair use (pack-2). No clip length is safe: using content without permission may cause copyright issues "even if it's just a few seconds" (pack-m12).
- The Partner Program's reused-content rule allows reuse only when "viewers can tell that there's a meaningful difference". It rejects clips "edited together with little or no narrative" and copies with no substantive changes. It applies "even if you have permission from the original creator", and reviewers judge the whole channel (pack-3). The 15 Jul 2025 log entry renamed a different policy, "repetitious content", to "inauthentic content", and says there is no change to the reused-content policy (pack-3). The reused-content rule decides monetisation, not removal (policy-7).
- The impersonation policy also lists "Copying someone else's videos and reposting them as your own without changing anything" (or without significant original commentary) as impersonation. That is a third policy, next to spam and reused content, under which a minimal-edit clip channel can be actioned (pack-m13).
- Strikes block uploading, scheduling and custom thumbnails for 1-2 weeks. Three strikes in 90 days can end the channel, and a terminated owner is barred from using or creating other channels (policy-14).
- With 3 copyright strikes, the account "along with any associated channels" is subject to termination, and if a channel linked to yours has 3 active copyright strikes, your channel is also subject to termination. The page does not define "linked". A clip channel under the same Google account as the company channel therefore puts the company channel at risk (pack-m9).
- A Short over one minute long with an active copyright claim of any type, including a manual claim, is blocked worldwide: it cannot be played or recommended and cannot earn money. Shorts under one minute are not affected. Clipped Shorts should therefore be 60 seconds or less (pack-m8).

##### Titles

- The hard limits are 100 characters, and no `<` or `>` (pack-11). The app already enforces both (`publish/describe.py` lines 9-10 and 33-34).
- YouTube's advice is to put key words first and branding or episode numbers last, and to use the same 1-2 main words in the title and the description (packaging-1, pack-17).
- **Where titles get cut off.** YouTube publishes no cut-off. A vendor (vidIQ, updated 5 Jun 2026) says Shorts titles are cut at about 40 characters in the mobile feed and at 55-70 on desktop. It calls 4-6 words, or 20-40 characters, the best-performing band but gives no dataset for that claim. The only dataset it cites, more than 10,000 trending Shorts (no author or date), found an average trending title of about 51 characters, which is longer than its own recommended band (pack-20). Other vendor pages put the cut on the long-form mobile home feed at about 40-65 characters, and they disagree with each other (search results only, not opened).
- **Title length and style for long videos.** In a correlational vendor study of 18,080 English channels (AIR Media-Tech, updated 12 Jun 2026), titles of 30-50 characters did best in most niches and titles of 90 or more did worse. Question marks helped in Education, Business and Science & Tech. Brackets helped a little. Numbers helped in Science & Tech and Business (pack-21). The metric was engagement rate, and titles were not separated from thumbnails (pack-21). Channels where 80% or more of uploads were Shorts were excluded, so the study says nothing about Shorts titles (pack-21). Earlier vendor data also favoured specific titles over generic ones and found word-level effects to be small (packaging-5).
- **Shorts title length is vendor opinion only.** The one study with a Shorts-heavy sample (vidIQ) points the other way from its own advice, and AIR excluded Shorts channels. Treat the Shorts length band as a style preference, not evidence (pack-m7).
- **Clip-channel patterns.** We found no study of clip-channel titles. One clipping-tool vendor (AutoClip, 30 May 2026, updated 6 Oct 2026, selling its own product) gives this advice (pack-22):
  - Lead with the creator's or show's name, spelled the way people search for it, then the claim, then a short specific hook.
  - Keep the name and topic in the first 45 characters and the whole title under about 60.
  - Avoid hooks that say nothing, such as "you won't believe…".
  - Never suggest that the original creator runs or endorses the clip channel.
- Podcast guides disagree on putting the guest's name first. Some say to do it only when the guest is well known; others say to lead with the topic (search snippets only, not opened; treat as unverified).
- We did not open any top clip channel's pages, so we have no checked real-life example titles.
- **Earlier rules that still apply.** Titles generated by an LLM need a check that every claim is said in the transcript, because LLMs add unsupported content to some summaries (packaging-10). The app already checks titles against the transcript (`publish/describe.py`: `_grounded`, line 426). It also checks titles against recent ones to avoid repeats (`_posted_titles`, line 513).
- AI-written titles, descriptions and thumbnails need no AI disclosure (packaging-9, api-15).

##### Descriptions, credit and links

- **The opening lines.** Use the first few lines to describe the video, because viewers see them first. Keep every description unique, use the 1-2 main words, and stay within 5,000 characters (pack-17, packaging-8). The API limit is 5,000 bytes (pack-11).
- **Clickable links.**
  - Clickable links in long-form descriptions need "advanced features". A new channel gets them through channel history (YouTube gives no time frame) or right away by verifying with ID or a video, which is not available to all creators (pack-8).
  - Links in Shorts descriptions and comments have not been clickable since 31 Aug 2023. YouTube moved links to the channel profile, near the Subscribe button (pack-9, packaging-14). The official Help page "Sharing links with your audiences" says URLs in Shorts comments and descriptions are non-clickable, and that a channel profile can show up to 14 links (pack-m4).
  - So the credit link on a Short is plain text only. The only in-player link from a Short is the Related video link, which points only to the channel's own videos and is set in Studio, not by API (channel_features-3).
- **Credit wording.** For Creative Commons (CC BY) sources, YouTube says to credit the title of the work, its author, a source URL and the licence, for example "is licensed under CC BY". On-screen text or a voiceover also counts (pack-23). For sources that are not CC BY, YouTube gives no credit format, and credit gives no rights (pack-2).
- **Timestamps.** Chapters need at least 3 timestamps in ascending order, the first at 00:00, and each chapter at least 10 seconds long. They need advanced features (pack-14). Chapters are unavailable if the channel has any active strike, so after one copyright or guidelines strike the template's chapters silently stop working (pack-m6). Google uses description timestamps as "key moments" in search (offsite_search-3).
- **Pinned comment.** The API can post a comment (50 units) but cannot pin it. Pinning needs advanced features and is done in Studio or the app (channel_features-9).

##### Hashtags, tags and other fields

- **Hashtags.** Up to 3 hashtags "considered most engaging" show by the title. More than 60 makes YouTube ignore them all. Hashtags have no spaces and must relate directly to the video, and over-tagging can remove a video from uploads or search (pack-10, packaging-13). The hashtag page itself warns that "Misleading or unrelated hashtags may result in the removal of your video or playlist" (pack-m5).
- #Shorts is not needed: any vertical or square video of 3 minutes or less is a Short (shorts_views-12).
- **Tags.** Tags "play a minimal role in your video's discovery" and mainly help with misspellings (pack-12, packaging-13). All tags together are capped at 500 characters. Commas count, and a tag with a space counts 2 extra characters for its implied quotes (pack-11).
- **Category.** YouTube's only stated purpose for the category is "so viewers can find your video more easily" (pack-12). The valid ids come from `videoCategories.list` (pack-11). We found no evidence on how much the category matters.
- **Language.** `defaultLanguage` is the language of the title and description, and `defaultAudioLanguage` is the spoken language (pack-11). When the language is wrong or missing, dubs and subtitle tools break (localization-5).
- **Required declarations.** Every upload must say whether it is made for kids (`selfDeclaredMadeForKids`) and whether it is realistic altered or synthetic content (`containsSyntheticMedia`) (pack-11, pack-12).
- **Licence.** The licence is `youtube` or `creativeCommon`. A video with a Content ID claim cannot carry a CC BY licence (pack-11, pack-23).
- **Upload defaults.** These "only affect videos uploaded through your browser on youtube.com/upload". Mobile and video-editor uploads ignore them. The page does not mention API uploads (pack-13).

##### Search versus feed

- New Shorts go first to a small seed audience in the Shorts feed. Reach then grows or shrinks with how those viewers respond. Posting time, hashtags and posting frequency do not change this (shorts_views-1).
- Search is a smaller but real route for Shorts. Since 8 Jan 2026, search has a "Shorts" type filter, a "3-20 minutes" length filter, and a "Popularity" sort that weighs view count and watch time. The "Last hour" upload-date filter was removed (pack-15, shorts_views-14).
- YouTube search ranks on relevance (title, tags, description, video content), on engagement for that query, and on quality (algorithm-5).
- **Where to find search words without scraping.**
  - YouTube's Terms forbid automated access to the service (channel_features-15). So scraping autocomplete or other channels' pages is out.
  - Allowed sources: the Studio Trends tab and Research tools, which show top searches from our audience over 28 days, content gaps for Shorts and audience-interest levels, with no API mentioned (pack-16, analytics-12). These cards are built from "your audience", so a brand-new channel with no viewers will probably get little from them at first (our inference); do not plan early title vocabulary around them.
  - Google Ads Keyword Planner, which YouTube itself suggests (pack-17).
  - Per video, once there are views, the Analytics API's top 25 YouTube search terms (api-10).
  - The Search Console platform property, for Google queries (whats_new-12).
  - The Google Trends API is still an alpha for "a very limited number of testers". It gives relative interest, not volumes, and its announcement does not mention YouTube search data (pack-18).

##### Thumbnails

- Custom thumbnails need phone verification, which is the intermediate tier (pack-8).
- `thumbnails.set` works with the upload permission we already have. It costs about 50 units and takes files up to 50 MB. Since 3 Nov 2026 it also works on Shorts once processing has finished, and the image is cropped to 9:16 (packaging-4, whats_new-4, api-1).
- In 2026 vendor data, faces appear about as often on weak thumbnails as on breakout ones (82.2% vs 84.2%). Text overlays are the norm, and thumbnails with no text lean toward the weak ones (packaging-6).
- YouTube's own automatic picker favours sharp, well-framed frames centred on one subject (packaging-7).
- Test & Compare works only on long videos, picks the winner by watch time, and has no API (packaging-12).
- YouTube's impersonation policy bans copying another creator's "profile pictures, banners, or specific color schemes" (pack-5). It says nothing specific about thumbnails, so whether copying a source's thumbnail style breaks the rule is our inference.

##### Quota

- On the official quota page, `videos.insert` costs 1 unit in its own bucket with a default limit of 100 calls a day, so 24 uploads a day fits. `thumbnails.set`, `videos.update`, `playlistItems.insert` and `commentThreads.insert` cost 50 units each. `captions.insert` costs 400. Everything outside the upload bucket shares 10,000 units a day, reset at midnight Pacific Time. 24 thumbnails (1,200 units) plus 24 caption uploads (9,600 units) would use 10,800 units and go over the limit, so caption tracks cannot go on every hourly upload by API (pack-m10).
- The `videos.insert` page also says videos uploaded from unverified API projects are not restricted to private viewing mode (pack-m10).

##### A new channel

- **Name and handle.**
  - A fan channel must "state so explicitly in your channel name or handle", and it must be obvious that the channel doesn't represent the original creator.
  - Banned: putting "Real" or "Official" in the name; "Pretending to be a backup channel by adding words like "Backup," "Shorts," or "Live" to a creator's name"; and names that sound or look like an established entity, including deceptive misspellings (pack-5). A name like `<Creator> Shorts` is exactly the pattern the policy lists. `<Creator> Clips` is not listed but is close (inference). Use a topic or niche name, or put "fan" explicitly in the name, and never use a creator's name plus a format word (pack-m1).
  - Handles are 3-30 characters: letters or numbers, plus `_ - . ·`, but not at the start or end. They cannot look like a URL or a phone number, and YouTube can reclaim them (pack-6).
  - The name and handle can each change only twice in 14 days (channel_features-7).
- **Images.**
  - Profile picture: JPG, GIF, BMP or PNG (no animated GIF), at most 15 MB, shown at 98 x 98 px.
  - Banner: at least 2048 x 1152 px (16:9), 2560 x 1440 px recommended, at most 6 MB. Keep text and logos inside the 1235 x 338 px safe area.
  - Watermark: square, at least 150 x 150 px, under 1 MB (pack-7).
- **Fields the API can set.** `channels.update` can set the description (at most 1,000 characters), keywords (at most 500), country, default language, localisations and the trailer for non-subscribers. The name and handle can only be changed in Studio (channel_features-7).
- **Verification tiers.**
  - Standard features come at once, as long as the channel has no active Community Guidelines strikes (pack-8).
  - Phone verification unlocks videos over 15 minutes and custom thumbnails (pack-8).
  - ID or video verification, or enough channel history, unlocks clickable description links, chapters, higher daily limits and A/B testing (pack-8). Pinned comments and the Shorts Related video link are also advanced features (channel_features-2).
  - ID and video verification "isn't available to all creators", and advanced features stay only while the channel keeps a positive history with no strikes. Any Community Guidelines violation may result in a strike or restrict feature access (pack-m2).
- **Playlists.** Playlists can be made and filled by API (50 units a call), but only with the broader `youtube` or `youtube.force-ssl` permission (channel_features-5).
- **Studio-only settings.** The header links, Home sections, end screens, cards and pinned comments can only be set in Studio. YouTube's Terms forbid driving Studio with a bot (channel_features-15, api-16).
- **Notifications.** One finding says a channel can send each viewer at most 3 notifications a day, with a 24-hour pause after bulk publishing (channel_features-1). A later finding says the current help page states no such cap (shorts_views-15). The two findings disagree.

##### Languages

- **Auto-dubbing.**
  - It is enabled by default for eligible creators. English can be dubbed into 20 languages. On a computer, it is switched off in YouTube Studio at Settings > Channel > Advanced settings by unchecking "Allow automatic dubbing". The same screen has "Manually review dubs before publishing". Settings > Content > Automatic dubbing is the path in the Android Studio app (pack-4, pack-m3).
  - Videos over 120 minutes, videos with little speech and videos that contain "copyrighted content" are not dubbed (pack-4).
  - The dubs cannot be edited and are weakest with jargon and overlapping speakers (localization-3).
  - YouTube says dubs do not hurt the original video's discovery (localization-4).
- **Translated titles and descriptions.** These can show in search for viewers of those languages. They go in the upload call at no extra quota (localization-1). YouTube's developer rules forbid adding translations without the owner's explicit consent (api-14). The app already has this feature, off by default (`publish/translate.py` lines 1-18).

##### Posting times

- YouTube says upload frequency, breaks and publish time do not drive long-term performance. Uploading private and publishing later costs nothing (algorithm-8, algorithm-9).
- Buffer, a vendor of scheduling tools, studied 1.8 million videos (24 Jul 2026). It measured median engagement, not views. Its best Shorts slot was Friday at 4 p.m., with evenings from 6 to 11 p.m. strong. Its best long-form slot was Sunday at 10 a.m. Buffer adjusted its times to the viewer's local time, says they "may not be the right fit for your audience", and its 2025 results pointed to different hours (pack-19). Buffer also says Shorts launch time matters less because Shorts are resurfaced over days or weeks (pack-19).
- Scheduling works through `status.publishAt` with today's upload permission (channel_features-4).

#### What this means for our build

**Channel.** Post clips on a new channel, not the company channel, and do not link it to the company's account. Reused content is judged across the whole channel, and three strikes can end the channel and bar its owner from other channels (pack-3, policy-14). Three copyright strikes on a linked channel also put the other channel at risk, and the page does not define "linked", so a Brand Account under the company's Google account is not safe (pack-m9). Whether a separate Google account fully isolates the two is a question for the policy strand; we did not check it.

**Title rules for the program (one `clip_title()` per format):**
1. Shorts: aim for 20-45 characters, never more than 60. The main topic or claim goes in the first 40 characters (pack-20). No hashtags in the title. This length band is a style preference from vendor advice, not evidence (pack-20, pack-m7).
2. Long clips: aim for 40-70 characters. Put the searchable words (the guest's name, the topic) in the first 45 characters, and the show name or brand last (packaging-1, pack-21, pack-22).
3. Use a guest's or creator's name only when it is spoken or shown in the clip, or is in the source video's own title. Write it as the source writes it. Never add "official", or anything that suggests the person runs or backs our channel (pack-5, pack-22).
4. Every claim, number and name in the title must appear in the clip's transcript. Reuse `describe.py`'s `_grounded` and `_names_someone` checks, with a cleared-names list replaced by "names found in the source metadata" (packaging-10).
5. Create curiosity only by leaving out the answer, never by stating something the clip does not show. Ban phrases such as "you won't believe", "SHOCKING" or "gone wrong" unless the clip shows it (pack-1, pack-22).
6. Use several title shapes and refuse a title too close to any of the last 50. Identical templates at high volume look like mass production (pack-1, packaging-11).
7. Illustrative shapes (ours, not observed on real channels):
   - `<Guest>: <specific claim>`
   - `<Specific claim> (<Guest> on <Show>)`
   - `Why <topic> <outcome>`
   - `<Number> <things> about <topic>`
   - A question only when the viewer already has that question (pack-21).

**Description template (fill in order, check in bytes):**
1. Lines 1-2, unique: what the clip shows, in plain words, with the title's 1-2 main words (pack-17).
2. One line on what we added, such as context, a summary or commentary. This line must be true, and it does not make reuse allowed by itself (pack-3).
3. Credit block:
   - `Source: "<source title>" by <channel name>`
   - `Full video: <source watch URL>`
   - `Channel: <source channel URL>`
   - For CC BY sources, add `Licensed under CC BY` (pack-23).
   - These lines are not clickable on Shorts, or on long clips until advanced features are on (pack-8, pack-9). Keep them anyway, as visible credit.
4. Long clips only: chapters, if there are 3 or more segments of at least 10 seconds, starting at 00:00. They stop working after any active strike (pack-14, pack-m6).
5. A short fixed footer of at most 3 lines: the channel's purpose and a contact line for takedown requests. No keyword lists and no repeated sentences (policy-9). Never write "no copyright infringement intended" (pack-2).
6. 1-3 hashtags on the last line: topic, guest and show. Never generic trending tags (pack-10, pack-m5).

**Tags and fields on every upload** (send all of them, because upload defaults will not fill them in, pack-13):
- `tags`: at most 10, within 500 characters as counted by YouTube's rule. Include the guest's and the show's spellings and the topic (pack-11, pack-22).
- `categoryId`: one fixed per source type, looked up once from `videoCategories.list` (pack-11).
- `defaultLanguage` and `defaultAudioLanguage`: the source's language (localization-5).
- `selfDeclaredMadeForKids=false`, `containsSyntheticMedia=false`, `license=youtube` and an explicit privacy setting, read back after the upload (pack-11, api-2).

**Clip length and look.** Cap clipped Shorts at 60 seconds or less, because a claimed Short over a minute is blocked worldwide (pack-m8). Vary the template, the music and the on-screen look, not only the titles (pack-m11).

**Pinned comment.** Skip it in the automation. It cannot be pinned by API (channel_features-9).

**Thumbnails.** For long clips, take a sharp frame of the speaker at the moment the title is about. Add a 2-4 word label from the title (high-contrast text, no more than 4 words) and size it to 1280 x 720 (packaging-6, packaging-7). Never reuse the source's thumbnail or its colour scheme (pack-5). For Shorts, leave the automatic frame at first. API thumbnails on Shorts are 11 days old and unproven (whats_new-4). Thumbnails cost 50 units each from the shared 10,000-unit daily allowance (api-1), so 24 a day would use 1,200 units. Do not upload caption tracks by API on every hourly upload: `captions.insert` costs 400 units each, and 24 a day would break the daily limit (pack-m10).

**Search words.** Build each clip's vocabulary from the source video's own title, chapters and transcript, and from our own Analytics search terms once they exist (api-10). Once a week, a person reads the Studio Trends tab (pack-16). Do not scrape YouTube (channel_features-15).

**Posting slots.** The posting hour is a minor lever (algorithm-8, shorts_views-1). If the owner keeps several posts a day, place them in the main audience's evening for Shorts and its morning for long clips. Use US Eastern time as a guess until Studio shows our own viewers' hours (pack-19). Use `publishAt` from one queue (channel_features-4). Hourly posting is a volume decision for other strands. Packaging cannot make it safer.

**Languages.** Turn auto-dubbing off on day one, as an owner decision. Dubbing would synthesise other people's voices, and clips with copyrighted content are not dubbed anyway (pack-4, localization-3). Keep translations off. Test them only after the channel has steady English views, because the earlier research expected a small effect (localization-1).

**Set-up checklist, before the first upload** (the owner does this in Studio unless marked API):
1. A new Google account, not linked to the company's, with 2-Step Verification (pack-m9). A Brand Account under the company's account is not enough.
2. Name and handle: a topic-niche name, or one with "fan" in it. Never a creator's name plus "Shorts", "Live", "Backup" or a similar format word, and not "Clips" after a creator's name either (pack-5, pack-6, pack-m1).
3. Phone verification. Try ID or video verification for advanced features, but it may not be offered; do not plan the first uploads around description links, chapters or the Related video link (pack-8, pack-m2).
4. A square profile picture, large enough to stay sharp (it is shown at 98 x 98; we did not confirm a recommended upload size), and a 2560 x 1440 banner with text inside the safe area (pack-7).
5. Description (at most 1,000 characters, saying it is a clips channel and how creators can ask for removal), keywords (at most 500), country, default language. API or Studio (channel_features-7).
6. Profile links near Subscribe, up to 14 (Studio). Each source creator's main link can go in the description instead (pack-9, pack-m4).
7. Automatic dubbing off: Settings > Channel > Advanced settings > "Allow automatic dubbing" on a computer. Comments on, with held-for-review filters (Studio) (pack-m3).
8. Upload defaults: set them anyway, for manual uploads (pack-13).
9. Playlists, one per source show and one per topic. These need the broader API permission (channel_features-5). No trailer until there is a strong clip (channel_features-7).
10. Add the channel to Search Console as a platform property (whats_new-12).

#### Risks and unknowns

- **The main risk is not packaging.** A clips channel that adds little can be removed under the scraped-content, mass-production and impersonation rules whatever its titles say (pack-1, pack-3, pack-m13). The policy strand must define what "adding something of our own" means. This section assumes it does.
- **Clip-title patterns are unverified.** The patterns above come from one vendor and from our own reasoning (pack-22). Cheap check: a person reads 50 titles from 5 successful clip channels in the niche, and we compare length, name position and shape.
- **Cut-off numbers are vendor figures** (pack-20, pack-21). The Shorts length rule rests on vendor opinion only (pack-m7). Cheap check: look at 10 of our own titles on a phone and on desktop.
- **We don't know whether upload defaults apply to API uploads.** The page does not say (pack-13). Cheap check: upload one private test video by API with no category and read it back.
- **We don't know whether Shorts get auto-dubbed, or whether claimed clips count as "copyrighted content"** (pack-4). Check the Studio Languages page on the first few uploads.
- **The notification cap is disputed** (channel_features-1 vs shorts_views-15). It does not matter for a new channel with almost no subscribers.
- **Category weight is unknown.** YouTube only says the category helps viewers find the video (pack-12).
- **Advanced features take time and may not be offered.** ID verification is the fast route but is not available to all creators; channel history has no published time frame (pack-8, pack-m2). Until then, description links and chapters do not work, so the first uploads should not depend on them. One strike also removes chapters (pack-m6).
- **Copyright strikes can reach linked channels.** The page does not define "linked" (pack-m9).
- **A single fixed template is the pattern YouTube names as mass production.** Varying only the titles will not fix that (pack-m11).
- **A title that names a guest may attract privacy or impersonation complaints** if the clip misrepresents them. The grounding check lowers this risk but does not remove it.
- **Practitioner pages may be written for AI readers.** We saw no instructions aimed at AI readers in the pages we opened. Several pages were vendor marketing and are labelled as such.
- **Not re-checked by the fact-checkers:** the earlier-research ids cited here (packaging-*, policy-*, channel_features-*, shorts_views-*, api-*, localization-*, algorithm-*, whats_new-*, offsite_search-*, analytics-12), and `publish/describe.py` line 34. Whether hashtags and @mentions in Shorts descriptions are clickable, and whether the Google Trends API is still alpha in November 2026 on a Google-owned page, were also not confirmed.

### A11. What we can reuse from the app we have

**The short answer.** The app is a meeting machine that happens to contain three parts a clips channel can use: a careful ffmpeg Shorts renderer, an "upload each video at most once" journal with a release-slot planner, and a YouTube download plus captions fetcher. Everything else (the job record, the pipeline, the autopilot, the never-post check, the titles, the web page) is shaped around Zoom meetings and the one company channel, and should be written new, not bent. Nearly every file the app keeps (YouTube token, upload journal, settings, quota count, release slots, cost database, job folders) is found through one setting, `STORAGE_DIR`. So a second process started with its own `STORAGE_DIR`, its own Google Cloud project and its own `.env` gets all of those separate with no change to the existing code. That is the safest way to keep the company channel untouched. I would build a new `clips/` package on the `clp` branch that only adds files, runs as its own container, and imports a short, listed set of stable modules. Four things need care: the app's single job queue (one job at a time, and a separate process on the same t3.large still shares one CPU with production renders), the look object (it exists only in uncommitted code, and the committed classic renderer takes none), the never-post check inside the uploader (it would refuse clip titles such as "5 PM" or "Interview"), and the deploy script (`--remove-orphans` would delete a clips container defined in the same compose project).

#### What we found

Status words used below. **Committed** means the file matches the last commit (3b6c4bb, 14 Nov 2026) and git shows no change. **Changing** means git shows a change that the second build, still running, has made (37 files changed, about 4,588 lines added and 213 removed in the working tree when the checkers ran; the count kept moving). **New, untracked** means the second build is adding the file and git does not know it yet. Line numbers for changing files are as read on 14 Nov 2026 and may move (code-18).

##### 1. The flow, module by module

- **api/ (jobs, queue, auth).** `api/main.py` is one FastAPI app (1,942 lines, changing). Routes create a job from an upload (`POST /jobs`), a YouTube link (`POST /jobs/youtube`) or a Zoom recording (`POST /jobs/zoom`), then serve progress, files, publish, autopilot, costs, publishing settings and storage pages. `api/queue.py` (committed) runs jobs on one worker thread, one at a time, with a heartbeat, cancel, a wall-clock limit (13 h) and a restart sweep that marks half-finished jobs failed. `api/jobs.py` (committed) keeps each job as `storage/jobs/<id>/job.json`, written atomically, with an in-memory cache. `api/auth.py` (committed) checks an `X-API-Key` header or cookie before routing. It reads and writes only under `STORAGE_DIR`. (code-1, code-24)
- **ingest/.** `ingest/zoom.py` (917 lines) signs in to Zoom and downloads recordings and Zoom's transcript. `ingest/youtube.py` runs yt-dlp and saves `source.<ext>` or `videos/<id>.<ext>`. `ingest/store.py` saves an uploaded file into the job folder (`.mp4`, `.mkv`, `.mov`). `ingest/validate.py` checks audio/video sync and the maximum length (8 h). All committed. (code-11)
- **transcribe/.** `transcribe/native.py` parses Zoom and uploaded `.vtt`/`.srt` and YouTube's own captions into sentence-level segments. `transcribe/whisperx_backend.py` runs WhisperX (speech to text, word alignment, speaker separation) and needs a Hugging Face token. Both committed. (code-13)
- **decide/.** One caller layer for Anthropic, OpenAI or Gemini (`LLM_PROVIDER`) with a rate limiter and token counting. `judge_segments` marks every sentence keep or remove and scores it for highlights. `rerank_moments` picks and titles the best moments, with an on-screen hook and a "makes sense alone" score. Also chapters, a word-count check (`decide/content.py`) and `decide/pricing.py`. Committed, except `decide/topics.py` (new, untracked, topic cuts). (code-14)
- **edl/.** `edl/builder.py` (changing) turns the keep/remove marks into frame-exact keep ranges for the cleaned meeting. `edl/highlights.py` (committed) groups scored sentences into moments and picks the reel and the Shorts. (code-14)
- **slice/ (render).** ffmpeg graphs and commands (`ffmpeg_wrapper.py`, `plan.py`, `profile.py`), the Short renderer, captions (`captions.py`), fonts, silence detection and the new `layout.py`. `plan.py`, `fonts.py`, `silence.py`, `transcript.py` and `intro_outro.py` are committed; `pipeline.py`, `ffmpeg_wrapper.py`, `captions.py`, `profile.py` are changing; `layout.py` is new and untracked. (code-15, code-16)
- **deliver.py and outputs.py (both changing).** `outputs.render_outputs` renders the final video, the highlight reel, the removed-parts video and the Shorts into the job folder. `deliver.py` adds transcripts, chapters, a PDF report, thumbnails, topic cuts, `manifest.json` and `bundle.zip`. All of it is meeting-shaped (code-15).
- **publish/.** `youtube.py` (sign-in, token, one resumable upload), `once.py` (upload one item at most once), `run.py` (plans and runs a meeting's uploads), `schedule.py` (release slots), `settings.py` (the owner's publishing choices), `describe.py` (titles and descriptions), `media.py` and `cleanup.py` (committed), and new, untracked files for quota, thumbnails, playlists, caption tracks, translations, follow-up queue and team lists. (code-3 to code-10)
- **autopilot/.** `engine.py` (changing) is one step run every 60 s by `loop.py` (committed): follow jobs, post what finished, look for new Zoom recordings, start the oldest ready meeting. `store.py` (changing) keeps each meeting's state in `autopilot.json`. `never_post.py`, `emails.py`, `webhook.py` are committed. It never starts a job while one runs. (code-1)
- **ledger/.** `files.py` and `prefs.py` (committed) write small JSON and JSON-lines files safely (atomic write, fsync, backup copy). `uploads.py` (changing) is the upload journal that stops a video going up twice. (code-2, code-7)
- **costs/ and analytics/.** `costs/` (committed except `record.py`) is a SQLite cost meter, AI tokens only. `analytics/` (new, untracked) pulls views into its own SQLite file. (code-22)
- **web/ and settings.** `web/app.html` is one page of 4,081 lines in the working tree (3,270 at the last commit, so it is changing) with a side panel of fold-away sections. It calls the API and holds no server state. Choices made on the page are saved in `state/prefs.json`. (code-17, code-18)

The new look is Zoom-tuned and not committed (code-15). | changing |

##### 3. YouTube publishing in detail

- **Where the token lives and how the channel is chosen.** One file, `STORAGE_DIR/youtube_token.json`, mode 600, written after the admin signs in at `/youtube/connect` (youtube.py:73-74, 192-237). The function that finds it takes no argument. The channel is whichever channel the signed-in grant belongs to: uploads and checks call `channels().list(mine=True)` and take the first item (youtube.py:308-314, 512-530). The app stores only the channel's title, not its id (`channel_title` at youtube.py:225-229; a search of the Python code for `channel_id` or `channelId` finds nothing). So nothing in the code can tell "this is the company channel" from "this is the clips channel" except by title. (code-3)
- **The Google client.** One OAuth client (ID and secret in `.env`) and a redirect address `PUBLIC_BASE_URL/youtube/callback` (youtube.py:77-95). The app asks for upload and read access, plus wider permissions (force-ssl, analytics) in the second build (youtube.py:29-37). Google's OAuth page (opened 14 Nov 2026) confirms that refresh tokens from a project with an External consent screen in "Testing" status expire after 7 days (unless only basic profile scopes are asked, which does not apply to youtube.upload); we do not know whether the current project is in Testing (research 05:222; finding api-6 in research data). The same page caps refresh tokens at 100 per Google Account per OAuth client (the oldest is invalidated silently) and says tokens unused for six months stop working. An unverified project set to In production shows a warning screen and is capped at 100 new users, which is fine for one admin. (code-10, code-m2)
- **Privacy, publishAt and the release plan.** `insert_body` always writes `selfDeclaredMadeForKids: false` and `containsSyntheticMedia: false`; with a `publish_at` the video goes up private and YouTube makes it public at that time (youtube.py:408-440). `publish/schedule.py` hands out slots on a quarter hour, inside a daily window, spaced apart, with a daily cap, and lets only the first video of a team day notify subscribers (schedule.py:1-30). Defaults: 12 h review, 2 h gap, 6 videos a day with at most 3 Shorts a day (`shorts_per_day`), window 10:00-22:00, 7 days ahead (settings.py:43-62). One video an hour all day is possible only with several settings raised together: `max_per_day` 24 (range 1-24), `shorts_per_day` 24 (range 0-24; left at 3, a Shorts-only channel gets 3 a day), gap 1 h or less (range 0-24), window 0-24, review 0-72 h, up to 30 days ahead (settings.py:167-176). Shorts never notify subscribers; only the first full video or topic cut booked on a day may (schedule.py:214-233). The autopilot's own public default is `public` (config.py:330). (code-8)
- **Quota.** The app keeps its own daily count in `state/quota.json`, resets it at midnight Los Angeles time, reserves 2,000 of 10,000 units for uploads, and counts each upload start in a separate "upload calls" bucket (quota.py:1-15, 114-119; settings.py defaults). The earlier research, citing Google's pages, says each Cloud project gets 100 upload calls a day at 1 unit each, 100 searches, and 10,000 units for everything else; thumbnails, playlist inserts and video updates cost 50 each, captions 400 (research 01:1014-1022, id api-1). Google's quota page and revision history (opened 14 Nov 2026) confirm this: `videos.insert` and `search.list` have their own buckets of 100 calls a day at 1 unit each since 1 June 2026, 10,000 units a day cover everything else (thumbnails.set, playlistItems.insert and videos.update 50, captions.insert 400, channels.list 1), reset at midnight Pacific. Those buckets belong to the project, so a separate Cloud project for clips is a separate allowance. YouTube's help page says the channel's own upload limit is unpublished and varies with channel history; copyright and Community Guidelines strikes can cut it (code-m10). (code-9)
- **How uploads are recorded and found again.** `upload_once` claims the item in a journal before opening the file, records YouTube's upload link before the first byte, resumes a cut-off upload through the same link, and if the link is gone searches the channel for a hidden tag (`hc` + a hash of the item key) and otherwise stops as "check needed" (once.py:1-10, 70-136; uploads.py:1-30). Files: `state/uploads.jsonl` (journal) and `state/posted.jsonl` (what is on the channel), each copied to `state-backup/` after every write (files.py:36-41, 166-178). One link makes at most one video. This is the best piece to reuse. (code-5, code-7)
- **What must change to post to a second channel with no way to reach the company channel.**
  1. Run clips as its own process with its own `STORAGE_DIR` (not a sub-folder of the company's data). Then the token, journal, settings, quota, slots and costs are all separate files (code-2).
  2. Give the clips token a different file name (for example `clips_token.json`) and a different Google Cloud project and OAuth client. Today a clips process started by mistake on the company's `STORAGE_DIR` would load the company token (youtube.py:73-74).
  3. Store the channel id at connect time and, before each upload, compare it with a configured `CLIPS_CHANNEL_ID` and with a denylist holding the company channel id. One `channels.list` call costs 1 unit. This guard does not exist today.
  4. Do not share the backup folder: `files.py` copies every file to `backup_dir()/<file name>` under the settings' `STORAGE_DIR`, so two ledgers sharing a `STORAGE_DIR` would overwrite each other's `posted.jsonl` backup (files.py:166-171). It is worse than an overwrite: `read_jsonl` merges records found only in the backup copy back into the main file, so the two ledgers would import each other's posted and journal records (files.py:75-96). Separate directories avoid this (code-m7).
  5. Wrap `upload_once` so the item carries an empty `meeting` and no topic (the never-post match of an empty title returns nothing, never_post.py:149-160), and keep the company's never-post list out of the clips process. Note that `upload_once` checks only the item's meeting, topic and meeting id, never the video title or description, so an empty meeting also switches off every never-post check and clips needs its own block list; in a fresh `STORAGE_DIR` the built-in default list is active unless those fields are empty, and its first use writes a flag into `state/prefs.json` (harmless only with a separate `STORAGE_DIR`) (code-5).
  6. Set a separate `STORAGE_DIR` in the clips environment explicitly: settings are cached per process (one `STORAGE_DIR` each) and the Dockerfile defaults it to `/data` (code-m8).

##### 4. The source side

- **What `ingest/youtube.py` does.** `download_youtube(url, dest_dir=None)` runs yt-dlp with a fixed format string (H.264 at 720p or lower, else anything), merges to mp4 and returns an id, the file path, the title and the upload date (youtube.py:99-137). `ydl_base_opts` adds a cookies file and a proxy if set, and every JavaScript runtime found on `PATH`, but only `deno` and `node` are looked for (youtube.py:20-26, 48-75). yt-dlp's own wiki (last edited 12 July 2026) says YouTube needs an external JavaScript runtime: Deno 2.3.0 or later by default, Node 22 or later only when enabled, QuickJS also supported. `requirements.txt:15` installs yt-dlp unpinned from the git main branch, so every image build can change download behaviour (code-m5). The settings comment says YouTube blocks cloud servers (Codespaces, EC2) with "Sign in to confirm you're not a bot" and that cookies and/or a proxy get past it (config.py:146-150). The Dockerfile installs no Node or Deno (it installs ffmpeg, git and certificates only), and the README says yt-dlp wants one on `PATH`. The company app has never needed this on the server, because the autopilot only reads Zoom. (code-11)
- **How a job is created from a URL.** `POST /jobs/youtube` makes a `JobRecord`, queues `run_youtube_pipeline`, which downloads then runs the whole meeting pipeline (api/main.py:424-433; pipeline.py:595-616). That pipeline judges every sentence for cleaning, builds the cleaned video, a reel, a removed-parts video, a PDF and a zip, so it is far more than a clip needs. Only the two functions (download, captions) are worth reusing. (code-12)
- **Transcript with word timings for a non-Zoom video.** First choice: YouTube's own captions through yt-dlp, creator-made preferred over automatic, English only (native.py:616-681). They come as sentence-level segments with no speakers; the json3 format is read per caption event and trimmed so events do not overlap (native.py:498-535). As the code reads it, real word times do not exist on this path (whether YouTube's automatic json3 tracks carry per-word offsets was not verified, and a cheap word-timing path may exist; worth one test): `slice/captions.py` splits each sentence into words and spreads the time by word length (captions.py:1-12, 55-76). Second choice: WhisperX, which gives real word times but always runs speaker separation and fails without `HF_TOKEN` (whisperx_backend.py:41-59). The research already measured the estimated word times as off by a median 0.3-0.4 s and up to 2.3 s (research 02:131). (code-13)
- **What the Shorts picker and renderer expect.** Picker input is a list of `Segment(speaker, start, end, text)`; output is `ShortClip(start, end, title, hook, screen_hook, stands_alone, category, score)` with start and end in source seconds, 20-60 s (config.py:124-126; edl/highlights.py:259-320). The AI cost is about $0.08 per 30 minutes of source with Sonnet 5.5, thinking off (config.py:23-27, a developer comment; it is an estimate, and the comment's cache-read price of $0.20 per million is out of date, since `decide/pricing.py:13` now prices Sonnet 5.5 cache reads at $0.10). `select_shorts` itself takes `Moment` and `SegmentJudgment` lists (outputs of judge and rerank); the `Segment` input is at `judge_segments`; and its count is capped by `shorts_per_meeting`, default 2. The renderer expects: the source file, a FLAC of its audio (`extract_audio_flac`), a `MediaInfo` from `probe_media`, the word list, and output paths (outputs.py:150-160, 320-336; pipeline.py:667-690). (code-14, code-15)

##### 5. Rendering

- **Classic Short (committed).** The frame is scaled to fit 1080x1920 over a blurred, zoomed copy of itself, with burned-in captions (libass), a title at the top, and audio from the FLAC with short fades; frame counts and audio length are checked after the render (ffmpeg_wrapper.py:515-531; pipeline.py:667-735). Captions are cut into cues of up to 6 words and 30 characters (captions.py:31-37).
- **New look (not committed).** The second build adds, per Short: a picture analysis that sorts a clip into screen share, speaker or gallery and crops accordingly; a speaker fills the frame or sits in a 4:5 panel (the crop centres on a motion centroid, not a face finder); a hook card from frame 0; two-line captions; loudness levelling to a target; optional HD encode; optional trimming of pauses; and a blur over Zoom's burned-in timestamp (ffmpeg_wrapper.py:584-664; pipeline.py:737-863; layout.py:1-60). The layout limits were measured on one real recording and the file says to treat them as a first guess (layout.py:31-37). Gallery, screen share and the Zoom timestamp are Zoom ideas; they will not fit talking-head or gameplay clips from other channels without new tuning. (code-15)
- **Render time.** There is no measured time per Short on the server in the notes (research 02:200 says nobody has looked). The command timeout is 12 times the clip length for the classic look and 18 times for HD, with a floor of 120 s (profile.py:71-73; ffmpeg_wrapper.py:540-542, 716). The README records 312-327 s on the owner's laptop for rendering a 98-minute meeting (README.md:408). The timeouts are limits, not render times; the classic HD path is about 26 times (code-16). The server is a t3.large with 1 core and 2 threads, a 30% baseline and 36 CPU credits earned an hour, launched in Unlimited mode by default with surplus billed at $0.05 per vCPU-hour (AWS docs, 14 Nov 2026). A checker's estimate, not measured: 24 Shorts a day at about 5 min each of 2-vCPU render is about 4 vCPU-hours against about 14.4 earned. The second build's own target is "new plus HD at most about 2 times classic" and it measured 2.15 times for HD on full videos (research 05:173, 218). (code-16)
- **How settings choose the look.** Only in the uncommitted working tree, `publish_settings.looks()` builds frozen `ShortsLook` and `FullLook` objects from the saved Publishing settings once per job and passes the look to the renderer, which uses it only for new-style Shorts (settings.py:362-418; outputs.py:139; pipeline.py:692-695). At the last commit `publish/settings.py` (196 lines) has no `looks()`, `ShortsLook` or `FullLook`, and the classic renderer takes no look. A separate clips look can be supplied only to the uncommitted new-style renderer. Style per Short is `classic`, `new` or `alternate` (pipeline.py:547-560). (code-17)

##### 6. Config, storage and state

- **Settings.** One pydantic `Settings` class reads `.env` from the working folder plus the process environment (config.py:14-15). Keys in `.env.example` (names only): `HF_TOKEN`; `LLM_PROVIDER`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`/`_MODEL`, `OPENAI_*`, `GEMINI_*`; `WHISPERX_*`; `STORAGE_DIR`; `FFMPEG_BIN`, `FFPROBE_BIN`; `MAX_VIDEO_HOURS`, `CONTENT_*`; `YOUTUBE_CLIENT_ID`, `YOUTUBE_CLIENT_SECRET`, `PUBLIC_BASE_URL`; `YTDLP_COOKIES_FILE`, `YTDLP_PROXY`; `HC_API_TOKEN`, `MAX_QUEUE_DEPTH`, `MIN_FREE_DISK_BYTES`, `JOB_RETENTION_HOURS`, `LOW_DISK_CLEANUP_BYTES`; silence, transition, title-card, intro/outro and font keys; `ZOOM_*`; `AUTOPILOT_*`; `REQUIRE_NATIVE_TRANSCRIPT`, `JOB_MAX_WALL_S`, `ASR_JOB_MAX_WALL_S`, `STATE_BACKUP_S3_URI`. The page also saves choices in `state/prefs.json`, and an unset page choice falls back to `.env`.
- **Files under `STORAGE_DIR/state/` (names from the code only; the folder was not opened).** `prefs.json` (retention, never-post list, publishing choices), `posted.jsonl`, `uploads.jsonl`, `autopilot.json`, `emails.json`, `quota.json`, `schedule.json`, `channel_check.json`, `series.json`, `extras.json` and `extras/`, `experiments.jsonl`, `costs.sqlite`, `views.sqlite`, and a `.deploying` flag. Beside it: `state-backup/`, `jobs/<id>/job.json` and media, `videos/`, `transcripts/`, and the token `youtube_token.json` at the top. (code-2)
- **SQLite.** Two databases, both in WAL mode with a short connection per call: costs (`events`, `prices`, `fixed_costs`, `settings`) and views (`videos`, `snapshots`, `yta_daily`, more). Both paths come from `settings.storage_dir`. Since commit 3b6c4bb (14 Nov 2026, "Cost meter shows AI token cost only") the cost database seeds only the model prices; the server's $70.08 monthly fixed cost is no longer seeded or shown (the `fixed_costs` table still exists, unread), so a clips instance has nothing to clear (costs/db.py:58-62,134-143). (code-22)
- **What a clips subsystem needs its own copy of.** Token file, ledger (`uploads.jsonl`, `posted.jsonl`), `prefs.json`, `quota.json`, `schedule.json`, `costs.sqlite`, the job folders, its own never-post-style rules (a "do not clip" list of channels), and a list of followed source channels. All come free from a separate `STORAGE_DIR`.

##### 7. Tests, CI and deploy

- **Tests.** 49 test files are committed (82 to 85 on disk, counts differ and keep changing). `tests/conftest.py` runs before every test: it sets `STORAGE_DIR` to a per-test temp folder, blanks every LLM key, Zoom and YouTube setting, and turns auth and the disk check off (conftest.py:8-58). YouTube is faked by `tests/fake_channel.py`, an in-memory channel that can crash at four points of an upload; yt-dlp is faked by putting a fake module in `sys.modules` (test_youtube.py:10-36); Zoom is faked by replacing the client. Render tests need a real ffmpeg: they skip on a laptop without it, and in CI they must run on the pinned build (`REQUIRE_FFMPEG=1`). At the last commit CI reported 1,284 passed, with 27 render tests included (research 04:209). (code-23)
- **What a new package must include to pass CI.** `.github/workflows/tests.yml` installs a fixed list of packages by hand, not `requirements.txt` (tests.yml:21-27), so any new library has to be added there or the import fails. It then runs `ruff check .` over the whole repo (line 30). No ruff config file is tracked (no `pyproject.toml`, `ruff.toml`), so CI uses ruff's default rules; the code's `noqa` tags for other rule families suggest the owner may lint with extra rules locally (we don't know). Then `pytest -q` with the pinned ffmpeg 9.0.1 and DejaVu fonts (lines 36-57), then `shellcheck deploy/*.sh` (line 60). `tests/test_gitignore.py` fails if secret paths stop being ignored.
- **When it runs.** The tests run on pushes to `main` and on every pull request (tests.yml:3-6). The security scan runs on every push and pull request. Only a push to `main` triggers the deploy job (tests.yml:68). A push to branch `clp` runs the security scan only; a pull request into `main` runs the tests but never deploys. (code-19)
- **What a deploy does.** `deploy/auto-update.sh` waits up to 45 minutes for jobs found under `data/jobs`, runs `git reset --hard origin/main` (line 64), then `docker compose up -d --build --remove-orphans` (line 69). The Dockerfile copies the whole repo into the image (`COPY . .`) except what `.dockerignore` lists (tests, deploy, `*.md`, research, `.env`). So (a) a new package merged to `main` ships in the production image even if nothing imports it; (b) the script never sees a clips job folder in a different data directory, so a deploy would not wait for it; (c) a clips container defined in the same compose project but not in `main`'s `docker-compose.yml` would be removed by `--remove-orphans`. Docker's docs say the project name defaults to the compose file's folder name (overridden by `-p`, `COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME` or a top-level `name:`), so a clips compose file in another folder or with its own name is a separate project and is not touched; (d) the production build is tagged `highlight-cutter:latest`, so a clips stack must use its own image name; the server checkout is reset to `origin/main`, so clips code cannot live there; and Caddy holds host ports 80, 443 and 443/udp, so a clips web page needs another port or host (code-m3, code-m4). (code-20)

##### 8. Three ways to add the clips subsystem

| | A. New package in this repo, branch `clp` | B. Separate small service that imports this repo as a library | C. Separate repo that copies what it needs |
|---|---|---|---|
| Reuse | Direct imports of the stable modules; no copying | Same code, but the repo has no packaging file, so it must be vendored or installed from git with extra setup (code-25) | Copy about 10,700 lines (slice, core, ledger, publish core, decide callers, costs); see the count below |
| Risk to production | None at runtime if the package is only added and run as its own process; merged to `main` it ships in the image (code-20) | None at runtime; but a change to the company code can break the clips service silently | None: no shared code, CI or deploy |
| Keeping up with `main` | `git merge main` into `clp` regularly (never force-push: house rule). The second build edits `publish/run.py`, `youtube.py`, `once.py`, `settings.py`, `uploads.py`, so imports of those drift most | A version pin or a git commit pin; breakage shows at install time | No merging, but fixes (such as ffmpeg pins, YouTube API changes) must be ported by hand |
| CI and deploy | Reuses CI; needs its own deploy script | Own CI and deploy | Own CI, own deploy, own security scan |
| Speed to first post | Fastest | Medium | Slowest (stand up CI, Docker, fonts and ffmpeg pin again) |

Line count for option C: `slice/` 3,402, `core/` 1,462, `decide` callers and prompts 1,712, `ledger/` 815, `publish` core (youtube, once, schedule, quota, settings) 1,622, `costs/` 466, plus download and captions; about 10,700 lines in the working tree, of 25,738 non-test lines in the app (wc -l, 14 Nov 2026). (code-18)

#### What this means for our build

1. **Go with A, run like C.** Build `clips/` as new files only, on branch `clp`, in this repo. Run it as its own container or process with its own `STORAGE_DIR`, its own `.env.clips`, its own Google Cloud project and OAuth client, its own domain or port, and its own deploy script. Do not edit `api/main.py`, `publish/*`, `ledger/*` or `web/app.html` from the clips branch: the second build is changing them and a long-lived branch would pay for every edit in merge conflicts. Reason: all state follows `STORAGE_DIR` (code-2), so isolation costs nothing in code, and import-only reuse keeps merges nearly conflict-free. Set a clips `HC_API_TOKEN` (an empty one leaves the routes open) and add a second backup job, since `deploy/backup-state.sh` copies only the production state to S3 (code-m6, code-m11).
2. **Add a channel guard before any upload.** Save the channel id when connecting, check it against a configured clips channel id and a denylist with the company channel id, and refuse on a mismatch. Use a different token file name and a startup check that refuses the company's `STORAGE_DIR`. This is the only part that needs new safety code, and it should be tested first (code-3).
3. **Give clips its own small worker and loop.** One hourly step: pick the next ready clip, upload it, record it. Do not use the company's `JobQueue` instance or autopilot loop: the app runs one job at a time and the autopilot starts nothing while a job runs (code-1). Reuse the `JobQueue` class only in the clips process.
4. **Reuse the uploader and the planner, not the meeting logic.** Call `upload_once` through a wrapper that sets an empty meeting and no topic. Use `schedule.book` with `max_per_day` 24, `shorts_per_day` 24 (default 3), a 1 h gap and a 0-24 window for a one-post-an-hour test, but start lower: we do not know the new channel's upload limit (code-8, code-9). Treat the hourly rate as a setting to be tested, not a given.
5. **Reuse the renderer through a wrapper.** Call `render_short_clip` with plain data. The committed classic renderer takes no look and ignores any look passed to it, so clips-specific styling needs either the second build's uncommitted new-style renderer (Zoom-tuned) or a new renderer with a talking-head and screen layout for other people's footage (code-15, code-17). Raise the 720p download cap if Shorts should look sharp.
6. **Transcribe on demand, near the clip.** Use YouTube captions first (free, sentence-level) for choosing the moment. For burned-in captions, plan a word-timing step (alignment only, no speaker separation, no HF token) because the estimated word times drift up to 2.3 s (code-13). Copy `whisperx_backend.py` and strip diarization rather than call it.
7. **Write new:** the source follower (channels and videos), the moment-picker prompt, titles and descriptions, a "do not clip" rule list, the small web page and the hourly loop. Copy `JobStore` and `api/auth.py` ideas (about 150 lines).
8. **CI.** Add clips tests under `tests/` with the same fakes (`FakeChannel`, `sys.modules` fake for yt-dlp), add any new library to the pip list in `tests.yml` on `clp`, and expect ruff to scan `clips/`. Add one import-contract test listing the functions clips takes from the app, so a rename on `main` fails loudly on the next merge.
9. **Merge routine.** Merge `main` into `clp` at least weekly, and always right before the second build's commit lands. Never rebase and force-push `clp` (the owner's rule; the history was already rewritten once for a malware clean-up).
10. **Deploy.** Put clips in a separate compose project and folder on the server, or a second small instance. Never put it in `main`'s `docker-compose.yml` until it is merged, because of `--remove-orphans`; give it its own image name, folder and ports. Prefer a separate host, or accept that on the same t3.large it competes with production renders for one CPU (code-m9). Add a rule that the deploy waits for clips jobs too, or accept a restart between posts.

#### Risks and unknowns

- **The second build is still running** (code-18). A function we plan to import may change shape. Cheap check: write the import-contract test first and run it after each merge.
- **Server downloads.** A cloud IP can be refused by YouTube with a bot check (a developer comment, not a YouTube source), and the production image has no JavaScript runtime although yt-dlp now needs one (Deno by default); yt-dlp is also installed unpinned (code-m5). Unknown: whether `download_youtube` works at all on the server today. Cheap check: one test download of a short public video from the server, outside production, with the cookie and runtime variants (code-11). Copyright and platform-policy limits on clipping other people's videos are covered by other parts of this report.
- **The channel guard does not exist.** Until it does, the only protection against a wrong-channel post is that the clips process has no company token. Check at connect time with a test channel (code-3).
- **Token life.** If the clips Cloud project's External consent screen is in Testing status, tokens expire after 7 days (research api-6, Google OAuth page), which would stop hourly posting weekly. Unknown for the existing project too. Cheap check: read the project's publishing status in the Google Cloud console (owner action).
- **Quota and upload limit.** 100 upload calls a day per project is enough for 24 a day, but a channel's own upload limit is unpublished and varies with channel history; strikes (likelier when posting other people's clips) can cut it, so 24 a day is not safe to plan on (research 01:1022; YouTube help page, code-m10). Since 2 November 2026 uploads from unverified API projects are no longer forced private, which supports a separate Cloud project for clips without an audit (code-m1). Cheap check: raise posting gradually and watch for `uploadLimitExceeded` (youtube.py:551-570 turns it into a plain message).
- **Single queue.** If clips ever shares the company worker or data folder, meeting jobs wait for clip jobs, and the deploy's wait, the retention sweep and the cost backfill would count clips jobs (code-1, code-2, code-20).
- **Never-post false refusals.** The company list contains words like "pm", "private", "partner", "interview", "internal", "legal", "hr" and would refuse clip titles that contain them, and `match_words` is also run on titles and descriptions in `publish/run.py:239` and `extras.py:255` (code-5). Keep the clips process on its own `prefs.json` and a wrapped uploader.
- **Same-box contention.** Option A's "no risk to production at runtime" holds only for data and code. A clips process on the same 1-core t3.large gets around the queue's one-job-at-a-time protection (queue.py:4-6) and could slow production renders (code-m9).
- **Auth and backup.** An empty `HC_API_TOKEN` leaves a clips process open, and its state has no off-server backup unless a second job is added (code-m6, code-m11).
- **No server timings.** We do not know how long a Short takes on the t3.large, or how it behaves when CPU credits run out (research 02:123, 200). Cheap check: render one Short on a staging copy and read `stage_timings`.
- **Disk.** The server's real disk size is unconfirmed (docs say 30 GB, the live one was 20 GB and filled once; research 02:250). Source downloads plus FLAC audio add up; clips needs its own cleanup.
- **Not checked.** We did not run the code or tests (read-only rule). Claims are from reading. Whether the second build will change the Settings class, the `Item` kind list or the token path is unknown.

### A12. Where it runs and what it costs

**The short answer.** Do not run the clips job on the production server. A second container there shares the same 8 GB of memory (no swap), the same CPU credits and the same disk, and every push to `main` restarts the production stack, which abandons running jobs and would remove any container of the same compose project that is not in `docker-compose.yml`; the 45-minute wait before a deploy counts only production's own jobs (host-1, host-2, host-3). For the first two weeks, run it on the owner's Windows laptop as a nightly batch: render the next 24 hours of posts, upload them as private with a publish time, and let YouTube release one per hour. That costs about $2-30 a month (mostly AI tokens), uses a home network address that YouTube downloads tolerate best, and keeps working if the laptop sleeps by day. A home address is the best bet for downloads but is not safe from blocks either (host-14, host-15, host-17, host-26, host-m16). The laptop has only about 13 GB free on D:, so transcription must be YouTube captions or a paid API, not local WhisperX (host-m15). For steady state, move to a small dedicated VPS only if a free test shows downloads work from its address. The cheap quotes (Hetzner EUR 6-9, Contabo EUR 4.40-5.50) are not buyable month to month today: Hetzner showed every cloud type unavailable and Contabo's price needs a 24-month term, so plan on about $24-50 a month (DigitalOcean $24 for 2 vCPU/4 GiB, $48 for 4 vCPU/8 GiB) (host-6, host-8, host-7). The ffmpeg-only design fits easily. Browser-rendered overlays on every Short roughly double the compute and need a 4-vCPU box. An AI agent per Short costs about $1,300 a month at 20 Shorts a day, which would also hit the company's shared $500 API cap in about 11 days and stop production's own AI step (host-18, host-24).

#### What we found

**1. Production today (what must not be touched)**
- One EC2 t3.large (2 vCPU, 8 GB), one uvicorn worker, jobs run inside that process one at a time (Dockerfile:73-77, DEPLOY.md:393-396). (host-1)
- A WhisperX job may run up to 13 hours (`ASR_JOB_MAX_WALL_S` 46800 s, core/config.py:320; DEPLOY.md:234-236). (host-1)
- Every push to `main` runs `deploy/auto-update.sh`. Deploy runs only on a push to `main` that passes the tests; a branch or pull request never deploys (tests.yml:5,68). The script counts the production app's own busy jobs (`data/jobs/*/job.json`, plus queued or uploading YouTube work) and waits up to 45 minutes for that count to reach zero. It runs `git reset --hard origin/main` and `docker compose up -d --build --remove-orphans` only once nothing is busy. If jobs are still busy after 45 minutes it exits with "Not updating" and does not deploy. The wait never counts work in any other container, so a clips container on the same host would get no grace period. A restart abandons any running job (auto-update.sh:12-13, 42-69, 104-124; DEPLOY.md:387-389). Docker documents `--remove-orphans` as removing containers for services not defined in the Compose file, so a container in the same project but missing from `docker-compose.yml` is removed; a service added to that file would instead be rebuilt and restarted on every deploy, and adding it means editing `main`, which the owner ruled out. (host-2)
- There is no swap on the live box and an out-of-memory kill takes down the single app worker (02-shorts-editing-and-cost.md:248). Disk: the docs say 30 GB, the live volume was 20 GB and filled up once (00-context.md:72-73; 02:250). (host-1)
- T3 instances launch in Unlimited credit mode by default. A t3.large earns 36 credits an hour (one credit = one vCPU-minute), so its baseline is 30% per vCPU, or 864 vCPU-minutes (14.4 vCPU-hours) a day. Above that, Unlimited mode bills $0.05 per vCPU-hour on Linux (AWS docs; AWS pricing page). The earlier research guessed Standard mode; the default is Unlimited, so "no credits" more likely means a small bill than a slowdown. Whether someone changed the mode is not known: an account can set its own default credit specification per Region, so read the instance's actual credit spec before relying on it. (host-3, host-m12)

**2. The work per day (24 posts: 20 Shorts of 30-60 s, 4 long clips of 5-10 min, 1-2 hours of source)**

All CPU numbers below are our estimates unless marked measured. The only measured data points are noted. One "vCPU-hour" means one virtual CPU busy for an hour.

| Step | CPU per day (est.) | Memory peak | Disk / network | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Download (yt-dlp, 1.5 h source) | under 0.2 vCPU-h | under 0.5 GB | about 2 GB in at 1080p if the whole video is fetched | One practitioner measured about 400 MB for a 17-minute 1080p video (host-15). Less if only the picked segments are fetched |
| Transcribe 1.5 h with WhisperX small, int8, CPU | 1.5-3 vCPU-h | 1.5 GB; 3.6 GB with batching; alignment model under 1 GB | audio only, small | Measured by faster-whisper's authors: 13 min of audio in 1 min 42 s on 8 threads of a desktop i7-12700K, 1,477 MB. Our box has 2 threads, so we scale by hand (host-20). Not measured on our server |
| AI calls (selection plus a title and hook per clip) | none | none | none | Section 4 (host-19) |
| Render 20 Shorts with ffmpeg at 1080x1920 | 0.6 vCPU-h at today's settings; 0.9-1.9 with the planned HD profile | about 0.3-0.5 GB each | about 15-45 MB per Short out | Earlier model: about 112 vCPU-s and about 1 min per Short, never measured on the server (host-21) |
| Render 4 long clips (5-10 min) with ffmpeg | 0 if cut without re-encoding; 1.3-3.8 vCPU-h if re-encoded with captions | 0.5 GB | 0.1-0.5 GB each | Same per-frame guess applied to 11,250 frames per 7.5-min clip (host-21) |
| Browser overlay on every Short (Hyperframes) | +3.5 to +14.4 vCPU-h (631-2,600 vCPU-s each) | Chrome 1-3 GB (guess); it drops to a single-worker low-memory mode at 8 GB or less | few GB scratch | Earlier model; the only real point is 9 min for one 44-s clip on a fast laptop (host-21, host-22) |
| Upload 24 posts | negligible | small | about 2-3 GB out a day | Shorts 15-45 MB, long clips up to about 450 MB at 8 Mbps (est.) |

- Totals for ffmpeg only: about 2.7-9 vCPU-hours a day. A t3.large's whole-day baseline is 14.4 vCPU-hours and its ceiling is 48 (2 vCPU x 24 h). So the job alone is 19-62% of the baseline, before production's own load, which nobody has read from CloudWatch yet (own arithmetic from host-3, host-20, host-21).
- Totals with a browser overlay on every Short: about 6-23 vCPU-hours a day, up to 160% of the baseline. If this ran on a burstable box in Unlimited mode, the extra above baseline (at most about 8.6 vCPU-hours) would cost up to about $0.43 a day, or $13 a month (own arithmetic from host-3). Wall time: 20 Shorts at 15-30 min is 5-10 hours a day on a 2-vCPU box. That still fits in 24 hours but leaves little room for a retry (est.).
- An agent per Short: 17-43 min each (earlier estimate), so 5.7-14.3 hours a day of wall time, and 12-40 hours a day if CPU credits run out. The slow end cannot keep up on one 2-vCPU machine (02:109-110, 123; host-21).
- Memory: transcription plus rendering plus Chrome together can exceed 8 GB. Run the stages one after another, never together (own reasoning; the earlier research gives the same advice for alignment, 02:248). (host-23)
- Upload traffic of about 60-90 GB a month (est.) is under AWS's 100 GB free allowance, but that allowance is shared across all AWS services in the account, including production's uploads (AWS EC2 pricing page). (host-5)
- Disk: keep source video for under 2 days and delete clips after upload. About 10-25 GB of scratch plus the Docker image and 1-2 GB of model weights (DEPLOY.md:129). Plan 40-50 GB on a server, 10 GB free on the laptop. (host-24)

**3. Prices (2026) and how each option fares**

*Cloud server prices read from provider pages on 2026-11-14:*
- AWS EC2 on demand, Linux: t3.large $0.0832/h (about $61 a month) on a price tracker, region not stated; the earlier research recorded $0.096/h, $70.08 a month in Frankfurt. t3.medium (2 vCPU, 4 GiB) $0.0416/h (about $30). c7i.xlarge (4 vCPU, 8 GiB) $0.1785/h (about $130). gp3 disk: the AWS EBS page example shows $0.08 per GB-month; the earlier research used $1.90 for 20 GB. A new instance also needs a public IPv4 address, charged $0.005 an hour (about $3.65 a month) on the AWS VPC pricing page. (host-4, host-5, host-m7)
- Hetzner Cloud: CX23 (2 vCPU, 4 GB, 40 GB) EUR 5.99; CX33 (4 vCPU, 8 GB, 80 GB) EUR 8.99; 20 TB traffic; excluding VAT. On 2026-11-14 every Cost-Optimized type showed "This product is currently unavailable" and the page says stock is limited. The dearer Regular Performance types also showed "currently unavailable" that day, so the fallback cannot be bought today either: CPX22 (2 vCPU, 4 GB) is EUR 16.99 in Helsinki (19.99 in Nuremberg); CPX32 (4 vCPU, 8 GB) is EUR 30.49 (35.99 in Nuremberg). The flag may be a stock signal that varies by visitor, so confirm in the console. No Hetzner cloud option is known to be orderable now. (host-6)
- DigitalOcean Droplets: Basic 2 vCPU/4 GiB $24, 4 vCPU/8 GiB $48; CPU-Optimized 4 vCPU/8 GiB $84; 4,000-5,000 GiB transfer. (host-7)
- Contabo Cloud VPS 4 (4 vCPU, 8 GB, 100 GB SSD): EUR 4.40 a month "for the first 24 months" (the page also shows EUR 5.50 without explanation; both are the effective monthly rate on a 24-month subscription including taxes). No 1-month or 12-month price is shown, so the real month-to-month cost is unknown. Minimum initial term 1 month, one-time setup fee on monthly plans (amount not shown), outgoing traffic "fair usage" with a right to throttle. (host-8)
- Railway: pay for use. $20 per vCPU-month, $10 per GB of RAM-month, $0.15 per GB-month volume, $0.05 per GB egress. Hobby plan $5 a month with $5 of usage included. Hobby limits per service: 48 vCPU, 48 GB RAM, 100 GB scratch disk, only 5 GB of volume. Railway says you are only charged for the resources you actually use, so the cron figures below that assume full allocated size for the whole run are an upper bound. (host-9, host-m6)
- Railway cron jobs: at least 5 minutes apart, UTC only, the job must exit on its own, a run is skipped if the last is still active, and start times can drift by a few minutes. (host-10)
