**4. YouTube downloads from datacenter addresses**
- yt-dlp's PO-Token guide (edited 2026-07-12) says YouTube is "at present rolling out changes to enforce PO Tokens". You pass a token yourself or use a third-party provider plugin such as bgutil; the page does not say yt-dlp makes tokens itself. Missing tokens can get the "account or IP address being blocked", which covers a home address too. (host-14)
- The Extractors page (edited 2025-06-11, so 17 months old) says guest sessions are limited to about 300 videos an hour and accounts about 2,000, advises a 5-10 second pause between downloads, and warns that using an account with cookies risks that account being banned. The FAQ (edited 2025-11-18) says 429/402 indicate the service is blocking your IP address because of overuse; fixes are a CAPTCHA plus cookies, or `--proxy` / `--source-address`. (host-14)
- yt-dlp now needs an external JavaScript runtime for YouTube. Deno is the recommended default; Node 22+ works only when enabled with `--js-runtimes node`; QuickJS is also supported. The production image has no Node or Deno, so any VPS, Railway or Docker download worker needs Deno added; the laptop's Node 24 needs the flag (ingest/youtube.py:70-74 already enables Node when it finds one). (host-m5)
- The home address has its own risk: a block on the owner's home IP would hit every YouTube user on that network, and cookies from a real account risk that account (the Extractors page advises a throwaway account). (host-m16)
- A practitioner post (dev.to, dated March; its text refers to 2026) found the same command and cookies worked at home and failed on a cloud server with "Sign in to confirm you're not a bot"; only a residential proxy worked (the author paid the same seller as host-16; the test covered one provider, Alibaba Cloud). Search results show many more such posts, but mostly from proxy sellers, so treat them as unverified. (host-15)
- The app already has a cookies file and a proxy setting for downloads (ingest/youtube.py:60-68; core/config.py:149-150), and DEPLOY.md:397-398 already warns about AWS. (host-15)
- Residential proxy price, one seller, undated page: $2.75-4 per GB (pay as you go $4). At about 32 GB a month (only the picked segments) that is about $90-150 a month (the 25 GB plan at $3.25 plus overage or the 50 GB plan at $3.00; the $2.75 rate needs a 100 GB plan); for whole 1080p videos (about 63 GB) about $175-250. Audio only, about 3 GB, is about $8-12 (own arithmetic). (host-16)
- We could not find a source that says what share of downloads fail from a given provider. We don't know. A cheap test is in "Risks and unknowns". (host-15)
- Whether copying other people's videos is allowed is another strand's question (policy), not covered here. 02-shorts-editing-and-cost.md:316-318 covers YouTube's mass-production and reused-content rules for our own footage.

**5. YouTube upload limits and scheduling**
- The Data API now charges `videos.insert` to its own bucket of 100 calls a day, at 1 unit a call, since 2026-06-01. Other calls share 10,000 units a day. Costs: `thumbnails.set` 50, `playlistItems.insert` 50, `captions.insert` 400, `videos.update` 50, `videos.delete` 50. 24 uploads a day is a quarter of the upload bucket. (host-17)
- `publishAt` works only on a video that is private and has never been published. If a request schedules a video in the past, the video is published right away, so a missed batch slot posts at once and does not fail (host-m1). Updating or deleting needs the `youtube`, `youtube.force-ssl` or `youtubepartner` scope; the production app holds only upload plus read-only, and cannot change a video afterwards (host-17; DEPLOY.md:192-195).
- Since 2026-11-02, videos uploaded by unverified API projects are no longer locked to Private. The same entry says that if `status.privacyStatus` is omitted on `videos.insert`, the video now defaults to public. The clips uploader must always send `privacyStatus=private` together with `publishAt`, and a test should assert it, or a render-ahead batch goes live at once. (host-17, host-m3)
- Since 2026-11-03, `thumbnails.set` supports custom thumbnails for Shorts once processing finishes (50 units each). (host-m4)
- A new channel is throttled by YouTube itself, not only by API quota: YouTube Help says uploads start with a "limited daily limit", phone verification unlocks more, and no number is published. A fresh clips channel posting 24 a day may hit "Daily upload limit reached". (host-m8)
- Quota is per Google Cloud project (publish/quota.py:3). A separate project for the clips channel keeps its quota and failures away from production. (host-17)
- Anthropic's monthly spend cap is per organization ($500 on Start, $1,000 on Build, $200,000 on Scale). At the cap every call returns HTTP 429 (`enforced_spend_limit_reached`) until 00:00 UTC on the first of the next month, with no retry-after. A limit the owner sets below the cap returns HTTP 400 `invalid_request_error` instead, so the job must treat both as stop signals. The company's tier was not checked (02:9,155 assumes Start), and a new organization may start in a lower Evaluation tier. (host-m10) Workspaces can have their own limit but the organization-wide limit always applies, and the default workspace cannot be limited. (host-18)

**6. AI token cost per day, from decide/pricing.py (US dollars per million tokens, in / out)**
- Sonnet 5.5 2.00 / 10.00; Haiku 5.5 0.10 / 0.50; Opus 5.5 4.00 / 20.00; cache read Sonnet 0.10, Haiku 0.01. (host-19)
- Per Short or clip, the earlier model uses 6K tokens in and 2K out: $0.0016 on Haiku 5.5, $0.032 on Sonnet 5.5. 24 clips a day for 30 days: about $1.15 on Haiku, about $23 on Sonnet. Picking clips from 1.5 h of transcript (about 20K tokens in, 3K out, once or twice): about $0.3 a month on Haiku, about $5 on Sonnet (own arithmetic). (host-19)
- The Batch API halves token prices (Sonnet 5.5 $1 in / $5 out, Haiku 5.5 $0.05 / $0.25, Opus 5.5 $2 / $10), which suits a nightly render-ahead batch and cuts the token lines in section 7 by about half. (host-m9)
- Agent per Short: the earlier research estimates $2.10-2.30 typical on Sonnet (range $1.13-7.26) and $4.30-4.60 on Opus, from an analogy, not a measurement (02:109-110, 155). (host-21)

**7. All-in monthly cost for 24 posts a day (600 Shorts + 120 long clips a month)**

| Cost line | L1: ffmpeg, cheap model | L2: ffmpeg + browser overlays | L3: AI agent per Short |
|---|---|---|---|
| AI tokens | $1.5 (all Haiku) to $28 (all Sonnet) | $2.5 to $47 (adds a brief per Short) | $1,260-1,380 typical on Sonnet; $680-4,360 range; $2,580-2,760 typical on Opus |
| Compute | $0 laptop; $24-50 VPS month to month ($6-10 only on a 24-month term or if Hetzner stock returns); about $17 Railway (upper bound) | $10-60 on a 4-vCPU VPS (Hetzner/Contabo); $37 Railway; $130 on c7i.xlarge | $25-130 plus a per-batch worker at higher volume (earlier model) |
| Transcription | $0 local (CPU time), or Groq $0.04/h = about $1.8, or OpenAI $0.006/min = about $16 | same | same |
| Storage and egress | $0-3 (VPS includes 80-100 GB; Railway egress $3-4.5) | $0-5 | $0-5 |
| Proxy, only if needed | $0, or $8-12 audio only, or $90-150 segments | same | same |
| **Total (no proxy)** | **about $8-30 on the laptop; up to about $55-80 on a month-to-month VPS** | **about $15-90** | **about $1,300-1,500 typical; over $4,000 at the heavy end** |

(own arithmetic from host-4 to host-9, host-16, host-19, host-20, host-21; token and compute ranges are estimates; the proxy range is $90-150 per host-m18)

- L3 at $44 a day typical would reach the $500 Start cap in about 11 days; the production decide step would then get HTTP 429 until the 1st (own arithmetic from host-18, host-21).
- 24 posts a day is 168 a week. Earlier research found about 35-50 Shorts a week from the company channel already sat at 5-10 times the 4-10 a week the data favours and near the pattern YouTube's spam policy describes (02:95-99). Whether the same applies to another channel is for the policy strand. (host-25)

**8. Scheduling: render ahead versus render each hour**

| | Render ahead, upload private with `publishAt`, YouTube releases | Render and upload each hour |
|---|---|---|
| If the machine is off at the post time | Post still goes out (YouTube holds it) | Gap in the hourly stream |
| Heavy work | Batch at night or any quiet time; laptop needs 3-8 h a night | Every hour, always |
| Kill switch | Needs `videos.update`/`videos.delete` (50 units each) on up to 24-48 pending videos, which needs the wider `youtube` scope | Stop the scheduler; at most one in flight |
| Crash mid-upload | Resumable upload; write the upload link before the first byte, like the app's `uploads.jsonl` (DEPLOY.md:261-270) | Same |
| Wrong content queued | Stays queued until deleted | Not queued |

(host-17, host-27)
- YouTube's videos resource doc says a `publishAt` in the past publishes the video right away (host-m1). So the code should never send one; if the batch misses a slot, shift it, or the video goes public at once.
- Always send `privacyStatus=private` with `publishAt` (host-m3).
- 24 posts a day from only 1.5 h of source means reusing about half of each source video every day. Either the best-moments bar drops sharply, or source hours, download volume, proxy GB and transcription cost all rise several-fold (own arithmetic from the section's table). (host-m17)
- Full disk: refuse to start a stage with under 3 GiB free (the app has a 3 GiB preflight, 00-context.md:85), delete finished work first. Lost network: resumable uploads continue; keep unsent clips and retry; never re-render. (host-24)
- Kill switch, in layers: (1) a file or setting that stops new renders and uploads at once; (2) a command that deletes all pending scheduled videos, newest first; (3) revoke the channel token in the Google account as a last resort. (own design, built on host-17)

**9. Monitoring with what the app already has**
- Already there: `/health` and the Docker health check (api/main.py:318, Dockerfile:70), a ledger of every video on the channel (`posted.jsonl`) and every upload in flight (`uploads.jsonl`, DEPLOY.md:261-270), the YouTube quota counter (publish/quota.py), the cost database (costs/db.py), the analytics pull (analytics/), "needs attention" with retries in the autopilot (DEPLOY.md:241-242), JSON logs rotated at 20 MB x 5 (docker-compose.yml:22-26), a daily S3 copy of state (DEPLOY.md:298-302). (host-28)
- A search for Slack, e-mail, Telegram, ntfy or Pushover senders in the app's code found none (matches were unrelated render code), so the app has no way today to tell the owner anything. We did not read every file. (host-28)
- Build for clp: (1) write `last_post_at` and `last_success_at` after each upload; (2) a dead-man's switch: a free ping service gets a call after each successful post and alerts if none arrives in 2 hours (we did not check any provider's price or limits); (3) alert on a failed upload after 3 retries, on HTTP 403 `quotaExceeded` or when the counter passes 80% of the day, and on a disk below 3 GiB; (4) daily total of tokens and dollars against a hard cap; (5) after each upload, check the video's processing status for `rejected` or a copyright or duplicate reason (the videos resource lists `status.rejectionReason` values claim, copyright, duplicate, inappropriate, legal, length, termsOfUse, trademark and more, and an `uploadStatus` of `rejected`, so the API supports this check; host-m2). (own design; host-28)
- Strikes and claims: we found no API call we have verified that reports them. Expect e-mail from YouTube to the channel owner, plus a weekly look at Studio. We don't know whether the Data API exposes them. (host-28)

**10. Added after fact-checking**
- A publishAt in the past makes the video publish right away; it does not fail. (host-m1)
- status.rejectionReason (claim, copyright, duplicate, inappropriate, legal, length, termsOfUse, trademark, account closed or suspended) and uploadStatus rejected exist, so the post-upload check is supported. (host-m2)
- Since 2026-11-02 a videos.insert without privacyStatus defaults to public; always send private with publishAt. (host-m3)
- Since 2026-11-03 thumbnails.set supports custom thumbnails for Shorts after processing (50 units). (host-m4)
- yt-dlp needs an external JavaScript runtime for YouTube: Deno default, Node 22+ with --js-runtimes node, QuickJS; the production image has none. (host-m5)
- Railway bills measured use, so the $17-37 cron figures are an upper bound. (host-m6)
- A new EC2 instance needs a public IPv4 at $0.005 an hour (about $3.65 a month). (host-m7)
- A new channel has a YouTube-side limited daily upload limit (no number published); phone verification raises it. (host-m8)
- Batch API halves token prices (Sonnet 5.5 $1/$5, Haiku 5.5 $0.05/$0.25, Opus 5.5 $2/$10). (host-m9)
- An owner-set spend limit returns HTTP 400, not 429; new organizations may start in a lower Evaluation tier; the company tier is unverified. (host-m10)
- GitHub prohibited-use bullet covers only GitHub-hosted runners; a self-hosted runner is not barred by it. (host-m11)
- An AWS account can set its default credit specification per Region, so T3 launching Unlimited may not hold here. (host-m12)
- Groq free tier accepts files up to 25 MB (100 MB on dev); 1.5 h of audio must be chunked or compressed. (host-m13)
- A t3.medium earns 24 credits an hour (9.6 vCPU-h a day baseline), so the 2.7-9 vCPU-h ffmpeg load can use 28-94% of it. (host-m14)
- Laptop disk does not fit as written: about 13 GB free on D: against 10-25 GB scratch plus WhisperX and torch. (host-m15)
- A home IP can be blocked for overuse too, and cookies risk the real account. (host-m16)
- 24 posts a day from 1.5 h of source means reusing about half of each video daily, or source, download and proxy volume rise several-fold. (host-m17)
- At about 32 GB a month the proxy plan steps give about $100-150, so the earlier $90-130 is slightly low. (host-m18)
- The repository is public, so a clip-bot branch would publish its code and source list. (host-m19)

#### What this means for our build

1. **Hosting (first two weeks):** the owner's laptop, as a separate project folder with its own token, its own ffmpeg, and a log folder. Nightly job: pick, download, transcribe, render, upload private with `publishAt` for the next 24 hourly slots. Cost about $2-30 (host-26, host-17, host-19).
2. **Steady state:** a small dedicated VPS in a different provider and account than production. DigitalOcean 4 vCPU/8 GiB at $48 a month is the only 4 vCPU/8 GB box checked that is sold month to month (2 vCPU/4 GiB is $24, ffmpeg-only). Hetzner CX33 (about EUR 9) is cheaper but was unavailable on 2026-11-14, as was its CPX fallback, and Contabo VPS 4 (EUR 4.40-5.50) needs a 24-month term. Realistic compute is about $24-50 a month unless a long term is accepted. A 4-vCPU box leaves room for Chrome if overlays prove worth it (host-6, host-7, host-8). Choose only after the week-1 download test below.
3. **Downloads:** make this a plug-in step with three settings: cookies file, proxy, and a PO-token plugin. Add Deno (or Node with `--js-runtimes node`) to any server image (host-m5). Fetch only the chosen segments and audio, with 5-10 s pauses. Keep downloading on the home machine if a datacenter address fails, and send finished files to the server (host-14, host-15, host-16).
4. **Transcription:** try the cheapest first. Use YouTube's own captions when present, else a paid API (Groq $0.04 an hour is about $1.8 a month) rather than 1.5-3 vCPU-hours a day of WhisperX on a small box (the laptop has only about 13 GB free, so local WhisperX is also a disk problem). Groq's free tier takes files of 25 MB at most (100 MB on dev), so 1.5 hours of audio must be chunked or compressed first (host-m13, host-m15). The source is public video, so privacy is not the concern here, but quality on our content is untested (host-20).
5. **Level of finish:** start at L1 (ffmpeg, cheap model). Render Hyperframes overlays once as a small asset library rather than per Short, as the earlier research suggested (02:167-169), so no Chrome runs on the box. L3 (agent per Short) is out: cost and cap (host-18, host-21).
6. **Isolation checklist:** separate Google Cloud project and OAuth client for the clips channel; separate Anthropic organization or at least its own key with a workspace limit AND a small organization cap, since the company's $500 cap is shared and a new organization may start in the lower Evaluation tier (host-18, host-m10); the repository is public, so a clip-bot branch would publish its code, source-channel list and scheduling logic and a private separate repo is better (host-m19); separate repo or branch that CI never deploys (merging to `main` triggers the production deploy, DEPLOY.md:315-322); no copy of production's `.env`; the Never-post list and consent register do not apply because these are other people's clips, but the clips job needs its own list of channels it must never copy.
7. **Scheduling:** render ahead with `publishAt`, about 24-48 hours of queue, never more than 100 uploads a day (upload bucket), always `privacyStatus=private` with `publishAt`, and the clips token needs the `youtube` scope for the kill switch (host-17, host-m3). A new channel may hit YouTube's own daily upload limit before the API quota (host-m8).
8. **Cost meter:** write each token call and each paid service to a separate cost table for clp, and stop the job if the day's spend passes a cap (the production app's cost meter, costs/record.py, is a pattern to copy, not to share).

#### Risks and unknowns

- **Download blocking** is the biggest unknown for any server. Cheapest test, $0 and no download: on each candidate (laptop, VPS, Railway) run a metadata-only yt-dlp check on 20-30 public video URLs spread over a day, with and without cookies, and count the failures. If a server fails more than a few percent, keep the download step at home. The test is read-only and fetches no media.
- **No timings on our hardware.** Render time per Short, ASR speed on 2 vCPU, and Chrome memory are all estimates (host-21). Read `stage_timings.render_shorts` in production's job files (read-only) and time one Short on the chosen machine before committing.
- **Production load unknown:** CloudWatch CPU and credit data for the t3.large has not been read. It does not matter if clp never runs there.
- **Provider stock and prices:** every Hetzner Cloud type we looked at (cheap and regular) showed as unavailable; Contabo's price is a 24-month deal; AWS Frankfurt versus US prices differ (host-4, host-6, host-8). Most price pages carried no date.
- **Railway billing detail:** we read the price list, not how it meters a cron run. The $17-37 figures assume billing for full run time; Railway says it bills only resources actually used, so they are an upper bound. Hobby's 5 GB volume limit applies if state lives there (host-9).
- **Laptop reliability:** sleep, updates and the 13 GB disk. The render-ahead design reduces but does not remove this.
- **Scheduled-video edge cases:** how many scheduled videos YouTube allows, and what happens to scheduled videos if the channel gets a strike are not in the pages we read.
- **YouTube's rules on volume and reused content** could end the channel regardless of hosting. Other strands cover this; the 24-a-day target is 3-4 times the company channel's rate that was already flagged (host-25).
- **Prices from pricing.py** are list prices, October 2026, and the file has no Gemini row (decide/pricing.py:10-11) (host-19).
- **Checker disagreements:** on Contabo, one checker read EUR 5.50 a month and the other EUR 4.40 for the first 24 months; we keep the more cautious reading (no month-to-month price known). On the proxy, the checkers put the monthly cost at about $96-128 and $100-150; we show $90-150.
- **Home address:** a home IP is not safe from blocks either (host-m16).
- **Instruction-like text:** none of the pages we read contained text addressed to us.

## 5. Answers to the gaps a critic found

- A13. How YouTube links a clips channel to the company channel and its people
- A14. Does a YouTube API suspension reach production's Cloud project?
- A15. Open the primary 1 Oct 2026 originality post and any follow-ups
- A16. Can automated commentary count as 'original'?
- A17. What a separate clips channel does for the company channel
- A18. How much rights-clear supply the recommended sources really give
- A19. The real daily upload limit for a new, unverified channel
- A20. Check the reported 'cluster termination' system

### A13. How YouTube links a clips channel to the company channel and its people

**The short answer.** YouTube's official pages never say how it decides two channels are "associated", "linked" or "related", and they don't define "repeatedly or prominently featured" (gap1-1, gap1-2). But the main rule is about the person, not the accounts. If your channel is terminated, *you* may not use, own or create any other channel, and that covers channels you are "repeatedly or prominently featured" in (gap1-1). So if the owner runs the clips channel and it is terminated, the owner breaks the rules by staying on the company channel, where he appears in the meeting videos and holds a role. Separate Google accounts, Brand Accounts, phone numbers or servers don't change that. The only official pages that name an identity check are about ID verification (it checks for past suspensions), the phone-number cap and the one-AdSense-account-per-payee rule (gap1-5, gap1-6). For a one-person company, the real protection is to make a termination very unlikely: licensed or permitted sources only, and stop at the first strike. Isolation alone won't protect the company channel.

#### What we found

**The rules bind the person.**
- If your channel is terminated, you may not use, possess or create any other YouTube channel. You also may not let others whose channels were terminated use your channel to get round it. This covers your existing channels, new or acquired ones, and channels where you are "repeatedly or prominently featured". The page lists reasons for termination but no test for linking, and it never uses the words associated, linked or related (gap1-1).
- At 3 copyright strikes, "your account, along with any associated channels" is subject to termination, and you can't create new channels. A channel linked to one with 3 active strikes is also subject to termination, and the other way round. Neither word is defined (gap1-2).
- A single Community Guidelines strike already restricts the channel: for one week it cannot upload, go live or make scheduled videos public, and the strike stays for 90 days. Using, creating or acquiring another channel to get round that freeze is circumvention, and "may result in termination of all your existing YouTube channels", including "channels in which you are repeatedly or prominently featured". A single copyright strike works differently: its help page names no upload freeze, only a 7-day live-streaming limit when the removed video was a live stream. YouTube's Terms of Service (in force since 15 Dec 2023) say "you must not use another channel to circumvent these restrictions" for any strike, and separately state that Google reserves the right to terminate your Google account (gap1-3).
- The monetisation policy says a demonetised or terminated creator must not create or use channels, or apply to the Partner Program (YPP, YouTube's monetisation scheme) with "related channels". This "may apply to … channels that you appear on regularly". Breaking it "could lead to termination of all channels" (gap1-4).

**The identity signals YouTube does document.**
- ID verification: only the primary owner can do it, and that includes Brand Account channels. YouTube uses the ID to confirm "that you haven't previously been suspended". It "restrict[s] repeat applications" and may keep ID and face data for up to 3 years (gap1-5).
- Phone: one number can verify at most 2 channels, "to help prevent abuse, we limit the number of channels that can be associated with each phone number" (gap1-5).
- Features can be restricted for "maintaining channels that are related to another policy-violating channel" and for "posting the same content repeatedly across one or more channels" (gap1-5).
- AdSense: one AdSense or AdSense for YouTube account per payee name. Several channels can share it. Duplicate accounts "will not be approved" and monetisation is turned off for the channel tied to the duplicate (gap1-6). AdSense also allows one account per publisher, plus a separate account for an organisation (gap1-6). That a shared AdSense account joins the channels in YouTube's eyes is our inference; no page says so.
- Google accounts: Google "automatically detects and disables accounts made for abuse". You must not create multiple accounts to break its policies, and it can stop a person signing in to all Google services (gap1-8).

**Brand Accounts and roles.** A Brand Account has exactly one primary owner, and people manage it through their own Google accounts. Deleting the primary owner's account deletes the channel (gap1-7). No page we opened says what happens to a Brand Account channel or a channel role when a manager's own account is terminated (gap1-7).

**Signals we could not confirm.** We opened no official page and found no 2025-2026 enforcement case that names a shared device, IP address, recovery email or payments profile as a linking signal (gap1-11). The one spillover case we found (one news report, so not a pattern) was linked through content: an original creator was terminated after re-posting his own clip, which a terminated channel had taken and uploaded without permission. Per the article's account of YouTube support's replies, he "violated YouTube's terms by posting a terminated user's content"; the article calls it an apparent misfire of YouTube's automated system and reports no shared account (gap1-10). The second-chance pilot (help page undated; we did not confirm its launch year) opens only one year after termination, is rolled out gradually, and excludes creators terminated for copyright infringement or for breaking the Creator Responsibility policies (gap1-9).

#### What this means for our build
1. **Treat the operator as the link.** Whoever owns, verifies or runs the clips channel puts every channel they use or appear in at stake. If the owner runs it, the company channel is exposed by the text of the rules (gap1-1, gap1-3, gap1-4). The plan should say this plainly. It should not promise isolation.
2. **The owner has to make one decision before the build.**
   - (a) Recommended: the owner runs it, and the system is built so it never gets a strike. That means licensed or permitted sources only (A3), an automatic stop and alert on the first copyright or Community Guidelines strike, no re-posting of removed clips, and no switching to another channel during a freeze (gap1-2, gap1-3).
   - (b) Another person runs it on their own Google account, phone, ID and AdSense, with no role on the company channel and no appearances in its videos. This person can't be the owner, and with one person in the company it may not exist.
   - (c) Don't build the unlicensed version at all.
3. **Brand Account (settles the A3 vs A2/A10 conflict).** Never create it under the company's Google account. A Brand Account owned by a new, separate Google account is fine, but it adds convenience, not separation. Its primary owner is the person who matters (gap1-7).
4. **Verification.** Phone-verify the channel for the features that unlocks. Whether to ID-verify is the owner's choice, and it does not change who is responsible: see point 1 (gap1-5).
5. **Phone.** One phone number can verify at most two channels, so check that limit before verifying (A9 api-m9). Under option (b), the operator uses their own number.
6. **Money.** Don't monetise the clips channel through the company's AdSense or the owner's personal AdSense in the first phase. One payee per account means monetising joins the channels (gap1-6; the joining is our inference). Under A3, unlicensed clips can't be monetised anyway.
7. **Roles.** No account that holds a role on the company channel gets a role on the clips channel, and the reverse (gap1-1, "letting others … use your channel").
8. **Content.** Never post the same video on both channels. Never feature, link or cross-promote the company channel from the clips channel. That last rule is our own precaution, not a documented rule (gap1-5, gap1-10).

#### Risks and unknowns
- How YouTube detects links (device, IP, recovery email, payments) is not published. Assume it can join accounts that share any of these (gap1-11). The cheap test: if the company channel has access to YouTube Creator Support (we don't know whether it does), ask them in writing whether a clips channel run by a person featured on the company channel is "related". Or pay for one hour with a media lawyer.
- "Repeatedly or prominently featured" has no threshold. The owner appearing in meeting videos likely counts, but we don't know (gap1-1, gap1-4).
- Automated enforcement errors happen. In the one known case, a creator was terminated through a content link and had not been reinstated as of 10 Dec 2025 (gap1-10). A copyright termination can't use the second-chance route (gap1-9).
- Our web search budget ran out during this task, so 2025-2026 Help Community threads and news cases were not searched. Rerun that search before the plan is final. The fact-check hit the same limit, so whether the creator in gap1-10 was later reinstated is also unchecked.
- A copyright strike does not simply expire. The copyright strike page says you can complete Copyright School "to have the strike expire in 90 days, otherwise it will remain active on your channel" (support.google.com/youtube/answer/2814000, read 2026-11-14). The "stop at the first strike" rule should therefore also make finishing Copyright School part of the response, or strikes will add up toward 3 for longer than 90 days.

### A14. Does a YouTube API suspension reach production's Cloud project?

**The short answer.** It can. A separate Cloud project lowers the risk but does not remove it. The YouTube API terms let YouTube suspend "you" or any single app, or both, and leave the choice of scope to YouTube (gap2-1). The policy that bans new projects after a suspension says you may not reach the API "via any means" once your credentials are suspended. It also applies when the Google account that made those credentials is suspended "for any reason" (gap2-3). Both systems are run for the same company, and the terms say "you" means that company (gap2-4), so a clips violation is a violation by the same "you" that runs production. Treat a clips-side API suspension as a real threat to production uploads. Build the separation described below, and fix the clips system's rule problems (downloading, reposting) rather than counting on project walls. The repo's own setup guide says production's Cloud project is made with the Google account that owns the company channel, as a free project with no card (gap2-9). If that was followed, the billing-account path is probably not a risk, and the weak points are the "you"-level clauses and that one channel-owning Google account, which the clips system must never use.

#### What we found
**What the API terms say about who gets suspended**
- YouTube "may suspend or terminate your access to, or use of, any aspect of the YouTube API Services", including credentials assigned to you or your apps, for any violation by you, any of your API Clients, or those acting for you (gap2-1).
- Section 24.2 lets YouTube act against "any specific user or API Client", a category of them, or all of them, at any time. YouTube says it will try to give reasonable notice but has no obligation to (gap2-1).
- Nothing in the terms limits a suspension to the one project that broke the rules. Nothing says it always spreads to every project either. The scope is YouTube's call (gap2-1).
- Audits and compliance messages are aimed at "you" and "your API Client(s)", plural. Compliance messages go to the email of the Google account used to log in to the developer console (III.D.5). Section III.J.3, in the rules for child-directed apps, also speaks of "You and your API Client's access" being suspended for breaking the terms (gap2-5).

**What the developer policies tie to a project, and what they tie to you**
- Credentials let Google "link API activity to a particular API Project and API Client". The only per-project examples of action (revoke credentials, cut a project's quota) are in III.D.4, which is about projects left inactive for 90 days, not about rule breaking. The policies give no per-project list of penalties for violations (gap2-2).
- III.D.6 is wider. It bars access "via any means" when your credentials are suspended, revoked or terminated. It also bars access when "the Google Account you used to create those credentials" is suspended or terminated for any reason. It forbids new Google accounts, credentials or projects made to get round this (gap2-3).
- Our reading: if the clips credentials are suspended, a strict reading of "via any means" covers production's existing project too, because both belong to the same "you". Google gives no example for one owner with two apps, and we found no ruling (gap2-3).
- The audit guide frames audits per project and mentions appeals after a failed audit. It does not say what a failed audit does to other projects (gap2-6).

**Who "you" is**
- When someone uses the API on behalf of an employer, "you" in the terms means that employer (gap2-4).
- Production and clips would both run for the same company, so separate Google accounts do not make two different "you"s (gap2-4).

**Google Cloud's own rules (separate from YouTube's)**
- The Cloud terms let Google suspend "all or part of Customer's use of the Services". Under 4.1 that is for Acceptable Use Policy breaches the customer has not fixed within 24 hours of Google's notice; under 4.2 it can be immediate, for example to protect the services, to comply with law, or for a breach of the restrictions or service-specific terms, and is lifted once the cause is resolved. The customer is the account holder, not one project (gap2-7). We did not find whether a YouTube API violation counts as a Cloud breach.
- If a Cloud billing account is suspended, every resource attached to that billing account is suspended too (gap2-8).
- A user who keeps breaking the Cloud terms can lose access to all their Cloud projects, while keeping Gmail and other services (gap2-8).
- If a Google account is disabled Google-wide, its owner loses access to their Cloud resources. A project is not suspended as long as it has at least one other active owner (gap2-8).

**What earlier sections already showed (not repeated)**
- Channel side: a terminated YouTube user may not use or own any other channel, existing or new (policy-14, policy-m11, growth-m2).
- Rules side: downloading other channels' videos and reposting them is already in conflict with III.E.1 and III.I.18, whichever project does it (api-m10, api-m1, ingest-23).
- Production uses one OAuth client whose ID and secret come from settings (gap2-9). The repo does not name the actual Google account, billing account or Cloud organisation. Its setup guides do say how the project is meant to be made: with the Google account that owns or manages the company channel (DEPLOY.md line 152; docs/BUILD_AND_DEPLOY_GUIDE_AR.md line 445), free and with no card, skipping any free-trial or card prompt (guide lines 443 and 447), with an External consent screen because the account is a regular Gmail account (guide line 449). If followed, production's credentials were created by the channel-owning account, probably with no billing account and no Cloud organisation. This is the written procedure, not proof of what was done (gap2-9).

#### What this means for our build
1. **Keep the separate Cloud project, but stop calling it a firewall.** It is required by the one-project-per-app rule (api-13, policy-m1). It does not protect production from a "you"-level suspension (gap2-1, gap2-3, gap2-4). The plan should say this plainly.
2. **Create the clips project from a different Google account** than the one that created production's credentials. Per the setup guide that is the channel-owning account (gap2-9), so the clips system must never sign in with it. This removes the mechanical link where a suspended creating account cuts off production's credentials (gap2-3). It does not remove the "you"-level reading of III.D.6, because both accounts act for the same company (gap2-3, gap2-4). Do this up front, as normal setup for a second app. Never do it after a suspension, which III.D.6 forbids (gap2-3).
3. **Do not attach the clips project to production's billing account or Cloud organisation**, so a billing or Cloud-account suspension cannot pull production down with it (gap2-7, gap2-8). If the setup guide was followed, production has neither, and the clips project should not need billing for the YouTube API either; check before assuming (gap2-9).
4. **Give production's Cloud project a second owner now**, a company admin account that never touches clips. A disabled owner then cannot freeze production (gap2-8). This is a console change, not a code change, and needs the owner's yes. Limit (our reasoning, not from a page we opened): this keeps the Cloud project alive, but production uploads through the channel owner's sign-in, so if that Google account itself were disabled, uploads would likely stop anyway.
5. **The real fix is to not break the rules.** No YouTube downloading through the clips system without written permission, and clips only from creators who give files or licences (api-m10, ingest-23). A clean clips app is the only thing that removes the "you"-level risk (gap2-1).
6. **Kill switch.** If the clips project gets any compliance email, audit request or quota cut, pause clips uploads at once and answer it. III.D.5 requires a reply to compliance messages about "your API Clients", and sends them to the email of the account that logs in to the developer console, so someone must read that inbox (gap2-5). Never open a new project to keep posting (gap2-3).
7. **Production stays the priority.** If the owner cannot accept any risk to production uploads, the clips system should launch only after rule items in A3 and A5 are settled.

#### Risks and unknowns
- We don't know how YouTube applies these clauses in practice. We found no public case of a YouTube API suspension spreading to another project, but we could not search forums because the shared web search limit ran out in this run (the fact-check hit the same limit). Next step: search Stack Overflow and the Google developer forums for "YouTube API" plus "suspended" and "other projects".
- We don't know for certain who owns production's Cloud project, its billing account, or whether it sits in a Cloud organisation; the setup guide only says how it was meant to be made (gap2-9). Cheap check: the owner opens the Cloud console, IAM page and Billing page, and notes the owners and billing account (5 minutes, no code).
- Using a second Google account for clips could look like hiding identity, which III.D.1.a forbids (gap2-2). Fill in the clips project's contact details truthfully with the company name.
- None of the pages we read shows a "last updated" date, so the wording could change without us noticing. The YouTube terms revision history (latest entry 1 June 2026) lists 2025-2026 changes only to the derived-metrics storage policy, the embedded player and the Android Player API; none touches suspension, III.D.6, audits or the meaning of "you".
- No page we read says that a YouTube API suspension disables a whole Google account. That path is our worst case, not a known outcome.

### A15. Open the primary 1 Oct 2026 originality post and any follow-ups

**The short answer.** We still could not read the primary text. The TeamYouTube thread renders only its title and menus (three URL variants tried across sections), and the Creator Insider video page shows only its title, though YouTube's own oEmbed lookup confirms the video exists under that title on the Creator Insider channel (gap3-1, gap3-2). Four news reports that did read the post agree on its wording. It gives no start date, no threshold or ratio for "primarily", and says nothing about licensed or permitted clips, clipping programmes, podcasts' own clips or long-form video (gap3-3, gap3-4, gap3-5). Between 1 Oct and 14 Nov 2026 we found no clarification, FAQ or change-log entry on the four official Help pages we opened, on YouTube's full policy changelog (it has October and November 2026 entries, none about originality, reused or scraped content) or on How YouTube Works (gap3-7). Plan as if licensed clips get no exemption on Shorts. Long horizontal clips are not named by this reach rule, but they still fall under the spam and reused-content rules (gap3-6, gap3-8).

#### What we found

##### The primary sources would not load
- The thread at support.google.com/youtube/thread/470890423 returned only the title "Prioritizing original content on Shorts" and site navigation. The A2 checker had tried the plain URL (clips-3); we tried the slug URL with ?hl=en (1,417 characters of page text, no body) and the Indonesian copy (?hl=id). An archive.org copy could not be fetched by our tool (gap3-1).
- The video page youtube.com/watch?v=XS2A6aExLaA (desktop and mobile) showed only menus, with no date, description or transcript. YouTube's public oEmbed endpoint (a small public lookup that returns a video's title and channel) confirms the title "Prioritizing Original Content on Shorts" and the channel Creator Insider (gap3-2).
- TeamYouTube's X page returned HTTP 402 (payment required), so no X posts were read. Our web-search allowance ran out on the first query, so we could not look for follow-ups by search (gap3-1). The fact-checker hit the same limit on 14 Nov 2026, re-opened the thread (title and menus only, no body, author, date or replies) and the watch page (title only), and re-ran the oEmbed lookup (title "Prioritizing Original Content on Shorts", channel Creator Insider, @creatorinsider).

##### What the post says, as quoted by four reports that read it
- PPC Land (2 Oct 2026) dates the English post 1 October 2026 and quotes it in fragments: YouTube is "updating our recommendation systems to further prioritize original" content and will "reduce the reach of content re-uploaded from other creators without adding anything of your own." Channels "identified as primarily aggregating or re-uploading other creators' videos without significant changes" "will likely see less distribution within the Shorts feed" (gap3-3).
- Dexerto (5 Oct 2026) and Social Media Today (1 Oct 2026) both quote a further line: "If you use clips from another creator, make sure you're adding real value through your own original commentary, unique edits" ... "or storytelling." The post also warns against "minor technical edits or template-based changes simply to alter a video" (gap3-3).
- Social Media Today links the post to YouTube's spam policy page (answer/2801973). That page defines "Scraped content" as re-posting other videos "without adding anything of your own; such as original commentary, educational value, or unique editing." Its example is "A channel that takes popular clips and re-uploads them in their entirety without any transformative editing, reaction, or educational breakdown" (gap3-6).
- The Creator Liaison's lines (the "not just VO descriptions..." quote, reach "re-evaluated" after a shift to original work, use the Posts tab to share others' videos) are already in growth-4 and sources-m7. Search Engine Journal (1 Oct 2026) is still their only source (gap3-3).

##### What the post does not say
- **Start date:** none. SEJ says the video gives none, and Dexerto cites 9to5Google saying YouTube gave no precise rollout date (gap3-4). SEJ adds that the post does not say how long a re-evaluation takes or where a channel can check whether its reach was reduced (gap3-4).
- **"Primarily":** no number. PPC Land notes there is no ratio, no lookback window (how far back YouTube looks) and no definition of "significant" (gap3-4).
- **Licensed or permitted clips, clipping programmes, podcasts:** none of the four reports says the post covers them. PPC Land raises licensed reposts only as an open question. SEJ and PPC Land both note that neither the post nor the video covers creators cutting Shorts from their own long videos (gap3-5).
- **Long-form or horizontal video:** the quoted wording is limited to "the Shorts feed". No report says the reach change covers long videos (gap3-5).

##### No follow-up found on official pages (1 Oct to 14 Nov 2026)
- Channel monetization policies (answer/1311392): last dated entry is 15 July 2025 ("There is no change to our reused content policy"). No Oct or Nov 2026 entry. It still says the reused-content policy "applies even if you have permission from the original creator" (gap3-7, gap3-8).
- Spam policy (answer/2801973), Shorts monetization (answer/12504220), Get started with Shorts (answer/10059070) and How YouTube Works on recommendations: no originality notice and no Oct or Nov 2026 entry (gap3-7).
- The full policy changelog (answer/10008196, linked from answer/1311392 as "View our changelog here") does have October 2026 and November 2026 entries, but they cover hate and harmful-acts monetization and AI labels for YouTube Music, not originality, reused, scraped or inauthentic content. The newest related entry is the July 2025 YPP update on "mass-produced and repetitious content" (gap3-7).
- The Shorts monetization page (answer/12504220) still lists as ineligible views "Non-original Shorts, such as unedited clips from others' movies or TV shows" and "reuploading other creators' content from YouTube or other platform, or compilations with no original content added". That is about revenue, not reach, but it points the same way (gap3-8).

#### What this means for our build
- **Treat the reach rule as covering licensed clips.** Nothing exempts them, the monetization page says permission does not help, and the spam definition is about added value, not rights. In A4 set (b), a licence or a clipping-programme deal buys copyright safety only, not Shorts reach. Keep set (b) only if each clip gets real added commentary or teaching (gap3-5, gap3-6, gap3-8).
- **Make every upload pass the spam-policy test, not just Shorts.** The written test is "original commentary, educational value, or unique editing", and "in their entirety" is the named bad case. So: never upload a whole source video; always add our own spoken or written point of view; log what was added per clip so a reviewer can see it (gap3-6).
- **Long clips are a hedge, not a loophole.** The Shorts reach cut does not name long video, so a mix leaning to longer horizontal clips with commentary is less exposed to this specific rule. Those clips are still judged by the spam and reused-content rules, which apply to all formats (gap3-5, gap3-6, gap3-8).
- **Do not plan around a grace period.** There is no start date, so assume the rule is live now (gap3-4).
- **Keep the ratio of our own content high from day one.** "Primarily" has no number. Reach is judged by channel and "re-evaluated" only after a shift (growth-4), so the first weeks set the label. Default: at most half of uploads are clips of others. That is our estimate, not a YouTube figure (gap3-4).

#### Risks and unknowns
- We have not read the primary post or the video ourselves. The wording rests on four reports that agree with each other. Cheap check: open the thread and the video in a normal signed-out browser and paste the text into clip.md (5 minutes).
- A clarification could exist on X, in thread replies (PPC Land saw six English replies) or in a later Creator Insider video. We could not search. Check TeamYouTube on X and the thread replies by hand before the build starts.
- The reach effect could spread to long-form later. Watch the Help pages above monthly and diff them.
- Whether licensed clips with light edits get reduced reach is unknown. A small test (about 20 clips over 2 weeks on a throwaway channel) would show it, but it costs a channel's early reputation.
- Realism: the owner's starting idea (a new channel posting other channels' clips every hour, up to 24 a day, with nothing of our own) is close to the pattern the post names, a channel "primarily aggregating or re-uploading other creators' videos". Expect reduced Shorts-feed reach for that plan as described, from the first weeks, with no stated way to check it or to know how long recovery takes (gap3-3, gap3-4).
- Also seen, outside this gap (unverified: read through a summarising fetch tool, check by hand): the Shorts monetization page (answer/12504220) appears to say that starting 1 Feb 2027, sharing in Shorts Creator Pool revenue needs at least 10 million qualified Shorts views in the last 90 days. If true, it matters for any revenue plan for this channel.

### A16. Can automated commentary count as 'original'?

**The short answer.** No official YouTube page or statement we could open says yes or no to AI-written or AI-voiced commentary over another creator's clip. YouTube judges the finished video, not the tool. Its policy says automated tools and AI script help are fine if the result shows "creative vision" and the creator's own "insights or perspective" (gap4-1, gap4-2). What fails is named clearly: voice-over that only describes the screen, reading text you did not write, template-based bulk changes, AI content that looks mass-produced, and AI clips stitched together for shock (gap4-1, gap4-3, gap4-4). The reused-content list also refuses short videos compiled from other sites and promotion of other people's content even with permission, so each clip has to be a review or commentary, not a repost (gap4-3). We found no documented case of an AI-commentary clips channel passing or failing review (gap4-9). So hourly automation is not ruled out by the rules, but it is only safe if each clip carries real, varied analysis. In practice that means a human checks the commentary at the start and samples it afterwards, and the build has to prove it with a test before the volume goes up.

#### What we found

**What the policy page says (and does not say)**
- The monetisation policy page (Help 1311392) never uses the words "text-to-speech" or "synthetic" and has no rule on narration voices. It does mention a "changed the voiceover" and "added voice commentary" in the reused-content examples (gap4-3). Its last dated change is 15 July 2025, a "minor update" that renamed "repetitious content" to "inauthentic content"; the note says the reused content policy did not change (gap4-1).
- Its AI rules are about outcomes, and there are three. AI content made "with generic or unoriginal templates giving the impression of mass production" fails when it lacks the creator's own insights or perspective. Under "Unsatisfying or off-putting content", "videos that stitch together unrelated or inconsistent AI clips to surprise or shock viewers" and realistic visuals faking a celebrity death or disaster fail. AI personas giving health, financial or legal advice also fail (gap4-1).
- Under "Unsatisfying or off-putting content" the page says: "If you use automated tools or templates to help create your content, the final product must still demonstrate your creative vision." It lists "using AI to edit your video scripts" as allowed when it helps deliver a "unique, well-researched, or creative narrative" (gap4-2). This section has no date of its own.
- The reused-content list is about what is said, not who or what says it. Allowed: explaining a competitor's moves over sports replays, rewriting dialogue and changing the voice-over, reaction videos that comment, "Using clips for a critical review", and "Edited footage from other creators where you add a storyline and commentary". Not allowed: content that "exclusively features readings of other materials you did not originally create", and mostly non-verbal reactions "without added voice commentary". For a clips channel the not-allowed list also names "Short videos you compiled from other social media websites", "Content uploaded many times by other creators" and "Promotion of other people's content (even if you have permission)" (gap4-3).

**What YouTube staff said**
- On 1 Oct 2026 the Creator Liaison said remixes need added value, "not just VO descriptions of what's happening on screen, minor technical edits, or template-based bulk changes". Creators should bring "commentary, analysis, and storytelling" instead. The coverage does not mention AI. We read this only through Search Engine Journal, because the video page gave no text (gap4-4, same as policy-m9 in section A3).
- In July 2025 the Liaison called the inauthentic-content change a "minor update". Per TechCrunch, a post by him said worries that reaction and clip videos would lose monetisation were unfounded; TechCrunch does not quote him directly on this. We could not open his video, only its title (gap4-6).
- In a July 2026 Creator Insider video, YouTube's VP of Trust and Safety said, per Search Engine Journal, that channels with too much "off-putting" content (emotionally manipulative or shock formulas) can lose Partner Programme access "whether or not the videos use AI". That remark was about that one category, not about all the rules. The journalist summed up in his own words: "Using AI to help make videos is still fine". The same article says a fixed intro and outro is fine as long as the body of each video differs (gap4-7).

**Synthetic voices and labels**
- The altered-content page (Help 14328491) requires a label when a real person is made to seem to say something they did not say. Cloning your own voice for voice-overs needs no label. "Disclosing AI content alone won't limit a video's audience or impact its eligibility to earn money" (gap4-5).
- Since May 2026 YouTube may auto-label undisclosed AI content its systems detect. Per Search Engine Journal this targets "significant photorealistic AI" but can also catch animated or slightly changed content. The Liaison said labels alone do not affect recommendations or earnings. The same article notes that if viewers see a label and do not click, or watch less, those viewer signals can still lower reach (gap4-5).

**Cases**
- One agency (vendor; it sells a monetisation recovery service) says an AI voice over your own script and edit "goes through the same test as a human voice". It says the voice "hurts when it's part of a pattern". It reports September 2026 rejections of sleep and prayer compilation channels that ran on one template. None of this cites a YouTube source, and it names no channels and gives no counts (gap4-8).
- We found no named AI-commentary clips channel that was approved, refused or demonetised. Nearby cases are different formats: a consented human clips channel removed for reused content (clips-6), templated AI-generated channels terminated (clips-7), and late-2025 wrongful spam terminations with no detail on voice or format (gap4-9).

**Money context**
- From 1 Feb 2027, new Partner Programme applicants need 8,000 watch hours in 365 days or 20M Shorts views in 90 days. Shorts revenue share needs 10M Shorts views in 90 days. The entry thresholds apply to new applicants only (existing partners are not affected); the Shorts threshold applies to partners too. So for a new clips channel, the originality test matters first for reach (the Oct 2026 Shorts change), not for ad money (gap4-10).

#### What this means for our build
1. **AI commentary is allowed in principle. Design for the test, not the tool.** Each clip must add something the clip itself does not say: context, a counterpoint, a link to another source, a "why it matters". An LLM recap of what is on screen is the named fail case (gap4-3, gap4-4). Make the prompt require a claim plus a reason, and reject drafts that mostly restate the transcript. A simple check: the share of words that overlap with the source transcript.
2. **No reading out other people's text.** Do not have TTS read the source's words, quotes, articles or news feeds (gap4-3).
3. **Break the template.** Vary the structure, opening, length, voice placement and visuals for each clip. A fixed intro and outro is fine only when the body differs (gap4-1, gap4-7, clips-2). Keep a rotation of at least 5-8 formats and log which one each post used.
4. **The voice must be ours or plainly synthetic.** Never clone or imitate the source creator (policy-13 and policy-21 in section A3; gap4-5). A recorded owner voice, or the owner's own cloned voice, is the safest choice and needs no label (gap4-5).
5. **Human gate, then sampling.** In weeks 1-4, a person approves each post's commentary in the web panel. After that, the system auto-posts and a person samples about 1 in 5 posts plus every flagged draft. This keeps most of the cost saving and is our estimate, not a YouTube rule.
6. **Volume follows proof.** Start with a few posts a day. Move toward hourly only if reach holds over 2-4 weeks (see A1 and A2 on cadence).
7. **Do not plan on ad revenue from Shorts.** It is out of reach for a new channel under the 2027 thresholds (gap4-10). Judge the test on views and reach.

#### Risks and unknowns
- **No official yes or no on AI commentary.** Reviewers judge case by case, and reviews may involve a human (Help 1311392, 10 Mar 2025 change note). A pattern of LLM framing at 24 posts a day may still read as "template-based bulk changes" (gap4-4).
- **Compilation and promotion are named fails.** A feed of other channels' clips with thin commentary matches the policy's own not-allowed examples ("Short videos you compiled from other social media websites", "Promotion of other people's content (even if you have permission)"), whatever voice is used (gap4-3).
- **AI labels can cost reach indirectly.** Labels do not change ranking by themselves, but viewers who skip labelled videos send weaker signals (gap4-5).
- **We could not watch the videos.** The Creator Insider videos (Jul 2025, Jul 2026, Oct 2026) returned only their titles. Rene Ritchie's X posts and the July 2025 Help Community post were not opened, and the web search budget ran out mid-task. Cheap fix: the owner watches the three videos, about 30 minutes in total, and notes any line on AI voice.
- **No precedent.** A one-month test on a throwaway channel with 30-60 posts is the cheapest evidence we can get. Track Shorts-feed share against views from other sources. The fact-checker's own counter-search for such cases could not run (search budget used up), so gap4-9 rests on the researcher's search plus the two cited articles.
- **Enforcement errors happen.** Late-2025 coverage describes automated terminations later reversed (gap4-9). The separate channel and the refusal to use the production token (A2 point 1) remain essential.

### A17. What a separate clips channel does for the company channel

**The short answer.** A separate clips channel sends almost nothing to the company channel unless we link them, and every working link also ties the two channels together in public. YouTube does give a separate channel ways to point at another one: up to 14 profile links, a "Channels" section on the Home tab, an end-screen element that promotes another channel, channel cards, @mentions in Posts, and Collaborations, which put a second channel's name and Subscribe button on the video (gap5-1 to gap5-6). But Shorts, the planned bulk of the posts, can carry none of these: their description links don't work, and their Related video link only points inside the same channel (gap5-8, pack-9, look-m6). We found no 2025-2026 study or case that measures traffic moving from a clips channel or sister channel to its parent. The one show team we found says its funnel "converts", but gives no numbers, says its long-form views "haven't changed at all" since it added Shorts, and now puts Shorts on the main channel because a separate Shorts channel can't link to the main channel's videos; it still runs a separate channel for horizontal 10-30 minute clips (gap5-8, gap5-9). The clips channel's subject also has to match the company's (robotics, AI, maker, space) for any transfer to be plausible. A GTA 6 clips channel would almost certainly send nothing (gap5-10, our estimate). Decide before building: either the clips channel is a separate views project that will not grow the company channel, or it runs in the company's niche, from permitted sources only, with a few deliberate links, and an 8-week test measured in the company channel's analytics.

#### What we found

##### The tools a separate channel has to point at the company channel
- **Profile links.** A channel can show up to 14 links on its channel page. The Help page does not say whether one may be another YouTube channel or what eligibility is needed. Clickable links in long-video descriptions and in Posts need advanced feature access (gap5-1). Viewers see these only if they open the clips channel's page.
- **"Channels" section on the Home tab.** The Home tab takes up to 12 custom sections. One type, "Channels", highlights subscriptions and featured channels (gap5-2).
- **End screens.** An end screen is the clickable panel in a video's last seconds. Its Channel element can "promote another channel with a custom message". It needs a video of at least 25 seconds, allows up to 4 elements on 16:9 video, and is not shown on mobile web (iPad excepted) or in the YouTube Music and Kids apps. The page does not mention Shorts (gap5-3). For Shorts this matches look-23.
- **Cards.** A card is a small pop-up link during a video. Video, playlist and channel cards can point to another channel's video or to another channel, up to 5 per video. The Help page is inconsistent about devices: its "Who can see cards?" part says "This feature is available to viewers on computers", while another part says that on mobile viewers see the card icon whenever the player controls show. Cards are not shown on videos set as made for kids. Cards are hidden when Content ID (YouTube's automatic copyright matching) has claimed the video and the owner has set up a campaign, which can happen to clips of other people's videos (gap5-4).
- **Collaborations.** Up to 10 collaborator channels per video, on long videos and on Shorts. After a collaborator accepts, each collaborator's name and Subscribe button show on the video. YouTube "aims to recommend the video to audiences of both" channels. Revenue stays with the posting channel. Invites are made in Studio's upload flow, and the API has no field for them (gap5-5, api-19). The page says nothing about eligibility, about invites after publishing, or about inviting a channel you own.
- **Posts and @mentions.** A Post can share any YouTube video, and an @mention in a Post is clickable on any device. Posts show on the Posts tab and may also show in Home and Subscriptions feeds, and image Posts may also show in the Shorts feed (gap5-6).
- **Shorts.** A Short's description links are not clickable. Its Related video link must point to a video on the same channel, needs advanced feature access, and can only be set in Studio (pack-9, growth-21, look-m6). So a Short on the clips channel cannot send a viewer straight to the company channel. We did not find a source on whether an @mention in a Short's title is clickable.

##### What the evidence says about traffic between channels
- The only team account is from Diary of a CEO's clips team (19 Mar 2026). They say clips "bring a different audience" and that people jump "over to the full length". They also say a separate Shorts channel can't link to the long video on the main channel, that "same channel is the best way", and that newer shows saw "a lot faster growth" after moving Shorts to the main channel. They give no conversion figures, and the main channel also uses Posts to promote clips (gap5-8; extends clips-13, clips-m7). Two points temper this: the speaker also says "Long form views haven't changed at all when we added shorts" (offered as proof of no cannibalisation, but it also reports no lift), and the team's separate DOAC Clips channel for horizontal 10-30 minute cut-downs is still running; only the separate Shorts channel is being made redundant. The speaker works for a media company behind a 14M-subscriber show, so this is a survivor's account, not a test a brand-new channel can repeat (gap5-8).
- The only large collaboration study is from 2018, before the Collaborations feature existed. The earlier research reports that in it the median channel gained nothing, and the gains clustered in same-category channels of 1K-100K subscribers; it does not keep the study's URL. The 2018 study we could open (Koch et al., arXiv:1805.01887, 1 May 2018) says in its abstract that collaborations are "in many cases significantly beneficial", often with more than 100% popularity growth over non-collaboration videos. We could not read its body, so we could not check the median figure or confirm it is the same study (unverified). The company channel has 261 subscribers (gap5-9; paid_partners-7).
- We found no 2025-2026 data on traffic from a sister or clips channel to its parent. Our web search budget ran out partway through this strand, and three vidIQ pages we tried directly returned 404, so the search was not exhaustive (gap5-9).

##### The subject match and the safety conflict
- The company channel's subject is robotics, AI, maker work and space (01-traffic-research.md:788). The clips research covers two possible directions: a tech, AI and podcast clips channel (A2, A4) and a GTA 6 gaming channel (G5-G8) (gap5-10).
- The safety advice in A2 and A9 is to keep the clips channel unlinked, because terminations and strikes reach "associated channels" and related channels can be restricted (clips-4, clips-m1, api-m8). Every tool above links the channels in public. We don't know whether YouTube treats a public link as making the channels "related" (gap5-11).
- In the company channel's Analytics, views from the clips channel would show up under these traffic sources: Channel pages ("other YouTube channels"), End screens, Video cards, and Suggested videos (which counts links in video descriptions). These totals also include traffic that has nothing to do with the clips channel (Channel pages counts the company's own channel page; Suggested counts every suggestion), so the totals alone do not isolate it. The YouTube Analytics API's insightTrafficSourceDetail dimension names the top referring video or channel page for one video at a time for Suggested (RELATED_VIDEO), End screens (END_SCREEN) and Channel pages (YT_CHANNEL), but lists no detail for the annotation/card type. So the funnel can be measured at no money cost, per company video, with cards counted only in total (gap5-7).

#### What this means for our build
1. **Make the funnel an explicit owner decision.** Recommended: say plainly that an unlinked clips channel adds nothing to the company channel's goal (00-context.md:8-9). If company traffic is the goal, the proven route is Shorts of the company's own content on the company channel, linked to its own long videos, which the existing build already does (gap5-8, growth-21).
2. **GTA 6 or any off-niche direction: build no funnel.** Treat it as a separate views project with zero Shorts revenue (growth-m3) and zero expected company traffic. Keep it fully unlinked (gap5-10, gap5-11).
3. **Same-niche clips channel from permitted sources only: a "soft link" kit, all done by hand in Studio, since none of it is in the API:**
   - one profile link to the company channel (gap5-1);
   - a Home-tab "Channels" section featuring it (gap5-2);
   - a saved end-screen template with a Channel element, applied to each long clip (gap5-3);
   - one channel card on each long clip (gap5-4);
   - one Post a week with an @mention of a company video (gap5-6).
   This is about 2-3 minutes per long clip at 1 long clip a day (our estimate). Shorts get no link.
4. **Do not invite the company channel as a Collaborator on reused clips.** Doing so would push other people's content to the company's audience, put the company's name on it, and needs a manual Studio invite for every upload (gap5-5, gap5-11).
5. **Measure it.** Before launch, save the company channel's 28-day baseline for Channel pages, End screens, Video cards and Suggested views, plus subscribers. After 8 weeks, a sensible kill line is under about 200 extra company views a month from those sources (our estimate) (gap5-7). Count only views whose traffic-source detail names a clips-channel video or the clips channel's page (insightTrafficSourceDetail), since the source totals include unrelated traffic (gap5-7). The clips app needs only a read-only analytics pull on the company channel. It must not get write access to the company channel.

#### Risks and unknowns
- **No 2025-2026 conversion data.** The DOAC account has no numbers, and the 2018 study is old and predates the feature (gap5-8, gap5-9). The 8-week test is the cheap way to find out.
- **Linking may count as association.** YouTube does not define when channels are "related". A public link may make a strike or termination easier to tie to the company (gap5-11). One way to lower the risk is to add the links only after 4 weeks without a strike or claim. That cuts risk but does not remove it.
- **Feature access.** A new channel may lack advanced features, which turns off clickable description links and Related video links (gap5-1, look-m6). End screens and cards have no feature-access requirement on their Help pages (gap5-3, gap5-4).
- **Content ID can switch cards off** on claimed clips, and the Help page says cards are "available to viewers on computers" while also describing a card icon on mobile, so reach on phones and TVs is unclear. We did not check what share of viewers watch on a computer (gap5-4).
- **Not checked:** whether profile links may point to another YouTube channel; whether Collaborations works between channels with the same owner; whether an @mention in a Short's title is clickable. Each takes about 5 minutes to try in Studio on the new channel.
