### A18. How much rights-clear supply the recommended sources really give

**The short answer.** Not much. In the 12 months to 14 Nov 2026, media.ccc.de released 383 English talks (236 hours) whose metadata says CC BY, but only about 23-27 of them (about 15-17.5 hours, depending on the keyword list) are about AI, robots or drones, and 40-50% of those came in one week (the December congress) (gap6-1, gap6-2, gap6-3). NASA's own video library added about 710 videos in the same 12 months, but most of the hours are briefings, interviews, live event coverage or silent B-roll. Narrated, edited pieces you can clip come to about 23 hours a year, by our sample-based estimate (gap6-5, gap6-6). At A6's assumed 6 usable clips per source hour (its figure for a 1-hour source; it assumes only 4 an hour for 3-hour sources, and neither is tested), the on-topic new supply gives about 4.5-5 posts a week, or about 8 a week if hardware and security talks count. Even Vizard's vendor figure of 13 clips an hour gives only 10-18 a week (gap6-8). That covers A1's floor of 7 a week (1 a day), only with help from the back catalogue. It is 5-9 times short of 42 a week and 20-36 times short of the 168 an hourly plan needs. Size the build for 1-2 posts a day, not 24.

#### What we found

##### media.ccc.de: counted from its public API
- The API lists 472 conferences. 67 of them released talks between 14 Nov 2025 and 13 Nov 2026, with 2,062 talks (1,244 h) in total. 1,261 are German and 799 English (434 h), by the `original_language` field (gap6-1).
- The API has no licence field. Most talk descriptions end with a line like "Licensed to the public under https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/". Of the 799 English talks, that line says CC BY 4.0 for 316 (205 h), CC BY 3.0 for 67 (32 h), CC BY-SA 4.0 for 333 (162 h) and CC BY-NC for 5. 78 talks (32 h) have no licence line (gap6-2).
- media.ccc.de says "The license displayed in the actual video file applies", usually as a logo in the intro or outro or in the file's metadata. Where none is shown, it says to ask the organisers. So the description line is a strong hint, and the build must still confirm it in the file. The site also says "Feel free to download as much as you like" (gap6-4).
- English CC BY talks (4.0 and 3.0) per release month: Nov 2025 0, Dec 105, Jan 0, Feb 1, Mar 24, Apr 70, May 14, Jun 43, Jul 2, Aug 26, Sep 39, Oct 23, Nov 2026 (to the 13th) 36. That is about 32 a month on average, but the flow is very uneven. Most of it is Linux and systemd, Godot game development, OpenStreetMap, programming languages and maths, not AI or robotics (gap6-1, gap6-2).
- On topic: about 23-27 of those 383 talks (about 15-17.5 h) have AI, LLM, machine learning, agent, robot, drone or autonomy in the title or subtitle; the count moves with the keyword list (the researcher found 27 and 17.5 h; the checker's own regex found 23 talks and 14.6 h, or 25 and 16.3 h with a broader list). 10-13 of them are from the 39C3 congress, released 27-30 Dec 2025. Several are about AI policy or society rather than technology, and at least one talk ("All Sorted by Machines of Loving Grace?") appears twice, at 39C3 and again at a June 2026 event. A rough second keyword pass found about 47 more CC BY 4.0 English talks (about 33 h) on hardware hacking, security and embedded topics (unverified) (gap6-3).
- The whole archive holds 17,417 talks (11,904 h; all 472 conferences loaded on the checker's pass). Only 1,074 English talks (664 h) carry a CC BY line in their metadata. Among them, about 57-65 talks (about 39-44 h, depending on the keyword list, all from 2024-2026) are on AI or robots, so the confirmed on-topic back catalogue is small. Another 580 English talks (288 h) carry a CC BY-SA line. 7,773 English talks (5,561 h), mostly older, have no licence line at all. Their licence can only be read from the video itself (gap6-7).

##### NASA: counted from images-api.nasa.gov
- The NASA Image and Video Library API returns 8,853 videos in all, 707 dated 2024 and 553 dated 2025. About 710 have a `date_created` between 14 Nov 2025 and 13 Nov 2026, with a spike in April 2026 (186, the Artemis II mission). Over half come from the Johnson (285) and Kennedy (233) centres (gap6-5).
- The search API has no duration field, so we read the per-video metadata.json files of a random sample of 200 videos (189 had a duration). By title: briefings, interviews, "discusses life in space with [a TV station or school]" events and ceremonies were 26% of the videos but 42% of the hours. Long live coverage of launches, dockings and landings was another 19% of hours. Silent B-roll, timelapses and high-speed film were 4%. Edited pieces under 15 minutes were 49% of the videos but only 9% of the hours, with a median of about 2.5 minutes (gap6-6).
- Scaled to the year, the sample gives about 190 h of NASA video in all. Of that, about 18 h is short edited pieces (about 345 of them) and about 5 h is longer edited features, so about 23 h of narrated, edited, non-live material. This is our estimate from one sample of 189 videos sorted by title words, so treat it as plus or minus about 50% (gap6-6). A checker's pass over all 715 window videos read a duration for 485 of them: 158 h in all, 301 pieces under 15 minutes (22.1 h, median 3.1 minutes), and 240 of those (15.2 h) with no briefing, interview, event or live words in the title. Scaled to all 715, that is about 22 h of short non-briefing pieces and 160-235 h in all, which fits the estimate.
- Silent B-roll has no speech. A6's picker works from the transcript, so it cannot pick from B-roll without a separate visual method (gap6-6; pick-20).

##### YouTube's CC BY pool: not counted
- `search.list` filters with `videoLicense=creativeCommon` (it needs `type=video`). Each call costs 1 unit from a Search Queries bucket of 100 calls a day and returns at most 50 results per page (more need paging, which uses more calls). The official quota page agrees: search.list has its own bucket, "100 quota per day", 1 per call. The page says totalResults "is an approximation". We could not count the pool, because the rules for this study forbid using an API key, so its size is unknown (gap6-9).

##### What the yield assumption means
- A6 assumes 6 posted clips per source hour (pick-22's cost table). That is its figure for a 1-hour source; for a 3-hour source it assumes 12, or 4 an hour, and says a quality floor and de-duplication may cut both (section A6 line 92). So 6 an hour is the upper of A6's two untested figures. Vizard says its model keeps about 13 "high-confidence" clips per hour, a vendor claim with no performance data (pick-2). The arithmetic below is ours (gap6-8).

| Supply (12 months to 14 Nov 2026) | Source hours a year | Posts a week at 6 an hour | at 13 an hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| CCC English CC BY, AI or robots | 15-17.5 | 1.7-2.0 | 3.8-4.4 |
| plus NASA narrated edited pieces (estimate) | 38-40 | 4.4-4.7 | 9.5-10 |
| plus CCC hardware and security talks (rough, unverified) | 71-73 | 8.2-8.4 | 18 |
| Every English CC BY CCC talk plus all NASA video (mostly off-topic or briefings) | 430 | 50 | 107 |
| Hours needed for 7 / 42 / 168 posts a week at 6 an hour | 61 / 364 / 1,456 | | |

#### What this means for our build
- **Default to 1 post a day and set the cap from the queue.** On-topic new supply supports about 5-8 posts a week. Start at A1's floor of 7 a week, use the 39-44-hour on-topic CCC back catalogue (about 230-260 clips once, at 6 an hour) to smooth the gaps, and only raise the cap when the approved queue holds more than 14 days of posts. Treat 42 a week as out of reach without written permission from the field channels (A4), and 168 a week as unworkable (gap6-7, gap6-8).
- **Buffer for uneven supply.** Half the on-topic CCC talks arrive in the week after Christmas. The scheduler should drain a queue at a steady rate and never post just to fill a slot (gap6-3; A6 quality floor).
- **Ingest by API, check the licence in three steps.** (1) Poll `api.media.ccc.de/public/conferences` daily (1 request, plus 1 per changed conference). (2) Keep only `original_language == "eng"` talks whose description line says CC BY 3.0 or 4.0. (3) After downloading from media.ccc.de, confirm the licence in the intro or outro, or the file's metadata, before cutting. Flag any mismatch for a person. Store the licence URL with each clip (gap6-2, gap6-4).
- **Topic gate before transcription.** Use a cheap title and description filter (the keywords above, then a Haiku yes/no) so we don't pay to transcribe systemd and OpenStreetMap talks. That cuts transcription from about 236 h to about 20-50 h a year (gap6-3).
- **NASA: use the library API, not YouTube.** Query `images-api.nasa.gov/search?media_type=video` and read duration from metadata.json. By default, drop briefings, media events with outside people, ceremonies and live coverage, and send B-roll to a separate visual-only path, or skip it (gap6-5, gap6-6; sources-9).
- **Size hosting and cost for about 6 source hours a month, not 24 posts a day.** That shrinks download, proxy, transcription and picking cost several-fold compared with the A12 hourly case (host-m17). The current server class is more than enough (gap6-8).

#### Risks and unknowns
- **Description licence lines may not match the file.** The licence that counts is the one in the video. A cheap check: download 10 of the 27 on-topic talks from media.ccc.de and read their intro and outro slides (gap6-4).
- **Topic counts come from title keywords.** They will miss on-topic talks with plain titles and include off-topic ones. A person reading the 383 titles once (about 30 minutes) would firm this up (gap6-3).
- **The NASA hours are a sample estimate.** They rest on 189 videos sorted by title words. Reading all 710 metadata files (about 710 small JSON requests) would give exact hours (gap6-6).
- **Yield is unmeasured.** Neither 6 nor 13 clips an hour has been tested on CCC talks or 2-minute NASA pieces. A 2.5-minute NASA piece gives one clip at most, and NASA posts many of these pieces itself, which crowds us out (gap6-8; A4 crowding).
- **Share-alike could double CCC supply.** 333 English talks (162 h, about 11 h on AI) are CC BY-SA 4.0 (580 English talks, 288 h, in the whole archive). A4 infers that share-alike can't be honoured on YouTube (sources-m2). A short legal opinion on stating "CC BY-SA 4.0" in the description could add them (gap6-2).
- **The YouTube CC BY pool is unknown.** Count it once with the owner's own key: about 20 topic searches with `videoLicense=creativeCommon`, then a person vets whether each uploader really owns the footage (gap6-9; A4).
- **Reach risk is the same.** A licensed-only clip channel still falls under the October 2026 reach cut for aggregation (sources-m6). Low supply simply forces the low, edited volume that A1 and A2 already recommend.
- **Data from pages.** API descriptions and titles were read as data only. None of them contained instructions to us (gap6-10).

### A19. The real daily upload limit for a new, unverified channel

**The short answer.** We still have no trustworthy number. YouTube publishes none, and we found no dated 2025-2026 report of a new channel's limit at the standard or phone-verified tier. Our web search budget ran out on the first query, and again during the fact-check, so Help Community and Reddit threads were not searched. The official pages say the limit counts uploads "across desktop, mobile, and YouTube API" and say nothing that exempts private or scheduled videos, so plan as if every upload counts, buffer included. On YouTube's feature table, the "Higher daily limit" sits in the column for verification by channel history or ID, not the phone-verification column, so phone verification alone is not shown to raise the upload limit (our reading of the table). YouTube gives no time for a new channel to earn "advanced" status through channel history. The only time figure ("usually ... within 2 months") is about channels getting access back after losing it. ID or video verification can unlock advanced features right away, but YouTube says it is not available to all creators. "Repeatedly uploading content you don't own" (unless educational, documentary, scientific or artistic) is on YouTube's list of things that can delay or restrict advanced access, which is what a clip channel does. Launch at A1's cap of 6 a day, treat A9's 24 a day as unproven, and fill the render-ahead buffer slowly instead of all at once.

#### What we found

**What the official pages say (all undated, footer ©2026, read 14 Nov 2026)**
- The limit covers uploads "across desktop, mobile, and YouTube API". No number is given. It varies by country or region and by channel history, strikes lower it, and the error says "Daily upload limit reached. You can upload more videos in 24 hours." The page does not mention private, scheduled or Shorts uploads (gap7-1). (The page is titled "Common uploading errors". It says "Community Guidelines strikes will affect how much you can upload" and "Copyright strikes may impact channel history eligibility.")
- The feature-eligibility page has one row, "Upload videos and Shorts", with only the labels "Limited daily limit" and "Higher daily limit". On intermediate access (phone-verified), hitting a limit may let you verify your ID to move up. On advanced access, you wait 24 hours. The page has no numbers and does not mention private or scheduled uploads (gap7-2). The table's columns are "No verification", "Verification via phone number" and "Verification via channel history OR identity". "Limited daily limit" sits under no verification and "Higher daily limit" under channel history or identity; the phone-number cell on that row is blank. So phone verification is not shown to raise the upload limit (fact-checker's reading of the table; the scraped text did not show column alignment with certainty). The same advanced tier also holds monetization applications, chapters, clickable description links, related video on Shorts, pinned comments and additional channels.
- The advanced-features page gives no number of days or videos for a new channel to qualify through history. It says history includes uploads, live streams, audience engagement, account age and how often the account is used. The only time figure, that active, rule-following channels "can usually rebuild sufficient channel history within 2 months", sits under "Restore feature access", so it is for channels regaining access, not for new ones (gap7-3). The other route is verifying identity with a valid ID or a video, which the eligibility page says unlocks advanced features right away but is not available to all creators.
- Things that delay or restrict advanced access (the page says the list is not complete): "Posting the same content repeatedly across one or more channels", "repeatedly uploading content you don't own" unless it is EDSA (educational, documentary, scientific or artistic), spam or misleading metadata, copyright strikes, and "Maintaining channels that are related to another policy-violating channel" (gap7-4). This adds to api-m7 in A9. The last item can work in both directions, so a flagged clip channel could in principle drag down a related company channel.

**What automated uploaders report (GitHub, porjo/youtubeuploader issue #119)**
- A YouTube email the maintainer quoted on 30 Nov 2022 said YouTube had "limited how many videos a channel can upload in a 24-hour period". It said this brings the Data API in line with "limits already in place for desktop and mobile". No number was given (gap7-5).
- On 28 Nov 2023, one user with a 650,000-unit quota got `uploadLimitExceeded` after 2 uploads in a day. It worked again the same day, and the user said "a handful of other folks" had hit the same thing starting the day before (27 Nov 2023). So a single refusal can be a YouTube-side glitch, not the real cap (gap7-6).
- In 2025, one user reported 8 uploads in one day using 800 units (comment of 18 Jul 2025, about "yesterday"), so about 100 units each. Another posted "10 Vid and 1600 of 10000 Credit" (24 Aug 2025, timeframe not stated), which is about 160 units per video if all of it was uploads; the post does not say whether thumbnails or other calls were included. Neither reported a limit error. Channel age and verification were not stated (gap7-7). These quota figures are now history: since 1 Jun 2026 `videos.insert` costs 1 unit from its own bucket of 100 calls a day (A9 api-1, api-3).
- The same tool's README says "~6 videos every 24 hours due to quota restrictions". That number comes from the old 1,600-unit upload cost (10,000 / 1,600 is about 6). Since the Dec 2025 cost cut (A9 api-3), it says nothing about the channel limit. Many "6 a day" claims online are probably this quota figure, not the channel limit (gap7-8). (The 1,600 figure is stated in the same issue thread, 16 May 2022. The revision history entry of 4 Dec 2025 says the docs were updated "to reflect a change" from about 1,600 to about 100 units, without saying when the change took effect; users were already seeing about 100 units in March-July 2025.)

**What we infer (our estimate, not a source)**
- A scheduled video is uploaded as private with a `publishAt` time. The limit counts uploads from every surface and never mentions visibility, so we expect private and scheduled uploads to count (gap7-9, unverified). The earlier research reached the same view (01:gap5-6, gap5-7). A steady rolling buffer uploads only as many videos a day as it releases. The risk is the day it is filled: building a 24-hour lead in one go adds a full day's worth of uploads on top of that day's normal uploads, so the fill day carries twice the steady rate (12 at a 6-a-day cap, 48 at 24 a day) (gap7-9).

#### What this means for our build
1. **Default daily cap: 6 uploads in any rolling 24 hours, counting every upload** (API, Studio, phone; private, scheduled, public). That matches A1. Raise it only through the ramp in A9 point 9, and only after 7 days with no refusal at the current level. 24 a day is a goal to test, not a plan (gap7-1, gap7-9).
2. **Fill the buffer slowly.** Never upload a batch to build the render-ahead queue. Upload at the steady rate (cap / 24 hours) and let the queue lengthen by at most 1-2 extra uploads a day, still under the cap. Render ahead on disk, not on YouTube: keep finished files locally and upload them only when their slot is 12-24 hours away (gap7-9).
3. **The upload counter is the channel's, not the app's.** Store a log of every upload with its time, including any done by hand in Studio, and check `count(last 24 h) < cap` before each `videos.insert` (gap7-1).
4. **Handle `uploadLimitExceeded` in two steps.** On the first refusal, pause uploads 24 hours, log the 24-hour count, then retry once at the same cap, because refusals can be glitches (gap7-6). On a second refusal at the same cap within 7 days, lower the cap one step. Never retry within the hour (A9 point 8).
5. **Expect to stay on the standard or intermediate tier.** Phone-verify on day one, as A9 point 10 says, for custom thumbnails, but do not count on it to raise the upload limit (gap7-2). Do not build anything that needs advanced access (higher limits, related video, pinned comments, chapters, clickable description links) into the first 60 days, and assume it may never come (gap7-3, gap7-4). ID or video verification is the only fast route YouTube names; whether it is offered to this channel is visible only in Studio, and it ties a real person's ID to a clip channel, which is the owner's call.
6. **Keep the clip channel apart from the company channel** (separate Google account, phone number and Cloud project), because of the "related to another policy-violating channel" item (gap7-4; A1 growth-m4; A9 point 1).

#### Risks and unknowns
- **No real number.** We don't know the cap for a new standard or phone-verified channel in 2026. Cheap check: the ramp itself (6, 8, 12, 16, 24 a day), logging the count at every refusal. The undated 16-a-day anecdote (A1 growth-11) is the only higher figure, and the 2025 reports of 8-10 a day come from channels of unknown age (gap7-7).
- **Not searched.** The WebSearch budget for this run was used up before our first query, and again when the fact-checker tried one search. Help Community threads, r/NewTubers, r/PartneredYoutube, and the n8n and Postiz issue trackers were not searched. The yt-dlp tracker is about downloading, so it would not show upload limits. Cheap fix: the owner or a later run searches YouTube Help Community for "daily upload limit reached" with "new channel" and notes thread dates.
- **Whether scheduled uploads count** is unconfirmed (our inference, gap7-9). Cheap test: in week one, upload some private scheduled videos and log whether the refusal count includes them. The rolling design above is safe either way.
- **Tier status is visible.** Studio, then Settings, then Channel, then Feature eligibility shows which tier is on (gap7-3). Check it weekly and log it next to the cap.
- **Advanced access may be withheld for clip content** (gap7-4, api-m7). If it is, the cap may never pass the standard level, and hourly posting would not be reachable on this channel.
- **Phone verification may not lift the cap.** On our reading of the feature table, the higher upload limit belongs to the channel-history-or-ID column, not the phone column (gap7-2). If that reading is right, a phone-verified new channel stays at the "limited" level until history or ID verification moves it up.

Checked on 2026-11-14 by one independent fact-checker (both lenses): 6 confirmed, 2 corrected, 0 removed, 1 unverified.

### A20. Check the reported 'cluster termination' system

**The short answer.** The paper is real. It is a Google-authored PDF, "Scalable Detection of Adversarial Synthetic Slop and Coordinated Media Abuse: A LoRA-Enabled Multimodal Defense System", by four Google staff. It describes S-CTS, the "Scalable Cluster Termination System". It never names YouTube. It names few signals: "proprietary infrastructure signals" similar to "API usage patterns" and "event time series", plus upload pacing (how often a channel uploads, and how soon its first upload comes; the paper does not define the second). It does not name OAuth clients, API projects, payment or device as its own signals; shared IP and device IDs appear only in its survey of how the field links accounts. Neither Google nor YouTube has confirmed it runs on YouTube, and the "130,000 channels" figure is not in the public PDF. Our reading: treat it as a credible description of the kind of system YouTube could run. An hourly bot is exactly the "non-human, high-frequency publishing" its upload-pacing features are meant to catch. It flags a cluster only where cluster signals and "synthetic-tagged" content occur together, but the content model that does the tagging also takes upload pacing and templated titles as inputs, so AI narration is not the only way in. And whatever S-CTS does, YouTube's own Spam Policy, which certainly applies, gives "a channel that takes popular clips and re-uploads them in their entirety" without transformative editing as an example of spam. Real clips alone are not safe; each clip must add something of our own.

#### What we found

**The paper exists, and is written by Google staff**
- The PDF sits on Google's own storage host (storage.googleapis.com, path "gweb-research2023-media/pubtools/1039291.pdf"). Its four authors list Google affiliation and google.com addresses. The file metadata says it was made with LaTeX on 2026-05-13. No venue, journal or arXiv id is given (gap8-1).
- Search Engine Journal (Roger Montti, 2026-06-19) was the first outlet we found that linked this PDF. Fstoppers (Alex Cooke, 2026-07-19) gives the same title but no link, and cites that article and Jim Louderback's "Inside the Creator Economy" newsletter (gap8-1).
- The paper talks about "online video platforms (OVP)" throughout. A text search of the extracted PDF found no mention of "YouTube" (gap8-2).

**How it groups accounts (what it actually says)**
- Part A, "Coordinated Bot-Net Detection", uses "proprietary infrastructure signals" that it calls "very similar to known behaviors like API usage patterns, event time series analysis, and GenAI-specific metadata". It clusters accounts "statistically likely to be controlled by the same actor or automated generation script" (gap8-3).
- Its related-work section says the field links accounts with "shared IP addresses and device identifiers". It then says "our work" uses internal algorithms on "infrastructure-level signals and inorganic behavioral patterns" to build "Generation Clusters": accounts likely using "the same generative API or script". "Generative API" most likely means the AI tool that makes the content, but that is our reading; the paper does not define it. Part A's "API usage patterns" is not defined either and could include how accounts use the platform's own APIs, such as an upload API, so that cannot be ruled out (gap8-3).
- The content model's named features are video text embeddings, title and description "salient terms" (to find "repetitive, templated narratives"), visual embeddings, and upload pacing: `Feature_avg_log_upload_pace` and `Feature_time_to_first_upload_secs`. The paper says these pick up "non-human, high-frequency publishing behaviors characteristic of automated scripts" (gap8-4). These features sit in Stage 1 of the content rater (Part C), not in the cluster detector (Part A), so posting pace feeds the "synthetic" score as well. The paper does not say what `time_to_first_upload` is measured from; "from channel creation" is our guess.
- Not named anywhere in the paper: OAuth client, Google Cloud API project, payment profile or script fingerprints (gap8-3).

**When it terminates**
- A cluster is flagged only where a high Part A (cluster) score meets "similar synthetic-tagged content" from Part C (the AI-content model). The paper calls the cluster requirement a safeguard that targets "coordinated, mass-produced behaviors rather than isolated uploads" (gap8-5).
- High-confidence scores trigger automatic enforcement. Unclear cases go to human reviewers. Auto-enforcement thresholds are tuned for 92-95% precision (share of flagged items that really are bad), so roughly 1 in 12 to 1 in 20 automatic actions could still be wrong (our arithmetic). The paper reports a "<1%" overturn rate; that is overturned decisions, not the false-positive rate, and the paper does not say how many decisions were appealed. Average turnaround was 32% shorter for cluster checks and 50% shorter for content review "compared to humans", reported under a "6-Month Baseline" heading (gap8-5).
- The target areas it names are synthetic impersonation, procedural gore, AI scams, AI text-to-speech narratives and generative NSFW content (gap8-6).
- The abstract says clusters were terminated "at a high precision" but gives no counts. The public PDF does not contain the "50,000 clusters" or "130,000 channels" numbers, and SEJ does not have them. Fstoppers gives no source for them: it puts them right after "Google researchers have published a paper", and credits the Louderback newsletter only with surfacing and analysing the paper. The newsletter returned HTTP 403 for us (gap8-7).

**Has Google or YouTube confirmed it runs on YouTube? No.**
- Fstoppers says to treat it "as published research rather than a confirmed description of live YouTube infrastructure". SEJ says only that it "could conceivably be in use" (gap8-8). Fstoppers' own headline ("How a Google Machine Terminated 130,000 AI Slop YouTube Channels in Six Months") states as fact what its body calls unconfirmed.
- YouTube's CEO letter (Neal Mohan, 2026-01-21) says YouTube is "actively building on our established systems" for spam and clickbait, to cut low-quality, repetitive content. It does not mention clusters, upload frequency, channel terminations or this paper (gap8-9).
- IBTimes UK (2026-06-02, the source behind clips-7) reports the 16 AI channels and their reach from outside analyses and The Verge, not from YouTube. YouTube's side is only paraphrased: a spokesperson "noted that the platform terminated several channels for breaching spam policies", for "spam, deceptive practices and inauthentic content production". It mentions no clustering, shared infrastructure or paper (gap8-10).
- YouTube's Spam Policy (YouTube Help, no date shown, read 2026-11-14) lists "Scraped content": "Re-posting material from other websites or platforms, or other videos without adding anything of your own", with the example of a channel that re-uploads popular clips "without any transformative editing, reaction, or educational breakdown". It also says that using automated or AI tools "to flood our platform with repetitive content" is not allowed, and that YouTube "may suspend your monetization or terminate your channel or account" (chk-1).

#### What this means for our build
1. **Keep growth-m8 at low confidence for "is this live on YouTube?". Raise it to medium for "this is how Google designs such systems."** The method is real and Google-authored. Running it on YouTube is unconfirmed (gap8-1, gap8-8).
2. **Make upload timing look human (cheap).** Upload pace and time-to-first-upload are named features (gap8-4). So: no uploads in the first days after the channel is created; start at 3-6 a day and build up over weeks; add ±10-25 minutes of random jitter to every publish time; skip a few slots each day; never upload 24 videos in one burst with `publishAt`. Spread the real uploads across the day as well. The figures are our own estimate, not from a source. The hourly target becomes a ceiling to work up to, not day-one behaviour. Checker's note: the named feature is an *average* pace, so jitter does not change it; only fewer uploads per day does. Jitter targets the unnamed "event time series" signals, which is a guess.
3. **Stay out of the "synthetic" half of the test.** The paper terminates only when cluster signals and synthetic content coincide (gap8-5). No AI voice-over or text-to-speech narration (a named target, gap8-6), no AI-generated visuals, and no single title/description template. Vary the LLM-written titles and add human-edited hooks. Note that the content rater also scores upload pacing and title/description terms (gap8-4), so high volume and templated titles push toward the "synthetic" tag even with no AI media.
4. **Add network and device separation to the isolation checklist (A3 point 1, A11 point 1, A12 point 6).** The paper names only "infrastructure signals" and "API usage patterns", and mentions IP and device IDs as standard practice in the field (gap8-3). The clips uploader must never run on the production EC2 host. It must not share an outbound IP with the box that uploads to the company channel. It must not use a browser profile or machine signed in to the company channel's managers. Keep the separate Google Cloud project and OAuth client already planned (A3, policy-m1). These steps are cheap insurance, not proven requirements.
5. **Keep the company channel out of any cluster.** Production already posts on a schedule from a script (the autopilot). If the clips bot shares its infrastructure and both look automated, they could fall into one "same actor" group. That is the scenario that puts the company channel at risk. It argues for a separate VPS (A12 point 2) over the laptop the owner also uses for company work.
6. **Passing S-CTS is not the bar; the Spam Policy is (checker's addition).** Re-uploading other channels' clips without commentary, educational value or unique editing is listed spam on its own, for a single channel, with or without any cluster (chk-1). Every clip needs a real added layer, and the plan should not count on "real clips, no AI" as protection.

#### Risks and unknowns
- We don't know which signals YouTube really uses. The paper keeps them "proprietary". Our separation steps target likely signals, not known ones.
- We don't know whether a single-channel operation counts as a "cluster". The paper targets groups of accounts. If clips and company channels are linked, that makes two. A single channel is still fully exposed to the Spam Policy (chk-1).
- We could not open the Louderback newsletter (HTTP 403, again for the checker on 2026-11-14), the YouTube Transparency Report (renders only with JavaScript, so we got no data) or a research.google listing for the paper. The search budget ran out before we could look for one. So the 130,000 figure stays unverified.
- The checker's web search budget was also used up, so no search was made for a Google or YouTube statement after 2026-07-19 confirming or denying S-CTS. "Not confirmed" holds as of the newest source we opened (Fstoppers, 2026-07-19), not necessarily as of 2026-11-14.
- Cheap checks: open the Transparency Report in a normal browser for the latest "spam, misleading and scams" channel removals; ask YouTube Creator Support whether channels in separate Brand Accounts owned by one company are treated as linked.
- The PDF text was pulled out with a short standard-library script that drops spaces. Quotes above have their spacing restored, but words were not changed. The checker re-extracted the text independently on 2026-11-14 and found the same wording.
